"In which direction did the one of vast wisdom go? O youths, tell me this matter. We shall go to him and make amends for this fault; perhaps then we may obtain our son's life." (Ja. 1.15.13)

Those attendants replied:
"The seer of vast wisdom went through the air, like the moon on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon. Furthermore, that seer of good character, who is true to his word, went towards the East." (Ja. 1.15.14)

The Great Being, from the place where he descended onto the main road, made a resolution: "Let my footprints not be obliterated by elephants, horses, and so on. Let only Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā see them, and no one else." Having wandered for alms and taken a portion of mixed rice just enough for sustenance, he sat in the refectory and ate, leaving a small portion of the food in the alms-bowl.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā also descended from the palace and, while walking on the main road, saw the footprints. Thinking, "These are the footprints of the noble one who bestowed glory upon me," she followed the trail of footprints. Having reached him, she paid homage and said: "Venerable Sir, please forgive the fault committed by your servant Maṇḍavya. Indeed, you are not ones who are under the power of anger. Please grant life to my son." Having spoken thus—
59:
"His head is twisted backwards, his arms are stretched out unable to perform any action, and his eyes are white like those of a dead man. Who has done this to my son?" Thus she spoke in verse. (Ja. 1.15.15)

The Great Being said: "We do not do such things. However, seeing an ascetic being harmed, it must have been done by the spirits, ogres, and deities who have respect for ascetics."

"Venerable Sir, let there be no malice in your mind. Let it be the work of the deities. Venerable Sir, the deities desire happiness. But Venerable Sir, how should I proceed?" she asked. "If you wish for his well-being, I will tell you the remedy. There is leftover rice in my alms-bowl. Pour a little water into those leftovers, take a small amount, and place it in your son's mouth. Stir the remainder in a water jar and place it in the mouths of the eighty thousand Brahmins," he instructed. The lady replied, "I will do as you say, Venerable Sir," took the leftover rice, paid homage to the Great Being, and went to do exactly as told.

As soon as it was placed in his mouth, the chief of the deities thought, "Since the noble ascetic himself is providing the remedy, we cannot do anything further," and released young Maṇḍavya. The youth sneezed and regained his natural complexion as if he had never suffered any pain. Then his mother said to him, "Look, dear son, at the corruption of these Brahmins who frequent your house but lack shame and moral dread. Ascetics are not of such a nature. Dear son, you should feed the true ascetics."

Furthermore, she had the water remaining from what was given to Maṇḍavya stirred in a large jar and placed in the mouths of the Brahmins. At that very moment, the spirits released them and fled. The Brahmins sneezed, stood up, and wiped themselves, asking, "What was put into our mouths?" When told, "The leftovers of the ascetic Mātaṅga," they thought, "We have been made to eat the leftovers of a Caṇḍāla. Now we are no longer Brahmins. Now the pure-bred Brahmins will no longer associate or eat with us." Thinking thus, they fled from that place and went to the Middle Country. In the city of the King of Majjha, they lived and ate in the royal palace, claiming, "We are Brahmins who deserve the highest seats."

At that time, the Bodhisatta, wishing to suppress the wicked, wandered about to humble those of proud nature. Then, an ascetic named Jātimanta, thinking "There is no one equal to me," did not even acknowledge others.
60:
"There is no one equal to me," he thought, not even forming a perception of others as his equals. The Bodhisatta, seeing that ascetic living on the bank of the Ganges, thought, "I will humble his pride," and went to that place. The ascetic Jātimanta asked him, "Of what caste are you, sir?" "Teacher, I am a Caṇḍāla," he replied. "Begone, Caṇḍāla! Begone, Caṇḍāla! Live only in the lower part of the Ganges. Do not defile the water in the upper part of the Ganges," the ascetic said. The Bodhisatta said, "Very well, teacher. I will live in the place you have mentioned." While living in the lower part of the Ganges, he made a resolution: "May the waters of the Ganges flow upstream."

In the early morning, the ascetic Jātimanta went down to the Ganges to rinse his mouth and wash his matted hair. The Bodhisatta, while chewing a tooth-stick, spat out lumps of phlegm into the water. He also let the chewed tooth-stick float away in that same water. He resolved that these things should not go elsewhere but should stick only to the ascetic's matted hair. Accordingly, the phlegm and the tooth-stick stuck to the ascetic's matted hair. The ascetic, feeling displeased and thinking, "This must be the work of that Caṇḍāla," went and asked, "O Caṇḍāla, did you make this water of the Ganges flow upstream?" "Yes, teacher," he replied. "If so, do not live in the lower part of the Ganges, but live in the upper part," the ascetic said. "Very well, teacher. I will live in the place you have directed," he said. While living in the upper part, he withdrew his psychic power, and the water flowed normally. However, the ascetic encountered the same trouble again. That ascetic went again and asked the Bodhisatta, "O Caṇḍāla, do you make this water of the Ganges flow upstream at one time and downstream at another?" "Yes, teacher," he replied. "Caṇḍāla, you do not allow the ascetics who live in comfort to live in peace. On the seventh day, may your head split into seven pieces," he cursed. "Very well, teacher. I, too, will not allow the sun to rise," the Bodhisatta replied.

Then the Great Being thought, "This curse of his will fall back upon himself. I shall protect him." Out of compassion for living beings, on the following day, he prevented the sun from rising by his psychic power. The range of psychic power of those possessed of it is indeed unthinkable. From then on, the dawn did not appear, and there was no distinction between night and day. No one could engage in work such as farming or trade.

People, falling into distress, wondered, "Is this a disturbance caused by Yakkhas, or by spirits, devas, Nagas, or Garudas?" and thought, "What should be done?" They consulted each other, saying, "The royal family is of great wisdom and can consider the welfare of the world. Let us go to the King's palace," and they went to the palace...
61:
(The people) went and reported the matter. When the King heard this, although he was afraid, he put on a fearless appearance and said, "Friends, do not be afraid. The ascetic Jātimanta, who lives on the bank of the Ganges, will know the cause of this. After questioning that ascetic, we shall be free from doubt." Accompanied by a few men who served his interests, he approached the ascetic, exchanged greetings, and asked about the matter. The ascetic said, "Great King, it is true; there is a Caṇḍāla. He can make this water of the Ganges flow downstream at one time and upstream at another. I have said something to him regarding that; ask him, he will know."

The King went to the ascetic Mātaṅga and asked, "Venerable sir, do you not allow the dawn to rise?" "Yes, Great King," he replied. "For what reason, venerable sir?" he asked. "Great King, it is because of the ascetic Jātimanta. When the ascetic Jātimanta comes, pays homage to me, and asks for forgiveness, I will release it (the dawn), Great King." The King went and said, "Teacher, come and ask the ascetic for forgiveness." "Great King, I will not pay homage to a Caṇḍāla," he said. "Teacher, do not do this; consider the faces of the subjects," the King said, but the ascetic refused again. The King approached the Bodhisatta and said, "The teacher does not wish to ask for forgiveness." "As long as he does not ask for forgiveness, I will not release the sun," he said. The King thought, "This one does not wish to ask for forgiveness, and that one will not release the sun unless forgiven. What benefit do we have from this ascetic? I must look after the world." He then said, "Friends, go to the ascetic. Seize him by his hands and feet, bring him to the feet of the ascetic Mātaṅga, make him prostrate, and have him ask for forgiveness out of compassion for these subjects." The King's men went, did as the King had said, brought him, made him prostrate at the feet of the ascetic Mātaṅga, and had him ask for forgiveness.

"I forgive those who should be forgiven. However, the words of this ascetic will fall back upon himself. When I release the sun, the sun's rays will fall upon this ascetic's head, and then his head will split into seven pieces. But let not that ascetic come to ruin. You all should make him descend into water deep up to his neck and place a large lump of clay on his head. Then I will release the sun. The sun's rays will fall upon the lump of clay and split it into seven pieces. Then tell him to discard the lump of clay, dive into the water, and come up from another landing place. If he does this, he will be safe," the Bodhisatta said. The people said, "We will do so," and acted accordingly. Thus, safety was brought to that ascetic. From that time on, that ascetic—
62:
"Birth is not the cause; virtue within those who have gone forth is the only cause." Having abandoned the pride born of birth and lineage, he became free from the intoxication of conceit. After the ascetic Jātimanta was thus disciplined, the multitude recognized the power of the Bodhisatta, and a great commotion arose. The King invited the Bodhisatta to come to his city. The Great Being gave his promise, thinking, "I shall discipline those eighty thousand Brahmins and fulfill my promise," and went to the city of King Majjha. 

As soon as the Brahmins saw the Bodhisatta, they consulted among themselves: "Friends, this great thief has come. Now he will make it known that all of us have become non-Brahmins by eating his scraps. If this happens, we will have no place to live here. Let us kill him beforehand." They approached the King and said, "Great King, do not regard this Caṇḍāla ascetic as a virtuous man. He knows a powerful mantra. He can take the earth and make it the sky, and take the sky and make it the earth. He can make far places near and near places far. He can make the Ganges River flow upstream. If he wishes, he is capable of lifting the earth and throwing it down. One can never know the mind of another. If he gains a footing here, he might destroy your kingdom, cause danger to your life, and end your royal lineage. Great King, listen to our words; it is proper to kill him this very day."

Kings are often led by others' words; thus, he reached a decision based on the talk of the many. The Bodhisatta, however, wandered for alms in the city, ate the mixed food in a place pleasant with water, and went to the royal garden. Being innocent and without suspicion, he sat upon the auspicious stone slab. Although he possessed the knowledge capable of recollecting eighty aeons—forty in the past and forty in the future—due to not reflecting, he was without mindfulness for a moment. The King, without letting others know, went himself and struck the Great Man (Mahāpurisa), who was sitting heedlessly without reflection, with a sword and cut him into two pieces. In this King's realm, the eighth rain of iron hammers and the ninth rain of mud fell. Thus, nine kinds of rain fell in this King's country. That King, along with his retinue, was reborn in the great hell. Therefore, the wise Saṅkicca said:
63:
“By offending the famous Mātaṅga with his mind,
Majjha, along with his retinue, was destroyed;
From that time on, that place became the Majjha forest.”

Thus, the state of the Majjha forest becoming a wilderness should be understood. Because of the sage Mātaṅga, that same forest is called the Mātaṅga forest.

'Pañhapaṭibhānāni' means the answering of questions. 'Paccanīkaṃ kattabbaṃ' means that opposition should be made. 'Amaññissaṃ' means it was as if taking the side of the opposition.

'Anuviccākāraṃ' means "Do what should be done after investigating, thinking, and weighing." 'Sādhu hoti' means "It is excellent." If people see someone like you seeing the Buddha and taking refuge in the Buddha, or seeing a Nigaṇṭha and taking refuge in a Nigaṇṭha, the reproach will arise: "This Upāli takes refuge in whoever he sees!" Therefore, it is shown that for people like you, acting after investigation is excellent.

'Paṭākaṃ parihareyyunti' means that if those Nigaṇṭhas obtain such a disciple, they would raise a banner and proclaim throughout the city, "The King of such a name, or a great royal minister, or a wealthy merchant has come to us for refuge and become our disciple." Why? Because they think, "In this way, our greatness will become manifest," and also, if that person should feel regret, thinking, "Why did I take refuge in these people?", they do this so that he might not turn back, thinking, "Many people know that I have taken refuge in them; it is difficult to turn back now." Therefore, it is said, "They would carry a banner."

'Opānabhūtanti' means existing like a prepared well. 'Kulanti' means your house. 'Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsīti' means that just as in the past, seeing ten, twenty, or sixty people arrive, you gave without saying "There is nothing," now do not cut off the gifts to them just because you have taken refuge in me; continue to give to the recipients who arrive as you always have. This is the advice given.

'Sutametaṃ, bhante' means "Venerable Sir, I have heard this before." From whom was it heard? From the Nigaṇṭhas. Those Nigaṇṭhas proclaim in the houses of supporters: "We say that gifts should be given to anyone who arrives, but the ascetic Gotama says, 'Gifts should be given only to me... etc... giving to the disciples of others is not of great fruit.'" Referring to what the Nigaṇṭhas said, the householder Upāli said, "I have heard this."
64: The gradual talk (anupubbikathā) refers to the discourse taught in sequence: virtue after generosity, heaven after virtue, and the path after heaven. Among these (four talks), the talk on generosity (dānakathā) is as follows: This generosity is the cause of happiness, the root of attainments (sampatti), and the basis of wealth. It is the refuge, the shelter, the destination, and the resort for those who have fallen into distress. In this world and the world beyond, there is no support, basis, object, refuge, shelter, destination, or resort equal to generosity. This generosity is like a lion throne (sīhāsana) made of jewels because it is a support. It is like the great earth (mahāpathavī) because it is a basis. It is like a rope to be grasped because it is something to hold onto. This generosity is like a boat because it enables one to cross over suffering. It is like a hero on the battlefield because it provides relief. It is like a well-fortified city because it protects from danger. It is like a lotus (paduma) because it is untainted by the stains of stinginess (macchariya) and so forth. It is like fire because it burns away those stains. It is like a venomous snake because it is difficult to approach (with mantras, etc.). It is like a lion because of its fearlessness. It is like an elephant because it is endowed with strength. It is like a white bull because it is regarded as a noble blessing. It is like the horse-king Valāhaka because it leads to a place of safety. This generosity is the path I have traveled; it is my lineage. When I was fulfilling the ten perfections, I performed many great sacrifices such as the great sacrifice of Velāma, the great sacrifice of Mahāgovinda, the great sacrifice of Mahāsudassana, and the great sacrifice of Vessantara. When I was the king of hares, I sacrificed myself into the blazing mass of fire and satisfied the hearts of those who came to beg. In the world, generosity gives the splendor of Sakka, the splendor of Māra, the splendor of Brahmā, and the splendor of a Cakkavatti. It also gives the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa), the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment (abhisambodhi-ñāṇa). Thus, he gave a talk connected with the virtues of generosity. Because one who gives is able to undertake virtue, he taught the talk on virtue (sīlakathā) immediately after the talk on generosity. The talk on virtue is this: This virtue is the support, the basis, the object, the refuge, the shelter, the destination, and the resort. This virtue is my lineage. In countless past lives, such as when I was the Naga king Saṅkhapāla, the Naga king Bhūridatta, the Naga king Campeyya, the Naga king Sīlava, the elephant king who cared for his mother, and the Chaddanta elephant king, I fulfilled virtue. For the attainments of this world and the world beyond, there is no support, basis, object, refuge, shelter, destination, or resort equal to virtue. There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no scent like the scent of virtue. Adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the flower of virtue...
65:
...and anointed with the scent of virtue, even the world with its devas cannot get enough of looking at such a person. In this way, He delivered the discourse connected with the virtues of virtue.

To show that this heaven can be obtained by relying on this virtue, He taught the talk on heaven (saggakathā) immediately after the talk on virtue. The talk on heaven is as follows: This thing called heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; here, there is constant play and enjoyment, and attainments are always obtained. The Cātumahārājika devas enjoy divine bliss and divine splendor for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsa devas for thirty-six million years. In this way, He delivered the discourse connected with the virtues of heaven. Even the mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the splendor of heaven. It has also been said: "Monks, I could tell of the talk on heaven in many ways," and so forth.

After thus enticing them with the talk on heaven, just as if one were to adorn an elephant and then cut off its trunk, He taught the danger, the baseness, and the corruption of sensual pleasures in this manner: "This heaven is also impermanent and unstable; one should not form strong desire (chandarāga) for it. The sensual pleasures I have spoken of have little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger (ādīnava) in them is far greater." In that context, 'ādīnava' means fault or danger. 'Okāra' means the state of being base or low. 'Sankilesa' means the corruption of beings within Saṃsāra through those sensual pleasures. It is as He said: "Alas, sirs, beings are indeed corrupted."

Having thus threatened them with the danger of sensual pleasures, He revealed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). 'Kallacitta' means a mind free from illness (a ready mind). 'Sāmukkaṃsikā' means the teaching peculiar to the Buddhas, which they have taken up and delivered by themselves, seen through self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), and not shared with others (such as Paccekabuddhas and disciples). What is that teaching of the Noble Truths? He said: "Suffering (dukkha), the origin (samudaya), the cessation (nirodha), and the path (magga)."

It is called 'virajaṃ' (stainless) because of the absence of the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth. It is called 'vītamalaṃ' (pure) because the stain of passion and so forth has departed. The name 'Dhamma-eye' (dhamma-cakkhu) is a name for the lower three paths in the Brahmāyu Sutta above, and a name for the destruction of taints (Arahattamagga) in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta; however, in this context, the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga) is intended. To show the manner of the arising of that Path of Stream-entry, He said: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." That path-knowledge arises by taking cessation (Nibbāna) as its object and penetrating all conditioned things (sankhata) by way of its function.
66:
This householder Upāli has seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths; therefore, he is called 'Diṭṭhadhamma' (one who has seen the Dhamma). The same method of interpretation should be applied to the remaining terms. This householder has crossed over doubt; therefore, he is called 'Tiṇṇavicikiccha'. Indecision has vanished for this householder; therefore, he is called 'Vigatakathaṃkatha'. 'Vesārajjappatta' means he has attained fearlessness. Where has he attained fearlessness? In the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed One. This householder does not have to rely on others for his faith; in this Dispensation, it does not occur through the persuasion of others; therefore, he is called 'Aparappaccaya'.

Accepting with the mind is called 'Abhinanditvā'. Praising with words is called 'Anumoditvā'. 'Āvarāmi' means I block or I cover. 'Anāvaṭaṃ' refers to that which is unobstructed, opened, or revealed.

'Dīghatapassī heard' means that from the time the householder Upāli left, Dīghatapassī remained listening, thinking: 'The householder is wise, and the ascetic Gotama is of inspiring appearance and speaks words that lead out of Saṃsāra. Upāli might become devoted just by seeing him; he might become devoted upon hearing the Dhamma talk. Having become devoted, he might go for refuge. Has the householder gone for refuge yet, or has he not?' Thus, he was the first to hear the news.

'Tena hi samma' (Therefore, friend) refers to being overwhelmed by intense grief; even upon hearing the gatekeeper's words, 'Stay right here,' he could not grasp the meaning and kept conversing with the gatekeeper repeatedly.

'In the middle gate-hall' means that in a house with seven gate-towers, the fourth gate-tower, whether counting from the innermost or the outermost, is called the middle gate-hall. If there are five, it is the third; if there are three, it is the second gate-tower. In a house with only one gate-tower, the area near the auspicious pillar in the center is called the middle gate-hall. It is said that the house of the householder Upāli had seven gate-towers, though some say five.

All terms starting with 'Agga' are synonyms of one another. In the phrase 'Yaṃ sudaṃ', 'Yaṃ' refers to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. 'Sudaṃ' is merely a particle. 'Pariggahetvā' means wrapping and holding the belly with that single outer robe. 'Nisīdāpeti' means he caused him to sit down gently, saying, 'Sit down slowly, teacher; sit down slowly, teacher,' as if placing down a large jar of oil. 'Dattosi' means 'Why have you become a fool?'. 'Paṭimukko' means (wrapped/taken) on the head.
67:
Wrapped and taken with the single outer robe. Due to the intense grief arising from the change in the behavior of the householder Upāli, who was his supporter, he spoke harsh words such as 'Aṇḍahāraka' without realizing, 'I am saying such a thing.'

When saying, 'Venerable sir, the enticing speech is excellent,' the Nigaṇṭha spoke referring only to his own sense of trickery, but the householder Upāli spoke referring to the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga) which he himself had realized. The term 'Tena hi' is merely a particle, meaning, 'Venerable sir, I will make a simile for you.' Or it is a statement of reason, meaning: 'Because your dispensation does not lead out of Saṃsāra, and the dispensation of my teacher, the Blessed One, alone leads out of Saṃsāra, for that reason I will make a simile for you.'

'Upavijanyā' refers to a female monkey that has reached the time of giving birth. 'Makkaṭacchāpaka' is a young monkey. 'Buy and bring it' means to bring it only after paying the price. In shops, they sell playthings such as living monkeys and inanimate monkey-figures; this was said in reference to such selling. 'Dyed' means this young monkey is desired after being dyed with a very thick, golden-colored dye. 'Beaten and washed' means struck and washed, or turned over and struck and washed repeatedly. 'Smoothed on both sides' refers to a cloth whose appearance has been made smooth by rubbing both sides well with a gem-stone.

'It can take the dye' is said because both animate and inanimate objects can absorb (drink) the dye. 'It cannot withstand beating' means that if a living young monkey is placed on a washing board and beaten on the belly, the belly will burst and excrement will come out; if beaten on the head, the head will crack and the brain will come out. An inanimate monkey-figure would break into pieces. Therefore, this was said. 'It cannot withstand smoothing' means that if a living young monkey is rubbed with a gem-stone, its hair and skin will fall off; an inanimate monkey-figure would turn into powder. Therefore, this was said. 'It takes the dye only for fools' means it causes delight (taking the dye) only for those of dull wisdom and becomes dear to them. For the wise, however, the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭha or other useless paths of stories such as the battles of the Bharata kings or the abduction of Sītā by King Rāma are only unpleasant. 'It cannot withstand application' means it cannot withstand questioning or investigation. It is as empty and hollow as seeking rice by pounding husks or seeking heartwood in a banana tree. 'It takes the dye (is delightful) only for the wise' means the words of the Blessed One, which demonstrate the Four Noble Truths, are so dear and pleasing to the wise that they cannot be satiated even if they listen for a hundred years. Therefore, the householder Upāli said this. 'I will make a simile for you' is to make that point clear. The householder Upāli meant that the word of the Blessed One is so profound that it can withstand investigation, just as the Great Ocean becomes deeper and deeper as one descends. With the words, 'Listen to whose disciple I am,' he endeavored to speak of the virtues of the Blessed One.
68:
"To the wise" means that the word of the Blessed One, which explains the Four Noble Truths, is dear to the wise. Even if they listen for a hundred years, they do not reach satiety. Therefore, it was said so. Just as the great ocean becomes deeper the further one descends into it, so too is the word of the Buddha. Thus, it was said, "It is capable of investigation and scrutiny." "Listen to [the qualities of] Him whose disciple I am" means "Listen to the virtues of that Blessed One," thus beginning the praise of the Blessed One's excellence.

"Dhīrassa" (of the wise) refers to being wise. I am the disciple of that wise Blessed One who is endowed with that wisdom, that full understanding, that right view... and who is skilled in the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna). He is my Teacher—this connection should be understood in all the following terms. "Pabhinnakhīlassa" (who has broken the spikes) means the Blessed One who has broken the five mental spikes (cetokhila). All worldlings have been conquered, are being conquered, or will be conquered by the Māras. Therefore, those Māras are called "victors" (vijaya). Who are they? They are the Māra of Death (maccu-māra), the Māra of Defilements (kilesa-māra), and the Māra as a Deity (devaputta-māra). Because He has conquered those conquering Māras, He is called "Vijitavijaya" (the Victor of victors). I am the disciple of that Blessed One, the Victor of victors. "Anīghassa" (free from suffering) means the Blessed One who is free from suffering, both the suffering of defilements and the suffering of results (vipāka). "Susamacittassa" (of perfectly even mind) means the Blessed One who has a perfectly even mind towards Devadatta, the elephant Dhanapālaka, Angulimāla, the Elder Rāhula, and so on, as well as towards all gods and humans. "Vuddhasīlassa" (of developed virtue) means the Blessed One whose conduct and virtue are fully developed. "Sādhupaññassa" (of excellent wisdom) means the Blessed One who possesses beautiful wisdom. "Vesamanntarassa" (who has crossed the uneven) means the Blessed One who stands having crossed over the unevenness (visama) of lust and so forth. "Vimalassa" (stainless) means the Blessed One who is free from the stains of lust and so forth.

"Tusitassa" (contented) means the Blessed One whose mind is satisfied. "Vantalokāmisassa" (who has vomited the world's bait) means the Blessed One who has relinquished the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Muditassa" (joyful) means the Blessed One who is joyful by way of dwelling in appreciative joy (muditā-vihāra). Alternatively, this is a repetition. Indeed, out of devotion, one may repeat even a single quality again and again. "Katasamaṇassa" (who has completed the recluse's task) means the Blessed One who has performed the duties of a recluse, meaning He has reached the summit of the recluse's practice. "Manujassa" (the human) refers to a single being according to conventional worldly usage. "Narassa" (the man) is also a repetition. If explained otherwise, there would not be ten qualities in each verse.

"Venayikassa" (the discipliner) means the Blessed One who is the guide of beings. "Ruciradhammassa" (of splendid Dhamma) means the Blessed One who possesses pure Dhamma. "Pabhāsakassa" (the illuminator) means the Blessed One who makes the light [of wisdom] shine. "Vīrassa" (the heroic) means the Blessed One who is endowed with energy (vīriya). "Nisabhassa" (the pre-eminent bull) means the Blessed One who is like the bulls Usabha, Vasabha, and Nisabha, in the sense of being peerless and unshakable in all assemblies. "Gambhīrassa" (the profound) means the Blessed One who has profound qualities, or who is profound because of His qualities. "Monapatassa" (who has attained sagehood) means the Blessed One who has attained omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Vedassa" (possessing knowledge) means knowledge is called veda; the Blessed One is endowed with that knowledge. "Dhammaṭṭhassa" (established in Dhamma) means the Blessed One who stands firm in the Dhamma. "Saṃvutattassa" (of restrained self) means the Blessed One whose self (personality) is guarded and restrained.
69:
Nāgassa means the Blessed One who does no evil due to four reasons. Pantasenassa means the Blessed One who habitually dwells in secluded lodgings. Paṭimantakassa means the Blessed One who is endowed with the wisdom to refute the doctrines of others. Monassa means the Blessed One who is endowed with the quality of mona, which is called wisdom, or one who has vomited out defilements. Dantassa means the Blessed One who is tamed (disciplined).

Isisattamassa means the Blessed One who is the seventh Sage, beginning from the six Buddhas such as Vipassī. Brahmapattassa means the Blessed One who has reached the supreme Omniscient Knowledge. Nhātakassa means the Blessed One who has washed away defilements. Padakassa means the Blessed One who is skilled in composing verses (gāthā) by combining syllables and words. Viditavedassa means the Blessed One who possesses the knowledge that should be known. Purindadassa means the Blessed One who was the very first to give the gift of Dhamma. Sakkassa means the Blessed One who is capable of enduring objects that are difficult to endure. Pattipattassa means the Blessed One who has fully attained all the qualities that should be attained. Veyyākaraṇassa means the Blessed One who explains the meaning in detail. For the Blessed One, there is no Pali term that is without meaning; He taught the meaning of all Pali terms.

Vipassissa means the Blessed One who possesses the wisdom of insight (vipassanā). Anabhinatassa means the Blessed One who has no inclination toward defilements. No apanatassa means the Blessed One who is not angry (does not reject). Ananugatantarassa means the Blessed One whose mind does not follow after defilements. Asitassa means the Blessed One who is free from the bond of craving.

Bhūripaññassa means the Blessed One who is endowed with wisdom that is vast, great, and extensive like the earth, which is called 'bhūri'. Mahāpaññassa means the Blessed One who is endowed with great wisdom. Anupalittassa means the Blessed One who is untainted by the defilements of craving and views. Āhuneyyassa means the Blessed One who is worthy of receiving offerings and honor. Yakkhassa: the Blessed One is called 'Yakkha' because He manifests great power (ānubhāva) or because He possesses a profound and hidden meaning. Mahato means the Blessed One who is great.

Tassa sāvakohamasmī means "I am the disciple of that Teacher who is endowed with such various extraordinary qualities." The householder Upāli attained analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) through the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Thus, established in the domain of analytical knowledge, he answered the question of the Nigaṇṭhas, "Householder, whose disciple do you consider yourself to be?" by praising the Blessed One's quality of destroying defilements with a hundred verses.

Kadāsu refers to the thought that arose in Nātputta: "This householder Upāli went to the ascetic Gotama just now and has returned; when did he collect and bring back so many qualities?" Mālaṅkayavatī means that just as a skilled florist weaves flowers of various colors into an exquisite garland, the householder Upāli wove and praised the collection of the Blessed One's qualities, which are as vast as Mount Meru.
70:
"When were they collected?" means "When were they combined?" It is said that Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had this thought: "This householder Upāli just went to the presence of the recluse Gotama and came back; when did he combine these praises?" Therefore, he asked this. "As if weaving an exquisite garland" means weaving an exquisite garland with various features, such as having stalks on one side, due to one's own skill and the various colors of the flowers. "Even so, venerable sir"—in this context, the Blessed One's collection of virtues, which is as vast as Mount Sineru, should be understood like a great heap of various flowers. Upāli the householder should be understood like the skilled florist. Upāli's composition of verses praising the Tathāgata's diverse virtues should be understood like the florist's weaving of an exquisite garland.

"Hot blood gushed from his mouth" means that the Nigaṇṭha, unable to bear the respect shown to the Blessed One by Upāli, had this thought: "Now this householder no longer wants us; from tomorrow onwards, I will not be able to take fifty or sixty Nigaṇṭhas to enter this householder's home to eat; my rice pot is broken." Then, due to the change in his supporter, intense grief arose. Indeed, these beings think only of their own benefit. When such grief arose in that Nigaṇṭha, internal heat intensified, and his blood melted; driven upward by a strong wind, about a cup of blood, like dye poured into a pot, gushed from his mouth. Very few beings are able to survive after vomiting stored blood. The Nigaṇṭha fell on his knees right there; then they carried him out of the city on a litter, took him by a palanquin, and went to the city of Pāvā. That Nigaṇṭha died in Pāvā not long after. In this sutta, the Dhamma teaching was concluded for a person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū).

## The Commentary on the Upāli Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.

## 7. Kukkuravatika Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Kukkuravatika Sutta. Therein, "among the Koliyans" (Koliyesu) means in the country of that name. Although it is a single country, it is so called in the plural because it is the residence of the Koliyan princes established in the city of Kola. It occurred in that Koliyan country. "Haliddavasanaṃ" means at the time when that market town was founded...
71:
People wearing saffron-colored clothes celebrated a festival of the stars. At the end of the festival, when naming the township, they called it 'Haliddavasana'. It means that the Blessed One lived depending on that Haliddavasana township. Although the specific monastery where he stayed is not designated here, it should be understood that he stayed only in a dwelling suitable for Buddhas.

'Govatika' refers to one who has undertaken the ox-duty; he lives by attaching horns to his head and tying a tail, wandering and eating grass together with cows. 'Acela' refers to one who is naked and without clothes. 'Seniya' is the name of that person.

'Kukkuravatika' refers to one who has undertaken the dog-duty; he performs all the actions of a dog. Both of these individuals were childhood friends who played in the dirt together. 'Crouching like a dog' means that when a dog sits near its master, it sits scratching the ground with its two paws and making a whimpering sound; this person also, thinking 'I will perform the actions of a dog,' greeted the Blessed One joyfully, then scratched the ground with his two hands, shook his head, made the sound 'Bhu bhu,' and sat like a dog with his hands and feet curled.

'Placed on the ground' refers to the food placed on the ground. 'Fully undertaken' means it was taken up to completion. 'What is the destination (gati)?' is a question asking what the result will be. 'What is the future life?' is a question asking in which realm one will be reborn in the hereafter. Because such a question would be unpleasant for him, the Blessed One prohibited it up to three times. 'Kukkura-vata' means the undertaking of the dog-duty.

'Develops' means increases. 'Fully' means without deficiency. 'Constantly' means continuously without interruption. 'Dog-virtue' (kukkura-sīla) means the habits of dogs. 'Dog-mind' (kukkura-citta) means the thought that arises as 'From today onwards, I will do what must be done by dogs.' 'Dog-behavior' (kukkura-kappa) means that dogs have a way of walking, a way of standing, a way of sitting, a way of sleeping, a way of excreting, and a way of walking with bared teeth upon seeing other dogs; this is called dog-behavior, and it means he develops that. In the words 'I, by this virtue,' etc., it means 'I, by this habit, or by this undertaking of duty, or by this practice of difficult austerities, or by this holy life of refraining from sexual intercourse.' 'Deva' refers to one of the deities such as Sakka or Suyāma. 'One of the deities' refers to a deity of the second or third rank among those deities. 'Wrong view' (micchā-diṭṭhi) is the false view that arises from taking a path that does not lead to the deva world as the path that leads to the deva world.
72:
That person's view is called wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). Since there is no other destination for one with such a view except hell or the animal realm, the Blessed One said, 'I declare one of two destinations.' 'Sampajjamānaṃ' means being fully established in that practice without mixing it with other views.

'Venerable Sir, I am not crying because the Blessed One said this to me' means 'Venerable Sir, I do not weep, lament, or wail over this explanation of the Blessed One.' Here, the meaning should be understood through the power of the transitive verb (sakammaka), not merely as the shedding of tears.

'O Mother, they weep for the dead, or for one who is alive but not seen; O Mother, why do you weep for me whom you see alive?' This verse is the application (example) here. Furthermore, 'Venerable Sir, this dog-duty has been undertaken by me for a long time; even if it is perfected, there is no benefit, and if it fails, there is no benefit. I weep, Venerable Sir, reflecting on my own ruin, thinking: "The work I have done for so long has become futile."' 

Ox-duty (govata) and others should be understood in the same manner as described for the dog-duty. 'Gavākappa' means the behavior of an ox. The remaining words are just like what was said regarding dog-behavior. However, the distinction is that while in the dog-duty there is the behavior of walking with bared teeth upon seeing other dogs, here in the ox-duty, it should be understood as the behavior of walking with ears pricked up upon seeing other cattle. The rest is the same.

'Puṇṇa, there are these four kinds of kamma'—why did He begin this discourse? This discourse came by way of the performance of certain kammas, and He began it intending that when these four kammas are explained, the actions (practices) of these people will become clear. Alternatively, He began this discourse knowing that if these four kammas are taught, these people will understand; then one (Puṇṇa) will go for refuge, and one (Seniya) will ordain and attain Arahantship, and this alone is suitable for them.

In that discourse, 'kaṇha' (dark kamma) refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action. 'Kaṇha-vipāka' (dark result) means having a dark result because of being reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). 'Sukka' (bright kamma) refers to the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Sukka-vipāka' (bright result) means having a bright result because of being reborn in heaven (sagga). 'Kaṇha-sukka' refers to mixed kamma. 'Kaṇha-sukka-vipāka' means having a result mixed with pleasure and pain. Because of performing mixed kamma, one might be reborn as an auspicious elephant, etc., in the animal realm due to unwholesome kamma, yet experience happiness during the course of life (pavatti) due to wholesome kamma; or one might be reborn in a royal family due to wholesome kamma, yet experience suffering during the course of life due to unwholesome kamma.
73: Having performed karma that is a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome, one may be born as an auspicious elephant or similar creature in the animal realm due to unwholesome karma, yet experience happiness during the course of life due to wholesome karma. Conversely, one may be born into a royal family due to wholesome karma, yet experience suffering during the course of life due to unwholesome karma. "Neither dark nor bright" refers to the volition of the four paths, which brings about the destruction of karma. If this volition of the four paths were dark in nature, it would yield dark results. If it were bright, it would yield bright results. However, because it does not yield either dark or bright results, and because its results are neither dark nor bright, it is called "neither dark nor bright." This is the meaning in the brief exposition (uddesa). In the detailed exposition (niddesa), "sabyābajjha" means "accompanied by suffering." Regarding body-formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) and so forth, the twelve unwholesome volitions that reach the state of movement through actions such as grasping at the body-door are called "afflictive body-formations." Those same twelve unwholesome volitions that bring about the breaking of silence by moving the jaw at the speech-door are called "speech-formations." For one who is contemplating in private without reaching either of these two types of movement, the volitions occurring at the mind-door are called "mind-formations." Thus, in all three doors, only the unwholesome volitions categorized as bodily misconduct and so forth should be understood as "formations." In this sutta, volition (cetanā) is the principal factor, whereas in the Upāli Sutta, karma is the principal factor. "Abhisaṅkharitvā" means "having accumulated" or "having gathered together." "Sabyābajjhaṃ lokaṃ" means they reappear in a world characterized by suffering. "Sabyābajjhā phassā phusanti" means that resultant contacts accompanied by suffering touch them. "Ekantadukkhaṃ" means continuous suffering. "Bhūtā" is a term in the ablative case signifying cause; the arising of a being (satta) occurs because of the karma that brought it into being. The intended meaning is this: as beings perform karma of a certain nature, their rebirth occurs according to that karma and by way of similarity to it. Therefore, it is said, "Whatever karma one performs, by that one is reborn." Here, although "by that" (tena) is spoken as if by karma, rebirth actually occurs through resultants (vipāka). However, since karma is the cause of the resultant, the meaning here is that one is reborn because of that karma which is the root cause. "Phassā phusanti" means the resultant contacts of that karma touch the one who is reborn. "Kammadāyādā" means "heirs to karma" (kammadāyajjā); it means I declare that karma alone is their inheritance and property. "Abyābajjha" means "without suffering." In this section, the eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) occurring at the body-door are called "body-formations." When these same volitions occur at the speech-door, they are called "speech-formations." Those eight volitions occurring at the mind-door, as well as the three lower jhāna volitions, are called "non-afflictive mind-formations." Let the jhāna volitions be; how do the sense-sphere volitions become "non-afflictive mind-formations"?
74: They are obtained both at the time of reflecting on a kasiṇa and at the time of repeatedly cultivating it. The eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions are connected with the first jhāna volition, and the fourth jhāna volition is connected with the third jhāna volition. Thus, in all three doors, only the wholesome volitions categorized as bodily good conduct and so forth should be understood as "formations." The third section should be understood by way of a mixture of both wholesome and unwholesome. In the passage beginning with "Just as for humans" (seyyathāpi manussā), the fact that humans experience happiness at times and suffering at times is quite evident. Among the deities, it should be understood that Bhumma deities (earth-bound) and among the fallen spirits, Vemānika petas (mansion-ghosts) experience happiness at times and suffering at times. This mixture of happiness and suffering is also found among animals such as elephants. "Tatra" means "among those three types of karma." "The volition for its abandoning" (tassa pahānāya yā cetanā) refers to the path-volition (magga-cetanā) for the purpose of abandoning that karma. Regarding karma, there is no state purer than path-volition. In relation to this karma quadruplet, the twelve unwholesome volitions are called "dark" (kaṇha), the wholesome volitions of the three planes are called "bright" (sukka), and the path-volition is called "neither dark nor bright" (akaṇha-asukka). Seniya said, "Venerable Sir, may I receive [ordination]," thinking: "For a long time indeed, I have weary myself by being joined to a side that does not lead to liberation. Like one turning back and forth on the bank of a dry river thinking 'I will bathe,' or like one pounding husks, I have achieved no benefit. Now, let me apply myself to the proper practice." Then, the Blessed One, referring to the probation (parivāsa) for wanderers prescribed in the Mahāvagga Khandhaka, said: "Seniya, one who was formerly a wanderer..." This refers to the probation undertaken by one who was formerly a wanderer, who, while in the stage of a novice, says: "Venerable Sir, I, named so-and-so, formerly a wanderer, desire full ordination in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for a four-month probation," and so forth. In that context, the word "pabbajjā" (going forth) is mentioned only for the sake of smooth phrasing. For one can indeed receive the going-forth without undergoing probation. However, one who desires full ordination (upasampadā) must undergo probation while fulfilling the eight duties (vatta), such as entering the village at the appropriate time. "Āraddhacittā" refers to the monks whose minds are pleased by the fulfillment of the eight duties. This is a summary here. The details of this probation for wanderers should be understood according to the method stated in the Pabbajjākhandhaka description of the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary. The phrase "api ca mettha" should be resolved as "api ca me ettha." In this Dispensation, the Blessed One knows the difference between individuals. It is shown that He knows the distinction among persons, such as "This person is fit for probation" and "This person is not." Then Seniya thought: "In the Dispensation of the Blessed One, they investigate systematically in this way, taking only what is suitable and rejecting what is not. The Dispensation of the Buddhas is truly wonderful!" Then, with a mind extremely eager for the state of a monk, he concluded his request with the words "Venerable Sir, if..." At that time, the Blessed One [recognized] the state of Seniya's sharp wisdom...
75: It should be understood. In the phrase "api ca mettha," the words should be divided as "api ca me ettha." Indeed, in this Dispensation, the Buddha knows the distinction between individuals. He shows, "This person is worthy of probation (parivāsa), this person is not worthy of probation," thus the distinction between individuals is clear to me. Then Seniya thought, "Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha's Dispensation, where they sift and grind in this way, accepting only what is suitable and discarding what is unsuitable." Thereafter, with a well-aroused effort toward monkhood, he said, "Venerable Sir, if..." and so forth. Then the Blessed One, knowing his intense desire, said, "Seniya is not worthy of probation," and addressed a certain monk, "Go, monk, bathe Seniya, ordain him as a novice, and bring him back." That monk did so, ordained Seniya, and brought him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, gave him the higher ordination. Therefore, it was said, "The naked ascetic Seniya received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he received the higher ordination." "Acirūpasampanno" means not long after receiving the higher ordination. "Vūpakaṭṭho" means withdrawn in body and mind from the cords of sensual pleasure and the defilements of sensuality. "Appamatto" means not abandoning mindfulness in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "Ātāpī" means having effort that burns away defilements, known as bodily and mental energy. "Pahitatto" means having a mind directed toward Nibbāna without regard for body or life, having relinquished the self-identity. "Yassatthāya" means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. "Kulaputtā" means sons of good family by conduct. "Sammadeva" means only through the root cause. In the word "tadanuttaraṃ," it should be divided as "taṃ anuttaraṃ." "Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ" means the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the noble holy life of the path. Indeed, for the sake of that fruit of Arahantship, sons of good family go forth. "Diṭṭheva dhamme" means in this very life. "Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā" means having realized it for oneself through the wisdom of Arahantship, knowing it personally without depending on others. "Upasampajja vihāsī" means having reached it, fulfilled it, and dwelt therein. Dwelling thus, the Elder Seniya understood, "Birth is exhausted..." and so forth. Having thus shown the stage of his reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa), and concluding the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship, it was said, "The Venerable Seniya became one of the Arahants." There, "aññataro" means one. "Arahatāṃ" means he became one among the Arahants who are disciples of the Blessed One; this is the intended meaning here. The remaining text is clear in all respects. ## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, ## the Explanation of the Kukkuravatika Sutta is finished.
76:
## 8. Explanation of the Abhayarājakumāra Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Abhaya Sutta (Abhayarājakumāra Sutta). Therein, "Abhaya" is the name of that prince. "Rājakumāra" means the biological son (breast-born son) of King Bimbisāra. "Vādaṃ āropehi" means "refute his doctrine" (find fault). "Nerayika" means one destined to be reborn in hell. "Kappaṭṭha" means one who remains for an entire aeon. "Atekiccho" means one who cannot be cured even by a thousand Buddhas. "Uggilituṃ" means that the ascetic Gotama, being unable to release the two ends (of the dilemma) and answer, will not be able to spit it out. "Ogilituṃ" means that the ascetic Gotama, being unable to show the fault in the question and reject it, will not be able to swallow it.

Regarding "Yes, venerable sir," it is said that Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta thought: "The ascetic Gotama takes my disciples by enticing and subverting them. Now, I shall devise a question such that, when asked, the ascetic Gotama will be unable to rise from his seat while sitting in a squatting position." That Nigaṇṭha, while eating the delicate food brought from Prince Abhaya's house, devised many questions, thinking: "In this question, the ascetic Gotama will show such a fault; in that question, he will show such a fault." Having discarded all of them, after four months, he saw this "Ovaṭṭikasāra" question. Then he thought: "In the asking or answering of this question, it is impossible to find fault. This question is like a pouch (extremely secure). Who can take this and refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama?" Then, concluding that "Prince Abhaya is wise; he will be able to do it," he taught it to the prince. The prince, desiring to refute the doctrine, accepted his words and said, "Yes, venerable sir."

"It is not the time today" means this question had been prepared for four months; he thought that if this meaning were taken and answered in this way, half a day would not be enough. "So dāni" means "tomorrow at this time." Regarding "himself as the fourth," why did he not invite many monks? It is said that the prince thought: "While many monks are sitting, if I give a small gift and speak, the ascetic Gotama will bring forth other suttas, other reasons, and other such stories to demonstrate. If that happens, there will be only a quarrel or a loud commotion. But if I invite only the Blessed One alone, then I will be blamed: 'How stingy is this Abhaya! Even though he sees the Blessed One traveling daily with hundreds or thousands of monks...'"
77:
If I think, 'I will invite only the Blessed One,' then the criticism might arise: 'This Prince Abhaya is very stingy; although he sees the Blessed One traveling daily with a company of monks, he invites him alone.' However, thinking, 'If I invite [four monks], there will be no fault,' he invited the Buddha along with three other monks, making himself the fourth [host] to the monks.

'Na khvettha rājakumāra ekaṃsena' means 'Prince, in this matter, there is no one-sided (categorical) answer.' The Tathāgata might or might not speak such words. The meaning is that if he sees a benefit arising from speaking, he speaks; if he does not see a benefit, he does not speak. Thus, the Blessed One, with a single word, crushed the problem that the Great Nigaṇṭha had prepared for four months, just as a thunderbolt crushes a mountain peak into powder. 'Anassuṃ nigaṇṭhā' means the Nigaṇṭhas were ruined.

'Aṅke nisinno' means sitting on the lap. Sophists (lesavādino), when presenting their doctrines, usually sit holding some fruit, flower, or a book. When they are victorious, they overwhelm others; when others are victorious, they show distraction as if eating fruit, smelling a flower, or reading a book. This Prince Abhaya, however, thought: 'This Sammāsambuddha is a veteran of many battles [of debate] and a crusher of others' doctrines. If I am victorious, that is good. If I am not, I will poke this child and make him cry. Then I will say, "Look, sirs, this child is crying; please stand up for a moment, we shall see to this later," and so I will remain.' Thus, he sat holding the child. The Blessed One, however, possessing a doctrine thousands and hundreds of thousands of times superior to that of Prince Abhaya, thought, 'I will destroy his doctrine by using this very child as a simile,' and said, 'What do you think, Prince?' and so on.

In that context, 'mukhe āhareyya' means to place in the mouth. 'Āhareyyassāhaṃ' means 'I would take it out [from his mouth].' 'Ādikeneva' means with the very first effort. 'Abhūtaṃ' means an unreal nature. 'Atacchaṃ' means an untrue nature. 'Anatthasaṃhitaṃ' means not connected with benefit, not tending toward growth. 'Appiyā amanāpā' means neither liked nor agreeable. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all places.

Among those categories mentioned, in the unpleasant side, the first type of speech is calling a non-thief a thief, a non-slave a slave, or one who has not misbehaved as one who has. The Tathāgata does not speak such words. The second type of speech is saying of an actual thief, 'This person is a thief,' and so on.
78:
The Tathāgata does not speak that [second type of speech] either. The third type of speech is such as: 'Because you did not perform merit in this life, you have reached poverty, ugliness, and lack of influence; if you do not perform further merit while staying in this life, how will you escape the four woeful states in the next life?' This is the kind of speech spoken with a view toward the benefit of the people, with a view toward the Dhamma, and with a view toward instruction. In that context, 'The Tathāgata is a knower of the right time' means that in that third explanation, the Tathāgata knows the time to speak those words; he speaks only after knowing the time when the people will listen and remember. In the pleasant side, the first type of speech is called 'groundless talk' (fable). It should be understood thus: It is said that many scoundrels, wishing to deceive an old villager who had come to the city and was drinking in a tavern, stayed at the drinking place and, while drinking liquor with the old man, planned: 'We will take all of this old man's clothes and the goods in his hands.' They made an agreement: 'We will each tell a story as if we experienced it ourselves. Whoever says "It is false" or does not believe what is told, we will make him our slave and take him.' They asked the old man, 'Father, do you also agree?' The old man said, 'My lads, let it be as you say.'

One scoundrel said: 'Sirs, when my mother was pregnant with me, she had a craving to eat wood-apples (kapiṭṭha). Since there was no one else to get the wood-apples, she sent me, even though I was in her womb. I went but could not climb the tree, so I grabbed myself by the feet and threw myself up the tree like a mallet. Then, moving from branch to branch and picking the wood-apples, I could not get down, so I went home, brought a ladder, and after descending the tree, went to my mother and gave her the fruits. Those wood-apples were as large as water jars. Then my mother, sitting in one session, ate sixty fruits. Among the fruits I brought in a single fold of my garment, those remaining after my mother ate were for the elders and youngsters in the village belonging to our clan. Our house is sixteen cubits high; after removing the household furniture, it was filled with wood-apples up to the roof. Then, taking the surplus, they made a pile in front of the house. That pile was like a mountain eighty cubits high. Sirs, can such a story be believed?'
79:
The old villager remained silent, and when everyone had finished speaking, being asked, he said, "Friends, it may be so. The kingdom is very vast; because of the vastness of the kingdom, it is possible to believe it." Just as he spoke, when the others also spoke such groundless words, he said, "Friends, listen to my words too. It is not only your clans that are great; our clan is also a great clan. However, our cotton field is much larger than other fields. In the middle of that large cotton field of many karīsas, there once was a great cotton tree eighty cubits high. It had five branches; the other branches did not bear fruit, but on the eastern branch, there was a single large fruit the size of a large water jar. It had six sections, and in those six sections, six cotton pods blossomed. After I had trimmed my beard, bathed, and applied perfumes, I went to the field, saw those blossoming cotton pods, and while standing, I stretched out my hand and plucked them. Those six cotton pods became six strong slaves. All those slaves left me alone and fled. For such a long time, I did not see them, and only today have I found them; you six people are those very slaves. You are named Nanda, you are named Puṇṇa, you are named Vaḍḍhamāna, you are named Citta, you are named Maṅgala, and you are named Poṭṭhiya." Saying this, he rose from his seat and stood holding the topknots of those who were sitting. They could not even say, "We are not slaves." Then, dragging them away, he took them to the court, had them marked, and made them serve as slaves for the rest of their lives. The Blessed One does not speak such words.

The second type of speech consists of various words of praise for others for the sake of material gain and flattery, as well as pointless talk (tiracchāna-kathā) such as talk about thieves, talk about kings, and so on. The Tathāgata does not speak such words either. The third type of speech is talk based on the Noble Truths, which wise men never tire of hearing even if they listen for a hundred years. Thus, the Tathāgata speaks neither all unpleasant words nor all pleasant words. However, he speaks the third type of speech without letting the proper time for speaking it pass. In that context, it should be understood that the simile of the young boy follows below, referring to the third type of unpleasant speech.

"Udāhu ṭhānasovetaṃ" means asking whether it occurs to the Tathāgata at that very moment through spontaneous knowledge (ṭhānupattika-ñāṇa). "Saññāto" means known, well-known, or evident. "Dhammadhātu" means the nature of things (dhamma-sabhāva). This is a name for Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).
80:
This is a name [for Omniscient Knowledge]. That knowledge has been perfectly penetrated by the Blessed One and is held in the Blessed One's hand. Therefore, whatever meaning he desires, all that meaning occurs to his knowledge on the spot. The remaining words are clear in all sentences. This Dhamma teaching was concluded according to the capacity of a person to be led (neyya-puggala).

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Abhayarājakumāra Sutta is finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Bahuvedanīya Sutta

The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Bahuvedanīya Sutta. In that sutta, in the phrase 'Pañcakango thapati', 'Pañcakanga' is the name of that carpenter. Alternatively, he is known as 'Pañcakanga' because he is equipped with five tools: an adze, an axe, a chisel, a mallet, and a bamboo tube for the marking line. 'Thapati' means a master carpenter. 'Udāyī' refers to the wise Elder Udāyī.

'Pariyāyaṃ' means reason or method. 'Dvepānanda' means 'Ananda, (two feelings) also (have been taught by me)'. 'Pariyāyena' means by way of a method. In this context, two feelings should be understood by way of bodily and mental feelings. There are three by way of pleasant feeling, etc.; five by way of faculties such as the faculty of pleasure; six by way of doors such as those born of eye-contact; eighteen by way of mental explorations (upavicāra) such as 'having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy'; thirty-six as follows: six joys related to the household, six joys related to renunciation, six griefs related to the household, six griefs related to renunciation, six equanimities related to the household, and six equanimities related to renunciation. These thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present make one hundred and eight feelings to be understood.

'Ananda, these are the five cords of sensual pleasure'—this is a separate sequence (anusandhi). The Blessed One did not only designate feelings starting from two; he also spoke of feeling as one by way of a method. Desiring to show that one feeling, the Blessed One began this teaching to support the view of the master carpenter Pañcakanga.

'Abhikkantataraṃ' means more excellent. 'Paṇītataraṃ' means more sublime in the sense of being more unsatisfying (due to its high quality). In this context, from the fourth jhāna onwards, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; that too is called 'pleasure' (sukha) because of its peaceful and sublime nature. The six [feelings] related to the household are also called 'pleasure'. The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)...
81:
The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is called happiness (sukha) by virtue of being a bliss that is not felt (avedayita). Indeed, happiness arising by virtue of the five cords of sensual pleasure and by virtue of the eight attainments is called felt happiness (vedayita-sukha). The attainment of cessation is called unfelt happiness (avedayita-sukha). Thus, whether it be felt happiness or unfelt happiness, both are truly happiness in the sense of being blissful, which is defined as the state of being free from suffering.

"Wherever and wherever" (yattha yattha) means in whatever place. "Happiness is found" (sukhaṃ upalabbhati) means that either felt happiness or unfelt happiness is obtained. The Tathāgata designates all that as happiness based on the absence of suffering, in the sense of bliss. In this sutta, the Blessed One, making the attainment of cessation the head, concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship for the sake of the person to be led (neyya-puggala).

## Within the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Bahuvedanīya Sutta is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Apaṇṇaka Sutta
"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Apaṇṇaka Sutta. In that sutta, "wandering" (cārikaṃ) means wandering without haste.

Why did He ask, "Householders, is there any [teacher] you favor?" It is said that the village was situated at the entrance of a forest. Various ascetics and brahmins of different views, having traveled the road all day, would approach that village in the evening for lodging. The villagers would spread out couches and stools, wash their feet, anoint their feet, give them allowable drinks, and on the next day, invite them and offer alms. Those villagers, with confident hearts, would converse with those ascetics and brahmins, who would ask, "Householders, do you hold any view?" When they replied, "No, venerable sirs," the ascetics would say, "Householders, without a view, the world cannot be led out [of suffering]. You should take up a view that you like and find acceptable. Take up the view 'The world is eternal'." Then they would leave. On another day, others arrived and asked the same. The villagers told them, "Yes, venerable sirs, on previous days, ascetics and brahmins like you came and made us take up the view 'The world is eternal'." Then those others said, "What do those fools know? Take up the annihilationist view 'This world is annihilated'." Thus they made them take up the annihilationist view and left. In this way, some taught the partial-eternalism view, others...
82:
...taught the view of the finite and the infinite, others the eel-wriggling view (amarāvikkhepa); thus they made them learn the sixty-two views. Those villagers were unable to stand firm even in a single view. Finally, the Blessed One arrived. Wishing to ask for their benefit, He said, "Householders, is there any [teacher you favor]?" and so on. In that context, "reasoned" (ākāravatī) means having a reason, with a cause. "Apaṇṇaka" means unfailing, without hesitation, taking a certain side.

The ten-based wrong view beginning with "There is no [result of] giving" was explained in detail below in the Sāleyyaka Sutta. Likewise, the right view which is its opposite was also explained.

"Blessing in renunciation" (nekkhamme ānisāṃsaṃ) means they do not see the benefit of emerging from unwholesome states and the side of purification and purity. "Persuasion in false Dhamma" (asaddhamma-saññatti) means making known the false Dhamma. "Exalts oneself" (attānukkaṃseti) means praising oneself by saying, "Apart from me, who else can make others accept their own view?" "Disparages others" (paraṃ vambheti) means belittling others by saying, "Among all these people, not even one is able to make others accept their own view."

"But previously indeed" (pubbeva kho pana) means that for one who first takes up a wrong view, good virtue disappears and immorality stands before them. "Thus to him these" (evamassime) means thus these seven states, such as wrong view, arise in that person. By way of successive arising, many evil unwholesome states arise due to that wrong view as a cause.

"Therein" (tatra) means in those views of the ascetics and brahmins. "Losing throw" (kaliggaho) means taking the losing side or defeat. "Badly grasped, badly handled" (dussamatto samādinno) means poorly taken up and poorly practiced. "Standing having pervaded one side" (ekaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati) means standing having thoroughly reflected only on one's own one-sided view. "If there is no other world," even if it were so, it brings safety. "Neglects" (riñcati) means avoids.

"Persuasion in true Dhamma" (saddhamma-saññatti) means making known the true Dhamma.

"Winning throw" (kaṭaggaho) means taking the winning side or victory. "Well grasped, well handled" (susamatto samādinno) means properly taken up and properly practiced. "Standing having pervaded both sides" (ubhayāṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati) means standing having thoroughly reflected on both sides—one's own view and the other's view. "If there is another world, and if there is no other world," even if it were so, it brings safety. In the subsequent mentions of "one-sided" (ekaṃsa) and "both-sided" (ubhayāṃsa), the meaning should be understood in this same way.
83:
"Karoto" means one who acts with one's own hands. "Kārayato" means one who causes another to act by command. "Chindato" means one who cuts off the hands, etc., of others. "Pacato" means one who oppresses or threatens with a stick. "Socayato" means one who causes sorrow, such as by stealing others' property, either by oneself or by causing others to do so. "Kilamato" means one who causes weariness, such as by cutting off food or imprisonment, either by oneself or by causing others to do so. "Phandato phandāpayato" means one who trembles oneself or causes others to tremble when another is trembling. "Pāṇamatipātayato" means one who kills a living being oneself or causes another to kill. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances through the power of doing oneself and causing others to do.

"Sandhiṃ" means house-breaking. "Nillopaṃ" means great plunder. "Ekāgārikaṃ" means plundering by surrounding only a single house. "Paripanthe tiṭṭhato" means one who waits on the road to rob those who come along. "Karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ" means that even if one acts with the perception "I will do some evil," it is not called doing evil; evil does not exist. However, it means that beings have the perception "We are doing [it]." "Khurapariyantena" means with a disc that has a sharp edge like a razor, or a disc with a rim similar to a razor's edge. "Ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ" means a single mass of flesh. "Puñjaṃ" is a synonym for that "ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ." "Tatonidānaṃ" means because of the cause of making such a single mass of flesh. The people living on the south bank of the Ganges are harsh and cruel; "killing," etc., is said in reference to them. The people living on the north bank of the Ganges are faithful and devout, cherishing the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; "giving and donating," etc., is said in reference to them.

In that context, "yajanto" means one who performs a great sacrifice. "Damena" means by the act of observing the Uposatha, which is the restraint of the senses. "Saṃyamena" means by restraint through virtue (sīla). "Saccavajjena" means by speaking the truth. "Āgamo" means coming or arising. In every way, they reject the very performance of demerit and merit. The white side (sukkapakkha) should also be understood in the same manner as already stated. The remaining terms here are just like what was said in the previous section.

"Natthi hetu natthi paccayo"—in this sentence, the word "paccaya" is a synonym for "hetu." By both these words, they reject the cause of defilement, such as bodily misconduct, which is clearly present, as well as the cause of purity, such as bodily good conduct. "Natthi balaṃ, natthi vīriyaṃ, natthi purisathāmo, natthi purisaparakkamo" means that for beings, whether for defilement or for purity...
84:
...there is no strength, no energy, no such thing as human power or human effort to be performed by a man.

By the term "sabbe sattā," they point to all beings without exception, such as camels, oxen, and donkeys. By the term "sabbe pāṇā," they speak by way of beings with one sense-faculty, beings with two sense-faculties, and so on. By the term "sabbe bhūtā," they speak in reference to beings born within an egg-shell or a womb. By the term "sabbe jīvā," they speak in reference to hill paddy, barley, wheat, and so on. In those cases, they perceive these as "living" (jīva) because of their nature of growing and flourishing. "Avasā abalā avīriyā" means that those beings have no power, strength, or effort of their own. In the phrase "niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā," "niyati" means the state of being fixed (necessity). "Saṅgati" means the wandering into the six classes of birth (abhijāti) here and there. "Bhāva" is just nature (sabhāva). Thus, they have reached various states, being transformed by necessity, by wandering, and by nature. They show that if a person is to be a certain way, he becomes exactly that way. If a person is not to be a certain way, he does not become that way. "Chasvevābhijātīsū" means that they experience pleasure and pain only while staying within the six classes of birth; they show that there is no other ground for experiencing pleasure and pain.

Those six classes of birth (abhijāti) are: Kaṇhābhijāti, Nīlābhijāti, Lohitābhijāti, Haliddābhijāti, Sukkābhijāti, and Paramasukkābhijāti. Among them, bird-catchers, pig-butchers, hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, or whoever else performs cruel deeds, are called Kaṇhābhijāti. They call the monks (bhikkhus) Nīlābhijāti. It is said that those monks eat by putting "thorns" into the four requisites. "Monks have a thorn-like practice" is their very text. Or else, they speak of certain monks named Kaṇṭakavuttika. "Samaṇakaṇṭakavuttikā" is also their text. They call the Nigaṇṭhas, who wear a single cloth, Lohitābhijāti. These are said to be whiter than the first two. They call the laymen who are disciples of the naked ascetics (Acelakas) Haliddābhijāti. In this way, they make their own donors, who provide them with requisites, even more noble than the Nigaṇṭhas. They call the group of people such as Nanda, Vaccha, and Saṅkicca Sukkābhijāti. They are said to be whiter than the previous four. They call the Ājīvakas Paramasukkābhijāti. They are said to be whiter than all others.
85:
In that doctrine, all beings are first bird-hunters and the like. From there, as they become purified, they become Sakyan ascetics (Sakyasamaṇā). From there, as they become purified, they become Nigaṇṭhas; then disciples of the Ājīvakas; then Nanda and others; then Ājīvakas. This is their doctrine. The bright side (sukkapakkha), however, should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. The remaining text here is also similar to what was said in the previous section.

Among these three views, the nihilistic view (natthika-diṭṭhi) denies the result (vipāka). The view of non-action (akiriya-diṭṭhi) denies the action (kamma). The view of causelessness (ahetuka-diṭṭhi) denies both. Among them, one who denies action also effectively denies the result; one who denies the result also effectively denies the action. Thus, in meaning, all of these are nihilists, non-causalists, and non-actionists who deny both.

Those who, having adopted their doctrine, sit in places for the night and places for the day, reciting and investigating: "There is no result of giving, no result of sacrifice; for one who acts, no evil is done; there is no cause, no condition." For them, wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati) is established on that object, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the impulsion-moments (javanas) run. In the first impulsion-moment, it is still curable; likewise in the second and so on. But in the seventh impulsion-moment, even the Buddhas cannot cure it; they are irreversible, like the Ariṭṭhakaṇṭaka thorn.

Among them, some enter one view, some two, and some all three. Whether entering one, two, or three, such a person is one of fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). He is a hinderer of the path to heaven and a hinderer of the path to liberation. Immediately after that existence, he is incapable of going even to heaven, let alone to liberation. Such a being is called a "stump of the round" (vaṭṭakhāṇu) and an "earth-guardian" (pathavīgopaka).

If it is asked, "Is he fixed only in this existence or in another as well?" He is fixed only in this existence. However, due to the power of habitual practice, he will surely delight in those various views in other lives as well. For such a person, there is generally no such thing as emerging (vuṭṭhāna) from existence. Therefore, a wise person desiring prosperity should avoid a wicked person from afar, like a venomous snake.

"Natthi sabbaso āruppā" means that the formless Brahma realm does not exist in any manner. "Manomayā" means made by the mind of meditative absorption (jhāna). "Saññāmayā" means made by the perception of formless absorption. "He is one who practices for the revulsion, fading away, and cessation of forms" means this person is either an attainer (lābhī) or a reasoner (takkī). An attainer is one who has attained the meditative absorptions of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-jhāna). He has no doubt about the fine-material sphere, but he has doubt about the formless sphere. He hears the words of those who say, "Formless realms exist," and the words of those who say, "Formless realms do not exist." In reality, he does not know truly whether they exist or not. [He thinks:] "Based on the fourth fine-material absorption, I will produce a formless absorption. If formless realms exist, I will be reborn there; if not, in the...
86:
...(formless realm) exists. That person [thinks]: "I hear the words of those who say, 'Formless realms exist,' and the words of those who say, 'They do not exist,' but I myself do not know whether they exist or not. Based on the fourth fine-material absorption, I will produce a formless absorption. If formless realms exist, I will be reborn there; if not, I will be reborn in the Brahma world of form (rūpāvacara-brahmaloka). Thus, my infallible practice (apaṇṇaka-dhamma) will be truly infallible and unerring." Thus he practices.

The reasoner (takkī), however, is one who has not yet attained absorption. He also has no doubt about the fine-material absorptions but has doubt about the formless world. He [thinks]: "I hear the words of those who say, 'Formless realms exist,' and the words of those who say, 'They do not exist,' but I myself do not know whether they exist or not. Having performed the preliminary work for the kasina and produced the fourth absorption, and based on that, I will produce a formless absorption. If formless realms exist, I will be reborn there. If not, I will be reborn in the Brahma world of form. Thus, my infallible practice will be truly infallible and unerring." Thus he practices.

Cessation of existence (bhavanirodha) means Nibbāna. "Near to lust" (sārāgāya santike) means being near to delighting in the round of rebirth through the power of lust. "For bondage" (saṃyogāya) means for the purpose of binding through the power of craving.
