"For delighting" (abhinandanāya) means for the purpose of greatly delighting through the power of craving and views. "He is one who practices" means this person is also either an attainer (lābhī) or a reasoner (takkī). An attainer is one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). He has no doubt about the formless realms but has doubt about Nibbāna. He [thinks]: "I hear it said that 'Cessation (nirodha) exists' and 'It does not exist,' but I myself do not know. Based on the meditative attainment, I will develop insight (vipassanā). If cessation exists, I will reach the fruit of Arahantship and attain Parinibbāna. If it does not exist, I will be reborn in a formless realm." Thus he practices.

The reasoner, however, is one who has not attained even a single meditative attainment. Yet, he has no doubt about the formless realms but has doubt about the cessation of existence (bhavanirodha). He [thinks]: "I hear it said that 'Cessation exists' and 'It does not exist,' but I myself do not know. Having performed the preliminary work for the kasina and produced the eight meditative attainments, and based on those attainments, I will develop insight. If cessation exists, I will reach the fruit of Arahantship and attain Parinibbāna. If it does not exist, I will be reborn in a formless realm." Thus he practices.

In this context, it is asked: "Let the views such as 'There is what is given' be infallible (apaṇṇaka), but how can the views such as 'There is nothing given' be called infallible?" It is because of the power of grasping. Because those views are grasped as "infallible, infallible," they come to be called "infallible" (apaṇṇaka).
87:
The phrase "Cattārome" is a separate connection (anusandhi).

The five types of persons—those who hold the views of Nihilism (natthikavāda), the Theory of Non-causality (ahetukavāda), the Theory of Non-action (akiriyavāda), and the two types of persons who hold the views that "there is no formless realm" and "there is no cessation (Nibbāna)"—are the same as the three types of persons mentioned below (the self-tormentor, the tormentor of others, and the one who torments both self and others). The five persons beginning with the proponent of the Theory of Existence (atthikavāda) are the single fourth person (the one who torments neither self nor others).

The Blessed One began this teaching to demonstrate this meaning. In this teaching, the entire sequence of words is clear in its meaning.

88:
## 2. Bhikkhu Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta. In that sutta, the phrase "staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā" (Ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ viharati) means that he was dwelling, developing seclusion, in a mansion named Ambalaṭṭhikā, which was built in the form of a meditation hut near the Veḷuvana monastery for the use of those desiring solitude. Just as a thorn is sharp from the moment it sprouts, so too did this Venerable Rāhula dwell there developing seclusion even from the time he was a seven-year-old novice. "Arisen from seclusion" (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito) means having arisen from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). "The seat" (āsanaṃ) refers to a seat that was already prepared there in the usual manner, which he shook out and set down. "In a water vessel" (udakādhāne) means in a water container. There is also a variant reading "udakaṭṭhāne."

"He addressed the Venerable Rāhula" means he called him for the purpose of giving advice. Indeed, the Blessed One gave many Dhamma teachings to the Elder Rāhula. The Novice's Questions (Sāmaṇerapañhā) were spoken only to the Elder. Likewise, he taught the Rāhula Saṃyutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, and this Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta.

This Venerable Rāhula, at the age of seven, held the corner of the Blessed One's robe and asked for his inheritance, saying, "O Ascetic, give me my inheritance." The Blessed One then handed him over to the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, and had him ordained. Then the Blessed One thought, "Young boys speak words that are both fit and unfit; I will give him advice." He then called the young Rāhula and said, "Rāhula, it is not proper for one who is a novice to engage in animal talk (tiracchānakathā); if you wish to speak, you should speak in this manner." He then taught the Novice's Questions (Sāmaṇerapañhā), consisting of ten questions and fifty-five answers, which are never omitted by any Buddha. It proceeds: "What is the one question, the one recitation, the one explanation? What are the two questions... up to... the ten questions, the ten recitations, the ten explanations?" "What is the one? All beings subsist on nutriment... What is the ten? One endowed with ten factors is called an Arahant." He taught these Novice's Questions.

Again, he thought, "Young boys are fond of lying (musāvāda); they say they have seen what they have not seen, and they say they have not seen what they have seen. I will give him advice." Thinking thus, so that he might easily understand even by just looking with his eyes, he first presented four...
89:
The Blessed One taught this Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta by showing four similes of the water vessel, followed by two similes of the elephant and one simile of the mirror. Furthermore, he taught the Rāhula Sutta (in the Sutta Nipāta) showing the greatness of relying on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), the abandoning of desire and lust (chandarāga) in the five cords of sensual pleasure, and the absence of craving for the four requisites. He taught the Rāhula Saṃyutta to show that desire and lust should not be formed towards existences in whatever place one arrives. He taught the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta to show that desire and lust based on the household life and the physical body—thinking "I am beautiful, my appearance is clear"—should not be formed.

Among those suttas, it cannot be said exactly when the Rāhula Sutta was spoken. This is because it was spoken repeatedly by way of frequent advice. The Rāhula Saṃyutta was spoken from the age of seven until the time he was a monk who had not yet spent a vassa. The Mahārāhulovāda Sutta was spoken when he was an eighteen-year-old novice. The Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta was spoken when he was a monk who had not yet spent a vassa. The Kumārakapañhā and this Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta were spoken when he was a seven-year-old novice.

Among them, the Rāhula Sutta was for the purpose of frequent advice; the Rāhula Saṃyutta was for the purpose of the Elder's conceiving the womb of insight (vipassanā); the Mahārāhulovāda was for the purpose of dispelling desire and lust based on the household life; and the Cūḷarāhulovāda was for the purpose of making him attain Arahantship when the fifteen factors for the maturation of liberation (vimutti) had matured in the Elder. Referring to this instruction of the Blessed One, the Elder Rāhula, wishing to speak of the virtues of the Tathāgata in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, said this:

"As a lapwing (kikī) would protect its egg,
Or as a yak (cāmarī) its noble tail,
So did the Wise One, perfect in virtue,
The Tathāgata, protect me."

The Novice's Questions (Sāmaṇerapañhā) were spoken for the purpose of abandoning improper speech, and this Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta was spoken for the purpose of not telling intentional lies (sampajānamusāvāda).

In those passages, "passasi no" means "do you see?" "Parittaṃ" means "a little." "Sāmaññaṃ" means "the Dhamma of a recluse." "Nikkujjhitvā" means "having turned it face down." "Ukkujjhitvā" means "having turned it face up."

"Rāhula, for example, the King's elephant"—this simile was spoken for the purpose of showing a comparison for one who lacks restraint in telling intentional lies. In that context, "īsādanto" means...
90:
It is an elephant with tusks like the shafts of a chariot (slightly long and uneven). 'Uruḷhavā' means an elephant that is well-grown and accomplished in being mounted. 'Abhijāto' means an elephant of noble birth and lineage. 'Saṅgāmāvacaro' means an elephant that has previously entered the battlefield. 'Performing its task' means killing the enemies as they come. With its forebody, it knocks down the wooden platforms, watchtowers, turrets, and plain walls of the enemy's army; likewise with its hindbody. 'Performing its task with its head' means it turns and looks with the intention, "I will trample this area." By merely looking in this way, a hundred or a thousand troops are split in two. 'Performing its task with its ears' means striking and bringing down the incoming arrows with its ears. 'Performing its task with its tusks' means goring the enemy kings' elephants, horses, elephant-riders, horse-riders, and infantry. 'Performing its task with its tail' means cutting or breaking with a long sword or an iron club tied to its tail. However, it protects its trunk by placing it in its mouth.

In the performance of that elephant's battle-task, if it is said that it 'has not yet sacrificed its life' (apariccattaṃ), the elephant-rider thinks, "We shall see the victory of others and our own defeat." 'Performing its task with its trunk' means it tramples an area of eighteen cubits around it, holding an iron mace or a catechu-wood pestle. If it is said that it 'has sacrificed its life' (pariccattaṃ), he thinks, "Now the elephant is no longer afraid of the soldiers; we shall see our victory and the defeat of the enemy." For one who tells a deliberate lie, there is no evil deed that cannot be done, whether it be the transgression of an offense or deeds such as matricide. Therefore, one should train with the thought, "I will not speak a lie even in jest or for the sake of fun." The purpose of reflection is the purpose of looking; it means it is like looking to see a blemish on the face. One should act after reflecting (looking) again and again.

Indeed, one should not do what should not be done, but should withdraw from it. One should perform the task that should be done repeatedly, giving it support. One must be one who trains day and night.

One should feel oppressed by unwholesome acts, be ashamed of them, and feel disgust as if seeing excrement. Since the mental action (manokamma) is not a basis for the confession of an offense, it is not said here that "it should be confessed." To what extent should bodily and verbal actions be purified, and to what extent should mental actions be purified? I shall answer this inquiry. Bodily and verbal actions should be purified even in the morning. A monk staying in a secluded place after his meal should reflect: "From the time of dawn until sitting in this place, have I committed any bodily or verbal action that is displeasing to others?" If he knows he has, he should say as follows:
91:
To what extent should bodily and verbal actions be purified, and to what extent should mental actions be purified? Bodily and verbal actions should be purified first, only during the time before the morning meal. A monk who has finished his meal and is sitting in a place for the day's rest should reflect: "From the time of dawn until sitting in this place, during this interval, have I committed any bodily or verbal action that is displeasing to others?" If he knows he has, he should confess what is fit to be confessed and disclose what is fit to be disclosed. If he has not, he should abide in that very joy and gladness. Mental actions, however, should be purified in the place of seeking alms. How? He should reflect: "In the place of seeking alms today, did I have any desire, lust, or resentment toward forms and so on?" If he did, he should resolve in his mind, "I will not do so again." If he did not, he should abide in that very joy and gladness.

'Samaṇa' or 'Brāhmaṇa' refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or the disciples of the Tathāgata. "Tasmātiha" means: because they purified themselves in this way in the past, will purify themselves in the future, and are purifying themselves now, therefore you too, following their example, should train in this way. The remaining words are clear in all places. The Blessed One concluded this teaching according to the capacity of the person to be led (neyya puggala), as if placing a gem-stone of a hundred yojanas as the pinnacle upon a pile of jewels raised as high as the peak of existence (bhavagga).

## The Explanation of the Ambalaṭṭhika-rāhulovāda Sutta is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta. Therein, "followed closely behind" (piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi) means going without losing sight, following the postures closely behind. At that time, the Blessed One was walking ahead with a graceful gait, placing step after step, while the Elder Rāhula followed behind, keeping pace with the steps of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala).

As they went, the Blessed One shone like a noble elephant king emerging from the midst of a blossoming Sāla grove to descend onto level ground, and the venerable Rāhula was as beautiful as a young elephant following behind a noble elephant king. The Blessed One was as beautiful as the king of lions (Kesara) emerging from a jewel cave in the evening to reach his hunting ground, and the venerable Rāhula was as beautiful as a young lion following the lion king. The Blessed One was as beautiful as a great tusker tiger emerging from a forest like a mountain of jewels, and the venerable Rāhula was as beautiful as a young tiger following the tiger king. The Blessed One was as beautiful as a king of Garudas emerging from a grove of silk-cotton trees, and the venerable Rāhula was as beautiful as a young Garuda emerging after the Garuda king. The Blessed One was as beautiful as a king of Haṃsas (swans) flying into the sky from Mount Cittakūṭa, and the venerable Rāhula was as beautiful as a young Haṃsa flying in pursuit of the Haṃsa king. The Blessed One was as beautiful as a great golden boat entering a large lake, and the venerable Rāhula was as beautiful as a small golden boat following the great golden boat.
92:
(Prince Rāhula was as beautiful) as a young elephant following a noble great elephant. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a maned lion king (kesarājā) emerging from a jeweled cave in the evening and heading towards his hunting ground; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as a young lion following the lion king. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a powerful tiger emerging from a forest that resembled a jeweled mountain; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as a young tiger following the tiger king. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a Garuḍa king emerging from a silk-cotton forest; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as a young Garuḍa following the Garuḍa king. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a golden swan king flying into the sky from Mount Cittakūṭa; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as a young swan following the swan king. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a great golden ship entering a great lake; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as a small golden boat following the great golden ship. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a Wheel-turning Monarch traveling through the sky by the power of the wheel-treasure; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as the counselor-treasure following the monarch. The Blessed One was as magnificent as the moon traveling through a cloudless sky; Rāhula Bhadda was as beautiful as the pure morning star following the path of the moon.

The Blessed One was born into the Okkāka royal dynasty, the lineage of Mahāsammata; Rāhula Bhadda was also born likewise. The Blessed One was born into a most pure Khattiya caste, like milk poured into a conch shell; Rāhula Bhadda was also born likewise. The Blessed One renounced the throne and went forth into homelessness; Rāhula Bhadda did the same. The Blessed One’s body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as delightful as a jeweled portal erected in the cities of the gods, or like a coral tree (pāricchattaka) in full bloom; Rāhula Bhadda’s body was also the same. Thus, both had fulfilled their past aspirations; both were monks of royal birth; both were delicate nobles; both had golden complexions; both were endowed with the marks. As they walked together on the same path, they shone brilliantly, outshining with their own glory the splendor of two moons, two suns, two Sakkas, two Suyāmas, two Santusitas, two Sunimmitas, two Vasavattis, and two Mahābrahmās.

While walking thus, the Venerable Rāhula, following closely behind the Blessed One, gazed upon the Tathāgata from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair. Seeing the magnificent beauty of the Buddha’s appearance, he thought: "The Blessed One is truly beautiful, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, he is like one in the midst of scattered gold dust, like a golden mountain surrounded by streaks of lightning, like a golden shrine adorned with jewels pulled by mechanical strings. Even when covered with his red rag-robes, he is like a golden mountain wrapped in a red woolen blanket, like a golden shrine adorned with coral vines."
93:
The Blessed One was beautiful, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Surrounded by a fathom-long aura of radiance, he appeared as if he were in the midst of scattered gold dust, like a great golden mountain surrounded by streaks of lightning, or like a great golden stupa beautifully decorated with jewels and well-constructed with mechanisms. Clad in a rag-robe the color of a red bladder, he was like a great golden mountain enveloped in a thick red woolen blanket, like a golden stupa adorned with coral vines, like a golden stupa honored with vermilion powder, like a golden pillar anointed with lacquer, or like the full moon emerging at that moment from between red clouds. 

Rahula thought, "Oh, how endowed with the splendor of a physical form fashioned by the power of the thirty perfections!" Then, looking back at himself, he thought, "I, too, am beautiful. If the Blessed One had exercised the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch over the four great islands, he would have given me the position of heir-apparent. In that case, the surface of Jambudīpa would have been exceedingly beautiful." Thus, based on his own physical form, he gave rise to strong lustful desire (chandarāga) associated with the household life.

While walking ahead, the Blessed One also thought: "Now Rahula's physical form is replete with skin, flesh, and blood. The time has come for his mind to leap toward desirable forms and other sense objects. On what object does Rahula mostly spend his time?" Then, as soon as he reflected, he saw that thought of Rahula's, just as one might see a fish in clear water or a reflection of a face in a pure circular mirror. Having seen it, he thought: "This Rahula, though being my own son and following behind me, thinks 'I am beautiful, my appearance is clear,' and thus, based on his physical form, gives rise to strong lustful desire associated with the household life. He is rushing toward a place that is not a landing-place, following a wrong path, and wandering in an improper resort. Like a traveler lost in direction, he is going toward a destination where one should not go. Indeed, if this defilement increases within him, it will not allow him to see his own welfare, the welfare of others, or the welfare of both as they truly are. Because of such inability to see, it will cause him to take rebirth in hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras, or in the cramped confines of a mother's womb, and will cause him to fall into the beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra)."

Greed gives rise to misfortune, greed agitates the mind;
People do not perceive this danger born from within.
A greedy person does not know the benefit, a greedy person does not see the Dhamma;
When greed overcomes a person, there is then utter darkness. (Itivuttaka 88)

"Just as a large ship filled with many treasures must not be neglected for even a moment if water enters through a gap in the planks, but the hole must be quickly plugged, even so, this defilement must not be neglected. I will subdue it right now, before this defilement destroys the treasures of virtue and so forth within him." Such was his intention. In such matters, the Buddhas have a gaze like that of a great elephant. Therefore, turning his entire body like a statue moved by a machine, he stood and called Rahula. Based on that address, the words beginning with "Atha kho bhagavā apaloketvā" were spoken. In that text, the terms beginning with "yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ" have been explained in every aspect in the Khandhaniddesa of the Visuddhimagga. The terms beginning with "netaṃ mama" have been explained in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta.
94:
It is what is called the "elephant's gaze" (nāgavilokana). Therefore, turning with his entire body like a golden statue moved by a machine, he stood and addressed the fortunate Rahula. With reference to that address, it is said: "Then the Blessed One, having looked back..."

In that Pali, the terms beginning with "yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ" (whatever kind of form) have been explained in detail in every aspect in the Khandhaniddesa of the Visuddhimagga. The terms beginning with "netaṃ mama" (this is not mine) have been stated in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta. Why did he ask, "Is it only form, O Blessed One?" It is said that to the young Rahula, having heard the words, "All form is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self," the following method of reasoning arose: "The Blessed One says that all form should be seen in this way with insight-wisdom; how then should one practice regarding feeling and the other aggregates?" Therefore, established in that method, he asked. For the venerable Rahula was skilled in the methods of reasoning; if it were said, "This should not be done," he would understand through a hundred or a thousand methods that "this also should not be done, and this also should not be done." If it were said, "This should be done," the same method applied.

Indeed, this venerable one was desirous of training (sikkhākāma). Early in the morning, he would scatter a handful of sand in the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) and reflect: "Today, may I receive this much instruction and this much reproof from the presence of the Fully Enlightened One and from the presence of my preceptor." The Fully Enlightened One, wishing to appoint him to a foremost position, placed him as the foremost in training, saying: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are desirous of training, Rahula is the foremost." (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.209). That venerable one also roared this lion's roar in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks:

"Having fully understood all this, the King of Dhamma, my father,
In the presence of the Saṅgha of monks, appointed me to this foremost position.
I am the foremost among those desirous of training, praised by the King of Dhamma;
And among those who have gone forth out of faith, my companions are excellent.
The King of Dhamma is my father, and the Treasurer of Dhamma is my uncle;
Sāriputta is my preceptor; he gave me all the instructions of the Conqueror."

Then, because not only form but also feeling and the other aggregates should be seen in this way, the Blessed One said: "Rahula, form also..." and so forth. "Ko najjā" means "Ko nu ajja" (Who is it today?). It is said that this thought occurred to the Elder Rahula: "The Fully Enlightened One, knowing the lustful desire associated with my physical form, did not speak indirectly, saying 'A monk should not think such a thought,' but rather said, 'Go, monk, to Rahula...'"
95:
He did not send a messenger to say, “Do not think such thoughts again.” Standing right before me, He gave the Sugata’s instruction to my face, like catching a thief with the stolen goods by the topknot. The instruction of the Buddha is difficult to obtain even in incalculable aeons. Having received such an instruction in the presence of the Buddha, he thought, “What wise person of prudent nature would enter the village for alms today?” Then, that Venerable (Rāhula) abandoned the matter of food and, turning back from the very spot where he had stood and received the instruction, sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The Blessed One, seeing that Venerable turning back, did not say, “Rāhula, do not go back yet; it is time for your alms-round.” Why? It is said that He thought, “Let him today eat the ambrosial food that is mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati).”

“Venerable Sāriputta saw him” means he saw him while following behind after the Blessed One had departed. This Venerable (Sāriputta) had one routine when living alone and another when living with the Blessed One. When the two Chief Disciples live alone, they sweep the lodgings early in the morning, attend to their physical needs, enter into meditative attainments, and then, after sitting together in harmony, go for alms according to their wish. However, when living with the Blessed One, the Elders do not do so. At that time, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, goes for alms first. When the Blessed One has departed, the Elder leaves his own lodging and, reflecting, “In a place where many people live, some may be able to make everything pleasant to look at, while others may not,” goes here and there and sweeps the unswept places. If the rubbish has not been discarded, he discards it. If there is no water pot at the place for drinking water, he places one there. Going to the sick monks, he asks, “Friends, what shall I bring for you? What do you need?” Going to the junior monks who have not yet spent a rainy season, he advises, “Friends, find delight; do not be dissatisfied; the Buddha’s Dispensation has practice as its essence.” Having done this, he goes for alms last of all.

For example, just as a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), wishing to go somewhere, sets out first surrounded by his army, but the Treasurer-Jewel (the eldest son jewel) sets out last after organizing the army units; in the same way, the Blessed One, the Universal Monarch of the True Dhamma, sets out first surrounded by the community of monks, but the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), who is like the Treasurer-Jewel to the Blessed One, sets out last of all after performing these duties. The Elder, having set out in this manner, saw the Venerable Rāhula sitting at the foot of a certain tree on that day. Therefore, it is said, “He saw him while following behind.” Why did Venerable Sāriputta urge him to practice the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (anāpānasati)? He urged him because it was suitable for his sitting posture. The Elder, without reflecting that “The Blessed One has taught the meditation on form (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) to this Rāhula,” thought, “This Rāhula is sitting in a manner that is unshakable and unmoistened by craving; this meditation on mindfulness of breathing is suitable for this sitting posture of his,” and thus he spoke...
96:
Why did Venerable Sāriputta urge him to practice the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (anāpānasati)? He urged him because it was suitable for his sitting posture. The Elder, without reflecting that “The Blessed One has taught the meditation on form (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) to this Rāhula,” thought, “This Rāhula is sitting in a manner that is unshakable and unmoistened by craving; this meditation on mindfulness of breathing is suitable for this sitting posture of his,” and thus he spoke. In those words (urging him to develop mindfulness of breathing), “mindfulness of breathing” (anāpānasati) means to grasp the in-breaths and out-breaths, to produce the fourfold and fivefold jhānas therein, to develop insight (vipassanā), and thereby to attain Arahatship.

“It is of great fruit” (mahapphalā hoti)—how great is the fruit? In this Dispensation, a monk devoted to mindfulness of breathing can exhaust all taints (āsavas) and reach Arahatship even while sitting in a single seat. If he is unable to do so, he becomes a samasīsī (one who simultaneously ends defilements and life) at the time of death. If he is unable to do so, having been reborn in the deva realm and hearing the Dhamma from a deva-son who is a preacher of Dhamma, he reaches Arahatship. If he misses that, he realizes Paccekabodhi-knowledge in a time when no Buddha has arisen. If he does not realize that, he becomes one with swift intuition (khippābhiññā) in the presence of Buddhas, like Venerable Bāhiya and others. Thus, it is of great fruit. “It is of great benefit” (mahānisaṃsā) is a synonym for that very “great fruit.” This has also been said:

“For whom mindfulness of breathing is perfected and well-developed,
Practiced in due order as taught by the Buddha,
He illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.”

Seeing this great fruit, the Elder urged his co-resident (saddhivihārika) in that mindfulness of breathing.

Thus, the Blessed One taught the meditation on form, and the Elder taught mindfulness of breathing; both departed after teaching meditation. Venerable Rāhula remained behind in the monastery. Although the Blessed One knew that Rāhula had remained behind, He did not take hard or soft food Himself and go to him, nor did He send it through the hand of Venerable Ānanda, nor did He give a sign to King Pasenadi, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others. If He had given even a mere sign, they would have brought meals in baskets. Just like the Blessed One, Venerable Sāriputta also did nothing. Venerable Rāhula was without food and missed his meal. However, in that Venerable, not even a thought of dissatisfaction arose, such as: “The Blessed One, though knowing I remained in the monastery, did not Himself bring the alms-food He received, nor did He send it through another, nor did He inform King Pasenadi and others; my preceptor (Venerable Sāriputta), though knowing I remained behind, did nothing along with the Blessed One.” Since he did not have such thoughts, how could low pride or excessive pride arise? On the contrary, he was reflecting on the meditation taught by the Blessed One, both in the morning and in the afternoon: “For such reasons, the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is impermanent; for such reasons, the aggregate of form is suffering; for such reasons, the aggregate of form is...”
97:
(The Blessed One) did not send him away, nor did he give any sign to the people. The thought, "My preceptor also knows that I have been left behind, yet he has done nothing," did not even arise in the Venerable Rāhula. Because of that lack [of attention], how could there arise in him low pride (omāna) or excessive pride (atimāna)? Indeed, he continuously applied his mind to the meditation subject taught by the Blessed One, both before and after the meal—"Thus form is impermanent, thus it is suffering, thus it is foul, thus it is non-self"—like one rubbing sticks to start a fire. In the evening, he thought: "I was told by my preceptor to develop mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). I shall not fail to follow his word. One who does not follow the words of one's teachers and preceptors is called 'difficult to admonish' (dubbaca). There is no affliction more harsh than being blamed, 'Rāhula is difficult to admonish; he does not even follow the word of his preceptor.'" Desiring to ask about the method of meditation, he went to the presence of the Blessed One. To show this, it was said: "Then the Venerable Rāhula..." and so on.

In that text, "seclusion" (paṭisallānā) means being alone. Why is it said, "Whatever, Rāhula"? Although the Buddha was asked about mindfulness of breathing, he taught the meditation on form (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna). This was for the purpose of abandoning desire and lust (chandarāga) for form. It is said that this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Desire and lust have arisen in Rāhula depending on his own physical body (attabhāva). Previously, I taught him the meditation on form in brief. Now, I will make him disillusioned with the physical body through forty-two aspects, and by deconstructing it, I will bring the desire and lust dependent on that body to the state of never arising again." If so, why did he explain the space element (ākāsadhātu) in detail? It was to show derived form (upādārūpa). Previously, only the four great elements were taught, not derived form. Therefore, he explained the space element in detail to show it through this method. Alternatively, form delimited by internal space also becomes clear.

Form delimited by space reaches clarity;
For the sake of making it manifest thus, the Leader revealed it.

Regarding the first four elements here, what should be said has already been stated in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta. In the space element, "gone to space" (ākāsagata) means having reached the state of space. "Clung to" (upādinna) means taken, grasped, or touched by craving and views, meaning "situated in the body." "Ear-hole" (kaṇṇacchidda) means the opening of the ear not touched by flesh, blood, etc. The same method applies to the nostrils and so on.
98:
"And by which" (yena ca) means by which opening (one swallows). "Swallows" (ajjhoharati) means taking inside. From the base of the tongue to the stomach lining, humans have an opening about four finger-breadths wide. This was said in reference to that opening. "And where" (yatta ca) means in which place. "Stays" (santiṭṭhati) means remains. Humans have what is called a stomach lining (stomach) as large as a cloth-strainer. This was said in reference to that stomach. "Exits below" means the opening through which it exits downwards. This was said in reference to the intestines, which are about thirty-two cubits long and coiled in twenty-one places. By the phrase "or whatever else there is," he shows the very subtle space situated within the skin, flesh, etc., as well as the space existing as pores. The remaining terms should be understood in the same way as mentioned for the earth element and others.

Now, wishing to explain the characteristic of steadfastness (tādibhāva) to the Venerable Rāhula, he spoke the words beginning with "like the earth." One who is neither attracted to the pleasant nor repelled by the unpleasant is called "steadfast" (tādī). In the phrase "agreeable and disagreeable," the eight types of contact associated with consciousness rooted in greed are called "agreeable." The two types of contact associated with consciousness rooted in displeasure are called "disagreeable." "Will not remain overwhelming the mind" means these contacts, having arisen, will not be able to remain by taking over and grasping your mind as if holding it in a fist. The desire and lust based on the physical body—thinking "I am beautiful, my appearance is clear"—will not arise again. In terms such as "gūthagata," "gūtha" itself is "gūthagata" (excrement). It should be understood thus in all instances.

"Not established anywhere" means not being established in any object such as the earth, mountains, or trees. If it were established in the earth, it would break along with the earth when it breaks. If it were in a mountain, it would fall when the mountain falls. If it were in a tree, it would be cut when the tree is cut.

"Rāhula, develop loving-kindness"—why did he begin this teaching? It was to show the cause of steadfastness (tādibhāva). The characteristic of steadfastness was shown below. It is not possible to become steadfast without a cause, saying "I am steadfast." Nor does one become steadfast because of reasons such as "I am born of a high family, I am learned, I am a recipient of gains, kings and royal ministers associate with me." One becomes steadfast only by developing meditations such as loving-kindness. Therefore, to show the cause of steadfastness, he began this teaching: "Rāhula, develop loving-kindness."
99:
In that [Mahārāhulovāda Sutta], 'bhāvayato' refers to a person who is attaining either access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā). 'Yo byāpādo' means whatever anger exists towards beings; that anger will be abandoned. 'Vihesā' means the harming of beings with hands, etc. 'Arati' means boredom in secluded dwellings and in the higher wholesome states. 'Paṭigho' means the defilement of impingement upon beings or formations anywhere. 'Asubhaṃ' means the access and absorption concentration obtained regarding [corpses] such as the bloated one (uddhūmātaka). This development of the perception of foulness (asubhabhāvanā) has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'Rāgo' means lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Aniccasaññaṃ' refers to the perception that arises together with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). Alternatively, this insight wisdom itself is called 'perception of impermanence' (aniccasaññā). Although it is not perception, it is called 'perception' by way of taking perception as the head. 'Asmimāno' means the conceit that clings as "I am" regarding the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha), etc.

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to elaborate on the question asked by the Venerable Rāhula, spoke the words beginning with "ānāpānassati." In that passage starting with ānāpānassati, this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of mindfulness of breathing, the method of developing the meditation, the meaning of the Pali text, along with the discourse on its benefits (ānisamsakathā), have all been explained in every detail in the Anussatiniddesa of the Visuddhimagga. The Blessed One concluded this teaching for the sake of a person who is to be led (neyyapuggala).

## The Commentary on the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta
## in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## 3. Commentary on the Cūḷamālunkyasutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mālunkya Sutta. In that sutta, 'Mālunkyaputtassa' refers to the elder of that name. 'Ṭhapitāni paṭikkhittāni' means that views are set aside and rejected, in the sense that they should not be declared. 'Tathāgato' means a being. 'Taṃ me na ruccati' means "I do not like that non-declaration." 'Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya' means having rejected the training.

'Ko santo kaṃ paccācikkhasi' means: for either a beggar might reject the one who was begged, or the one who was begged might reject the beggar. You, Mālunkyaputta, are neither the beggar nor the one who was begged. Thus, the meaning is: "Who are you, and whom are you rejecting?"
100:
'Viddho assa' means he would be shot by an archer standing within the enemy's army. 'Gāḷhapalepanena' means by a thick smearing of poison. 'Bhisakka' refers to a doctor (physician). 'Sallakatta' refers to the extraction of an arrow or a surgeon who extracts arrows. 'Akkassa' means they take the fibers of the akka plant and make a bowstring; therefore, it is said "akkassa." 'Saṇhassa' refers to the fibers of bamboo strips. They also make bowstrings from maruvā hemp and khīrapaṇṇi hemp; therefore, it is said "whether of maruvā hemp or khīrapaṇṇi hemp." 'Gaccha' refers to a plant growing in mountain clefts, rivers, etc. 'Ropima' refers to an arrow made from grass taken from a thicket of reeds, which has been planted and grown. 'Sithilahanu' refers to the feathers of a bird of that name. 'Bherava' refers to the hair of a black lion (kāḷasīha). 'Semhāra' refers to the hair of a monkey. 'Evaṃ no' means if this (eternalism) wrong view exists, the (path) holy life (brahmacariya) is not possible.

'Attheva jāti' means if this wrong view exists, only the holy life does not exist, but birth (jāti) certainly exists. Likewise, it shows that aging, death, etc., also exist. 'Yesāhaṃ' should be resolved as "yesaṃ ahaṃ." 'Nighāta' means oppression or destruction. The meaning is that my disciples, being disenchanted with those views, reach Nirvana in this very life.

'Tasmātiha' means because I have not declared this view, but have declared only the Four Noble Truths, therefore [this is so]. 'Na hetaṃ mālunkyaputta atthasaṃhitaံ' means neither this view nor this declaration is connected with the goal (benefit). 'Na ādibrahmacariyakaံ' means it is not even the preliminary morality (pubbabhāgasīla) which is the beginning of the holy life. In the passage beginning with 'na nibbidāya,' it means it does not lead to disenchantment with the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), to dispassion, to the cessation of the round, to the stilling of lust, etc., to direct knowledge of things to be known, to the enlightenment consisting of the four paths, or to the realization of the unconditioned Nirvana. 'Etaṃ hi' refers to this declaration of the Four Noble Truths. 'Ādibrahmacariyakaံ' means the dhamma which is the beginning and the proximate cause of the holy life. The rest should be understood by the method of opposites to what has been stated. The Blessed One concluded this teaching also for the sake of a person who is to be led (neyyapuggala).

## The Commentary on the Cūḷamālunkyasutta
## in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
101:
## 4. Commentary on the Mahāmālunkyasutta

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāmālunkyasutta. In that sutta, "orambhāgiyāni" refers to those states that exist as a group in the lower sensual realm (kāmabhava) and lead to rebirth in that sensual realm. "Saṃyojanāni" refers to the states that act as bonds. "Kassa kho nāma" is a question: "Whose teachings, whether of a deva or a human, do you remember? Did you alone hear it, or did anyone else hear it?" "Anuseti" means lying latent because it has not yet been abandoned by the Path (magga). A defilement that continuously lies latent is called a fetter (saṃyojana).

In this context, the Blessed One asked about the fetters, and the Elder also answered regarding the fetters. Nevertheless, the Blessed One reproached the Elder's doctrine. Why was he reproached? It was because the Elder held such a view. His view was: "One is associated with defilements only at the moment they arise (samudācāra); at other moments, one is not associated." Because of this view, the Blessed One reproached the Elder. Then, the Venerable Ānanda thought: "The Blessed One began this Dhamma teaching by his own nature, intending to teach the Sangha of monks. This unwise monk has distorted that teaching. Now, I shall request the Blessed One and teach the Dhamma to the monks." The Venerable Ānanda did so. To show this, the passage beginning with "Evaṃ vုtte āyasmā ānando" was spoken.

In that text, "sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitena" means one who is possessed and overwhelmed by identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). "Sakkāyadiṭṭhiparetena" means one who is driven by identity view. "Nissaraṇaṃ" refers to Nibbāna, which is the escape from view; he does not know that Nibbāna as it truly is. "Appaṭivinītā" refers to states that have not been removed or abandoned. "Orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ" refers to the fetters belonging to the lower sensual realm. The same method applies to the remaining terms. The "white side" (sukkapakkha, the wholesome part) has an obvious meaning. However, because it is said here that "sānusayā pahīyati" (it is abandoned along with latencies), some teachers say, "The fetter is one thing, and the latency (anusaya) is another." Their view is that just as when one says "rice with curry," the curry is something other than the rice, so because of the word "sānusayā," the latency must be a different state from the identity view that has arisen (pariyuṭṭhāna). These teachers should be refuted by phrases such as "covering [the body] along with the head." This is because there is no man other than the head. Furthermore, "If that state itself is the fetter and that state itself is the latency, then in that case, the Blessed One..."
102:
"...would be making a reproach against the Elder like that against a child." It was not poorly reproached. Why? Because the Elder held such a view; this has been explained in detail. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke the words "abandoned along with latencies" (sānusayā pahīyati) with the intention that the same defilement is called a 'fetter' (saṃyojana) in the sense of binding, and a 'latency' (anusaya) in the sense of not being abandoned.

In the words beginning with "tacaṃ chetvā" (cutting the bark), this is a comparison with a simile. The meditative attainments (samāpatti) should be understood as cutting the bark; insight (vipassanā) as cutting the softwood (pheggu); and the Path (magga) as cutting the heartwood (sāra). The practice (paṭipadā), however, is suitable as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. "Thus those people should be regarded" means that such individuals should be regarded in this way.

"Upadhiviveka" means by way of seclusion from the bases (detachment from the five cords of sensual pleasure). By this, seclusion from the five cords of sensual pleasure is taught. By the phrase "by abandoning unwholesome states," the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is taught. By the phrase "by the subsiding of bodily discomfort," the subsiding of bodily sluggishness (kāyaduṭṭhulla) is taught. "Secluded from sensual pleasures" means being without objective sensual pleasures (vatthukāma) through upadhiviveka. "Secluded from unwholesome states" means being without unwholesome states due to the abandoning of unwholesome states and the subsiding of bodily sluggishness. "The states occurring therein" refers to the group of states such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) that arise due to the attainment at the very moment of being within that meditative attainment. "Those states" refers to the states such as form taught by the method beginning with "rūpagataṃ."

"As impermanent" (aniccato) means not as permanent. "As suffering" (dukkhato) means not as pleasant. In the terms beginning with "as a disease" (rogato): it is seen as a disease because of the sense of oppression; as a boil (gaṇḍato) because of the sense of internal corruption; as a dart (sallato) because of the sense of piercing and causing pain; as a calamity (aghato) because of the sense of suffering; as an affliction (ābādhato) because of the sense of disease; as alien (parato) because of the sense of not being one's own; as disintegrating (palokato) because of the sense of breaking down; as empty (suññato) because of the sense of being devoid of a being; and as non-self (anattato) because of the sense of not being a self. Among these, the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) is taught by the two terms "as impermanent" and "as disintegrating." The characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) is taught by the six terms beginning with "as suffering." The characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) is taught by the three terms "as alien," "as empty," and "as non-self."

"That person, by those states" means that the practitioner contemplates by means of the five aggregates within the attainment, which are seen by applying the three characteristics. "Turns the mind away" (cittaṃ paṭivāpeti) means he withdraws the mind, frees it, and removes desire and lust. "Directs it" (upasaṃharati) means he first directs the insight-mind to the deathless Nibbāna-element as "This Nibbāna is peaceful" by way of hearing, praising, learning, and designation. The Path-mind (magga-citta) directs it by taking Nibbāna as an object, bringing it in as "This Nibbāna is peaceful, this Nibbāna is sublime." It means the practitioner who knows through penetration directs the mind to that Nibbāna. "Ṭhitvā" (standing/established) means being established in insight that has the three characteristics as its object. "Reaches the destruction of the taints" means progressively...
103:
One directs the insight-mind towards the unconditioned and deathless element of Nibbāna, thinking 'This Nibbāna is peaceful,' by way of hearing the Dhamma, praising the qualities of Nibbāna, learning the scriptures, and the designation of the name 'Nibbāna.' The path-mind (magga-citta) does not say 'This Nibbāna is peaceful, this Nibbāna is sublime' solely by making Nibbāna its object; rather, it means that while penetrating Nibbāna in this manner, it directs the mind towards it. 'He stands therein' means standing in insight (vipassanā) which has the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) as its object. 'He reaches the destruction of the taints' means he reaches it by developing the four paths in succession. 'By that very lust for the Dhamma' refers to the desire and lust (chandarāga) for the states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Indeed, one who is able to completely exhaust desire and lust for serenity and insight attains the fruit of Arahantship; one who is unable becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmī).

In the phrase 'whatever state there is among the group of feelings,' materiality (rūpa) is not included here. Why? Because it has been transcended. Since this person has previously attained the fine-material jhānas (rūpāvacara-jhāna), transcended materiality, and entered the immaterial attainments (arūpāvacara-samāpatti), materiality is transcended by the power of serenity. Furthermore, since he has previously fully comprehended materiality and, having transcended it, is now comprehending immaterial states (nāma), materiality is also transcended by the power of insight. Because materiality is entirely absent in the immaterial realm, materiality is not included here with reference to that immaterial realm.

'But then, what?' (atha kiñcarahi) is a question asking how to inquire. For one who proceeds by the power of serenity, one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) is the precursor, and that person is called 'one delivered by mind' (cetovimutta). For one who proceeds by the power of insight, wisdom (paññā) is the precursor, and that person is called 'one delivered by wisdom' (paññāvimutta). Regarding these two types of persons, the Venerable Ānanda had no doubt. This is simply the nature of things. However, he asks: among those who proceed by the power of serenity, why is one called 'delivered by mind' and another 'delivered by wisdom'? And among those who proceed by the power of insight, why is one called 'delivered by wisdom' and another 'delivered by mind'?

'I speak of the diversity of faculties' (indriyavemattataṃ vadāmi) means I speak of the difference in faculties. This is what is meant: 'Ānanda, because you have not yet penetrated the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) by fulfilling the ten perfections, this point is not clear to you. But for Me, because I have penetrated it, this point is clear. Here, the diversity of faculties is the cause.' Indeed, among the monks who proceed by the power of serenity, for some, one-pointedness of mind is the precursor, and that monk is called 'one delivered by mind.' For some, wisdom is the precursor, and that monk is called 'one delivered by wisdom.' Among the monks who proceed by the power of insight, for some, wisdom is the precursor, and that monk...
104:
... is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta). For some monks, one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā or concentration) is the predominant factor; that monk is called one liberated by mind (cetovimutta). The two chief disciples reached the fruit of Arahantship through the power of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Among them, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) became one liberated by wisdom, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna became one liberated by mind. Thus, it should be understood that the difference in the faculties (indriya) is the reason here. The remaining words are clear in meaning in every respect.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya
## The Explanation of the Mahāmālukya Sutta is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Bhaddāli Sutta
"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Bhaddāli Sutta. In that sutta, "eating in one sitting" (ekāsanabhojana) means the food or meal eaten at a single sitting during the morning. The terms beginning with "freedom from illness" (appābādhatā) have been explained in detail in the Kakacūpama Sutta. "I am not able" (na ussahāmi) means "I cannot."

"There might be remorse, there might be regret" (siyā kukkuccaṃ siyā vippaṭisāro) means that if one has to eat only once, there might be worry or anxiety, thinking, "Will I be able to lead the holy life for as long as I live, or will I not?"

"Having eaten a portion" (ekadesaṃ bhuñjitvā): It is said that the ancient Elders, after putting almsfood in their bowls and being offered ghee, would eat a little of the hot food with the ghee, wash their hands, take the remaining food outside, and eat it while sitting in a comfortable place with shade and water. Referring to this practice, the Blessed One said, "having eaten a portion."

But Bhaddāli thought: "If I were to eat the food offered to fill the bowl once, then wash the bowl, receive it full of rice again, take it outside, and eat it in a place with shade and water, that would be suitable; otherwise, who could manage?" Therefore, he said, "Venerable Sir, even so, I am not able."

This Elder Bhaddāli, it is said, was born in the lineage of crows in a past life immediately preceding this one. Crows are known to be very hungry. Therefore, he was known as "Elder Chātaka" (the Hungry Elder). While that Elder was complaining, the Blessed One, subduing and overwhelming him, laid down the training rule: "Should any bhikkhu eat or consume food, whether soft or hard, at the wrong time (vikāla), it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)." Therefore, it is said, "Then the Venerable Bhaddāli... expressed his inability."
105:
"Yathā taṃ" means that just as any other monk who does not habitually fulfill the training would not come into the presence of the Blessed One even while living in the same monastery, so too he did not come (did not show his face). He did not go to the place where he could serve the Blessed One, nor to the place where the Dhamma was preached, nor to the pavilion of reflection, nor did he walk on the same alms route as the Blessed One. He did not even stand at the doorway of the house where the Blessed One was sitting. If the Blessed One were to come to the place where the Elder Bhaddāli resided, the Elder would know in advance and go elsewhere. It is said that this son of good family had gone forth out of faith and possessed pure virtue. Therefore, no other thought occurred to him except this: "For the sake of my stomach, I have obstructed the Blessed One's laying down of a training rule; I have done what is unbefitting." Because of this shame, even though he lived in the same monastery, he did not dare to come into the presence of the Teacher.

"Cīvarakammaṃ karonti" means that people offered robe-cloth to the Blessed One, and taking that cloth, they were making robes. "Etaṃ dosakaṃ" means to reflect well on this blameworthy fault, this offense, the reason for obstructing the Teacher as he was laying down a training rule. "Dukkharataraṃ" (more difficult) is said because monks who have lived through the three months of the rainy season and are departing for other regions are asked, "Where did you spend the Vassa?" When they reply, "We stayed at Jetavana," people will ask, "Friends, what Jātaka did the Blessed One preach during this Vassa? What Sutta did he teach? What training rule did he lay down?"

Then they will say, "He laid down the training rule on eating at the wrong time, and an Elder named Bhaddāli obstructed it." Upon hearing this, the monks will say, "It is improper and groundless to obstruct the Blessed One as he lays down a training rule." Thinking that in this way, this fault of yours will become public among the multitude and become difficult to remedy, they spoke thus. Furthermore, other monks will come to the Teacher after performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony. Then you will have to assemble the Saṅgha, saying, "Friends, come and be my companions as I ask the Teacher for forgiveness." At that assembly, the visiting monks will ask, "Friends, what has this monk done?" Then, hearing of this matter, they will say, "This monk has done a grievous thing; he would obstruct the Ten-Powered One! This is improper." Thinking that for this reason too, this fault of yours will become public among the multitude and become difficult to remedy, they spoke thus. Otherwise, the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour after the Pavāraṇā. Then you will have to assemble the Saṅgha wherever he goes in order to ask the Blessed One for forgiveness. In that place...
106:
Monks living in various directions will ask, "Friends, what has this monk done?" and so on... Thinking that it would become difficult to remedy, they spoke thus.

"Etadavoca" (He said this): Thinking, "I have done what is unbefitting, yet the Blessed One, without clinging to even great faults, will accept my confession," he spoke these words beginning with "Accayo maṃ, bhante" (Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me). In that passage, "accayo" means an offense. "Maṃ accagamā" means it occurred by surpassing and overwhelming me. "Paṭiggaṇhātu" means "may he forgive." "Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya" means for the sake of restraint in the future, so as not to commit such an offense, fault, or lapse again. "Taggha" means "certainly." "Samayopi kho te Bhaddāli" means "Bhaddāli, there is a reason that you ought to have penetrated, but you did not penetrate or notice it."

In the passages beginning with "ubatobhāgavimutta," the two persons—the follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī) and the follower by faith (saddhānusārī)—are those who possess the Path in a single mind-moment. However, just as it would be improper for the Blessed One to command these seven types of Noble Persons in such a way, it would also be improper for them to act in such a way even if commanded by the Blessed One. Nevertheless, this was said by way of an impossible hypothesis to show the easy-to-admonish nature of Noble Persons and the difficult-to-admonish nature of the Elder Bhaddāli.

Why did he begin the teaching with "Api nu tvaṃ tasmiṃ samaye ubatobhāgavimutto"? It was to rebuke the Elder Bhaddāli. The meaning here is: "Bhaddāli, these seven Noble Persons are worthy of offerings in the world and are masters in my Dispensation; if there were a valid reason to obstruct a training rule while I was laying it down, it would be proper for them to obstruct it. But you are one who stands outside my Dispensation; it is not proper for you to obstruct the training rule while I am laying it down."

"Ritto tuccho" means empty and hollow due to the absence of noble qualities within; it means not accepting even a little of the Master's word. "Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi" means he acts according to the nature of the Dhamma; it means he asks for forgiveness. "Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma" means "we forgive that offense of yours." "Vuḍḍhi hesā Bhaddāli ariyassa vinaye" means "Bhaddāli, in the Dispensation of the Blessed One who is a Noble One, this is called growth." In what way? Seeing a fault as a fault, making amends according to the Dhamma, and achieving restraint in the future. Wishing to give the teaching in terms of persons (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna), he said, "Whoever sees a fault as a fault, makes amends according to the Dhamma, and achieves restraint in the future."
107:
The phrase "The Teacher also censures" means: Having heard that "A monk named so-and-so, a co-resident of such-and-such a teacher, a pupil of such-and-such a mentor, living in such-and-such a monastery, has entered the forest to realize the supramundane Dhamma," the Buddha censures him thus: "What is the use of forest-dwelling for that monk who does not fulfill the training in my Dispensation?" The same method applies to the remaining terms. Indeed, in this context, the deities not only censure him but also make him flee by showing terrifying objects.

"Self also [censures] self" means: To a monk of bad conduct who reflects on his own virtue, the point of defilement becomes clear, and his mind wanders; it does not stick to the meditation subject. That monk, feeling remorse, thinking, "What is the use of forest-dwelling for a monk of bad conduct like me?" gets up and leaves. "Attāpi attānaṃ upavadito" means he is accused by himself, or this is simply the reading. The "bright side" (the side of purity) should be understood by the opposite method already mentioned. The words "He, secluded from sensual pleasures..." etc., are spoken to show that he realizes it in this way.

"They punish by oppressing and oppressing" means they punish repeatedly, rebuking even for a slight fault. "Not like that" means they do not punish by oppressing even for a great offense, as they do to the other. It is said that the Elder Bhaddāli expected favor from the Saṅgha of monks, [thinking they might say,] "Friend Bhaddāli, do not worry, such a thing happens; come, ask the Teacher for forgiveness," or from the Teacher, who might send for him through a monk and say, "Bhaddāli, do not worry, such a thing happens." Then, thinking, "I have not been consoled by the Saṅgha of monks, nor by the Teacher," he spoke thus.

Then the Blessed One, to show that both the Saṅgha of monks and the Teacher exhort only the person who is worthy of being exhorted and not the other, said, "Here, Bhaddāli, a certain person..." etc. Therein, the words "aññenaññaṃ" (prevarication) etc., are explained in detail in the Anumāna Sutta. "Does not behave properly" means he does not practice the proper duties. "Does not lower his hair" means he does not practice the duties of conformity but takes the opposite way. "Does not practice the way out" means he does not practice the duties that lead to emergence from an offense; he has no urgent desire to emerge from the offense. "In that matter" means in that matter of being difficult to speak to. "Frequent offender" means one who constantly falls into offenses. "Full of offenses" means the time he has offenses is much, and the time he is pure and without offenses is little. "Not quickly settled" means it is not settled quickly; the legal issue becomes long-drawn-out.
108:
The Vinaya experts, at the time of washing their feet, say to the monk (who has an offense) who has come, "Go, friend, it is the time for duties." When he comes again, having noted the time, they say, "Go, friend, it is the time for you to sweep the monastery; go, friend, it is the time for giving lessons to novices and others, the time for us to bathe, the time to attend to the elders, the time to wash our faces," and so on; they just send away that monk who comes during the day or night. Even when asked, "Venerable sir, at what time will there be an opportunity?" they say, "Friend, you only know this place; the Vinaya-expert elder named so-and-so is drinking medicinal oil, so-and-so is taking a purgative; why are you in such a hurry?" and so on, making the legal issue long-drawn-out.

"Settled very quickly" means it is settled quickly and is not long-drawn-out. The energetic monks, [thinking,] "Friends, this monk is easy to admonish; for those living in the countryside, the places for staying, standing, and sitting in a village-boundary monastery are not comfortable, and going for alms is also difficult; let us quickly settle this monk's legal issue," gather together, make him emerge from the offense, and establish him in a state of purity.

"Adhiccāpattiko" means one who falls into an offense occasionally. Even if that monk is a conscientious monk of natural character, if he is difficult to admonish, the Vinaya-expert monks treat him in the same way (making it long-drawn-out).

"Carried by mere faith, carried by mere love" means he subsists on a small amount of house-based faith and a small amount of house-based love for the teachers and preceptors. Indeed, this going forth is like taking rebirth; a newly ordained monk, not yet knowing the virtues of the monkhood, subsists merely on love for the teachers and preceptors; therefore, such newly ordained monks should be supported. For, having received even a small amount of support and remaining in the monkhood, they will become Great Recluses who have attained direct knowledge. By this much sequence of words, the Blessed One showed this meaning: "They exhort only the one worthy of being exhorted, not the other."

"Established through knowledge" means they were established in Arahantship. "When beings decline" means when practice (paṭipatti) declines, beings are said to decline. "When the True Dhamma disappears" means the disappearance of the True Dhamma of practice. For the True Dhamma of practice disappears when there are no beings who fulfill the practice.
109:
The term 'āsavaṭṭhāniya' (taint-producing) means that the taints (perils) reside in these things. In the transgression of those training rules, there truly reside the taints (perils) such as reproach by others, remorse, killing, and imprisonment, which occur in this present life and in future lives, as well as those that are the specific causes of the suffering of the lower realms. The meaning is that the transgression of those training rules is the cause of such perils as the accusations of others. As long as those taint-producing states, which are of the nature of transgression, have not become manifest in the Saṅgha, the Teacher does not yet prescribe training rules for his disciples; this is the connection of the meaning in this passage.

Having thus shown the time when it is not yet appropriate to prescribe training rules, the Teacher spoke the words beginning with "Yato ca kho, Bhaddāli" (But when, Bhaddāli...) to show the time when it is appropriate. In that passage, "yato" means 'at which time' or 'when'. The remaining words should be understood according to the method already mentioned. Alternatively, the summary of the meaning here is: at the time when the faults of transgression, known as taint-producing states, become manifest in the Saṅgha, then the Teacher prescribes training rules for his disciples. Why does he prescribe them? He prescribes them solely to counteract those faults of transgression known as taint-producing states.

Having thus stated that the non-arising of the faults of transgression, which are the causes of perils, is the time when it is not yet appropriate to prescribe training rules, and their arising is the time when it is appropriate, the Teacher now spoke the words beginning with "Na tāva, Bhaddāli, idhekacce" (Not yet, Bhaddāli, do some here...) to show the time of the non-arising and the time of the arising of those states. In that passage, "mahattaṃ" (greatness) refers to the state of being large in number. This is because as long as the Saṅgha has not reached greatness in terms of elders, newly ordained, and those of middle standing, the lodgings and bedding are sufficient for living, and some taint-producing states of transgression do not yet arise in the Dispensation. However, when the Saṅgha reaches greatness, those states do arise; then the Teacher prescribes training rules. The training rules prescribed when the Saṅgha reaches greatness are to be understood in this manner:

"If a monk should lie down together with one who is not ordained for more than two or three nights, it is an offense entailing expiation (Pācittiya). If a bhikkhunī should give ordination (to a candidate) every year, it is an offense entailing expiation. If a bhikkhunī should give ordination to two (candidates) in one year, it is an offense entailing expiation."

"Lābhaggaṃ" (peak of gains) refers to the excellence of gains. This is because as long as the Saṅgha has not reached the peak of gains, taint-producing states of transgression do not yet arise based on gains. However, when the Saṅgha reaches the peak of gains, those states do arise; then the Teacher prescribes training rules—
110:
"If a monk should give with his own hand food or edibles to a naked ascetic, a wanderer, or a female wanderer, it is an offense entailing expiation (Pācittiya)." This training rule was prescribed when the Saṅgha reached the peak of gains.

"Yasaggaṃ" refers to the peak of fame and retinue. As long as the Saṅgha has not reached the peak of fame and retinue, taint-producing states of transgression do not yet arise based on fame. However, when the Saṅgha reaches such greatness, they do arise; then the Teacher prescribes the training rule: "In the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors, there is an offense entailing expiation." This training rule was prescribed when the Saṅgha reached the peak of fame and retinue.

"Bāhusaccaṃ" refers to the state of having great learning. As long as the Saṅgha has not reached the state of great learning, taint-producing states of transgression do not yet arise. However, when the state of great learning is reached, because individuals who have learned one Nikāya, two Nikāyas, or even all five Nikāyas emerge improperly, they mix the essence with other essences and represent the Teacher's Dispensation by presenting what is not Dhamma as Dhamma and what is not Vinaya as Vinaya. Then the Teacher prescribes training rules in the manner beginning with: "If a monk should speak thus: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One...' ... If a novice should also speak thus..."

In the phrase "rattaññutaṃ patto" (reached seniority), they are called "rattaññū" (those who know the nights) because they know many nights. It means those who have been ordained for a long time, knowing many nights from the day of their own ordination. The state of being a rattaññū is called "rattaññuta". In that context, it should be understood that when the Saṅgha reached seniority, the training rule was prescribed concerning the Venerable Upasena, the son of Vanganta. That venerable one, seeing monks with less than ten years of seniority acting as preceptors and giving higher ordination, himself gave higher ordination to a co-resident when he had only one year of seniority. Then the Blessed One prescribed the training rule: "Monks, one with less than ten years of seniority should not give higher ordination. Whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (Dukkaṭa)." After the training rule was thus prescribed, monks who were foolish and incompetent gave higher ordination, saying, "I have ten years, I have ten years." Then the Blessed One prescribed another training rule: "Monks, a foolish and incompetent monk should not give higher ordination. Whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, a competent and capable monk with ten years of seniority or more than ten years of seniority to give higher ordination." Thus, two training rules were prescribed when the state of seniority was reached.
111:
"He preached the Dhamma discourse similar to a young thoroughbred horse" means he preached the Dhamma by using a young thoroughbred horse as a simile. "Tatra" means in that state of being without refuge. "Bhaddāli, this is not the only reason" means that not fulfilling the training rules is not the sole reason.

"Training in the mouth" means training the horse to hold its neck well by placing bits and reins in its mouth. With the words "visūkāyitāni" and so on, he spoke of unrefined behavior. In truth, all these words are synonyms of one another. "In that place" (tasmiṃ ṭhāne) means in that unrefined behavior. "He is completely extinguished" (parinibbāyati) means he becomes refined; it means he abandons that unrefined behavior. "Placing in the yoke" (yugādhāne) means for the purpose of holding the yoke well.

"In the sequence" (anukkame) means in the lifting and setting down of all four feet at the same time. Indeed, enemy soldiers stay in pits, hold swords, and cut the legs of the approaching horse. At that time, they teach this skill using a rope-binding method so that this horse can lift all four feet at once. "In a circle" (maṇḍale) means training in a circular area so that the rider can pick up a weapon that has fallen to the ground while still seated on the horse. "In treading with hooves" (khurakāse) means in treading the ground with the tips of the hooves. Indeed, it is intended to mean teaching the horse to walk only with the tips of its hooves by giving a signal at a certain place so that the sound of footsteps is not heard during night patrols. "In speed" (jave) means in moving swiftly. There is also a variant reading "dhāve". This skill is taught for the purpose of fleeing when one is defeated and for chasing and capturing a fleeing enemy. "In playfulness" (davatte) means for the purpose of frolicking. During battle, when elephants trumpet like cranes, horses neigh, chariots rumble, or soldiers shout, this skill is taught so that the horse can enter the enemy lines without being afraid of those sounds.

"In the royal qualities" (rājaguṇe) means in the qualities that should be known by kings. It is said that King Kūṭakaṇṇa had a horse named Guḷavaṇṇa. The King went out through the eastern gate to Cetiya Mountain...
112:
...thinking, "I will go," and arrived at the bank of the Kalamba River. The horse named Guḷavaṇṇa stood on the bank and did not wish to enter the water. The King called the horse trainer and said, "Hey, the horse you trained does not wish to enter the water!" The teacher said, "Great King, the horse is well-trained. In this horse's mind, there is the thought: 'If I enter the water, my tail will get wet; if the tail is wet, water will splash on the King's body.' Thus, it does not enter out of fear of splashing water on your body. Please have someone hold the tail." The King had it done so. The horse entered swiftly and reached the other side. This training is done for that purpose. "In the royal lineage" (rājavaṃse) means in the lineage of the king of horses. This is the lineage of the king of horses; even if their bodies are broken and pierced by such blows, they do not let the rider fall into the midst of the enemy's army but carry them out. It means that the training is given for that purpose.

"In the highest speed" (uttame jave) means in the perfection of speed. It means the training is given so that there may be the highest speed. "In the noble horse" (uttame haye) means in the state of being a noble horse. It means the training is given so that it may be a noble horse. In that situation, only a naturally noble horse is worthy of the training of a noble horse, not any other. And only through the training of a noble horse does a horse attain the highest speed, not any other.

Regarding this matter, there is this story: It is said that a certain king, having obtained a Sindhava colt but not knowing it was a Sindhava horse, gave it to a teacher saying, "Train this horse." The teacher, also not knowing it was a Sindhava horse, put it through the training of common bean-eating horses. That horse did not practice that training because it was not suitable for him. The teacher, unable to tame it, had it released, saying, "Great King, this is a deceitful horse."

Then one day, a young man who was formerly a horse trainer, while carrying his preceptor's belongings, saw that horse grazing at the edge of the moat and said to his preceptor, "Venerable sir, this is a priceless Sindhava colt!" He said, "If the King knew, he would make this his state horse." The Elder said, "Dear boy, the King is one of wrong view; perhaps he might gain faith in the Buddha's Dispensation. Tell the King." He went and said, "Great King, there is a priceless Sindhava colt." You...
113:
"Did you see it, dear ones?" (he asked). "Yes, Great King, we saw it," (they replied). "What is it fit for you to receive?" (he asked). "The rice from your golden bowl that you eat, the liquid that you drink, your perfumes, and your flowers (are fit for me to receive)," (he replied). The King had everything given. The young monk had them taken and departed.

As soon as the horse smelled the scent, it thought, "I think there is a horse trainer who knows my qualities," and stood looking up with its head raised. The young monk went there, snapped his fingers, and said, "Eat the rice." The horse came and ate the rice from the golden bowl and drank the liquid. Then, after anointing the horse with perfumes and decorating it with the King's ornaments, he snapped his fingers and said, "Go ahead of me, go ahead." The horse went ahead of the young monk and stood in the place of the auspicious horse. The young monk said, "Great King, this is your priceless Sindhava colt. Have it looked after in this very manner for a few days," and then he departed.

Then, after a few days had passed, he came and said, "Great King, you shall see the horse's power." "Very well, teacher, where should we stand to watch?" (the King asked). "Great King, go to the garden," he said. The King had the horse brought and went there. The young monk snapped his fingers and gave a signal to the horse, "Go around this tree." The horse galloped, went around the tree, and returned. The King saw neither its going nor its coming. "Did you see it, Great King?" (he asked). "Dear ones, I did not see it," (he replied). "Place the golden staff you use against this tree," he said, and snapping his fingers, (gave the signal), "Go and bite the golden staff and bring it back." The horse galloped, bit it with its mouth, and returned. "Did you see it, Great King?" (he asked). "Dear ones, I have seen it," (he replied).

Again, he snapped his fingers (and signaled), "Go around the top of the garden wall and come back." The horse did so. "Did you see it, Great King?" (he asked). "Dear ones, I did not see it," (he replied). He had a red woolen blanket brought and tied to the horse's feet, then gave the signal in the same way. The horse leaped up and went around the top of the wall. It appeared on top of the garden wall like the tip of a torch waved by a strong man. The horse went and stood nearby. "Did you see it, Great King?" (he asked). "Dear ones, I have seen it," (he replied). He gave the signal, "Go around the top of the wall of the auspicious pond."

Again, he gave the signal, "Descend into the pond and walk upon the lotus leaves." It descended into the pond and walked upon all the lotus leaves. One...",
114:
...not even a single lotus leaf was stepped on (crushed), split, cut, or broken. "Did the Great King see it?" he asked. "Dear ones, I saw it," he replied. Snapping his fingers, he held out his palm. The horse, being firm in its physical nature, leaped and stood upon the palm. "Did the Great King see it?" he asked. "Dear ones, I have seen it," he replied. In this way, a noble horse, through noble causes, attains noble speed.

"Uttame sākhalye" means with gentle speech. Indeed, through gentle speech, such as "Dear one, do not worry, you will become the King's auspicious horse, you will receive the King's food and so on," the cause for a noble horse should be made. Therefore, it is said "Uttame sākhalye." "Rājabhoggo" means the King's possession. "It is recognized only as an organ (limb) of the King" means that when going anywhere, it must be gone with without being abandoned, like a hand or a foot. Therefore, it is recognized as an organ, or it is one of the four limbs of the army.

"Asekha-sammādiṭṭhi" refers to the Right View associated with the fruition of Arahantship. Right Intention and the others are also those associated with that fruition of Arahantship. Right Knowledge is the same Right View mentioned previously. Excluding the eight factors of fruition, the remaining states should be known as Liberation (Vimutti). The remaining words are clear in all places. This teaching, however, was concluded by placing the fruition of Arahantship at the summit for the sake of a person of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū).

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Bhaddāli Sutta is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Laṭukikopama Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Laṭukikopama Sutta.
