In that sutta, "yena so vanasaṇḍo" is because this Elder Mahā Udāyī also entered for alms with the Blessed One and returned together. Therefore, it should be understood that he approached that forest grove where the Blessed One had gone. "Apahattā" means one who abandons. "Upahattā" means one who brings. "Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" means arising from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
115: "Yaṃ bhagavā" means "at the time when the Blessed One [was present]." "Ingha" is an indeclinable particle used in the sense of a command. "Aññathattaṃ" refers to a change of mind (a state other than joy). It should be understood that this change of mind was not because of the Blessed One, but rather arose because of the fine food, thinking, "If we do not get such fine food, how shall we survive?" "Bhūtapubbaṃ" (In the past) indicates the excellence of the evening meal. "Sūpeyya" refers to things to be served with soup, such as fish, meat, bamboo shoots, and so on. "Samaggā bhuñjissāma" means "we shall eat together." "Saṅkhatiyo" refers to prepared delicacies. All those prepared delicacies are abundant only at night, while during the day they are few and limited. Indeed, although people survive on gruel, sour rice water, and so on during the day, at night they eat as much fine food as they can. Again, with the word "Bhūtapubbaṃ," the danger of eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana) at night is shown. In that context, "andhakāratimisāyaṃ" means in thick darkness. "Māṇavehi" means by thieves. "Katakammehi" means by thieves who have already committed a crime. It is said that thieves, having prayed to a certain deity for the success of their crime, kill people and take their throat-blood and so on to make an offering to that deity when the crime is completed. While those thieves are killing other people, they think, "There will be an uproar, and there is no one who would search for a monk," and so they seize and kill the monk. This was said in reference to such killing. "Akatakammehi" refers to thieves who, when coming from the forest to the village, wish to make an offering beforehand so that their crime may be successful. "Asaddhammena nimanteti" (invites with unrighteousness) means inviting with sexual misconduct, saying, "Come, monk, eat and stay here in this house for the whole night, enjoy this pleasure, and go tomorrow." Again, with the word "Bhūtapubbaṃ," he relates an incident he saw himself. "Vijjantarikāya" means in the moment of a lightning flash. "Vissaramakāsi" means he made a loud sound. In the word "abhumme," "bhu" means prosperity, and "abhu" means lack of prosperity or destruction. The meaning is "Destruction has come to me." "Pisāco vata maṃ" means "A demon has indeed come to eat me!" In the phrase "ātumārī mātumarī," "ātu" means father and "mātu" means mother. The meaning is this: If someone has a mother and father, those parents, saying "our little son," seek food in some way or another, give him delicacies and food, and make him sleep in one place. Such a person does not wander for alms at night. "I think your parents are dead, and that is why you wander for alms at such a time."
116: Just so, those [worthless men], not seeing any benefit, [say this] without any reason. The Blessed One said, "Thus they said," intending to criticize. In that context, "āhaṃsu" means "they say." They say, "What is there to be said because of this slight fault? Should one not act as if not seeing and not hearing?" "Oramattakassa" means of a very slight fault. "This monk scrapes excessively (or exerts excessively), like one squeezing butter or like one cutting lotus fibers with a saw." "Sikkhākāmā" refers to those who love the training, such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna; they [the worthless men] cause a lack of confidence toward them. Those worthless men have this thought: "If these [elders] were to say, 'This is a minor matter, Blessed One, please remove it,' would the Teacher not remove it? But instead of saying this, they sit surrounding the Blessed One and say, 'It is well, Blessed One; please prescribe it, Blessed One,' and thus they gain even greater zeal." Therefore, they cause a lack of confidence toward those who love the training. "Tesaṃ" refers to those certain worthless men. "Taṃ" refers to that minor fault that is to be abandoned. "Thūlo kaliṅgaro" means it is like a large block of wood tied to the neck. "Laṭukikā sakuṇikā" is a small female quail. It is said that she chirps a hundred times and dances a hundred times before taking food once. Seeing that bird descended from the sky to the ground, cowherds and others tie her with a rotten creeper for the sake of playing. This was said in reference to such binding. "Āgameti" means it approaches or arrives. "Tañhi tassā" means that binding with a rotten creeper is called a strong bond for her because of her small body and her lack of strength. Like a large coconut rope, it is difficult to break. "Tesaṃ" means that for those worthless men, because of their weak faith and weak wisdom, it is called a strong bond. Even a mere minor offense (dukkhaṭa) is difficult to abandon, like a major offense (pārājika). In the bright side (sukkapakkhē), "pahātabbassa" means: The Blessed One has told us to abandon a certain fault; is there anything for the Blessed One to say regarding that minor fault to be abandoned? [Yes, there is]. The meaning is that even after knowing the Blessed One's intention, it is something that must be abandoned. "Appossukkā" means they are without anxiety. "Pannalomā" means they have their hair lying flat. Such a person does not have hair standing on end due to the fear of having something to abandon. "Paradattavuttā" means they have their livelihood provided by others; the meaning is that they survive on what is received from others. "Migabhūtena cetasā viharanti" (They live with a mind like a deer) means...
117:
They dwell established in the state of not longing for the four requisites. When a deer is struck, it does not go to a human settlement with the intention of obtaining medicine or oil for its wound. Instead, immediately after being struck, it enters a forest where there are no villages, lies down with the struck side underneath, and only gets up and leaves when it is at ease. Thus, deer are established in the state of not longing. With reference to this, it is said: "They dwell with a mind like that of a deer."

"Taṃ hi tassa" means that the binding with that rope is called a weak bond for that great elephant because of its large body and great strength. It is easily broken like a rotten creeper. "Tesaṃ taṃ" means that for those sons of good family, because of the greatness of their faith and wisdom, even a major Pārājika matter is as easy to abandon as a mere Dukkaṭa matter.

"Daliddo" means a person endowed with poverty. "Assako" means a person without possessions. "Anāḷhiyo" means a person who is not wealthy. "Agārakaṃ" means a small house. "Olugga-vilugga" refers to a house whose rafters have become detached from the ridgepole and are hanging on the ring-beam, or have become detached from the ring-beam and are resting on the ground. "Kākātidāyī" refers to a poor man's house where, when sitting inside to eat something, there is no separate task of closing the door, and thus crows enter from here and there and surround him. Even when the bold crows flee, they exit and flee from whichever direction they are facing. "Naparama-rūpaṃ" means not having an excellent appearance like the houses of the meritorious. "Khaṭopika" means a small bed woven with bamboo strips. "Olugga-vilugga" means being uneven, sagging in some parts and raised in others. "Dhanyasamavāpakaṃ" means a mixture of grain and seeds. Among those two, "dhanya" refers to kudrūsa grain. "Samavāpakaṃ" refers to a collection of seeds such as gourd seeds and pumpkin seeds. "Naparama-rūpaṃ" means not being a pure type of seed like the fragrant sālī rice seeds of the meritorious. "Jāyikā" means a poor wife. "Naparama-rūpā" means having a repulsive appearance like an ogress, with a head the size of a basket, sagging breasts, and a large belly. "Sāmaññaṃ" means the state of a monk. "So vatassa, yohaṃ" means "Indeed, I should be that excellent man who, having shaved off hair and beard, would go forth."

"So na sakkuṇeyya" means that even though that poor man thinks thus, he returns home and reflects: "The state of a monk is one that respects gains, is difficult to practice, and difficult to attain. One might have to wander through seven or eight villages for alms and return with a bowl just as it was washed. For me, who is unable to subsist in this way, is there still a place to live? At that time, it is very difficult to collect building materials like grass, wood, rope, and creepers. What shall I do?" Then, that small house appears in his mind like the Vejayanta Palace.
118:
"For me, the poor man, who has returned, a place to live is needed. Building materials like grass, creepers, wood, and bamboo are very difficult to gather. What shall I do?" Thus he investigates and reflects. Then that small house appears to him like the Vejayanta Palace. Then, looking at the small bed placed there, he thinks: "When I am gone, they will break this bed and use it as firewood for the stove. When I return, it will be difficult to get the frame, legs, and bamboo strips. What shall I do?" Then that bed appears to him like a magnificent couch. Then, looking at the pot of grain, he thinks: "When I am gone, this housewife will eat this grain with various people. When I return, I must have a means of livelihood. What shall I do?" Then that pot of grain appears to him like twelve hundred and fifty great granaries. Then, looking at his wife, he thinks: "When I am gone, an elephant trainer, a horse trainer, or someone else will entice this woman. When I return, I must have someone to cook rice. What shall I do?" Then that woman appears to him like a beautiful celestial maiden. With reference to this inability, it is said: "He is unable," and so forth. "Nikkhagaṇānaṃ" refers to hundreds of pure gold nikkhas. "Cayo" means an accumulation made in order. "Dhanyagaṇānaṃ" refers to hundreds of carts of grain.

"Udāyi, there are these four persons"—what is shown here? Below, it was shown by way of groups: "They abandon those defilements, they do not abandon those defilements," showing those who abandon and those who do not, but they were not distinguished individually. Now, just as a man who goes for building materials cuts down trees in order, then turns back, discards the crooked ones, and takes only those suitable for the work, even so, this discourse is begun to show that there are four types of persons who abandon, after setting aside and making insignificant those who do not abandon.

"Upadhipahānāya" means for the abandoning of these upadhis: khandhupadhi (aggregates), kilesupadhi (defilements), abhisaṅkhārupadhi (volitional formations), and kāmaguṇūpadhi (sensual pleasures). "Upadhipaṭisaṃyuttā" refers to those whose thoughts repeatedly run towards the four upadhis. In the term "sarasaṅkappā," they are called "sarā" because they run, and "saṅkappā" because they plan. Both terms refer to thoughts (vitakka). "Samudācaranti" means they occur by way of overwhelming. "Saṃyutto" means association with defilements. "Indriyavemattatā" means the difference in the faculties.
119:
It is the state of diversity of the faculties (*indriya-nānattatā*). 'Kadāci karahaci' means after a long period of time has elapsed. 'Satisammosā' means due to a lapse of mindfulness. 'Nipāto' refers to the falling (of a drop of water) onto a hot iron pan. By this much, the three groups—'does not abandon, abandons, quickly abandons'—are shown. Among those groups, four types of persons are called those who do not abandon, four are called those who abandon, and four are called those who quickly abandon.

In that regard, these four types of persons—the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmī*)—are called those who do not abandon. Let alone the worldling and others who cannot yet abandon, why can the non-returner not abandon? The reason is that as long as that non-returner has greed for existence (*bhava-lobha*), he greatly delights in it, thinking, 'Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!' Therefore, he is called one who does not abandon. However, these same four types of persons are also called those who abandon. Let alone the stream-enterer and others who can abandon, why can the worldling abandon? It is because a worldling who has undertaken insight practice (*āraddha-vipassaka*), when defilements suddenly arise due to a lapse of mindfulness, feels spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, 'Defilements have arisen in a monk like me,' and by exerting effort and developing insight, he completely eradicates the defilements with the Path. Thus, that worldling is called one who abandons. These same four types of persons are also called those who quickly abandon. In this regard, it should be understood that although the third case ('quickly abandons') is taken in this sutta, as well as in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta* and the *Indriyabhāvanā Sutta*, the problem is explained only by way of the second case ('abandons').

In the phrase 'Upadhi is the root of suffering,' the five aggregates are called *upadhi*. Knowing that this *upadhi* is the root of suffering, one becomes free from *upadhi* (*nirupadhi*) due to the absence of the *upadhi* of defilements. It means one who is without craving and without grasping. 'Liberated in the destruction of upadhi' means one who is liberated from defilements by taking Nibbāna—the destruction of craving—as the object.

Having thus expanded on the four types of persons, he now spoke the words beginning with 'Udāyi, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure' in order to show that those who abandon 'abandon these many defilements of such a name,' and those who do not abandon 'do not abandon these many defilements of such a name.' In that context, 'miḷhasukha' (filthy pleasure) means impure pleasure. 'Anariyasukha' (ignoble pleasure) means the pleasure enjoyed by ignoble worldlings. 'Should be feared' means it should be feared both because of the acquisition of this pleasure and because of its result (*vipāka*). 'Nekkhammasukha' means the pleasure of renunciation from sensual desires. 'Pavivekasukha' means the pleasure of being secluded both from the group and from defilements. 'Upasamasukha' means the pleasure for the sake of the stilling of lust and so forth. 'Sambodhasukha' refers to the enlightenment called the Path...
120:
...the bliss of jhāna for the sake of the arising of enlightenment called the Path (should not be feared). One should not fear because of the acquisition of this bliss of jhāna or because of its result; this bliss of jhāna should only be developed.

Regarding the phrase 'in the agitated' (*iñjitasmiṃ*), it means agitation, movement, or wavering. What is the agitation in that first jhāna? The unceased initial and sustained thoughts (*vitakka-vicāra*) are the agitation in that first jhāna. The same method applies to the second and third jhānas. Regarding the phrase 'in the unagitated' (*aniñjitasmiṃ*), I, the Buddha, declare this fourth jhāna to be without agitation, without movement, and still.

Regarding the phrase 'not enough' (*analaṃ*), it means that attachment (*ālaya*) through craving should not be formed; it shows that the dwelling of craving (*taṇhā-ālaya*) should not be allowed to arise in this jhāna. Alternatively, 'analaṃ' means incomplete (*apariyattaṃ*); it means one should not make the conclusion, 'This much is enough.' Even if it is a peaceful attainment like the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I, the Buddha, declare the abandoning of even that attainment. 'Small or large' (*aṇuṃ vā thūlaṃ vā*) refers to whether they (the fetters) are small or large, or of minor fault or major fault. The remaining words are clear in all respects. This discourse was concluded by placing the peak on Arahantship through the influence of a person to be led (*neyya-puggala*).

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Laṭukikopama Sutta is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Cātuma Sutta

'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the *Cātuma Sutta*. In that sutta, 'Cātumāyaṃ' means in the village of that name. 'Pañcamattāni bhikkhusatāni' refers to five hundred monks who had just recently ordained. The Elders (Sāriputta and Moggallāna) thought: 'These sons of good family have ordained without having seen the Tathāgata; if we take them to the Blessed One and they hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, they will be established in the Dispensation according to their respective supporting conditions (*upanissaya*).' Therefore, they came bringing those monks.

'Greeting joyfully' (*paṭisammodamānā*) means engaging in courteous conversation such as 'Are you well, friend?' and so forth. 'Preparing lodgings' (*senāsanāni paññāpayamānā*) means asking for the dwelling places of their own teachers and preceptors, opening doors and windows, taking out, dusting, and arranging beds, stools, and mats in appropriate places. 'Setting aside bowls and robes' (*pattacīvarāni paṭisāmayamānā*) means taking care of the monks' requisites, saying, 'Venerable sirs, please take care of my bowl, robe, small bowl, water bottle, and staff.' 'Loud noise, great noise' (*uccāsaddā mahāsaddā*) refers to making rising sounds, spreading sounds, and sounds where one person's voice cannot be distinguished from another's. 'Like fishermen scrambling for fish' (*kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilope*) means just as many people gather at a place where fishermen keep their fish baskets and shout, 'Give me the fish from this basket, cut that fish for me,' or shout, 'He was given a large fish while I was given a small one.' Referring to such loud and great noises, the Blessed One spoke these words. In a place where fish are caught by casting nets, the fishermen...
121:
“This is my bowl, this is my robe, this is my cup, this is my water-jug, this is my walking staff”—thus they were putting away the monastic requisites of the monks.

“Uccāsaddā mahāsaddā” (loud noise, great noise) refers to a sound that is high-pitched because it rises upwards, and great because it spreads out, making a noise where individual voices cannot be distinguished. “Like fishermen scrambling for fish” means that in the place where fishermen have set down their fish baskets, many people gather and make a loud, great noise, saying, “Give me another fish here, give me a slice of fish, you gave him a big one, you gave me a small one.” This statement was made with reference to such behavior. Also, in a place where a net has been cast to catch fish, fishermen and others make a great noise, saying, “It’s in, it’s not in; it’s caught, it’s not caught.” This statement was also made with reference to that.

“Paṇāmemi” means “I dismiss” or “I drive away.” “You should not stay in my presence” means “You come to the dwelling place of a Buddha like me and make such a noise; living according to your own nature, how could you ever act appropriately? There is no reason for people like you to stay in my presence.” Not even a single monk among them was able to say, “The Blessed One is dismissing us just because of a little noise,” or anything else; all of them, accepting the words of the Blessed One, said, “Very well, Bhante,” and departed.

This thought occurred to those monks: “We came to see the Teacher, to hear the Dhamma, and to live in the presence of the Teacher. However, having come to the presence of such a venerable Teacher, we made a great noise. This is our own fault. We have been dismissed. We no longer have the opportunity to live in the presence of the Blessed One, to behold his golden-hued body, or to hear the Dhamma preached with his sweet voice.” They departed, filled with strong dejection.

“Tenupasaṅkamiṃsu” means that those Sakyans saw those monks sitting in that very place when they arrived. Then it occurred to those Sakyans: “Why have these monks returned immediately after entering? Let us find out the reason.” Thinking thus, they approached where those monks were. The word “handa” is a particle used in the sense of resolution. “Venerable sirs, where are you going, having just arrived? Is there some trouble for you, or is there some trouble for the Blessed One, who is endowed with the ten powers (Dasabala)?”

Although those monks could have replied with words like, “Lay followers, we came to see the Blessed One, we have seen the Blessed One, and now we are going back to our own places,” they did not speak such untruths but spoke according to the truth, saying, “The Blessed One has dismissed the community of monks.” Those Sakyans were those who bore the burden of the Dispensation (Sāsana). Therefore, they thought, “When the two Chief Disciples and the five hundred monks arrive at the feet of the Blessed One, we will act so that these five hundred monks get the chance to stay again.” Having thought so, they spoke the words beginning with “tenupasaṅkamiṃsu.” Among those dismissed monks, thinking, “The Blessed One dismissed us five hundred monks just for making a noise; we are not those who became monks because of difficulty in livelihood,” one monk...
122:
The Sakyan princes, without acting improperly, spoke only the truth, saying: "Venerables, the Blessed One has dismissed the Saṅgha of monks." Since those princes were bearers of the burden in the Sāsana, they thought: "If five hundred monks go together with the two Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka), they will reach the feet of the Blessed One. We shall act in a way that these monks return." Having thought thus, they spoke the words beginning with "Tena hāyasmanto." Among those dismissed monks, not even a single monk was rebellious, thinking, "The Blessed One has dismissed us merely by making a sound; we are not those who became monks because we were unable to make a living." Instead, they all unanimously accepted, saying, "Very well, sirs."

"Abhinandatu" means may he greatly rejoice, desiring the arrival of the assembly of monks. "Abhivadatu" means may he speak while giving rise to the thought, "Let the assembly of monks come." "Anuggahito" means being accomplished through material support (āmisa-anuggaha) and Dhamma support (dhamma-anuggaha). "Aññathattaṃ" (alteration) refers to a change from devotion into another state due to not having the opportunity to see the Blessed One. "Vipariṇāmo" (transformation) refers to the deviation of monks who leave the order when their devotion is destroyed. "Bījānaṃ taruṇānaṃ" refers to young crops. "Siyā aññathattaṃ" refers to the state of withering due to not receiving water at the time it should be given. Transformation (vipariṇāma) would occur through drying up and withering. In the case of a young calf, drying up due to thirst for milk is called "aññathatta," and dying after drying up is called "vipariṇāma."

"Pasādito bhagavā" (The Blessed One is pleased): It is said that while the Elder was sitting there, he saw the arrival of Brahma with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), heard the sound of the entreaty with his divine ear (dibba-sota), and knew the Blessed One’s state of pleasure through the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa). Therefore, thinking, "It is not pleasant to go only when being called by sending a monk; let us go even before the Teacher sends for us," he spoke thus. "Appossukko" means being without effort in other matters. Thinking that the Blessed One wished to dwell by entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought, "Now, let the Blessed One dwell as he pleases." "Mayampi dāni" (We too now) expresses the meaning: "We, who were instructing others, have also been dismissed from the monastery. What is the use of instructing others? Now, we too shall dwell only in the bliss of the attainment of fruition." At this point, Venerable Sāriputta erred and did not recognize his own burden. In truth, this assembly of monks is the burden of both Great Elders. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to restrain Venerable Sāriputta, spoke the words beginning with "Āgamehi" (Wait). Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, however, recognized his burden, and thus the Blessed One gave him praise (sādhukāra).

Why did he begin the discourse "Cattārimāni bhikkhave" (Monks, there are these four)? It is because there are four perils in this Sāsana. He began this teaching to show that only a monk who is unafraid of these perils can remain in the Sāsana, while one who is afraid cannot. In that text, "udakabhayaṃ" means...
123:
Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to restrain Venerable Sāriputta, spoke the words beginning with "Āgamehi." Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, however, recognized his own responsibility. Thus, the Blessed One gave him praise.

Why did he begin the discourse, "Monks, there are these four perils"? There are four perils in this Sāsana. He began this teaching to show that he who is unafraid of these perils can remain firm in this Sāsana, whereas he who is afraid cannot. In that passage, "udakoro-hante" refers to a person descending into the water. "Kumbhīlabhaya" is the danger of crocodiles. "Susukābhaya" is the danger of fierce fish (makara).

"Kodhupāyāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ" is a designation for anger and despair. Just as a person who has descended into external waters dies by sinking in the waves, even so, in this Sāsana, one sinks into anger and despair and leaves the order. Therefore, anger and despair are called the "danger of waves" (ūmibhaya).

"Odarikattassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ" is a designation for gluttony (seeking food for the belly). Just as a person who has descended into external waters dies by being bitten by a crocodile, even so, in this Sāsana, one is bitten by gluttony and leaves the order. Therefore, gluttony is called the "danger of crocodiles" (kumbhīlabhaya).

"Arakkhiteneva kāyena" means having an unguarded body by doing things such as moving the head (distractedly) and so on. "Arakkhitāya vācāya" means having unguarded speech by speaking coarse words and so on. "Anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā" means without establishing mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). "Asaṃvutehi" means with (sense-doors) that are not closed. "Pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ" is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure. Just as a person who has descended into external waters dies by sinking in a whirlpool, even so, in this Sāsana, a monk sinks into the whirlpool of the five cords of sensual pleasure and leaves the order. Therefore, the five cords of sensual pleasure are called the "danger of whirlpools" (āvaṭṭabhaya).

"Anuddhaṃseti" means it wearies or withers. "Rāgānuddhaṃsena" means with a mind afflicted by lust. "Mātugāmassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ" is a designation for women. Just as a person who has descended into external waters dies by being struck because of a fierce fish, even so, in this Sāsana, one leaves the order because of sensual lust that arises on account of women. Therefore, women are called the "danger of fierce fish" (susukābhaya).
124:
Just as for one who, fearing these four dangers, does not descend into the water, there is no benefit derived from the water, and they remain thirsty with a body soiled by dust and dirt; similarly, for one who, fearing these four dangers, does not go forth into the Sāsana, there is no benefit derived from this Sāsana, and they remain thirsty with the thirst of craving and a mind soiled by the dust of defilements. But for one who, without fearing these four dangers, descends into the water, there is the aforementioned benefit; similarly, for one who, without fearing these dangers, goes forth into the Sāsana, there is the aforementioned benefit.

The Elder, however, said this: "Just as one who, fearing the four dangers, does not descend into the water, is unable to cross the current and reach the other shore, while one who descends without fear is able; similarly, one who, out of fear, does not go forth into the Sāsana, is unable to cut the current of craving and see the other shore of Nibbāna, but one who goes forth without fear is able." The rest of the words are clear in all respects. This teaching was concluded for the sake of a person who is to be led (neyya-puggala).

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya
## The Explanation of the Cātuma Sutta is finished.
## 8. Explanation of the Naḷakapāna Sutta

'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so on is the Naḷakapāna Sutta. In that Naḷakapāna Sutta, Naḷakapāna is the name of the village where it took place. Long ago, our Bodhisatta was reborn in the animal kingdom as a monkey. He was a great-bodied monkey king, wandering at the foot of a mountain surrounded by many thousands of monkeys. Indeed, he was wise and possessed great merit. That monkey king advised his followers thus: "Friends, at the foot of this mountain, there are what are called poisonous fruits and ponds possessed by non-humans (amanussa). You should eat only the fruits you have eaten before and drink only the water you have drunk before. In these matters of what has been eaten and drunk before, there is no need to ask me again. But do not eat fruits or drink water that you have not eaten or drunk before without asking me."
125:
One day, while wandering, those monkeys reached the foot of another mountain, and after searching for food, they looked for water and saw a pond possessed by an ogre. Those monkeys did not drink the water hastily but sat surrounding the pond, waiting for the arrival of the Bodhisatta monkey king. When the Bodhisatta arrived, he asked, "Friends, why do you not drink the water?" The monkeys replied, "We are waiting for your arrival, Lord." Saying "Very well, friends," he searched for footprints around the pond and saw only footprints going down, but no footprints coming up. Seeing this, he knew for certain that this pond was a pond with danger.

At that very moment, a water-ogre (udakarakkhasa) born in that pond, with a white face, a blue-black belly, red hands and feet, large and curved tusks, and an ugly and terrifying appearance, emerged, parting the water in two. That ogre said, "Why do you not drink the water? Drink the sweet water. Why do you listen to the words of this monkey king?" The Bodhisatta asked, "Are you the non-human (amanussa) living here?" He replied, "Yes, I am." "Do you seize those who descend into this pond?" "Yes, I do, and I will eat all of you." "Ogre, you will not be able to do so." "In that case, will you drink the water?" "Yes, we will drink," the monkey king replied. "If so, not even one of you shall escape from my hands," said the ogre.

"We shall drink the water, but we shall not fall under your power," he said, and had a reed (naḷa) brought to him. Holding it by the end, he blew into it, and that reed became hollow throughout without any joints. Then, sitting on the bank, he drank the water. He also had reeds brought for the remaining monkeys, blew into them, and gave them. All the monkeys drank the water while the ogre was watching. Regarding this matter, it was also said:

"Seeing the footprints that did not come up, seeing the footprints that only went down,
We shall drink the water with a reed; you shall not be able to kill me."

From that time until today, the reeds in that place have been hollow without joints. Along with this, there are four world-enduring miracles (kappaṭṭhiya-pāṭihāriya) in this aeon: the sign of the rabbit in the moon, the cessation of the fire's progress at the place of the act of truth in the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the absence of rain at the dwelling place of the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter, and the hollow nature of the reeds on the bank of that pond. Thus, that pond received the name "Naḷakapāna" because the water was drunk through a reed (naḷa). Later, a village was established near that pond, and that village also came to be known as "Naḷakapāna". Referring to that village, it was said "at Naḷakapāna". Palāsavana means a forest of Butea monosperma (Flame of the Forest) trees.
126:
“Venerable Sir, we are indeed greatly delighted (in the holy life)” means that we are certainly delighted. It indicates that others who are delighted in your Dispensation (Sāsana) are delighted in the same way as we are.

In the passages beginning with ‘neva rājābhinītā’, the meaning should be understood as follows: A certain person commits an offense against the king and flees. The king asks, “Sirs, where is that man?” They reply, “Great King, he has fled.” The king says, “Even in the place where he has fled, he shall not escape my hands; however, if he becomes a monk, he shall be released.” A friend of his goes and informs him of this, saying, “If you wish to live, become a monk.” He ordains and wanders about, protecting his life. This person is called ‘rājābhinīta’ (one led to monkhood by the king’s danger).

A certain person wanders about cutting off the source of thieves. The thieves, hearing of this, say, “He does not yet know our power; we shall make him know.” Hearing this, the man flees. The thieves, hearing he has fled, say, “Even in the place where he has fled, he shall not escape our hands; however, if he becomes a monk, he shall be released.” Hearing this, he ordains. This person is called ‘corābhinīta’ (one led to monkhood by the danger of thieves).

A certain person consumes many debts and, being oppressed by those debts, flees from the village. The creditors, hearing of this, say, “Even in the place where he has fled, he shall not escape our hands; however, if he becomes a monk, he shall be released.” Hearing this, he ordains. This person is called ‘iṇaṭṭha’ (one oppressed by debt).

One who, out of fear of any kind of danger such as the king’s danger, becomes frightened and oppressed, comes out and ordains, is called ‘bhayaṭṭha’ (one oppressed by fear). One who ordains because of being unable to make a living during famines and so on is called ‘ājīvikāpakata’, which means one who is oppressed by the matter of livelihood. Among these monks (such as Anuruddha and others), there is not even one who ordained for these reasons; therefore, (the Buddha) preached the words beginning with ‘neva rājābhinīto’.

‘Vivekaṃ’ means being secluded from defilements. The meaning is: if one does not attain the joy and happiness (pīti-sukha) known as the first and second jhānas, which are obtained by being secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states; or if one does not attain a more peaceful happiness through the power of the higher two jhānas (third and fourth) and the four paths, then these states such as covetousness (abhijjhā) will overwhelm the mind and remain. Among them, ‘arati’ is discontent with higher wholesome states. ‘Tandī’ is the state of laziness. Thus, for one who, after ordaining, is unable to perform the duties of a monk, these seven evil states...
127:
Having shown that [unwholesome states] arise and overwhelm the mind, [the Buddha] now says, "Having followed seclusion... or another more peaceful than that," to show that for whomsoever those states remain overwhelming the mind, that person is unable to perform the duties of a recluse.

Having thus shown the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), he now speaks the words beginning with "seclusion" (vivekaṃ) in the same manner to show the bright side (sukkapakkha). The meaning of those words should be understood in the same way as previously stated.

"Saṅkhāya" means having known. "Ekaṃ" refers to a certain state. "Paṭisevati" means he associates with or uses what is suitable to be associated with. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. Regarding "upapattīsu vyākaroti" (he declares regarding rebirths), one might ask: "Let him first declare regarding those who are subject to rebirth; how does he declare regarding those who are not subject to rebirth (Arahants)?" One who says that for an Arahant, who is not subject to rebirth, there is no further rebirth in a future existence, is said to "declare regarding rebirths" (upapattīsu vyākaroti).

"Janakuhanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of impressing or deceiving people. "Janalapanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of coaxing the multitude. "Let people know me" means he does not declare for the reason that "if I speak thus, the multitude will know me; thus my fame will spread among the multitude." "Uḷāravedā" means those with great joy.

"So kho panassa āyasmā" refers to that venerable one who has attained Parinibbāna [as known] to this venerable one who is still present (either seen personally or heard by report). In the terms beginning with "evaṃsīlo" (of such virtue), virtue and so on should be understood as a mixture of mundane and supramundane. In this context, "evaṃdhammo" (of such qualities) refers to the states associated with concentration (samādhi). "Phāsuvihāro hoti" (he lives at ease) means that for a monk who fulfills the practice previously fulfilled by that [deceased] monk, there is pleasant living through the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) after realizing the fruit of Arahantship. For one who is still fulfilling the practice and has not yet reached Arahantship, but is practicing tranquility and insight, it is also called pleasant living. The meaning should be understood in this manner in all instances.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Nalakapāna Sutta is finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Goliyāni Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Goliyāni Sutta. Therein, "padasamācāro" means weak conduct or gross conduct. It is like the Elder Mahārakkhita who was concerned with the four requisites. While that Elder Mahārakkhita was sitting in the house of a supporter, the supporter said, "Venerable Sir, I offer a robe to the Elder named so-and-so." A monk who is greedy for requisites, thinking only of that object, says, "You have done a good deed." When the supporter says, "I will also offer to you, Venerable Sir," he says, "Very well, you shall do so." This monk also has weak and gross conduct. "Sappaṭissava" means there must be a leader; it means one should not live making oneself the leader. "Serīvihāra" means living according to one's own will, living without moral dread (ottappa). "Anupakhajja" means without pushing in, without entering. Regarding that "pushing in," a certain disrespectful monk, while two senior elders are sitting to the left and right, sits down without asking permission, touching them with his robe or his knee. This monk is said to "sit down by encroaching" (anupakhajja nisīdati).
128:
It is like the case of the Elder Rakkhita. It is heard that while the Elder was sitting in the house of a supporting lay devotee, the devotee said, "Venerable sir, I have offered a robe to the Elder named so-and-so." The Elder replied, "You have done a good deed; by offering a robe to that monk who is greedy for requisites (paccayalola) and lives only thinking of those four requisites, you have done well." When the devotee said, "Venerable sir, I will also offer one to you," the Elder replied, "If you intend to offer to a monk who constantly thinks of those requisites, then it is well; you shall do so." This too is an example of such gross behavior (oḷārikācāra). "Sappatissena" means living with deference; one should not live making oneself the superior. "Serivihārena" means living according to one's own will, living without restraint.

"Nānūpakhajja" means without encroaching or without pushing in. Regarding this encroaching, if a monk sits down by touching two senior elders with his robe or his knee while they are sitting on both sides, without asking their permission, this is called sitting by encroaching. Instead of doing this, he should stand near the seat he is entitled to according to his seniority, and sit only when told, "Friend, please sit." If they do not say so, he should ask, "Venerable sirs, may I sit?" and then sit. From the time he has asked, whether they say "Sit" or not, it is proper to sit. In the phrase "Na paṭibāhissāmi," if a monk bypasses the seat he is entitled to by seniority and sits in the place belonging to junior monks, he is said to be obstructing the junior monks from their seats. This is because when he sits there, the junior monks have to remain standing, complaining, "He does not give us a place to sit," or they have to wander around looking for a seat. Therefore, one should sit only in the seat one is entitled to by seniority. In this way, he is said not to be obstructing.

"Ābhisamācārikampi dhammaṃ" refers even to the mere minor duties and practices known as noble conduct. "Nātikālena" means one should not enter the village too early, nor should one leave too late; one should enter and leave only together with the Saṅgha of monks. For a monk who enters too early and leaves too late, the duties of the shrine terrace (cetiyaṅgaṇa-vatta) and the Bodhi tree terrace (bodhiyaṅgaṇa-vatta) etc., decline. Having washed his face early in the morning, breaking through spider webs and letting dew drops fall, he enters the village, seeks rice gruel, and then sits in the village until the time for alms-round, engaging in various kinds of lowly talk (tiracchānakathā). After finishing his meal, he leaves only when the day is late, returning to the monastery only at the time when other monks are washing their feet. "Na purebhattaṃ pacchābhattaṃ kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjitabbaṃ" means, by way of observing this training rule: "If a monk who has been invited and is provided with a meal, without informing an existing monk, should go among families either before the meal or after the meal, except on the proper occasion, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)."
129:
In the analysis (vibhaṅga) of that training rule, it is stated that one should not go among families (cāritta) before or after the meal. Being "restless and frivolous" (uddhata and capala) means being restless by nature. It also means being endowed with the frivolity of young children and the practice described as decorating robes, decorating bowls, decorating lodgings, or cherishing and decorating this foul body.

"One should be wise" (paññavatā) means one should be endowed with resourceful wisdom (upāya-paññā) that knows the reasons in duties such as robe-making and so on. "In the Abhidhamma and the Higher Vinaya" (abhidhamme abhivinaye) means that one should make an effort in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka and the Vinaya Piṭaka, both by way of the Pali text and the commentary. At the very least, in the Abhidhamma, it is not proper to live without knowing the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga along with the Matrix of Couplets and Triplets (duka-tika-mātikā). In the Vinaya, it is not proper to live without knowing the two Pātimokkhas, well-decided, along with the judgments on formal acts and non-acts (kammākamma-vinicchaya).

By the word "Āruppa," all eight attainments (samāpatti) are taught. If one is unable to practice all of them completely, one should make an effort in seven, six, or five. At the very least, one should master and take up one preparatory meditation object (parikamma-kammaṭṭhāna) of a Kasiṇa; it is not proper to live without this much. By the term "superhuman states" (uttari-manussadhamma), all supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are shown. Therefore, one should live striving to become an Arahant. If one cannot yet attain Arahantship, one should be established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), or Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). At the very least, one should master and take up one gateway of insight (vipassanā-mukha) until Arahantship is reached. The remaining words are clear in every respect. The Venerable Sāriputta concluded this teaching by leading the person to be led (neyya-puggala) from the minor conduct (ābhisamācārika-vatta) gradually to Arahantship.

## The Explanation of the Goliyaani Sutta
## in the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, Papañcasūdanī, is finished.
## 10. Kiṭāgiri Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so on is the Kiṭāgiri Sutta. There, "among the Kāsīs" (kāsīsu) means in the province of that name. In the passage "Here, monks, you too...", the meaning should be understood thus: "Monks, you too, seeing well these five benefits—namely, being free from illness, free from affliction, being light, strong, and living in comfort—should eat while abstaining from eating at night." In this way, the Blessed Lord did not make them give up both kinds of eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana)—at night and during the day—simultaneously. He first made them give up vikālabhojana at one time, and then, after that time had passed, He taught this because He wanted them to give up eating at the wrong time entirely. Why is that? Because these habits of eating, practiced repeatedly in saṃsāra, tend to run into the minds of beings like water flowing in a river. Delicate gentlemen who are used to eating fine food in houses sheltered from the wind would be distressed if they had to give up two meals at once. Therefore, without making them give up all at once... Bhaddāli...
130:
“Bhikkhus, you too, seeing clearly these five benefits—freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and living in comfort—should eat only by abstaining from eating at night,” said the Blessed One. In this way, the Blessed One did not make them give up both kinds of vikalabhojana (eating at the wrong time)—eating at the wrong time at night and eating at the wrong time during the day—at once. Instead, at one time He made them give up only the daytime vikalabhojana, and later, wishing them to give up the nighttime vikalabhojana, He spoke thus. Why? Because these two ways of eating, being repeatedly practiced in the cycle of existence, have entered and attached to the continuity of beings like water flowing in a river. If noble sons who are very delicate and have been raised eating fine food in houses sheltered from the wind were to give up eating twice at once, they would become exhausted. Therefore, without making them give up both at once, He made them give up daytime vikalabhojana in the Bhaddāli Sutta, and in this sutta, He made them give up nighttime vikalabhojana. In making them give it up, He did not do so by threatening or by oppressing them; rather, He made them give it up only after showing the benefits, saying, “By abandoning these vikalabhojana, you will realize freedom from illness.”

Kīṭāgiri is the name of that market town. “Assajipunabbasukā” refers to the two bhikkhus named Assaji and Punabbasukā, who were the two group leaders among the six Chabbaggiya bhikkhus. These six—Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, Mettiya, Bhummajaka, Assaji, and Punabbasukā—are known as the Chabbaggiya bhikkhus. Among them, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka took their followers and lived in Sāvatthī. Mettiya and Bhummajaka lived in Rājagaha. These two, Assaji and Punabbasukā, were resident monks (āvāsika) in the market town of Kīṭāgiri. Resident monks are those who live there permanently; being committed to that place, they build unfinished dwellings, repair dilapidated ones, and become the masters when they are completed. “Kālikaṃ” refers to the benefit to be obtained in the future.

What meaning is shown by this passage, “Maya cetaṃ, bhikkhave”? Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who eats three times a day and produces only pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) is not one who does his duty in this Dispensation. Rather, He began this teaching to show this meaning: “This much feeling should be cultivated; this much feeling should not be cultivated.” “Abandon such pleasant feeling” was said with reference to joy based on the household life (gehassita-somanassa). “Strive to reach and dwell” was said with reference to joy based on renunciation (nekkhammasita-somanassa). In the next two sections as well, the meaning should be understood by way of displeasure (domanassa) and equanimity (upekkhā) based on the household life and based on renunciation.

Having shown the feelings to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, He now spoke the words beginning with “Nāhaṃ bhikkhave sabbesaṃyeva” to show the sekha (trainees) who must perform their tasks with heedfulness (appamāda) and the Arahants whose tasks are finished and need not be performed. In that Pali, “kataṃ tesaṃ appamādena” means that those persons have performed the beneficial task through heedfulness. “Ālekanī” refers to monasteries where one delights in meditation with a sequence of practice; a bhikkhu living in such a monastery is called Ālekanī because he can reach the Path and Fruit. “Indriyasamasamodhānā” refers to the noble ones who act to balance the faculties such as faith (saddhā). What meaning is shown in this Kīṭāgiri Sutta by the phrase “Sattime bhikkhave puggalā”? He showed the account of these seven persons in total: two Arahants who have no more tasks to perform with heedfulness, and five sekha persons who still have tasks to perform. Such is the meaning...
131:
Bhikkhus, He spoke the words beginning with “Sabbesaṃyeva.” In that Pali, “kataṃ tesaṃ appamādena” means that those persons have already performed the task that should be performed with heedfulness. “Anulomika” refers to monasteries and places that are suitable for meditation and conducive to practice, where one can reach the Path and Fruit while residing there. “Indriyāni samannānayamāna” means balancing the faculties such as faith (saddhā).

“Bhikkhus, there are these seven types of persons.” What is shown here by these words? The intention is to show all seven types of persons: the 2 types of persons who have no more tasks to perform with heedfulness, and the 5 types of persons who still have tasks to perform.

Among those seven, “ubhatobhāgavimutta” means one who is released in both ways. Such a person is released from the material body (rūpakāya) by formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) and from the mental body (nāmakāya) by the Path. That person is of 5 kinds: four kinds who reach Arahantship after emerging from each of the four formless attainments and contemplating formations (saṅkhāra), and the Non-returner (anāgāmī) who reaches Arahantship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). However, the Pali text here—“What kind of person is ubhatobhāgavimutta? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations (vimokkha) with the mental body, and by wisdom, having seen (the Four Noble Truths), his taints (āsava) are destroyed”—thus appears in the Abhidhamma with reference to one who obtains the eight liberations.

“Paññāvimutta” means one who is released by wisdom. That person is of 5 kinds: the dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) and the four kinds who reach Arahantship after emerging from the four jhānas. In this context, the Pali text appears only as one who does not obtain the eight liberations. It is taught: “He does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with the mental body, but by wisdom alone, having seen (the Four Noble Truths), his taints are destroyed. This person is called paññāvimutta.”

One who realizes the touched (jhāna) is called a “kāyasakkhī” (body-witness). It should be understood that the person who first touches the contact of jhāna and later realizes the cessation of Nibbāna is of 6 kinds, starting from one established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphalaṭṭhan) up to one established in the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggaṭṭhan). Therefore, He said: “Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the mental body, and by wisdom, having seen (the Four Noble Truths), some of his taints are destroyed. This person is called kāyasakkhī.”
132:
One is called 'attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta) because one has reached the end of the path of stream-entry. The brief characteristic of such a person is this: because one has known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom that 'conditioned things are suffering, and cessation (Nibbāna) is happiness,' one is called 'attained to vision.' In detail, however, this person, like the 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī), is of six kinds. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Here in this teaching, a certain person understands as it really is, "This is the truth of suffering"... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are also well seen and examined by him with wisdom... This person is called "attained to vision."' 

'Liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta) means one who is liberated from defilements through faith. This person also has six kinds according to the method mentioned before. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Here in this world, a certain person understands as it really is, "This is suffering"... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are also well seen and examined by him with wisdom... but not in the same way as the one attained to vision. This person is called "liberated by faith."' Between these two types of persons, for the one liberated by faith, at the moment of the mundane path which precedes the supramundane path, the exhaustion of defilements is slow and not sharp, as if one is believing, as if one is convinced, or as if one is resolving. For the one attained to vision, however, at the stage preceding the supramundane path, the knowledge that cuts off defilements is not slow but arises sharply and courageously.

Therefore, for example, for a person who cuts a banana tree with a dull sword, the cut is not smooth, the sword does not enter quickly, the sound of cutting is heard, and more effort must be exerted; the development of the preceding path of the one liberated by faith should be understood as having such a nature. On the other hand, for a person who cuts a banana tree with a sharp sword, the cut is smooth, the sword enters quickly, no sound is heard, and no great effort is needed; the development of the preceding path of the one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) should be understood as having such a nature.

One is called a 'Dhamma-follower' (dhammānusārī) because one follows along according to the Dhamma (wisdom). 'Dhamma' means wisdom; the meaning is that one develops the path preceded by wisdom. The same method applies to the 'faith-follower' (saddhānusārī). Both of these are only those standing on the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimaggaṭṭha). Therefore, it was said: 'For a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the faculty of wisdom is predominant, and he develops the noble path preceded by wisdom; this person is called a Dhamma-follower.' Likewise: 'For a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the faculty of faith is predominant, and he develops the noble path preceded by faith; this person is called a faith-follower.' This is the summary here.
133:
In detail, the discussion on those such as the 'one liberated in both ways' (ubhatobhāgavimutta) has already been stated in the chapter on the development of wisdom in the Visuddhimagga. Therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated in that Visuddhimagga. The Pali text that appears here in this Kiṭāgiri Sutta is for the purpose of showing the classification of these persons; in that Pali, since there are no immaterial attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) apart from the fine-material attainments (rūpa-samāpatti), it should be understood that even though 'immaterial jhānas' are mentioned, the eight liberations (vimokkha) are indeed included.

'Touching with the body' (kāyena phusitvā) means touching with the mental body (nāmakāya) that arises together with the fine-material or immaterial jhānas. 'And seeing with wisdom' (paññāya cassa disvā) means that person sees the noble truths with the path-wisdom. 'Some taints' (ekacce āsavā) refers to certain taints that are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry and so forth. 'Proclaimed by the Tathāgata' (tathāgatapavedita) refers to the four noble truths taught by the Blessed One. 'Are well seen with wisdom' (paññāya vodiṭṭhā honti) means: in this context, virtue is taught; in this, concentration; in this, insight; in this, the path; in this, the fruit. Thus, because of having practiced and familiarized oneself with the effect as effect and the cause as cause in terms of virtue and so forth, they are well seen by the path-wisdom. 'Practiced' (vocaritā) means familiarized. 'Faith is established' (saddhā niviṭṭhā hoti) means that faith characterized by conviction is firmly established. 'They endure reflection to a certain extent' (mattaso nijjhānaṃ khamanti) means they endure observation within measure. 'Mere faith' (saddhāmattaṃ) means just faith; any other word is merely a synonym or an alternative phrasing for that 'mere faith.'

Among these persons whose tasks are to be performed with heedfulness, three are trainees (sekha) who have penetrated the paths and fruits. These persons, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and balancing the faculties such as faith, gradually attain Arahantship. Therefore, for these three persons, the meaning of the Pali should be understood just as it stands. At the end, however, two persons are those possessed of the path of stream-entry. By them, suitable lodgings must be resorted to for that path of stream-entry, good friends must be associated with, and the faculties must be balanced. Resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and balancing the faculties for the sake of the three higher paths, they will gradually reach Arahantship—this is the meaning of the Pali in this context.

The contentious debater (vitaṇḍavādī), however, taking this very Pali, says: 'The supramundane path does not consist of a single mind-moment, but of many mind-moments.' That contentious debater should be told: 'If you say that the path consists of many mind-moments, not a single mind-moment, by referring to the meaning that one resorts to lodgings with one mind, associates with good friends with another, balances the faculties with another, and the path-mind is yet another—if that were the case, a person resorting to lodgings would see a blue-colored mountain, see a forest...'
134:
One hears the sounds of birds and beasts, smells the scent of flowers and fruits, tastes the flavor while drinking water, and feels the touch while sitting or lying down. In this way, those endowed with these five consciousnesses would also be those endowed with supramundane states. If one were to accept this statement, one would be in opposition to the Teacher. For the Teacher has declared the group of five consciousnesses to be purely indeterminate (avyākata); for one endowed with those five consciousnesses, the occurrence of wholesome or unwholesome states is excluded, whereas the supramundane path is purely wholesome. Therefore, he should be instructed: 'Abandon this view.' If he does not accept the instruction, he should be dismissed, saying: 'Go now; enter the monastery early in the morning and drink the rice gruel.'

'Monks, I do not say [that the attainment of knowledge occurs] at the very beginning' means: Monks, I do not say that the realization of the fruit of Arahantship or the standing in the fruit of Arahantship occurs at the very beginning, like the leaping of a frog. 'Gradual training' (anupubbasikkhā) is a word in the nominative case used in the sense of the instrument. The same method applies to the two subsequent words. 'One in whom faith has arisen' (saddhā-jāto) means a person who possesses faith that has arisen through conviction. 'He approaches' (upasaṅkamati) means he goes near to the teachers. 'He attends' (payirupāsati) means he sits in the presence of the teachers. 'He remembers' (dhāreti) means he bears it in mind well. 'Desire arises' (chando jāyati) means the wholesome desire to act arises. 'He strives' (ussahati) means he puts forth effort. 'He examines' (tuleti) means he weighs things as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. 'Having examined, he strives' (tulayitvā padahati) means that while weighing things through investigative insight (tīraṇa-vipassanā) in this way, he exerts effort in the practice of the path. 'Resolute' (pahitatto) means having a mind directed toward Nibbāna. 'With the body, [he realizes] the supreme truth' (kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ) means he realizes the truth of Nibbāna with the mental body (nāmakāya). 'And through wisdom' (paññāya ca) means he penetrates and sees with the path-wisdom associated with the mental body.

Now, because those monks, Assaji and Punabbasu, did not even perform the simple act of welcoming the Teacher upon hearing of his arrival, the Teacher, wishing to censure their conduct, said: 'Monks, even that faith did not exist,' and so on. Therein, 'how far have these [gone]' (kīvadūrevime) means to what distant place have they departed. Although it would be appropriate to say they have departed a hundred leagues or a thousand leagues, the Teacher did not say anything of the sort. The phrase 'the four-line explanation' (catuppadaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ) was said with reference to the explanation of the Four Noble Truths. 'Of that which was pointed out' (yassuddiṭṭhassa) means of that Dhamma which was indicated. By the phrase 'Monks, that teacher also' (yo pi so, bhikkhave, satthā), he shows a teacher outside the Dispensation. 'Of such a nature' (evarūpī) means of such a kind. 'Like buying and selling' (paṇopaṇaviyā) refers to the act of purchasing and selling. 'Does not occur' (na upeti) means it does not happen. The meaning is that there is no increasing or decreasing of the price as there is at the time of buying and selling. This...
135:
One who says, 'How much is this ox worth? It is worth twenty,' is called 'paṇa' (valuing). One who says, 'It is not worth twenty, it is only worth ten,' is called 'opaṇa' (devaluing). Wishing to prohibit such buying and selling (increasing or decreasing the price), the Blessed One said: 'He does not enter into buying and selling.' Now, to show that buying and selling, he said: 'If it were to be for us at such a price, we would perform that purchase; if it were not to be for us at such a price, we would not perform that sale.'

'Monks, [how could it be] for me' means: Monks, since the Tathāgata dwells entirely unmixed with material things (āmisa), how could such buying and selling be appropriate for a Teacher who is thus unmixed? 'For a disciple who dwells having plunged into [the teaching]' (pariyogāhiya vattato) means for one who practices having plunged into, taken up, and grasped [the teaching]. 'This is the natural way' (ayamanudhammo) means this is the nature. 'The Blessed One knows, I do not know' means that out of faith in the Blessed One, thinking 'The Blessed One knows the benefit of eating at a single sitting, but I do not know,' one abandons eating three times a day and eats only at a single sitting. 'Ruḷahanīya' means that which causes growth. 'Ojavanta' means having sap or essence. By the words 'Let only the skin remain,' he shows the fourfold effort (caturaṅga-vīriya). Herein, the skin is one factor, the sinews are one, the bones are one, and the flesh and blood are one. He shows that one practices by resolving upon this fourfold effort, thinking: 'I shall not rise until I have attained the fruit of Arahantship.'

The remaining words are clear in all respects. The Blessed One concluded this discourse by emphasizing the fruit of Arahantship for the sake of a person who is to be led (neyya-puggala).

## The Explanation of the Kīṭāgiri Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Second Division (Vagga) is finished.
136:
## 3. Paribbājaka Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Tevijjavacchasutta

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Tevijjavacchasutta. In that sutta, regarding "ekapuṇḍarīke," the white mango tree is called *puṇḍarīka*. Because there is only one such white mango tree in that grove, it is called *Ekapuṇḍarīka*. "Etadahosi" means that such a thought occurred because of the desire to enter that grove. "Cirassaṃ kho bhante" is said in reference to the fact that [the Buddha] had naturally come there before. In the phrase "dhammassa cānudhammaṃ," omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) is called "Dhamma," and the teaching of it to the great multitude is called "Anudhamma." The remaining words are exactly as explained in the Jīvakasutta.

"Na me te" means that without consenting to the wanderer's words, [the Buddha] rejects even what should be consented to. For while the statement "The Blessed One is all-knowing, all-seeing, and claims absolute knowledge and vision" should be consented to, the statement "Whether I am walking... [it is always] present" should not be consented to. This is because he knows only after adverting with his omniscience. Therefore, standing on what is not to be consented to, he speaks thus, wishing to reject even what should be consented to.

In the phrase "āsavānaṃ khayā," the word "yāvadeva" is not used because once the taints (*āsavas*) are destroyed, they do not need to be destroyed again. Here, the Blessed One shows the quality of knowing the past through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), the quality of knowing the present through the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*), and the supramundane quality through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*). Thus, with these three knowledges (*vijjā*), he taught by summarizing all the qualities of a Buddha.

"Gihisaṃyojanaṃ" refers to the lay fetter, which is the craving (*taṇhā*) and attachment to lay requisites. "Natthi kho vaccha" means that there is no one who can make an end of suffering without abandoning the lay fetter. For even though Santati the Minister, Uggasena the merchant's son, and the youth Vītasoka attained Arahantship while in lay form, they did so only after drying up attachment to all formations (*saṅkhāras*) through the Path (*magga*). After reaching Arahantship, however, they did not remain in that form. The lay form is inferior and cannot sustain the supreme quality of Arahantship. Therefore, one who reaches Arahantship in lay form must either go forth [as a monk] or attain Parinibbāna on that very day. Earth-dwelling deities (*bhummadevā*), however, can remain [in their form] because they have places to hide and seclude themselves. In the remaining sense-sphere, among humans, the three types of persons beginning with Stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) can remain.
137:
Stream-enterers and Once-returners reside in the sense-sphere heavens. However, Non-returners and Arahants do not remain there in the form of those deities. Why? Because that place called the sense-sphere heaven is the abode of beings who delight in sensual pleasures, and there is no secluded place suitable for the seclusion of those Non-returners and Arahants. Thus, an Arahant attains Parinibbāna there, and a Non-returner, after passing away, is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). Above the sense-sphere heavens, however, all four types of noble disciples (ariyas) can reside in the form of those Brahmas.

"So pāsi kammavādī" means that the Bodhisatta was also a proponent of action (kammavādī); he did not reject the efficacy of action (kiriyā). This was spoken by [the Buddha] referring to himself ninety-one aeons ago. At that time, it is said the Great Being went forth to examine and take up a sect; even though he knew the fruitlessness of that sect, he did not diminish his effort, and being a proponent of action (kiriyavādī), he was reborn in heaven. Therefore, he spoke thus. The rest of the words are clear in all respects.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Tevijjavacchagotta Sutta is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Aggivacchagotta Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Aggivacchagotta Sutta. Therein, in the first instance of "na kho ahaṃ" (not I), it means "I am not one with an eternalist view." In the second instance, it means "I am not one with an annihilationist view." Thus, the rejection in all instances should be understood by way of the extremes of finitude and infinitude, etc. This view, "it both is and is not," is partial eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda). This view, "it neither is nor is not," should be understood as eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepa).

"Sadukkhaṃ" means suffering together with the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha) and the suffering of results (vipāka-dukkha). "Savighātaṃ" means being with distress by way of those two [types of suffering]. "Saupāyāsaṃ" means being with despair by way of those two. "Sapariḷāhaṃ" means being with feverish burning by way of those two.

"Kiñci diṭṭhigataṃ" is a question asking whether there is any single view that has been liked, accepted, and held. "Apanītaṃ" means removed or discarded. "Diṭṭhaṃ" means seen with wisdom. Therefore, it is because he saw the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. "Sabbamanyitānaṃ" refers to all three types of imaginings: imagining through craving (taṇhā-manyita), imagining through views (diṭṭhi-manyita), and imagining through pride (māna-manyita). "Mathitānaṃ" is a synonym for those same imaginings. Now, wishing to show them by analyzing them, he said, "of all I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency of pride" (sabba-ahaṃkāra-mamaṃkāra-mānānusayānaṃ).
138:
In this context, 'ahaṃkāra' (I-making), which is the clinging to 'I', is called 'diṭṭhi' (wrong view). 'Mamaṃkāra' (mine-making), which is the clinging to 'mine', is called 'taṇhā' (craving). 'Mānānusaya' is called 'māna' (conceit). 'Anupādā vimutto' means being liberated without clinging to any of the four types of clinging (upādāna) regarding any phenomena (dhamma).

'Na upeti' means it is not fitting (not logical). In this instance, although the statement 'na upappajjati' (does not reappear) should be permitted, if it were said so, that wanderer (paribbājaka) might adopt the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). If it were said 'upappajjati' (reappears), he might adopt eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi); if 'upappajjati ca na ca upappajjati', he might adopt partial-eternalism (ekaccasassata-diṭṭhi); and if 'neva upappajjati na na upappajjati', he might adopt the view of equivocation (amarāvikkhepa-diṭṭhi). Therefore, the Blessed One, intending that 'this wanderer should be without a footing and without a support, and should not find an opportunity for easy entry (understanding)', remained without giving permission and even rejected what should have been permitted. 'Alaṃ' means capable or sufficient. 'Dhammo' refers to the law of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). 'Aññatrayogena' means by other efforts. 'Aññatrācariyakena' means by living in the presence of other teachers who do not know the law of dependent origination.

'Then, Vaccha' means 'Since you say you have fallen into great confusion, I will question you again on this matter.' 'Anāhāro nibbuto' means extinguished without a cause (paccaya).

'Yena rūpena' means by whatever form (rūpa) one might designate the Tathāgata (the Buddha), who is called a 'being', as 'one having form'. 'Gambhīro' means profound in terms of qualities. 'Appameyyo' means immeasurable, such that its extent cannot be grasped. 'Duppariyogāḷho' means difficult to fathom or difficult to know. Just as the great ocean is profound, immeasurable, and difficult to know, so too is the Arahant (khīṇāsava). All statements such as 'reappears' and so on made in reference to that Arahant are illogical. How? Just as all statements such as 'gone to the eastern direction' and so on made in reference to an extinguished fire are not fitting, so it is here.

'Aniccatā' means because of impermanence. 'Sāre patiṭṭhitaṃ' means established in the essence of the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma). All the remaining words are clear in all places.

## In the Pappañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Aggivacchasutta is finished.
139:
## 3. Commentary on the Mahāvacchasutta

The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Mahāvacchasutta. In that sutta, 'sahakathī' means one who has conversed with. By saying, 'I have previously had many conversations with the Venerable One,' he recalls past conversations and establishes a friendly rapport. This is because the two previous suttas were also preached to this very wanderer. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the section called the Abyākata Saṃyutta was also preached to this wanderer. In the Ekuttara Nikāya (Aṅguttara Nikāya), there are also conversations held with this wanderer, such as 'Master Gotama, is the world eternal? Is only this true and the other futile?' and 'This is an undeclared (abyākata) issue.' Therefore, the wanderer Vaccha said 'sahakathī'. The Blessed One also showed favor and gave an opportunity to that wanderer who came repeatedly. Why did He give the opportunity? Because this wanderer held the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). Those with the view of eternalism do not quickly abandon their views. Like an old cloth (pilosika) smeared with animal fat and sesame oil, they can only be purified after a long time. The Blessed One saw: 'As time goes by, this wanderer will abandon his view, go forth (ordain) in my presence, realize the six direct knowledges (cha-abhiññā), and become a distinguished disciple.' Therefore, He showed favor and gave an opportunity to that wanderer whenever he arrived. This was the wanderer's final visit. In this sutta, he came with the firm resolve: 'Whether I can cross (the round of rebirths) or not, I will go to the ascetic Gotama and ordain, like one who descends into the water leaning on a staff.' Therefore, wishing to request a Dhamma teaching, he said, 'It would be good if the Venerable Gotama would [teach] me...' and so on. The Blessed One taught Vaccha a brief discourse by way of the roots (mūla) and a detailed discourse by way of the courses of action (kammapatha).

In this sutta, the teaching given by way of the roots is extremely brief, while the teaching given by way of the courses of action, though brief, is like a detailed one. In truth, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a detailed teaching in an absolute sense (nippariyāyena). Even the twenty-four books of the Paṭṭhāna and all seven books of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka are merely brief. Therefore, it should be understood that He taught only a summary, both by way of the roots and by way of the courses of action.

In that teaching on the courses of action, the seven factors in sequence beginning with 'abstaining from taking life is wholesome' (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī kusalaṃ) are only of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). However, the three factors beginning with non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) are applicable to all four planes (bhūmi).

In the phrase 'Vaccha, when for a bhikkhu...', although it is stated without specification (as to which bhikkhu), it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke this referring to Himself, just as in the Jīvaka Sutta and the Caṅkī Sutta.
140:
Regarding the question "Atthi pana" (Is there...?), why does he ask? His view is: "In various dispensations, only the teacher is an Arahant; the disciple is unable to reach Arahantship. The ascetic Gotama speaks as if referring to a single monk, saying 'Vacchā, for a monk...'. Is there any disciple of the ascetic Gotama who has reached Arahantship?" He asks with the intention of inquiring about this matter. In that question, "Tiṭṭhatu" means let the Venerable Gotama wait for a moment (meaning it is already known that the Venerable Gotama is a renowned Arahant in the world). When the Buddha answered thus, he further asked questions regarding bhikkhunīs and so forth, and the Blessed One answered him as well.

"Ārādhako" means one who accomplishes or fulfills the practice.

"Sekhāya vijjāya pattabbaṃ" means what should be attained through the three lower fruits. He says, "I have attained all that." A Vitaṇḍavādī (sophist), however, says: "Which states are trainee states (sekha)? According to the words 'The four paths and the three lower fruits of recluseship,' he has reached the path of Arahantship but not yet the fruit. He wants the Buddha to speak about the further exertion to reach that fruit." That Vitaṇḍavādī should be informed thus:

"He who has abandoned five defilements,
Is a fully perfected trainee (sekha) of non-declining nature,
Has attained mastery over the mind and has composed faculties—
Such a man is truly called one of steady nature."

An Anāgāmī (Non-returner) is indeed a fully perfected trainee. Referring to him, it was said: "What should be attained through the knowledge of a trainee." Since the path (magga) lasts only for a single thought-moment, there can be no questioning of one standing in that path. If it is said that according to this sutta, the path also has many thought-moments, that is not the word of the Buddha and contradicts the meaning of the quoted verse. Therefore, it should be understood that while standing in the fruit of Non-returning, he is made to speak about the insight (vipassanā) for the path of Arahantship. Because he had the potential (upanissaya) not only for pure Arahantship but also for the six higher knowledges (abhiññā), the Blessed One, thinking, "In this way, by working on tranquility (samatha), he will produce the five higher knowledges; by working on insight (vipassanā), he will reach Arahantship; thus he will become a great disciple with six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñño mahāsāvako)," did not teach insight alone but taught both tranquility and insight.
141:
"Sati satiāyataneti" means mindfulness in the cause of mindfulness. What is the cause here? It should be understood that the cause is either higher knowledge (abhiññā), or the meditative absorption (jhāna) which is the basis for higher knowledge, or ultimately, fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala), or insight (vipassanā) which is the cause of Arahantship.

"The Blessed One has been served by me" means that the seven types of trainees (sekha) are said to be currently serving the Blessed One, but only the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava/arahant) has completed the service to the Blessed One. Thus, the Elder Mahāvaccha spoke in this way, declaring his attainment of Arahantship in brief. Those monks, not understanding that meaning, accepted the Elder's words and reported them to the Blessed One. "Devatā" refers to a deity who possesses those qualities. All the remaining words are clear in meaning in every instance.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Mahāvacchasutta is finished.
## 4. The Explanation of the Dīghanakhasutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Dīghanakhasutta. In that sutta, "Sūkarakhatāyaṃ" means in the cave named Sūkarakhatā. It is heard that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, that cave became buried underground as the earth rose during the interval between two Buddhas. Then, one day, a pig dug the earth near the edge of the cave's roof. When it rained, the earth was washed away, and the edge of the roof became visible. A forest hunter saw it and thought, "This cave must have been used by virtuous ones in the past; I will renovate it." He removed the surrounding earth, cleaned the cave, built walls, and installed doors and windows. Having completed the plasterwork and painting, he spread sand that looked like silver plates, arranged couches and stools, and offered it for the Blessed One to reside in. The cave was deep, so one had to descend and ascend to use it. This was said in reference to that fact.

"Dīghanakha" is the name of that wanderer (paribbājaka). Why did he approach?
