It is heard that when the Elder Sāriputta had been ordained for half a month, Dīghanakha thought: "My uncle does not stay long when he goes to other sects. But now, it has been half a month since he went to the ascetic Gotama. I have not heard any news of him..."
142:
"Is the teaching potent? I shall find out," with such a desire to go, he (Dīghanakha) arose. Therefore, he approached (the Blessed One). "Standing to one side" means that at that time, the Elder Sāriputta was standing fanning the Blessed One. Dīghanakha the wanderer, out of shame and fear towards his maternal uncle (the Elder), asked the question while standing. Referring to that, it is said, "standing to one side."

"Everything is not pleasing to me" means "All rebirths (upapatti) are not pleasing to me; taking conception (paṭisandhi) is not pleasing to me." By saying this much, he indicates, "I am an annihilationist." The Blessed One, setting aside his (annihilationist) intention for a moment, wishing to show the fault in the phrasing "Everything is not pleasing to me" first, spoke the words beginning with "Even this [view] of yours." Therein, "Is even this view of yours not pleasing?" means "Is even this view, which you first liked, accepted, and held, not pleasing (to you)?"

"Master Gotama, if this view were pleasing to me" means "I have the view 'Everything is not pleasing to me'; to me who is such, this view 'Everything is not pleasing to me' would be pleasing." The statement "Everything is not pleasing to me" is just like that for him. Just as this view is pleasing even though it is included in the general grasp of "everything," so too would that view be pleasing. Thus, seeing the fault placed upon his own doctrine, he speaks with the intention, "I shall resolve that fault." However, in meaning, it follows for him that "This view is not pleasing to me." If this view is not pleasing or liked by someone, then for him, through that view, the view "Everything is not pleasing to me" is liked. If that is so, by not liking or not being pleased with the view, it follows that "He likes everything." But he does not admit that meaning; he merely holds onto the cessation (of life) through his annihilationist view.

Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Aggivessana, than those (who abandon) ... they cling to another view." Therein, "ato" is the ablative case (nissakka) used in comparison with those who abandon. It means that those who do not abandon (their views) are far more numerous than those who do. In "bahū hi bahutara," the word "hi" is a mere particle, and it means "are far more numerous." Later, in the phrase "tanū hi tanutara," the same method applies. "Those who spoke thus" means "those who say so." "They do not abandon that view and cling to another view" means they do not give up the original view but cling to another view.

Here also, having taken the eternalist view, it is not possible to take the annihilationist view or the partial-eternalist view without abandoning that (original) view. Having taken the annihilationist view, it is not possible to take the eternalist view or the partial-eternalist view without abandoning that view. Having taken the partial-eternalist view, it is not possible to take the eternalist view or the annihilationist view without abandoning that view. But the original eternalist view...
143:
Without abandoning the original eternalist view, it is possible to take only another eternalist view. How? At one time, having taken "Form is eternal," at another time one takes "Not only pure form is eternal, but feeling is also eternal, consciousness is also eternal." The same method applies to the annihilationist view and the partial-eternalist view. As it is applied to the aggregates, so should it be applied to the sense bases. Referring to this kind of grasping, it is said, "They do not abandon that view and cling to another view."

In the second instance, "ato" means "than those who do not abandon" (ablative case). Those who abandon are far fewer than those who do not abandon. "They abandon that view and do not take another view" means they abandon that original view and do not take any other view. How? At one time, having taken "Form is eternal," at another time, seeing the danger in that view, one abandons it, thinking, "This view of mine is gross." One relinquishes it, reflecting, "Not only is the view 'Form is eternal' gross, but the view 'Feeling is eternal ... consciousness is eternal' is also gross." The same method applies to the annihilationist view and the partial-eternalist view. As with the aggregates, so should it be applied to the sense bases. In this way, they abandon that original view and do not take another view.

Why did He undertake this teaching beginning with "Santa, Aggivessana"? This Dīghanakha the wanderer, who held an annihilationist view, was hiding his own view. Thinking that if the merits of that view were spoken, he would reveal his own view, the Blessed One undertook this teaching to show and analyze the three views together.

In the phrases beginning with "sārāgāya santike," it means being near to being attached to the round of rebirths by the power of lust, and being near to being fettered to the round by the fetters of craving and views. "Abhinandanāya" means being near to swallowing and grasping by the power of craving and views. In the phrases beginning with "asārāgāya santike," the meaning should be understood as being near to not being attached to the round, and so forth.

Among these views, the eternalist view is less blameworthy but hard to relinquish. The annihilationist view is more blameworthy but can be relinquished quickly. How? An eternalist knows that this world and the next world exist. He knows that there are results of good and bad deeds. He performs wholesome deeds and is afraid to perform unwholesome deeds. He enjoys and delights in the round of rebirths.
144:
A person with the eternalist view, even when coming face to face with the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha, is unable to quickly abandon their own view. Therefore, that eternalist view is said to be of little fault but slow to be dispelled. On the other hand, an annihilationist knows that this world and the next world exist, and knows that there are fruits of good and bad deeds; however, they do not perform wholesome deeds, do not fear when performing unwholesome deeds, do not delight in the cycle of rebirth, and without being greatly attached, they are able to quickly abandon their view when face to face with the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha. If they are able to fulfill the perfections, they become a Buddha and attain Parinibbāna; if unable to fulfill them, they make a resolution, become a disciple, and attain Parinibbāna. Therefore, the annihilationist view is said to be of great fault but can be quickly dispelled.

That wanderer Dīghanakha, without being able to note the meaning thus explained, thought, "The Buddha praises my view; my view is certainly very good," and spoke the words beginning with "Ukkāṃseti me bhavaṃ."

Now, this wanderer is filled only with the annihilationist view, like a bitter gourd filled with sour gruel. Just as it is impossible to put oil, molasses, etc., into a gourd without discarding the sour gruel, and even if put in, it cannot be received, similarly, without abandoning that view, one is not worthy of attaining the Path and Fruit. Therefore, to cause the abandoning of the view, the Blessed One exerted effort with the words beginning with "Tatragghivessana." "Viggaha" means dispute. "Thus there is the abandoning of those views" means that by seeing the faults such as dispute, those views are abandoned. That wanderer, reflecting "What benefit is there for me in this dispute and so forth?", abandoned that annihilationist view.

Then the Blessed One, intending to fill the heart of Dīghanakha with the deathless medicine, like putting ghee, molasses, etc., into a gourd from which the sour gruel has been vomited out, and wishing to show insight (Vipassanā), spoke the words beginning with "Ayaṃ kho pana Aggivessana kāyo." The meaning of those words has been explained in the Vammika Sutta. The words beginning with "Aniccato" have also been detailed below. "Yo kāyasmiṃ kāyachando" means the craving that arises in the body. "Sneho" is the very moisture of craving. "Kāyanvayatā" means the state of following the body, meaning the defilements that follow the body.

Having thus shown the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), now wishing to show the meditation subject of immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), He spoke the words beginning with "Tisso kho." Again, wishing to show the unmixed nature of those feelings, He spoke the words beginning with "Yasmiṃ Aggivessana samaye." In that text...
145:
The summary of the meaning is: At the time when one feels one of the feelings such as pleasant feeling, at that time, the feelings other than the one being felt are not "sitting" waiting for their turn or opportunity. In fact, those feelings have not yet arisen, or they have vanished like bursting water bubbles. The words beginning with "Sukhāpi kho" were spoken to show the manner of the total disintegration of those feelings.

"Na kenaci saṃvadati" means that by holding the eternalist view and saying "I am an eternalist," one does not dispute with an annihilationist; and by holding that same eternalist view and saying "I am an eternalist," one does not dispute with a partial-eternalist. In this way, the three views should be applied interchangeably. "Yañca loke" refers to the speech used and spoken in the world; without misinterpreting or clinging to any phenomenon, one speaks according to worldly usage. It has also been taught thus:

"The monk who is an Arahant, who has finished his task,
Whose outflows are exhausted, and who bears his final body,
He might say, 'I speak,'
And he might say, 'They speak to me.'
Being skilled in the designations used in the world, and understanding them,
He would speak merely by way of worldly usage." (from Saṃyutta Nikāya).

In another text, it is taught: "Citta, these are worldly designations, worldly expressions, worldly usages, worldly concepts, which the Tathāgata uses without clinging." (from Dīgha Nikāya).

"Abhiññāpahānamāha" means that in regard to eternalism and so forth, having known those various phenomena as eternal with higher knowledge, He taught the abandoning of the eternalist view; having known annihilationism and partial-eternalism with higher knowledge, He spoke of their abandoning. Having known form with higher knowledge, He spoke of the abandoning of form—in this manner, the meaning should be understood here.

"Paṭisañcikkhato" means for one who reflects. "Anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci" means the mind was liberated from defilements without clinging to the outflows which are ceased through the cessation of non-arising. By this much, just as one dispels hunger by eating rice cooked for another, the Venerable Sāriputta, by sending his knowledge into the teaching given for another, the wanderer Dīghanakha, and developing insight, reached the Fruit of Arahantship. He stood having reached the pinnacle of the disciple's perfection of knowledge and having penetrated the sixteen types of intellectual speed (javana). The wanderer Dīghanakha also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and was established in the Three Refuges. The Blessed One, having concluded this teaching, descended from Gijjhakūṭa Hill, went to the Veḷuvana Monastery, and held an assembly of the disciples.
146:
Venerable Sāriputta, directing his knowledge to the Dhamma teaching given for another (the wanderer Dīghanakha) and developing insight, attained the fruit of Arahantship. He stood having penetrated the peak of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection and the sixteen types of knowledge. The wanderer Dīghanakha, however, attained the fruit of Stream-entry and became established in the refuges.

The Blessed One, having concluded this teaching while the sun was still up (before sunset), descended from Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, went to Veḷuvana Monastery, and held an assembly of disciples. That assembly was endowed with four factors. These factors are: it was the full-moon Uposatha day associated with the Māgha constellation; one thousand two hundred and fifty monks assembled of their own accord without being invited by anyone; among those monks, there was not a single worldling, nor anyone among the Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, or dry-insight Arahants, but all were Arahants with the six higher powers; and among those monks, there was not a single one ordained by cutting the hair with a razor, but all were 'Ehi-bhikkhu' monks.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Dīghanakha Sutta is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. Therein, "aggāgāre" means in a fire-offering hall. Regarding the term "tiṇasanthārake"—there were two people named Māgaṇḍiya, an uncle and a nephew. Between them, the uncle had ordained and attained the fruit of Arahantship. The nephew also possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) and would soon ordain and attain the fruit of Arahantship. Then, the Blessed One, seeing his supporting conditions, left the delightful Gandhakuṭi chamber, which is like a divine chamber, and stayed for a few days in that fire-offering hall, which was soiled with ashes, grass, and rubbish, having a grass mat spread out for the sake of helping another. It was with reference to that stay that this was said. "Tenupasaṅkami" means he did not approach only on that day. The reason is that the fire-offering hall was located near the village and was crowded and not secluded due to boys and girls. Therefore, the Blessed One would always spend the daytime in that forest grove and go to that fire-offering hall in the evening to stay.
147:
The Blessed One, while usually putting away the grass mat and making a mark before leaving on other days, left it spread out on that day. Why? Because, having surveyed the world at dawn that day, he saw: "Today, Māgaṇḍiya will come here, see this grass mat, and start a conversation with Bhāradvāja concerning the grass mat. Then I will come and teach the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he will ordain in my presence and attain the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, I have fulfilled the perfections only for the sake of helping and supporting others." Thus, he left having spread out the grass mat.

"I think this grass mat is a place suitable for a recluse." This place is not the dwelling of an unrestrained recluse. For in this place, no marks of being pulled by the hand, pulled by the foot, or struck by the head are apparent; it is like a mat spread out by a skilled artist who has marked it with a brush, without disorder, without confusion, and without being broken. This is the dwelling place of a restrained recluse. He asked, "Friend, whose dwelling place is this?"

"It is the place of the Bhūnahu (the destroyer of growth, the maker of boundaries)," he said. Why did he say so? Because he [the Buddha] was perceived as having the doctrine of the cessation of growth in the six doors. For this was his [Māgaṇḍiya's] doctrine: "The eye should be increased, should be developed; the unseen visible form should be seen; the seen visible form should be surpassed. The ear should be increased, should be developed; the unheard sound should be heard; the heard sound should be surpassed. The nose should be increased, should be developed; the unsmelled odor should be smelled; the smelled odor should be surpassed. The tongue should be increased, should be developed; the untasted flavor should be tasted; the tasted flavor should be surpassed. The body should be increased, should be developed; the untouched tangible should be touched; the touched tangible should be surpassed. The mind should be increased, should be developed; the unknown mental object should be known; the known mental object should be surpassed." Thus, he prescribes growth in the six doors.

The Blessed One, however, taught:
"Restraint of the eye is good, good is restraint of the ear.
Restraint of the nose is good, good is restraint of the tongue.
Restraint of the body is good, good is restraint of speech.
Restraint of the mind is good, good is restraint in everything.
The monk restrained in everything is freed from all suffering."
(Dhp. 360-361)
148:
(The Blessed One) prescribes restraint in the six sense-doors. Therefore, that Māgandiya, thinking "The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth, a maker of restrictions," said "Bhūnahu (destroyer of growth/embryo)."

"Ariye ñāye dhamme kusale" refers to the pure and blameless causal Dhamma. What is shown by this? One who is to speak about such a famous, well-known, and influential person should speak after investigating and reflecting, keeping a guard over the mouth. Therefore, it shows: "Do not speak hastily; keep a guard over the mouth." In saying "It comes thus in our scripture," it means: "Because it comes thus in our scripture, we do not speak merely what comes to the mouth as we wish; what should those who speak what is found in the scripture fear? Therefore, we can say it even to his face." "Appossukka" means being unconcerned and without effort for the sake of protecting me. "Vutto va naṃ vadeyya" means: "Being exactly as I, Māgandiya, have spoken, and without being asked (by Master Gotama), starting the conversation and filling it in as if taking mangoes, rose-apples, etc., may Master Bharadvāja speak in the manner I have spoken; please speak."

"Assosi kho" means the Blessed One, having developed the light-kasina, saw Māgandiya who had arrived there with his divine eye. He also heard the sound of the two people talking with his divine ear. "Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" refers to the time when he emerged from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Saṃvigga" means being shaken and agitated with joyful emotion (pīti-saṃvega). To that Brahmin Bharadvāja, this thought occurred: "Māgandiya has not yet informed the ascetic Gotama, nor have I. Apart from the two of us, there is no third person; that person with sharp hearing must have heard our voices." Then, joy arose within him, and ninety-nine thousand hairs stood on end. Therefore, it is said: "Saṃvigga lomahaṭṭhajāta (agitated, with hair standing on end)." "Atha kho māgandiyo paribbājako" means that for the wanderer Māgandiya, his wisdom reached maturity like a seed with an opening face. Therefore, unable to remain seated, he wandered about and returned once more to the Blessed One and sat at a respectful distance. To show that sitting, it is said "Atha kho māgandiyo," and so on.

The Blessed One did not say, "Māgandiya, you said this about me," but instead began the Dhamma teaching to the wanderer Māgandiya with "Cakkhuṃ kho māgandiya..."
149:
In the sense of being the dwelling place of eye-consciousness, the visible form is the delight of the eye; therefore, the eye is called 'rūpārāma.' Because it delights in forms, it is 'rūparata.' Because forms greatly gladden eye-consciousness, it is 'rūpasamudita.' 'Danta' means tamed or not indulged in. 'Gutta' means secured. 'Rakkhita' means guarded. 'Saṃvuta' means closed off. 'Saṃvarāya' means for the purpose of restraint. 'Paricāritapubba' means formerly much enjoyed. 'Rūpapariḷāha' is the fever of defilements arising with visible forms as the object. The Blessed One asked, "Māgandiya, what would you say to this Arahant who, having comprehended visible forms with insight-wisdom, has reached the fruit of Arahantship? Would you say 'He is a destroyer of growth, a maker of restrictions,' or not?" Māgandiya replied, "Master Gotama, there is nothing at all to be said." In the case of the remaining sense-doors, it is the same way. Now, just as you, Māgandiya, have nothing to say to an Arahant who has reached the fruit of Arahantship by comprehending the five aggregates with insight-wisdom, so too have I reached omniscience by comprehending the five aggregates; therefore, to show "You should not say anything to me," He said "Ahaṃ kho pana," and so on. "Tassa mayhaṃ māgandiya" was said to show his own luxury during his life as Prince Siddhartha when he was a layman. Among those terms, "Vassika" refers to the palace comfortable for living in during the rainy season. In the remaining terms, it is the same way. Here, the word-definition is: living for the four months of the rains is "vassa"; because it is suitable for living in the rains, it is "vassika." In the remaining terms, it is the same way. 

Among those palaces, the Vassika palace used during the rainy season is neither too high nor too low. The main doors and air-windows of that palace are neither too thin nor too many. In this palace, only floor coverings, bedspreads, and food and snacks that are balanced in heat and cold are suitable. In the Hemantika palace used during the winter, the pillars and walls are low. The main doors and air-windows are thin with subtle openings. Wall-projections are removed to allow heat to enter. In this palace, floor coverings, bedspreads, and clothing such as blankets that have the power to provide heat are suitable. As for food and snacks, those containing ghee and butter with a pungent taste are suitable. In the Gimhika palace used during the summer, the pillars and walls are high. In this palace, the main doors and air-windows are numerous with large lattices. Floor coverings and so on made of dukūla silk are suitable. Food and snacks that have a sweet taste and cooling properties are suitable. In this palace, new pots filled with water are placed near the air-windows and covered with blue lotuses and so on. In various places...
150:
Just as streams of water appear when the rain-god pours down rain, water machines were made through which streams of water emerged.

Furthermore, for the Bodhisatta, one hundred and eight golden pots and one hundred and eight silver pots were filled with scented water, and after arranging clusters of blue lotuses in them, they were placed surrounding the bed. In large copper cauldrons, scented mud was filled, and blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses were planted; these were placed here and there to capture the coolness. The lotus flowers bloomed by the rays of the sun. Various groups of bees entered the palace and flew about, taking nectar from the flowers. The palace was filled with an exceedingly fragrant scent. Between the double walls, copper pipes were installed, and in the open air above the nine-story palace, a net with fine holes was fastened over a jeweled pavilion. In one place, a dried buffalo hide was spread out. When the Bodhisatta played in the water, they threw stone balls onto the buffalo hide; that sound was like the thundering of clouds. Below, they turned the machine; the water rose up and fell from above the net, appearing like falling raindrops. At that time, the Bodhisatta wore blue garments, covered himself with a blue robe, and adorned himself with blue ornaments. His retinue of forty thousand female dancers also wore blue clothes and ornaments and were anointed with blue unguents; surrounding the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), they went to the jeweled pavilion. During the day, while playing in the water, he enjoyed the comfort of the cool season.

In the four directions of the palace, there were four ponds. During the day, groups of birds of various colors would rise from the eastern pond and, chirping, fly over the palace to the western pond. Rising from the western pond, they would fly to the eastern pond; from the northern pond to the southern pond; and from the southern pond to the northern pond. (Their constant flying) was like the rainy season. The palace for the winter season had five stories, and the palace for the rainy season had seven stories.

'Nippurisehi' means devoid of men (consisting only of women). In this context, it was not only the musical instruments that were without men; all places were without men. The doorkeepers were only women, and those who performed services such as bathing were also only women. It is said that the King thought: "If a person enjoying such sovereign happiness and prosperity sees a man, doubt may arise; that doubt of mine..."
151:
"Let no (doubt) arise in my son," thinking thus, the King placed only women in all affairs. The phrase "delighting in that delight" was said with reference to the delight in the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) based on the fourth jhāna.

In the phrase "a householder or a householder's son," the meaning should be understood thus: because for nobles (khattiyas), there is only the aspiration for the white parasol (sovereignty), and their impediments (papañca) are many; and brahmins, never satisfied with the Vedas, wander about seeking the Vedas; but householders, from the time they learn the art of finger-counting (arithmetic), only enjoy prosperity. Therefore, without including nobles and brahmins, he said, "a householder or a householder's son." "Āvaṭṭeyya" means that one might return because of the cause of human sensual pleasures. "Abhikkantatarā" means more excellent. "Paṇītatarā" means more refined (or more difficult to be satisfied with). This was also said:

"If one were to take water from the ocean with the tip of a blade of kusa grass and compare it with the water in the ocean, even so, human sensual pleasures are very few in the presence of divine sensual pleasures."

"Samadhigayha tiṭṭhati" means that having attained divine happiness, one stands far surpassing that divine prosperity.

In this context, the comparison between the simile and the thing signified (opammasansandana) should be understood thus: the time when the householder is endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure is like the time when the Bodhisatta, Prince Siddhattha, delighted among forty thousand women in the three palaces. The time when that householder, having fulfilled good conduct, is reborn in heaven is like the time when the Bodhisatta renounced the world and realized omniscience upon the throne of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka). The time when that householder enjoys prosperity in the Nandana Grove is like the time when the Tathāgata passes time in the delight of the attainment of the fruit of the fourth jhāna. The time when that householder does not long for the five cords of human sensual pleasure is like the time when the Tathāgata, while passing time with the attainment of the fruit of the fourth jhāna, does not long for the happiness of inferior people.

"Sukhī" means one who, though having reached suffering first, later reaches happiness. "Serī" means one who, though living with a physician first, later becomes independent and alone. "Sayamvasī" means one who, at first, had to follow the will of a physician, sitting when told to sit, lying down when told to lie down, eating when told to eat, and drinking when told to drink, but later becomes self-controlled. Which...
152:
The ability to go wherever one wishes means that although at first one is unable to go to a desired place, later, when the illness has subsided, one can go wherever one wishes, such as to see forests, hills, or mountains. Wherever one desires to go, there one can indeed go.

In this comparison, the correlation between the simile and the thing signified is as follows: The time when the man was afflicted with leprosy is like the time when the Bodhisatta lived in the household. A single pit of glowing coals is like a single object of sensual pleasure. Two pits of glowing coals are like two objects. The two and a half crores of pits of glowing coals belonging to Sakka, the king of devas, are like the two and a half crores of dancers. Scratching the openings of the wounds with fingernails and heating them over a pit of glowing coals is like indulging in objects of sensual pleasure. The time of being free from illness through medicine is like the time when the Bodhisatta, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits in renunciation, went forth and became a Buddha, spending his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) based on the fourth jhāna. The time of not envying another person afflicted with leprosy is like the time when the Buddha, spending his time in that bliss, does not desire the pleasure of low people.

"One with impaired senses" refers to one whose physical sensitivity (kāyaprasāda) is destroyed by worm-leprosy. "Those with impaired senses" refers to those with an impaired wisdom faculty (paññindriya). Just as that leper with impaired physical sensitivity perceives the painful touch of fire as pleasant through a perverted perception, so too, because of the impairment of the wisdom faculty, they perceive sensual pleasures, which are of painful touch, as pleasant through a perverted perception.

Regarding the words "asucitarāni ceva" and so on: By nature, those wounds are impure, foul-smelling, and putrid. Now (during scratching and heating), they become even more impure, even more foul-smelling, and even more putrid. When that person heats the wounds and scratches the itch, small worms enter inside, and corrupt blood and pus flow out. In this way, there is only a mere measure of gratification for him.

In the verse beginning with "ārogayaparamā": Among whatever gains of wealth, gains of followers, or gains of children there may be, health is the highest and most excellent; there is no gain superior to it. Therefore, "health is the highest gain." Among whatever bliss of jhāna, bliss of the path, or bliss of fruition there may be, Nibbāna is the highest; there is no bliss superior to it. Therefore, "Nibbāna is the highest bliss." The Eightfold Path, which occurs in the preliminary stage of the supramundane path and leads to the Deathless, is secure; there is no other secure path superior to it. Alternatively, in the text "khemaṃ amatagāminī," both the names "khemaṃ" and "amataṃ" are names for Nibbāna. Those other doctrines of recluses and brahmins, which are held by the power of their own views as leading to the place of security and leading to the Deathless...
153:
In the verse beginning with "Ārogyaparamā," the meaning should be understood as follows: In the world, there are various types of gains, such as gaining wealth, gaining followers, and gaining children. Among these gains, being free from illness is the most excellent. There is no gain superior to being free from illness. Therefore, it is said, "Ārogyaparamā lābhā" (Health is the highest gain). There are all kinds of bliss, such as the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the Path, and the bliss of the Fruition. Among these, the bliss of Nibbāna is the most excellent. There is no bliss superior to the bliss of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, "Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ" (Nibbāna is the supreme bliss).

"Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggānaṃ" means that the Eightfold Path, which is the way to Nibbāna through practice in the preliminary stage of the Supramundane Path, is the secure way. There is no other secure path superior to this path. Alternatively, in the phrase "khemaṃ amatagāminī," both the names "khema" (security) and "amata" (deathless) are names for Nibbāna itself. There are other doctrines of recluses and brahmins who, according to their own views, hold that their paths lead to security and the Deathless. Among all those paths (views) claimed to lead to the security of Nibbāna, the Noble Eightfold Path is the most supreme and excellent; this is the meaning here.

"Ācariyapācariyānaṃ" means of the teachers and of the teachers' teachers (the lineage). "Sameti" means it is similar or identical, without distinction, like measuring with a single measure or weighing with a single scale. "Anomajjati" means stroking repeatedly by lowering the hand. "Venerable Gotama, this is health, this is Nibbāna," he says, stroking sometimes the head and sometimes the chest.

"Chekaṃ" means accomplished or skilled. "Sāhuḷicīrena" refers to taking a coarse cloth made of black sheep's wool. Some also call it "saṅkāracola" (rags collected from a dust heap). "Vācaṃ nicchāreyya" means he should speak while repeatedly stroking sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at the edge, and sometimes in the middle. "Pubbakehesā" should be analyzed as "pubbakehi esā." Indeed, the Blessed One Vipassī... and the Blessed One Kassapa, while seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly, spoke this verse. The great multitude learned it as "a verse based on welfare" (atthanissitagāthā). After the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, it entered among the wanderers (paribbājakas). Although those wanderers put it into books, they were only able to preserve the two lines: "Ārogyaparamā lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ." Therefore, He said, "That verse has now gradually become a verse of worldlings (puthujjanagāthā)."

"Rogova bhūto" means "rogabhūta" because the disease itself has become manifest. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Ariyaṃ cakkhu" refers to pure insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). "Pahoti" means being capable. "Bhesajjaṃ kareyya" means one should perform medical treatment such as emetics, purgatives, and eye drops.

"Na cakkhူni uppādeyya" means that if someone's visual sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) is impaired due to being enveloped by bile, phlegm, etc., they can produce eyes (gain sight) by relying on a skilled physician and using suitable medicine. However, for one born blind (jaccandha), the sensitivities were already destroyed even in the mother's womb. Therefore, such a person cannot obtain sight. Thus, He said, "He would not produce eyes." In the second instance, "jaccandha" refers to one who is blind from birth due to being enveloped by bile and so on. "Amitto" means that one should look upon the person who gave the coarse cloth made of black sheep's wool mentioned earlier as an enemy, thinking, "This person is my enemy." The same should be understood for the second term, "paccatthikato." "Anumiyamānaṃ" refers to that which is known by the mind that follows along in the beginningless Saṃsāra. With the words "tassa me upādānapaccayā," He taught the Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) which has one connection and two layers, and clearly showed the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). "Dhammānudhammapaṭipanno" refers to the practice that is in accordance with the Dhamma of Nibbāna and is the means of escape from the cycle. With the words "this disease, ailment, dart," He showed the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā). With the words "upādānanirodhā," He showed the cessation. The Buddha spoke thus, wishing to teach in this way. The remaining expressions in all places have the same meaning as previously stated.

## End of the Commentary on Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
## The fifth, Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, is finished.
155:
Unnādiniyā means crying out with a high voice. For that assembly crying out in such a way, it is called 'high sound' (ucca-sadda) due to the sound rising upwards, and 'great sound' (mahā-sadda) due to it spreading in all directions; thus, it refers to an assembly endowed with such high and great sounds.

Those wanderers (paribbājakas) do not have duties such as the duty to the stupa (cetiya-vatta), the duty to the Bodhi tree (bodhi-vatta), the duty to teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya-vatta), or wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) to be performed upon rising early. Therefore, having risen early, they sit in the morning sun or gather in the evening for the sake of pleasant conversation, saying, "This person's hand is beautiful, this person's foot is beautiful," and so on. Thus, referring to each other's hands, feet, etc., or the beauty of women, men, boys, and girls, or starting with other matters such as delight in sensual pleasures or delight in existence, they engage in various kinds of lowly talk (tiracchānakathā—talk contrary to the path to fruition), such as talk about kings (rājakathā), in sequence.

Such talk is called tiracchānakathā (lowly talk) because it does not lead out of the round of suffering and is contrary to the paths to heaven, the Path, and the Fruit. Among those lowly talks, talk proceeding in the manner of "King Mahāsammata, King Mandhātu, King Dhammāsoka were of such great power," etc., referring to kings, is called talk about kings (rājakathā). The same method applies to talk about thieves (corakathā), and so on.

Among those talks, only talk connected with sensual pleasures in the manner of "This king is very handsome and attractive," etc., is lowly talk. However, talk proceeding as "Even a king of such great power has come to destruction" stands as a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Regarding thieves, only talk connected with sensual pleasures, such as "Mūladeva was of such great power, Meghamāla was of such great power," and referring to their deeds as "Oh, how brave!" is lowly talk. In battles like the Bhārata war, talk such as "This person killed that person in this way, stabbed him in that way," spoken out of delight in sensual pleasures, is lowly talk. But talk in all these matters proceeding as "They too have come to destruction" is indeed a subject of meditation.

Furthermore, regarding food and so on, it is not proper to speak out of delight in sensual pleasures, saying, "I have eaten, consumed, drunk, and enjoyed such food endowed with color, aroma, taste, and texture." However, it is proper to speak beneficially, saying, "In the past, I offered such food, drink, clothing, bedding, flowers, and perfumes endowed with color, etc., to virtuous persons, and I made offerings at the stupa."

In talk about relatives (ñātikathā), etc., it is not proper to speak out of delight, saying, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we traveled with such magnificent vehicles." However, it is proper to speak beneficially, saying, "Those relatives of ours have also come to destruction," or "In the past, we offered such sandals to the Saṅgha." Talk about villages (gāmakathā) is also not proper if spoken out of delight, such as whether a village is well-situated or poorly-situated, has plenty of food or is famished, or "The villagers here are brave and capable." However, it is proper to speak beneficially, saying, "Faith..."
156:
...[Faithful] and devoted," or "They have come to the end and vanished." The same method applies to talk about market towns, cities, and districts.

Talk about women (itthikathā) is also not proper if spoken out of delight regarding their complexion, figure, etc. It is only proper to speak in this way: "That woman has faith, is devoted, or has come to the end." Talk about heroes (sūrakathā) is also not proper if spoken out of delight, such as "The great warrior named Nandimitta was very brave." It is only proper to speak in this way: "He had faith, was devoted, or has come to the end." Talk about streets (visikhākathā) is also not proper if spoken out of delight, such as "This street is well-constructed or poorly-constructed; those on this street are brave and capable." It is only proper to speak in this way: "They have faith, are devoted, or have come to the end."

Talk about the place of water jars (kumbhaṭṭhānakathā) refers to talk about the watering place of potters or talk about the slave-girls of potters. That too is not proper if spoken out of delight, such as "That slave-girl is charming, and she is skilled in dancing and singing." It is only proper to speak in the manner of "She has faith, is devoted," etc. Talk about departed ancestors (pubbapetakathā) is talk about deceased relatives. In that case, the judgment is the same as that for talk about living relatives.

Talk about various things (nānattakathā) refers to useless talk of various natures that is excluded from the talks mentioned before and after. Talk about world-speculation (lokakkhāyika) is talk based on the Lokāyata and Vitaṇḍa treatises, such as "Who created this world? Such a person created it. Crows are white because their bones are white; cranes are red because their blood are red," and so on.

Talk about ocean-speculation (samuddakkhāyika) is useless talk such as "Why is the ocean called sāgara? It is called sāgara because it was dug by the princes of Sāgara. It is called samudra because it was indicated by a hand gesture meaning 'It was dug by me,'" and so on. Talk about being and non-being (itibhavābhavakathā) is talk that proceeds by stating any useless reason, such as "It is thus being (bhava), it is thus non-being (abhava)." In this context, "being" (bhava) refers to the eternalist view (sassata), and "non-being" (abhava) refers to the annihilationist view (uccheda). Or, "being" means prosperity, and "non-being" means decline. Or, "being" means sensual happiness, and "non-being" means self-mortification. Together with these six kinds of talk about being and non-being, there are thirty-two kinds of lowly talk (tiracchānakathā). They were sitting there engaging in such lowly talk.

Then, Sandaka the Wanderer looked at those wanderers and said, "These wanderers are very disrespectful and discourteous toward one another; and we..."
157:
“Since the appearance of the ascetic Gotama, we have become like fireflies at sunrise, and our gains and honor have declined. Indeed, if the ascetic Gotama, or a disciple of Gotama, or even a lay attendant of Gotama were to come to this place, it would be very shameful. Thinking, ‘The fault of the assembly falls only upon the leader of the assembly,’ he looked here and there and saw the Elder Ānanda. Because he saw him, it is said: ‘The wanderer Sandaka saw... they became silent.’

In that passage, ‘saṇṭhapesi’ means to train (the disciples) and to conceal the faults of that assembly. It means placing that assembly so that it is well-established. For example, just as a person about to enter the midst of an assembly adjusts his lower robe to hide any fault, adjusts his upper robe, and wipes the place where dust has settled; similarly, to conceal the faults of that assembly, he trains them saying, ‘Sirs, do not make a noise,’ and places that assembly so that it is well-established. ‘Appasaddakāma’ means they desire quietude, they are accustomed to sitting alone, they are accustomed to standing alone, and they do not live in the company of a group. ‘Appasaddavinīta’ means those who are disciplined in quietude and silence by the Buddha. ‘Appasaddassa vaṇṇavādino’ means those who are accustomed to speaking in praise of a quiet and silent place. ‘Upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyya’ means he would think it fit to come to this place.

Why does this wanderer Sandaka long for the Elder’s approach? It is because he longs for his own growth. It is said that when the Buddha or the Buddha’s disciples come to them, the wanderers—in the presence of their own lay attendants—exalt themselves and place themselves in a high position, saying: ‘Today the ascetic Gotama has come to us, Sāriputta has come; indeed, these ones do not go to just anyone; look at our excellence!’ They also strive to win over the lay attendants of the Blessed One. When those wanderers see the Blessed One’s attendants, they say: ‘Even your teacher, the venerable Gotama, and Gotama’s disciples come to us; we are in harmony with one another. But you do not even wish to look at us with your eyes, nor do you pay respect; what fault have we committed against you?’ Some people, thinking, ‘Even the Buddhas go to these people, what need is there to speak of us?’ from then on, do not neglect those wanderers when they see them. ‘Tuṇhī ahesuṃ’ means they sat silently surrounding Sandaka.

‘Svāgataṃ bhoto Ānandassa’ means the welcome arrival of the venerable Ānanda. When you come, Ānanda, we are joyful; when you go...”
158:
The word ‘soko’ (sorrow) indicates the meaning that when the venerable Ānanda comes, those wanderers feel great joy, and when he leaves, they feel sorrow. ‘Cirassaṃ kho’ (It has been a long time) is a polite and affectionate expression. The Elder Ānanda would occasionally go to the wanderers’ park for the sake of wandering; referring to such previous visits, he said, ‘Cirassaṃ kho.’ Having said this, he did not sit down stiffly with pride, but rose from his own seat, dusted it, and invited the Elder to the seat, saying, ‘Let the venerable Ānanda sit; this seat is prepared.’

‘Antarākathā vippakatā’ (Interrupted talk) is a question: ‘From the time you all sat down together until my arrival, what talk was interrupted in the interval? What talk did not reach its conclusion because of my arrival?’ Then the wanderer Sandaka, wishing to show, ‘This talk is useless, without essence, and based on the round of rebirth; it is not worthy to be spoken before the venerable one,’ said ‘Tiṭṭhatesā bho,’ and so on. He showed: ‘If the venerable Ānanda wishes to hear it, this talk will not be difficult to find later; indeed, this talk is of no use to us. Having obtained the venerable one’s arrival, we only wish to hear a different talk on a good subject.’ Then, wishing to request a Dhamma teaching, he said ‘Sādhu vata bhavantaṃ ye vā,’ and so on.

In that passage, ‘ācariyake’ means in the teacher’s doctrine. ‘Anassāsikānī’ means states devoid of solace or delight. ‘Sasakkaṃ’ is an indeclinable in the sense of ‘certainly’; it means ‘a wise man certainly would not live there, and even if he lived there, he would not achieve or fulfill it.’ ‘Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ’ means the Dhamma which is the cause and is wholesome in the sense of being faultless. ‘Idha’ means in this world. The words ‘Natthi dinnaṃ’ (There is no gift), etc., have already been explained in the Sāleyyaka Sutta. ‘Cātumahābhūtiko’ means composed of the four great elements. ‘Pathavī pathavīkāyaṃ’ means the internal earth element follows and reaches the external earth element. ‘Anupagacchati’ is a synonym for ‘anupeti.’ It also means ‘anugacchati’ (follows). Both terms show the meaning of ‘approaching’ or ‘reaching.’ The same method applies to the liquid element (āpo), and so on. ‘Indriyāni’ means the six faculties, beginning with the mind, pass into space. ‘Āsandipañcamā’ means five, including the four men carrying the four legs of the bed and the bed on which the body lies. ‘Yāvāḷāhanā’ means as far as the cemetery. ‘Padānī’ means in the manner of saying, ‘This person was virtuous in this way, this person was immoral in this way,’ and so on...
159:
This refers to the qualities (guṇapada) that have arisen, such as 'This person was virtuous,' 'This person was virtuous in such a way,' and so on. Alternatively, in this context, the body itself is intended by the word 'pada'. 'Kāpotakāni' means having a color like that of a pigeon, or the color of a pigeon's wing.

'Bhasmantā' means ending in ashes; or this very word 'Bhasmantā' is the original Pali. 'Āhutiyo' refers to whatever gifts are given, characterized by offerings, honors, and the like; all such gifts end only in ashes. It means they do not go on to produce results beyond being reduced to ashes. 'Dattupaññattaṃ' means that which is prescribed by fools (dattu). The meaning is: this gift is prescribed only by fools who lack wisdom, not by the wise. It shows that fools give, and the wise receive. 'Atthikavādaṃ' refers to those who say, 'There is giving, there is the fruit of giving'; the words of those who speak this doctrine of existence (atthikavāda) are empty and are merely false speech. 'Bāle ca paṇḍite ca' means both fools and the wise.

'Akate na me ettha kataṃ' means: even by the work of a recluse (samaṇa) not yet performed by me, in this doctrine, the work is said to be done; even by the holy life (brahmacariya) not yet lived, it is said to be lived. 'Ettha' means in this recluse-dharma. 'Samasamā' means extremely equal, or equal by way of similar qualities. 'Sāmaññaṃ pattā' means having reached a state of equality.

The words starting with 'Karato' and so on were spoken in the Apaṇṇaka Sutta. Likewise, the words starting with 'Natthi hetu' and so on (were also spoken in the Apaṇṇaka Sutta).

In the fourth brahmacariyavāsa, 'Akaṭā' means not conditioned (by causes such as merit and demerit). 'Akaṭavidhā' means having no created arrangement; it means they are not made to be done by anyone saying, 'Do it like this.' 'Animmitā' means not created even by psychic power. 'Animmātā' means not caused to be created. Some teachers say the word 'Animmitabbā', but that word is found neither in the Pali nor in the Commentary. 'Vañjhā' means barren, like a barren animal or a sterile palm tree that bears no fruit; it means they do not produce any state. By this word 'Vañjhā', the ability of the earth-body (pathavīkāya) etc. to produce form (rūpa) etc. is rejected. Because they stand like mountain peaks, they are called 'Kūṭaṭṭhā'. 'Isikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā' means they stand like the stalks in muñja grass. The intention there is: what is said to be 'born' is merely something already existing that emerges, like a stalk from muñja grass. There is also the reading 'Esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā', meaning they stand like a well-planted gate-pillar that does not shake. By both these words, the absence of destruction of those (bodies) is shown. 'Na iñjanti' means they do not shake because they stand like gate-pillars. 'Na vipariṇāmenti' means they do not abandon their natural state. 'Na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti' means they do not oppress (destroy) one another. 'Nālaṃ' means they are not capable.
160:
In the terms such as 'Pathavīကာယော' (Pathavīkāyo), the earth element itself is the earth-body, or the collection of earth is the earth-body. In the word 'Tattha' (therein), it refers to those bodies among which the soul (jīva) is the seventh. 'Natthi hantā vā' shows that there is no one capable of killing, or causing to kill, or hearing, or causing to hear, or knowing, or causing to know. 'Sattannaṃ tveva kāyānaṃ' means that just as a weapon struck into a heap of beans etc. enters between the beans, so the weapon enters through the gaps and openings between the seven bodies. At that time, the thought 'I am depriving this person of life' is merely a mere perception (saññā). 'Yonipamukhasatasahassāni' refers to 1,400,000 primary or superior wombs, plus another 6,000 and another 600. 'Pañca ca kammuno satāni' refers to 500 karmas. This shows a useless wrong view based on mere speculation. In the phrases 'five karmas and three karmas' etc., it should be understood in the same way. However, some teachers say that 'five karmas' refers to the five senses, and 'three' refers to the three types of action: bodily action, etc. In the phrase 'in karma and half-karma' (Kamme ca aḍḍhakamme ca), his doctrine is that bodily action and verbal action are considered full karma, while mental action is considered half-karma (upaḍḍhakamma). 'Dwaṭṭhipaṭipadā' means 62 practices. 'Dwaṭṭhantarakappā' means that although there are 64 intermediate eons (antarakappa) in one eon (kappa), this person says 62 because he does not know the other two intermediate eons. The six types of births (abhijāti) have been explained in detail in the Apaṇṇaka Sutta.

'Aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo' refers to these eight stages of man: manda-bhūmi, khiḍḍā-bhūmi, vīmaṃsaka-bhūmi, ujugata-bhūmi, sekkha-bhūmi, samaṇa-bhūmi, jina-bhūmi, and panna-bhūmi. Among these eight, from the day of birth until seven days, because they have emerged from the narrow place of the mother's womb, beings are slow and greatly deluded. This stage is called manda-bhūmi. Beings coming from woeful states (duggati) constantly cry and wail. Beings coming from happy states (sugati) remember that happy state again and again and laugh. This stage is called khiḍḍā-bhūmi. Holding the hands, feet, couch, or stool of the parents and placing the feet on the ground is called vīmaṃsaka-bhūmi. The time when one is able to walk on foot is called ujugata-bhūmi. The time of learning arts and sciences is called sekkha-bhūmi. The time of leaving home and ordaining is called samaṇa-bhūmi. The time of knowing after serving a teacher is called jina-bhūmi. Just as it is said, 'The monk, the barren one, and the conqueror consume nothing,' a monk who receives nothing is called panna-bhūmi.
161:
"Ekūnapaññāsa ājīvasate" refers to four thousand nine hundred varieties of livelihoods. "Paribbājakasate" refers to one hundred lineages of wandering ascetics. "Nāgāvāsasate" refers to one hundred abodes of Nagas (or groups of elephants). "Vīse indriyasate" refers to two thousand faculties. "Tiṃse nirayasate" refers to three thousand hells. "Rajodhātuyo" refers to places where dust falls, specifically referring to the backs of hands, the backs of feet, and so on. "Satta saññīgabbhā" refers to sentient births such as camels, oxen, donkeys, goats, deer, buffaloes, and so on. "Asaññīgabbhā" refers to non-sentient births such as hill paddy, barley, wheat, green gram, millet, corn, and rye. "Nigaṇṭhigabbhā" refers to births from knots or joints, referring to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so on. "Satta devā" means that although there are many gods, he (Makkhali Gosāla) says there are seven. Humans are also infinite, but he says there are seven types. "Satta pisācā" means that although Pisācas (goblins) are numerous, he says there are seven types.

"Sarā" means great lakes. It refers to Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Anotatta, Lake Sīhapapāta, Lake Kuḷira, Lake Mucalinda, and Lake Kuṇāla. "Pavuṭā" means the knots of trees. "Papātā" means great precipices. "Papātasatāni" means hundreds of small precipices. "Supinā" means great dreams. "Supinasatāni" means hundreds of small dreams. "Mahākappino" refers to the number of great aeons (Mahākappa). Here, he says a great aeon is the period it takes to empty a lake by taking one drop of water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass once every hundred years, repeated seven times until the lake is dry. His doctrine is that only after passing through eight million four hundred thousand such great aeons will both fools and the wise make an end of suffering. It means that even a wise person cannot become pure in the interval, and a fool cannot go beyond that period.

"Sīlena" means by the practice of a naked ascetic or by any other kind of practice. "Vatena" means by such a vow. "Tapena" means by ascetic practice. One who tries to become pure within that interval by saying "I am wise" is called one who tries to ripen unripe kamma. One who goes beyond the fixed time by saying "I am a fool" is called one who exhausts ripe kamma by experiencing it. He shows that this cannot be done with "Hevaṃ natthi" (There is no such thing). It indicates that both are impossible to do. "Doṇamite" means as if measured by a bushel (doṇa). "Sukhadukkhe" means happiness and suffering. "Pariyantakate" means limited by the aforementioned time. "Natthi hāyanavaḍḍhane" means there is no decrease or increase. It means the saṃsāra of the wise does not decrease, and the saṃsāra of the fool does not increase. "Ukkaṃsāvakaṃse" means rise and fall (increase and decrease), which are just synonyms for decrease and increase. Now, to explain that meaning with a simile...
162:
Desiring to complete the meaning, Sañjaya the wanderer said "Seyyathāpi nāma," etc. In that text, "Suttaguḷe" means a ball of string that has been wound up. "Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paleti" means just as a ball of string thrown while standing on a mountain or a treetop unwinds as far as the length of the string and then stops and goes no further when the string is exhausted, even so, it is shown that one does not go beyond the stated time.

"Kimidaṃ" means "What is this ignorance of yours regarding things like this village empty of people? Are you called omniscient?" When asked thus, Assaka the wanderer, wishing to insert the doctrine of fatalism (Niyati-vāda), said "Suññaṃ me agāraṃ," etc.

"Anussaviko hoti" means one who relies on oral tradition. "Anussavasacco" means one who holds what is heard as the truth. "Piṭakasampadāya" means by the accomplishment of the Pitaka scriptures consisting of fifty vaggas.

"Mando" means one of weak wisdom. "Momūho" means one who is extremely deluded. "Vācāvikkhepaṃ အာပဇ္ဇတိ" means falling into verbal distraction. What kind of distraction? It means falling into the endless evasion called "Amarāvikkhepa." Alternatively, "Amarā" is a species of fish. Just as that fish cannot be caught because it darts about in the water by surfacing and diving, even so, this view darts here and there and cannot be grasped; therefore, it is called "Amarāvikkhepa." He falls into a distraction like that of the Amarā fish.

In the sentences "Evantipī me no," etc., when asked "Is this Dhamma wholesome?", he says "It is not my view thus." Then when asked "Is it unwholesome?", he says "It is not my view in that way." When asked "Is it otherwise than both?", he says "It is not my view otherwise." Then when asked "Is it your view that it is not even in these three ways?", he says "It is not my view that it is not." Then when asked "Is it your view that it is not 'not'?", he falls into distraction saying "It is not my view that it is not 'not'." He does not stand on any side. "Nibbijja pakkamati" means departing in weariness, thinking, "This teacher cannot even be a refuge for himself, how can he be one for me?" In the previous sections on "Anassāsika" (Unreliable doctrines), the method is the same.

"Sannidhikārakaṃ kāme paribhuñjituṃ" means just as when he was a layman before, he consumed sensual objects by storing them up, even so, it means it is now improper for him to consume things like sesame, rice, ghee, fresh butter, and so on, by storing them. Indeed, for an Arahant...
163:
If asked whether sesame, rice, and so forth are visible in the dwelling place, it is not that they are not visible; they are visible. However, this person does not store those items for his own benefit, but for the benefit of sick monks and others. If asked about an Anāgāmī (Non-returner), even though the five strands of sensual pleasure have been entirely abandoned by that Anāgāmī, he still examines and uses requisites obtained in accordance with the Dhamma.

'Puttamatāya puttā' means that the wanderer Sandaka, having heard this teaching and perceiving that 'the Ājīvakas are dead,' spoke thus. The meaning here is: the Ājīvakas are dead; the mother of those Ājīvakas is a mother whose sons have died; thus, the Ājīvakas are called the sons of a mother whose sons have died. 'Samaṇe Gotame' (In the ascetic Gotama) is intended to show that the holy life (brahmacariya) exists only in the ascetic Gotama and not elsewhere. The rest of the words are clear everywhere.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, Papañcasūdanī
## The Explanation of the Sandaka Sutta is finished.
## 7. The Explanation of the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta

'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta. In that sutta, 'Moranivāpa' (The Peacocks' Feeding Ground) is so called because in that place, peacocks were given sanctuary and fed. 'Annabhāra' is the name of a wanderer (paribbājaka). Similarly, 'Varadhara' is also a name. Not only these three, but there were also many other well-known wanderers. 'Appasaddassa vaṇṇavādī' (One who speaks in praise of quietness) is said here instead of saying 'appasaddavinīta' (one disciplined in quietness). Why? Because the Blessed One was not disciplined by another.

'Purimāni' (Former ones) refers to the words spoken previously, starting from yesterday. Those earlier than that are called 'purimatarāni'. 'Kutūhalasālā' (The Hall of Curiosity) is not a separate hall, but a place where ascetics and brahmins of various sects carry out various discussions, and because it is a place where the curiosity (kutūhala) of many people arises, thinking 'What is this person saying? What is that person saying?', it is called 'Kutūhalasālā'. There is also a reading 'Kotūhalasālā'. 'Lābhā' (Gains) means the opportunity to see such ascetics and brahmins and to ask questions...
164:
...or to listen to their Dhamma talk; for the people of Anga and Magadha, seeing these great teachers is a rare benefit (gain). This is the meaning.

In the words 'saṅghino' and so forth, because they have a community (Saṅgha) consisting of a group of renunciants, they are called 'saṅghī' (having a community). That very group is a 'gaṇa' (sect), and because they have that sect, they are called 'gaṇီ' (having a sect). Because they are teachers of that sect by way of teaching conduct and training, they are called 'gaṇācariya' (sect-teachers). 'Ñātā' means well-known and famous. Because they have a following and fame (yasa) that has spread through both true and false qualities, they are called 'yasassino' (famous). For teachers like Pūraṇa Kassapa, their fame spread through such means as: 'He has few desires, he is content; because of his fewness of desires, he does not even wear clothes.' For the Tathāgata, however, his fame spread through true qualities such as 'Itipi so bhagavā' (Thus indeed is the Blessed One). 'Titthakarā' means those who create doctrines (founders of sects). 'Sāဓုသမ္မတာ' (Sādhusammatā) means those who are regarded as 'These are good and virtuous people.' 'Bahujanassa' (of the manyfolk) refers to both the unlearned, blind, foolish worldlings and the wise, discerning people. Among them, the foolish people regard the sectarian teachers as virtuous, while the wise people regard the Tathāgata as virtuous. In this way, the meaning of the words 'Pūraṇa Kassapa is a saṅghī' and so forth should be understood. As for the Blessed One, because he analyzed the thirty-eight objects of meditation and created many 'fords' (tittha) for entering Nibbāna, it is appropriate to call him 'Titthakara' (The Ford-Maker).

Why did all those teachers gather there? It was to protect their attendants and to obtain gains and honor. For those teachers had this thought: 'If our attendants go to the ascetic Gotama for refuge, we will protect them. Seeing the honor paid by the attendants of the ascetic Gotama, our own attendants will also pay honor to us.' Therefore, wherever the Blessed One stayed, all those teachers also followed and gathered there.

'Vādaṃ āropetvā' means pointing out a fault in a doctrine. 'Apakkantā' means having departed; some departed to another region, some returned to the lay life, and some entered this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Sahitaṃ me' means my words are consistent, coherent, and endowed with meaning and reason. 'Asahitaṃ te' means your words are not consistent. 'Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ' means that which you have practiced and mastered for a long time has been overturned and destroyed by just one word of mine; nothing remains. This is the meaning. 'Āropito te vādo' means I have [pointed out a fault] in your doctrine...
165: A fault has been charged. 'Go about to release yourself from the doctrine' means go here and there to learn in order to be released from the fault. 'If you are able, resolve it right now' means if you are personally capable, provide an explanation now. 'Dhammakkosena' means by way of natural abuse. 'We shall listen to that Dhamma' means we shall listen to that Dhamma taught to us. 'Khuddamadhu' is honey on a branch (daṇḍakamadhu) made by small bees. 'Anelakaṃ' is pure honey, free from bee larvae and pollen. 'Pīḷeyya' means one should squeeze and give. 'Paccāsīsamānarūpo' describes one who has the appearance of standing and waiting, holding a vessel in hand, hoping, 'Will they fill our vessel and give almsfood?' 'Sampayojetvā' means having engaged in a slight dispute. 'Itaritarena' means with whatever inferior requisites. 'Pavivitto' (secluded): The wanderer says this referring only to physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), but the Blessed One is secluded by all three types of seclusion (viveka). 'Kosakāhārā': In donors' houses, there are small bowls for setting aside the first portion of food. Donors eat after placing the first portion there, and when monks arrive, they give that food. That small bowl is called a 'kosaka'. Therefore, those who subsist on just one such bowl of food are called 'kosakāhārā'. 'Beluvāhārā' are those who eat food only the size of a bael fruit. 'Samatittikaṃ' means being level with the lower rim of the bowl's edge. 'By this Dhamma' means by this practice of eating little food. In this context, the Blessed One should not be called one who eats little in every respect. During the six years of great exertion (padhānabhūmi), he indeed ate very little. In the city of Verañjā, he subsisted for three months on just a handful of steamed grain. In the Pālileyyaka forest, he subsisted for three months on only lotus stalks and roots. However, the meaning intended in this sutta is: 'I was one who ate little only at one time, but my disciples, from the time they undertook the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), do not break them for as long as they live.' Therefore, if those disciples were to respect me because of this practice of eating little, they would be even more exceptional than I in that regard. But he shows that there is also another reason why they respect me. In this manner, the connection of meaning should be understood in all remaining sections.
166:
Paṃsukūlikā are those who undertake the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes. Lūkhacīvaradharā are those who wear coarse robes cut and sewn with needles and knives. Nantakāni refers to pieces of cloth without borders; for if those pieces had borders, they would be called pilotikā (rags). Uccinitvā means picking out the strong parts and discarding the weak parts after tearing the cloth. Alābulomasāni indicates delicate robes with threads like the fuzz of a gourd seed. By this much, it should not be said that the Teacher lacks contentment with robes. For on the day he took the rag-robe made of hemp, which had been used as a shroud and discarded by the slave girl named Puṇṇā in the Atimuttaka cemetery, the great earth shook as far as the water's edge. In this sutta, however, the intended meaning is: 'I took a rag-robe only at one time, but my disciples, from the time they undertook the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.'

Piṇḍapātikā are those who reject extra gains and undertake the ascetic practice of eating only almsfood. Sapadānacārino are those who reject greedy wandering (loluppacāra) and undertake the practice of house-to-house almsround. Uñchāsake vate ratā means delighting in the natural practice of monks known as wandering for alms; it means they stand at the doors of houses, whether high or low, collect mixed food, and consume it. Antaraghara (inside the village): Although the Brahmāyu Sutta says it is from the threshold, in this sutta it is intended to mean from the gatepost (indakhīla). By this much, it should not be said that the Teacher lacks contentment with almsfood; everything should be understood in detail according to the method already mentioned regarding eating little food. In this sutta, however, the intended meaning is: 'I did not accept invited food only at one time, but my disciples, from the time they undertook the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.'

Rukkhamūlikā are those who reject covered dwellings and undertake the ascetic practice of living at the foot of a tree. Abbhokāsikā are those who reject both covered dwellings and the foot of a tree and undertake the ascetic practice of living in the open air. Aṭṭhamāse refers to the eight months of the winter and summer seasons. During the three months of the rainy season, however, they enter covered dwellings to protect their robes. By this much, it should not be said that the Teacher lacks contentment with lodgings; the Teacher's contentment with lodgings should be shown by his six years of great exertion and his stay in the Pālileyyaka forest. In this sutta, however, the intended meaning is: 'I did not enter a covered dwelling only at one time, but my disciples, from the time they undertook the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.'
167:
"Āraññika" refers to one who rejects a monastery near a village and undertakes the forest-dweller's practice (āraññaka-dhutaṅga). The phrase "descending into the midst of the Saṅgha" is spoken in relation to an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā); however, those living in a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) perform the Uposatha only in their own place of residence. By this much, it should not be said that the Teacher does not resort to seclusion. As he said, "Monks, I wish to go into seclusion for half a month," the Teacher's seclusion is very clear. In this sutta, however, it is intended to show: "Even though I go into seclusion only at such times, my disciples, from the time they undertake the dhutaṅga practices, do not break them for as long as they live." "Mamam sāvakā" means "my disciples."

"Sanidānaṃ" means being with a cause. It is not that he does not teach Nibbāna, which is without a cause; he teaches that Dhamma of Nibbāna also with a cause, not causelessly. "Sappāṭihāriyaṃ" is a synonym for the former and means "with a reason." In "taṃ vata," "vata" is merely a particle.

"Anāgataṃ vādapathaṃ" refers to the path of discourse that will come in the future regarding various questions—excluding today—tomorrow, the day after, in half a month, a month, or a year, etc. "Na dakkhati" (will not see): just as Saccaka Nigaṇṭha did not see the reason for his own defeat even when it was spoken specifically, there is no such case where the Blessed One does not see. "Sahadhammena" means with a reason. "Antarantarā kathaṃ opāteyyu" means "interrupting the sequence of my discourse to insert their own words in between." "Udāyi, even while I am engaged in great debates on doctrines with Ambaṭṭha, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, Saccaka Nigaṇṭha, and others, I do not teach the disciples with such an expectation as: 'Oh, if only one of my disciples would bring forward a simile or a reason!' In such situations, the disciples expect only the instruction and advice of the Blessed One."

I satisfy their minds by answering their questions; I win over, fulfill, and complete their minds; I do not answer one thing when asked another, like answering "star-fruit" (labuja) when asked about "mango" (amba), or "mango" when asked about "star-fruit." Here, in the context of "they honor [him] for higher virtue," it refers to the Buddha's virtue (Buddha-sīla). "Abhikkante..."
168:
In the context of "they honor [him] for knowledge and vision," it refers to Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). In the context of "they honor [him] for higher wisdom," it refers to situational wisdom (thānuppattika-paññā). In the context of "by which suffering," it refers to the wisdom that explains the Four Noble Truths (sacca-byākaraṇa-paññā). Among these three, excluding Omniscience and the wisdom explaining the Truths, the remaining wisdom belongs to the category of higher wisdom (adhipaññā).

Now, wishing to show the practice for attaining those various distinctions, he spoke again: "Furthermore, Udāyi," and so on. In that text, "abhiññāvosānapāramippattā" means having reached the Fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of the six direct knowledges and the reaching of the further shore of the six direct knowledges.

"Sammappadhāne" refers to strategic effort (upāyapadhāna). "Generates desire" (chandaṃ janeti) means generating a wholesome desire to act. "Strives" (vāyamati) means making an effort. "Arouses energy" (vīriyaṃ ārabhati) means bringing energy into play. "Upholds the mind" (cittaṃ paggaṇhāti) means lifting up the mind. "Exerts" (padahati) means performing strategic effort. "For the fulfillment of development" (bhāvanāya pāripūriyā) means for the sake of completing the growth. Furthermore, in these Right Efforts, according to the Vibhaṅga: "That which is stability is non-confusion (asammosa)... that which is abundance is the fulfillment of development (bhāvanāpāripūrī)." Thus, it should be understood that the preceding term is the meaning of the succeeding term.

What is taught by these Right Efforts? According to the method of the Kassapa Saṃyutta, it is the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā) of a disciple before the Path. It is said there:
"Friends, there are these four Right Efforts. Which four? Here, friends, a monk reflects, 'If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, they would lead to my harm,' and he makes a strenuous effort. He reflects, 'If arisen evil, unwholesome states in me are not abandoned, they would lead to my harm,' and he makes a strenuous effort. He reflects, 'If unarisen wholesome states do not arise in me, it would lead to my harm,' and he makes a strenuous effort. He reflects, 'If arisen wholesome states in me were to cease, it would lead to my harm,' and he makes a strenuous effort."

Here, "evil, unwholesome states" refers to greed and so on. "Unarisen wholesome states" refers to serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the Path (magga). "Arisen wholesome states" refers only to serenity and insight. As for the Path, although it arises once and then ceases, [it does not lead] to harm...
169:
The Path (Magga) does not arise for the sake of harm (when it ceases after arising once). This is because that Path ceases only after giving the cause for Fruition (Phala). Alternatively, although it was said in the previous sentence that only tranquillity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) should be taken, such a statement is not appropriate.

Among those samatha-vipassanā, there is this story as an illustration to clarify the meaning: "Arisen tranquillity and insight, when they cease, arise for the sake of harm." It is said that an Elder who was an Arahant (khīṇāsava), intending to worship the Mahācetiya and the Mahābodhi, arrived at the Mahāvihāra from the countryside together with a novice (sāmaṇera) who was a storekeeper and an attainer of meditative absorptions (samāpatti), and entered the monastery precinct. In the evening, while the great community of monks was worshipping the Cetiya, the Elder did not go out to worship. Why? Because Arahants have great reverence for the Triple Gem. Therefore, when the community of monks had finished worshipping and returned, at the time when people were having their evening meal, he went out alone to worship the Cetiya without letting even the novice know. The novice, thinking, "Why is the Elder going out alone at an unseasonable time? I shall find out," followed closely in the footsteps of his preceptor. The Elder, not reflecting and thus unaware of his coming, ascended to the courtyard of the Cetiya by the southern gate. The novice also ascended immediately after him.

The Great Elder, looking up at the Mahācetiya, aroused rapture (pīti) having the Buddha as its object, and with his mind fully concentrated on all the qualities, worshipped the Cetiya with great joy and delight. When the novice saw the Elder's manner of worship, he thought, "My preceptor is worshipping with an extremely devout mind; would he perform an offering if he obtained flowers?" After worshipping, the Elder stood up and remained looking at the Mahācetiya with his hands clasped in reverence over his head. The novice cleared his throat to let his presence be known. The Elder turned around, looked, and asked, "When did you arrive?" "I have been here since the time you were worshipping the Cetiya, Bhante. You worshipped the Cetiya with such great devotion; would you like to make an offering if you obtained flowers?" "Indeed, novice, there is no other place where such a vast enshrinement of relics exists as in this Cetiya. Who would not worship such an incomparable Mahācetiya if they obtained flowers?" "In that case, Bhante, please wait a moment; I shall bring them," he said. Immediately entering into meditative absorption (jhāna), he went to the Himavanta by psychic power (iddhi), filled his water-strainer (parissāvana) with flowers endowed with color and fragrance, and returned before the Great Elder had even moved from the southern side to the western side. Placing the water-strainer full of flowers in the Elder's hand, he said, "Please make the offering, Bhante." The Elder said, "Novice, these flowers are very few for us." "Go ahead, Bhante, and worship by reflecting on the qualities of the Blessed One," the novice replied.
170:
The Elder ascended by the staircase on the western side and began to offer the flowers on the terrace of the inner railing. The flowers that overflowed on the railing terrace fell down and filled the second terrace up to knee-height. Descending from there, he offered them at the row of the base pedestal, and that area also became full. Knowing it was full, he went along scattering flowers on the lower courtyard. The entire courtyard of the Cetiya became filled. When it was thus filled, he said, "Novice, the flowers are not exhausted." "Bhante, turn the water-strainer upside down," the novice replied. When he turned it upside down and shook it, only then were the flowers exhausted. Having given the water-strainer back to the novice, the Elder performed three circumambulations of the Cetiya including the elephant-wall, worshipped at the four sides, and while returning to the monastery precinct, he thought: "How great is the psychic power of this novice! Will he be able to protect this power?" Then, seeing that "He will not be able to," he said to the novice: "Novice, you are now of great psychic power, but after losing such power, in the future you will drink sour gruel (kañjiya) mixed by the hand of a one-eyed weaver woman." This is the natural fault of the young. Although the novice was startled by his preceptor's words, he did not request, "Bhante, please teach me a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)," but went along as if not hearing, thinking, "What is our preceptor talking about?"

After worshipping the Mahācetiya and the Mahābodhi, the Elder had the novice take the bowl and robes and gradually proceeded to the Kuṭeḷitissa Mahāvihāra. The novice, following in the footsteps of his preceptor, would not go for alms-round himself, but after asking, "Bhante, which village will you enter?" and knowing, "Now my preceptor will have reached the village gate," he would take his own and his preceptor's bowl and robes, travel through the air, hand the bowl and robes to the Elder, and then enter for alms. The Elder would constantly advise him: "Novice, do not do this. The psychic power of a worldling (puthujjaniddhi) is unstable and not permanent; it is destroyed by even a little thing upon encountering unsuitable objects such as visible forms. If the attained meditative absorptions are lost, one cannot maintain the holy life (brahmacariyavāsa)." The novice, not wishing to listen, thinking, "What is my preceptor saying?" continued to act as before. The Elder, while visiting Cetiyas in succession, arrived at the Kammubindu Vihāra. Even while the Elder resided at that monastery, the novice continued to act in the same manner.
171:
Then one day, a very beautiful weaver's daughter in her youth left Kammabindu village, went down to Padumma Lake, and picked flowers while singing. While she was singing, a novice monk was traveling through the air above Padumma Lake; he became attached to the sound of her singing, like a blind fly stuck in resin. At that very moment, the novice's psychic power disappeared, and he became like a crow with clipped wings. However, by the power of his peaceful meditative attainments, he did not fall into the water but drifted down like silk-cotton and landed gradually on the shore of Padumma Lake. The novice went quickly, handed over his bowl and robes to his preceptor, and returned. The Great Elder thought, "I have seen this beforehand; even if forbidden, he will not turn back," and without saying a word, he entered the village for alms.

The novice went and stood on the shore of Padumma Lake, waiting for the girl to come out of the water.
