The girl, seeing the novice traveling through the air and then returning to stand there, realized, "Surely this novice has become dissatisfied with the monkhood because of me," and said, "Novice, please step aside for a moment." The novice stepped aside. The girl came out of the water, dressed herself, approached the novice, and asked, "Venerable sir, what is the matter?" The novice told her the situation. Although the girl advised him by showing the disadvantages of household life and the advantages of living the holy life through many reasons, she was unable to dispel his dissatisfaction. Thinking, "This novice has lost such psychic power because of me; it is no longer proper to abandon him," she said, "Stay right here," went home, and told the news to her parents.

The parents also came and gave various advice, but when the novice would not listen to their words, they said, "Do you think we are of a noble caste? We are weavers. Will you be able to do the work of a weaver?" The novice replied, "Lay devotee, once one becomes a layman, one must do weaving or mat-weaving; why do you show greed for just this piece of cloth?" The weaver gave him a cloth to wear around his waist, took him home, and gave him his daughter.

He learned the craft of weaving and worked in the hall with other weavers. The wives of others prepared and brought food early in the morning, but his wife had not yet arrived. While the others stopped work and were eating, he sat turning the shuttle. She arrived late. Then he...
172:
He threatened her, saying, "You have come very late." It is the nature of a woman that once she knows a man's heart is attached to her, she regards even a universal monarch as a slave. Therefore, she said, "In other people's houses, wood, vegetables, salt, and so on are stored; there are also people who bring and deliver things from outside. But I am all alone. You do not even know what is present or absent in my house. If you want to eat, eat; if you do not want to eat, do not eat."

He became angry, thinking, "Not only does she bring food when the sun is high, but she also offends me with her words." Finding no other weapon to strike with, he pulled the shuttle rod from the shuttle and threw it. The woman saw the shuttle rod coming and turned her face slightly. The tip of the shuttle rod was very sharp; as she turned her face, it pierced the corner of her eye. Although she quickly held her eye with both hands, blood flowed from the wound. At that time, he remembered the words his preceptor had once spoken: "In the future, you will drink sour gruel pressed by the hands of a blind weaver woman." He thought, "The teacher must have said this with this event in mind; oh, how great is my lord's foresight!" and began to cry loudly. Others said to him, "Friend, do not cry; once an eye is destroyed, it cannot be restored to its original state just by crying." He replied, "I am not crying because of the destruction of this eye; rather, I cry because I remember what my teacher said regarding this matter," and he told the whole story in sequence. Thus, when the developed tranquility and insight cease, they lead to misfortune.

Another story: Thirty monks, after paying homage to the Kalyāṇī Great Stūpa, were descending from a forest path to the main road when they saw a man returning from working in a burnt field along the way. His body looked as if it were smeared with ink. He was wearing a single bark-dyed cloth, tucked up at the waist, which also looked as if it were smeared with ink; when looked at, he appeared like a burnt stump. Having worked during the day, he was carrying a bundle of firewood that was still smoldering, and with his hair disheveled, he came from the side of the road and stood in front of the monks. When the novices saw him, they looked at one another and, laughing, went and asked, "Friend, is this your father? Your grandfather? Your uncle?" and then asked, "Lay devotee, what is your name?" Being asked his name, he became displeased and [dropped] the bundle of firewood...
173:
(The farmer) discarded the bundle of firewood, adjusted his clothes, and after paying homage to the senior elders, said, "Please wait a moment, venerable sirs." The senior elders stopped.

Young novices came and mocked him even in the presence of the senior elders. The lay devotee said, "Venerable sirs, you see me and mock me; do not think that by this much you have reached the summit. I too was once a monk like you. In you, there is not even a trace of one-pointedness of mind, but I once possessed great psychic power and great majesty in this Dispensation. I could take the sky and make it earth, and take the earth and make it sky. I could make the far near, and the near far. I could penetrate a hundred thousand world-systems in an instant. Look at my hands; now they are like the hands of a monkey, but with these very hands, while sitting right here, I have touched the moon and the sun. With these very feet, I have sat using the moon and the sun as a footstool. Such psychic power has vanished due to negligence; venerable sirs, do not be negligent. Through negligence, one may encounter such ruin. Only those who live without negligence can make an end of birth, aging, and death. Therefore, venerable sirs, taking even me as an object of reflection, be diligent." Thus he warned and gave them advice. Even as he was speaking, those thirty monks were moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and, developing insight, attained Arahantship right there. Thus, it should be understood that even arisen serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), if they cease, can lead to disadvantage.

In the phrase "anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ" (of unarisen evil states), the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Sabbāsava Sutta, such as "the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise," and so on. In the phrase "uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ" (of arisen evil states), however, "arisen" (uppanna) is of four types: presently arisen (vattamānuppanna), arisen by having been and gone (bhutvāvigatuppanna), arisen by opportunity (okāsakatuppanna), and arisen by obtaining a ground (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Among these four, those defilements that are currently existing and are endowed with the moment of arising, etc., are called "presently arisen." When kamma has run through its seven impulsions (javana) and has experienced the taste of the object, the resultant consciousness that has ceased is called "arisen by having been and gone" (bhutvā-vigata). Kamma that has arisen and then ceased is called "arisen by having become and gone" (bhavitvā-vigata). Both of these are classified as "arisen by having been and gone" (bhutvāvigatuppanna). Wholesome or unwholesome kamma may obstruct the result of another kamma and create an opportunity for its own result; when an opportunity is thus made, the resultant that arises is called "arisen" from the time the opportunity was made. This is called "arisen by opportunity" (okāsakatuppanna).

The five aggregates are called the "ground" (bhūmi) of insight. These aggregates are distinguished as past, and so on. The latent tendencies (anusaya) lying within those aggregates, however, should not be called past, future, or present. For the latent tendencies lying within the past aggregates are simply unabandoned; in the future aggregates...
174:
...the latent tendencies lying within the present aggregates are also simply unabandoned. This is called "arisen by obtaining a ground" (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Therefore, the ancient teachers said: "The uneradicated defilements in those various planes (bhūmi) are known as 'arisen by obtaining a ground'."

There are another four types of "arisen" (uppanna): arisen through active occurrence (samudācāruppanna), arisen through being obsessed with an object (ārammaṇādhigahituppanna), arisen through not being suppressed (avikkhambhituppanna), and arisen through not being eradicated (asamugghātituppanna). Among these four, only the defilement currently occurring is called "arisen through active occurrence." It cannot be said that defilements will not arise in the moments of repeated recollection once the eyes have been opened and a sign has been taken in an object. Why? Because the object has been obsessed over. Like what? Just as it cannot be said that milk (latex) will not come out from whatever place a milk-tree is struck with an axe. This is called "arisen through being obsessed with an object." It cannot be said that defilements not yet suppressed by meditative attainment will not arise in such and such a place. Why? Because they have not been suppressed. Like what? Just as if one were to strike a milk-tree with an axe, it cannot be said that milk will not come out in such and such a place. This is called "arisen through not being suppressed." Defilements not yet eradicated by the Path can arise even in one who is reborn in the peak of existence (bhavagga); this should be elaborated according to the previous method. This is called "arisen through not being eradicated."

Among these eight types of "arisen" (defilements), the four types—presently arisen, arisen by having been and gone, arisen by opportunity, and arisen through active occurrence—are not to be abandoned by the Path. The four types—arisen by obtaining a ground, arisen through being obsessed with an object, arisen through not being suppressed, and arisen through not being eradicated—are the states to be abandoned by the Path. For when the Path arises, it abandons these defilements. Those defilements which the Path abandons should not be called past, future, or present. This has also been said:

"If it abandons past defilements, then it exhausts what is already exhausted, ceases what has already ceased, makes vanish what has already vanished, and makes disappear what has already disappeared. It would be abandoning the past which does not exist. If it abandons future defilements, then it abandons what is not yet born, what has not yet been produced, what has not yet arisen, and what has not yet become manifest. It would be abandoning the future which does not exist. If it abandons present defilements, then one who is lustful would be abandoning lust, one who is hateful would be abandoning hatred, one who is deluded would be abandoning delusion, one who is proud would be abandoning pride, one who misapprehends would be abandoning wrong view, one who is distracted would be abandoning restlessness, one who is indecisive would be abandoning doubt, and one who has reached the strength (of defilements) would be abandoning latent tendencies. Dark and bright states would occur simultaneously as a pair. The development of the Path would be accompanied by defilement... (pe)... In that case, there would be no development of the Path, no realization of the Fruit, no abandoning of defilements, and no breakthrough to the Dhamma."
175:
There is the development of the Path... (p)... there is the realization of the Dhamma. How is this so? It is like a young tree that has not yet produced fruit... (p)... those fruits that have not yet appeared simply do not appear.

In this way, the simile of the tree that has not yet produced fruit appears in the Pali text. However, it should be illustrated by a tree that has fruit. To illustrate clearly: suppose there is a young mango tree with fruit. People might consume the fruits of that young mango tree and fill baskets by shaking down the remaining fruits. Afterwards, another man might cut down that mango tree with an axe. By that cutting, the past fruits of that young tree are not destroyed, nor are the future or present fruits destroyed. Indeed, the past fruits have already been consumed by people, and the future fruits have not yet arisen, so they cannot be destroyed. As for not destroying the present fruits: at the time the tree is cut, there are no fruits at all, and thus the present fruits are also not destroyed.

However, if the young tree were not cut, then, depending on the essence of the earth and the essence of the water, whatever fruits would have been produced—those are the ones that are destroyed. Indeed, those fruits that have not yet been born simply do not take birth; those that have not yet arisen simply do not arise; those that have not yet appeared simply do not appear. In the very same way, the Path neither abandons defilements (kileśas) classified as past and so on, nor does it not abandon them. In truth, if the aggregates (khandhas) were not fully understood by the Path, those defilements would arise; but because the Path has arisen and the aggregates are fully understood, those defilements that have not yet been born simply do not take birth; those that have not yet arisen simply do not arise; those that have not yet appeared simply do not appear. This meaning should also be illustrated by the medicines taken by a woman with a young son to prevent further birth, and by those who are afflicted by disease to appease their illness.

Thus, the Path abandons those defilements; those defilements should not be called past, future, or present. It is not that the Path does not abandon defilements; it certainly abandons them. However, it is in reference to those defilements which the Path abandons that the words "uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ" (of arisen evil states) and so forth were spoken.

Furthermore, the Path does not only abandon defilements; it also abandons those grasped-at aggregates (upādinnaka-khandhas) which would have arisen because the defilements had not yet been abandoned. This has also been stated, and the details should be understood: "By the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, through the cessation of kammic-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa), whatever mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) would have arisen in the beginningless saṃsāra, setting aside seven existences—these cease right here." In this way, the Path emerges from grasped-at and non-grasped-at states. In terms of existence (bhava), the Path of Stream-entry emerges from the plane of misery (apāya-bhava); the Path of Once-returning emerges from a portion of the happy plane of existence; the Path of Non-returning emerges from the happy sensual plane of existence.
176:
The Path of Arahantship emerges from the fine-material and immaterial planes of existence. Some teachers also say that it emerges from all planes of existence.

If that is so, how is there development (bhāvanā) for the arising of unarisen wholesome states at the moment of the Path, or how is there development for the stability of arisen states? It is through the occurrence of the Path itself. Indeed, when the Path occurs, it is called 'unarisen' because it has never occurred before. Just as people who reach a place they have never reached before, or experience an object they have never experienced before, say, "We have reached an unreached place, we are experiencing an unexperienced object." And the very occurrence of this Path is called 'stability'; therefore, it is also appropriate to say that it develops for the sake of stability.

Brief talk regarding the Bases of Power (iddhipādas) was mentioned in the Cetokhila Sutta. It is called 'upasamagāmī' because it goes towards Nibbāna while calming the defilements, or because it goes for the sake of calming the defilements. It is called 'sambodhagāmī' because it goes towards Nibbāna while realizing the Four Noble Truths, or because it goes for the sake of penetrating with Path-knowledge.

The states such as 'dependent on seclusion' (vivekanissita) and so forth were explained in the Sabbāsava Sutta. This is just a summary here; the detailed explanation of the Factors of Enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-kathā) was stated in the Visuddhimagga.

In the discussion on Liberations (vimokkha-kathā), in what sense is it called 'vimokkha'? It is called 'vimokkha' in the sense of being intent upon the object (adhimuccanaṭṭha). What is this 'adhimuccanaṭṭha'? It means the sense of being well-released from opposing states and the sense of being well-immersed in the object by way of delight. It means occurring in the object with a sense of security and without restraint, like the sleeping of a child who has relaxed his limbs in his father's lap. However, this meaning does not exist in the last liberation; it exists in all the preceding ones. In the passage 'Possessing form, one sees forms' (rūpī rūpāni passati), 'form' (rūpa) refers to the fine-material jhana produced by way of the blue kasiṇa and so forth on internal parts such as hair; one who has that jhana is 'one possessing form' (rūpī). 'One sees external forms' means one sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa with the jhana-eye. By this, the four fine-material jhanas of a person who has produced jhana on kasiṇas that have internal and external bases are shown.

'Internally perceiving no form' (ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī) means one who does not perceive form internally; the meaning is a person who has not produced fine-material jhana on his own hair and so forth. By this, the fine-material jhanas of a person who, having performed the preliminary work externally, produces jhana only externally, are shown. By the passage 'One is intent only on the beautiful' (subhanteva adhimutto hoti), the jhanas occurring in very pure color kasiṇas such as the blue kasiṇa are shown. Therein, although in the midst of absorption...
177:
Although there is no reflection of 'it is beautiful' within the absorption-impulsion (appanā-javana), because a person dwells having made a very pure beautiful-kasina (subha-kasiṇa) their object, they reach a state where it can be said they are 'resolved on the beautiful'; thus this teaching was given. However, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said: "How is it a liberation resolved only on the beautiful? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... because of the development of loving-kindness, beings are not repulsive (beautiful). He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, with appreciative joy, with equanimity... because of the development of equanimity, beings are not repulsive. Thus it is a liberation resolved only on the beautiful."

All that should be said regarding the passages beginning with 'sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ' has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. 'This is the eighth liberation' means this is called the eighth and supreme liberation because of the complete relinquishment and liberation from the four mental aggregates.

In the discussion on the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana-kathā), 'abhibhāyatanāni' refers to the factors that are causes for overcoming. What do they overcome? They overcome both the opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the objects. These bases of mastery overcome the opposing hindrances by being their opposites, and they overcome the objects through the superiority of the person's knowledge. In the passages beginning with 'perceiving form internally' (ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī), one is called 'perceiving form internally' by virtue of performing the preliminary work (parikamma) on one's own internal form. One who performs the preliminary work on blue (nīla-parikamma) internally does so on the hair, the bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on yellow (pīta-parikamma) does so on the fat, the skin, the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on red (lohita-parikamma) does so on the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on white (odāta-parikamma) does so on the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. However, that object such as the hair is not perfectly blue, perfectly yellow, perfectly red, or perfectly white; it is indeed impure.

'Alone, he sees forms externally' (eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati) means that for someone, the preliminary work occurs internally, but the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) occurs externally; such a person is said to be 'perceiving form internally, alone he sees forms externally' by virtue of the internal preliminary work and the external absorption (appanā). 'Limited' (parittāni) means signs that are not expanded. 'Beautiful or ugly' (suvaṇṇa-dubbaṇṇāni) means whether they are of good color or bad color, it should be understood that this base of mastery is spoken of only in terms of being limited.
178:
"Overcoming those forms" (tāni abhibhuyya) means, for example, just as a person with good digestion (or a large stomach), upon receiving a mere ladleful of rice, thinks "What is there here to eat?" and gathering it together, makes it into a single mouthful. In the same way, a person with superior knowledge and clear wisdom thinks, "What is there here in this limited object to attain? This is no burden for me," and overcoming those forms, they enter the attainment. It means they reach absorption (appanā) in that object as soon as the sign arises. By the words "he knows and sees," his reflection (ābhoga) is described; and that reflection occurs only for one who has emerged from the attainment, not within the attainment. "He is one who has such a perception" means he has such a perception either through the perception of reflection or through the perception of jhāna. For him, the perception of overcoming exists within the attainment, but the perception of reflection exists only upon emerging from the attainment.

"Immeasurable" (appamāṇāni) means signs that have been expanded and are large. In this context, "overcoming" is like a gluttonous man who, upon receiving a tray of rice, thinks "Let there be another, and another; what can this much rice do for me?" and does not regard that tray of rice as large. In the same way, a person with superior knowledge and clear wisdom thinks, "What is there here to attain? This is not immeasurable; it is no burden for me in producing one-pointedness of mind," and overcoming those signs, they enter the attainment. It means they reach absorption in that object as soon as the sign arises.

"Not perceiving form internally" (ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī) refers to one who is devoid of the preliminary perception (parikamma-saññā) of internal forms, either because of not obtaining it or because of not desiring it. "Alone, he sees forms externally" means that for someone, both the preliminary work and the sign arise only externally; such a person is said to be "not perceiving form internally, alone he sees forms externally" by virtue of the external preliminary work and the absorption. The remaining explanation here is the same as that given for the fourth base of mastery. Among these four bases of mastery, the limited (paritta) object comes by way of one with a temperament of initial thought (vitakka-carita). The immeasurable (appamāṇa) object comes by way of one with a temperament of delusion (moha-carita). The beautiful (suvaṇṇa) object comes by way of one with a temperament of hatred (dosa-carita). The ugly (dubbaṇṇa) object comes by way of one with a temperament of greed (rāga-carita). For these persons, these objects are suitable. Their suitability is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the Description of Temperaments (Cariya-niddesa).

In the fifth base of mastery and so on, "blue" (nīlāni) is spoken of by way of inclusive grasping. "Blue-colored" (nīla-vaṇṇāni) is by way of color. "Showing blue" (nīla-nidassanāni) is by way of appearance. The meaning is that they appear as a single blue surface, with no gaps visible and with colors unmixed.
179:
This is the meaning. This word "nīlanibhāsāni" is spoken by way of the radiance of color; it means having a blue radiance or being endowed with blue light. By this, he shows the extreme purity of those bases of mastery (abhibhāyatanas). Indeed, these four bases of mastery are spoken of only by way of pure color. "Umāpupphaṃ" (flax flower): although this flower appears smooth and soft, it is simply blue. However, flowers like the "girikaṇṇikā" (butterfly pea), though appearing blue, have a white nature. Therefore, only this [flax flower] is taken, not those [butterfly pea flowers]. "Bārāṇaseyyakaṃ" means cloth produced in the Bārāṇasī region. In that Bārāṇasī region, the cotton is soft, the spinners and weavers are skilled, and the water is clean and smooth. Therefore, cloth from Bārāṇasī is smooth on both sides; it appears smooth, soft, and sleek on both surfaces. In the words "pītāni" (yellow) and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way. "One learning the blue kasina takes the sign (nimitta) in a blue object, or a flower, or a cloth, or a blue color-element," and so forth—all the methods for creating the kasina, the preliminary work (parikamma), and the procedure for absorption (appanā) have been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Abhiññāvosānapāramippattā" means: those who, having developed those dhammas in the previously mentioned foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on, have reached Arahantship, are called "those who have reached the perfection of the culmination of higher knowledge." However, in these eight bases of mastery (abhibhāyatanas), only those who have attained mastery (vasībhāva) through practice are called "those who have reached the perfection of the culmination of higher knowledge."

In the discussion of kasinas, they are called "kasiṇa" because of the sense of "entirety" (sakala). They are called "āyatanāni" (bases) because they are the field (khetta) or the standing-place (adhiṭṭhāna) for the states (dhammas) that take them as objects. "Uddhaṃ" means facing upwards toward the sky. "Adho" means facing downwards toward the ground. "Tiriyaṃ" means delimiting all around like the circumference of a field. Some practitioners expand the kasina sign only upwards, some downwards, and some all around. For various reasons, one spreads it thus, like one desiring to see a form spreads light. Therefore, it is said: "One perceives the earth kasina upwards, downwards, and across." "Adwayaṃ" means non-duality in the cardinal and intermediate directions. This is said to show that one kasina does not turn into another. Just as for one who has entered water, there is only water in all directions and nothing else, so too, the earth kasina is only the earth kasina; there is no mixing with another kasina. This method applies everywhere. "Appamāṇaṃ" (immeasurable) is said in terms of the immeasurability of the pervading. When pervading it with the mind, one pervades the whole; one does not take a measurement such as "this is the beginning, this is the middle." "Viññāṇakasiṇaṃ" means...
180:
In this consciousness kasina (viññāṇakasiṇa), it refers to the consciousness occurring in the space from which the kasina has been removed (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa). Therein, the state of being "upwards, downwards, and across" should be understood in the space from which the kasina has been removed by means of the kasina, and in the consciousness occurring there by means of the space from which the kasina has been removed. This is the summary here. However, by way of the method of meditation development (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā), these earth kasinas and so on have already been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Here too, it should be understood that they reach the perfection of the culmination of higher knowledge only through attained mastery (vasībhāva). Likewise, in the four jhānas immediately following this. What should be said regarding these four jhānas is to be understood as stated in the Mahā-assapura Sutta. In the case of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), the meaning of terms like "rūpī" has already been stated. Here, "dependent on this (body), bound up with this" means being supported by and bound to this body composed of the four great elements. "Subha" means beautiful (splendid). "Jātimā" means (a gem) arisen from a very pure source. "Suparikammakata" means well-prepared, with stones and grit removed, and smooth. "Accha" means having a thin skin (transparent/clear). "Vippasanna" means very bright/clear. "Sabbākārasampanna" means endowed with all qualities such as washing, piercing, and so on. By the words "nīla" (blue) and so forth, the perfection of color is shown. A thread strung through such (a ruby) is clearly visible.

"Just so"—in this context, the following comparison should be understood: The physical body (karajakāya) is like the ruby. Insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is like the strung thread. The bhikkhu who has attained insight knowledge is like the man with sight. Just as the time when the ruby becomes clear to one who holds it in his palm and reflects, "This is indeed a ruby," so should be understood the time when the physical body composed of the four great elements becomes clear to the bhikkhu who sits having directed his insight knowledge toward it. Just as the time when the thread becomes clear, saying "This thread is strung in that ruby," so should be understood the time when the states beginning with contact as the fifth (phassapañcamaka), or all the consciousness and mental factors, or insight knowledge itself, which take that body as an object, become clear to the bhikkhu who sits having directed his insight knowledge toward it. Does this become clear to the knowledge (ñāṇa) or to the person? It becomes clear to the knowledge; however, because it is clear to that knowledge, it is said to be clear to the person. This insight knowledge occurs immediately after the Path (magga); even so, since there is no intervening turn for this when the turn for higher knowledge (abhiññā) has begun, it is shown right here. And because one who has not yet performed comprehension (sammasana) through the power of impermanence and so on, might hear a terrifying sound with the divine ear element, or might recollect terrifying aggregates with the knowledge of recollection of past lives, or with the divine eye...
181:
Fear and terror arise in one who sees a terrifying form, especially for one who has not practiced contemplation through the lens of impermanence (anicca) and so forth. Therefore, this insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is shown right here (immediately after the fourth jhāna) for the purpose of fulfilling the cause for dispelling fear in one who has attained the superknowledges (abhiññā). In this insight knowledge as well, the attainment of the ultimate perfection of superknowledge (abhiññā-vosāna-pāramippattatā) should be understood only by the power of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala).

In the mind-made power (manomayiddhi), the attainment of the ultimate perfection of superknowledge is understood through the mastery (vasī) that has been practiced. In that context, 'manomaya' means created by the mind. 'Sabbangapaccangi' means complete with all limbs and parts. 'Ahīnindriya' means having sense faculties that are not deficient in form. If the possessor of power is fair-skinned, the form he creates is also fair. If his ears are not pierced, the created form also has unpierced ears. Thus, in every aspect, it is exactly like the creator. The three similes, such as pulling a reed from muñja grass, are mentioned only to show this similarity with the created form. Just as the reed inside the muñja grass is like the muñja grass itself, and the sword is like its scabbard; into a round scabbard, they sheath only a round sword, and into a flat scabbard, only a flat sword.

'Karaṇḍa' is also a name for a snake's slough (skin), not for a wicker basket. A snake's slough is indeed similar to the snake. In that simile, although it is shown as if 'a man would pull a snake out of its slough' with his hands, it should be understood as pulling it out by the mind alone. This is because a snake, remaining in its own nature, relying on the space between wood or trees, discards its slough by itself due to four reasons: by the strength of the effort of pulling its body out from the skin, as if biting its own body, and out of disgust for the old skin. It is not possible for another to pull it out. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to pulling it out by the mind. Thus, the body of this monk is like the muñja grass, and the created form is like the reed; this is the comparison of the similes here. The method of creation and the explanation of the five superknowledges, such as the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha), have been detailed in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga, and should be understood according to the method stated there. Here, only the similes are the additional distinction.

In those similes, the monk who has attained the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power should be regarded as the skilled potter and so forth. The knowledge of the modes of supernormal power should be regarded as the well-prepared clay and so forth. The monk's transformation (vikuubbana) should be regarded as the making of various kinds of vessels as desired. Here too, the attainment of the ultimate perfection of superknowledge should be understood by the power of practiced mastery. Likewise, it should be understood in the other four superknowledges.
182:
Among those (five superknowledges), in the simile for the divine ear element (dibbasota-dhātu), 'saṅkhadhammo' refers to a conch-blower. 'Appakasireneva' means without difficulty (easily). 'Viññāpeyya' means he would make it known. In that simile, just as when there is a conch-blower making it known in the four directions, the time when that conch sound becomes manifest to beings who note, "This is the sound of a conch," so too should be understood the time when divine and human sounds, both distant and near, become manifest to the meditator (yogī).

In the simile for the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa), 'daharo' means a young person. 'Yuvā' means one endowed with the prime of youth. 'Maṇḍanakajātiko' means that although he is young, he is not lazy or one with soiled clothes and body, but rather one who is naturally fond of ornaments, who has the habit of bathing two or three times a day, wearing clean clothes, and adorning himself. 'Sakaṇikaṃ' means (a face) with some defect such as a mole, freckle, blemish, or pimple. In that simile, just as the defect on the face becomes manifest to one who reflects on the image of his own face, even so, it should be understood that the sixteen types of minds of others become manifest to the monk who sits having directed his mind toward the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others. All that should be said regarding the similes for the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa) and so forth has already been stated in the Mahā-assapura Sutta.

In the phrase 'Ayaṃ kho udāyi pañcamo dhammo' (This, Udāyi, is the fifth Dhamma), nineteen factors are made into one Dhamma by way of the practice and called the 'fifth Dhamma.' Just as in the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta eleven factors are made into one Dhamma by way of questioning, so here nineteen factors should be understood as being made into one Dhamma by way of the practice. Among these nineteen factors, in the eight groups in sequence, and in insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), the attainment of the perfection of the end of superknowledge should be understood by the power of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala). In the remaining factors, it should be understood by the power of practiced mastery (vasībhāva). All the rest is clear in meaning.

## The Commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
183:
## 8. Commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta. In that sutta, "Uggāhamāna" is the name of that wanderer. "Sumana" is his natural name. However, because he is capable of learning (uggahituṃ) and teaching (uggāhetuṃ) a little at a time, he is known as "Uggāhamāna."

It is called "Samayappavādaka" because doctrines (samaya) are discussed (pavādanti) here. In that place, it is said that Brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, as well as ascetics such as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and Wanderers, gather and state, clarify, and demonstrate their own doctrines. Therefore, that park is called "Samayappavādaka."

That same park is called "Tindukācīra" because it is surrounded by a row of Tinduka trees, known as Tindukācīra. In this park, there was originally only one hall; later, many halls were built depending on the highly meritorious Wanderer Poṭṭhapāda. Therefore, it is called "Ekasalaka" (Single-hall) by the name obtained based on that one hall. It is known as "Mallikā’s Monastery" because it was the garden of Queen Mallikā, the queen of King Pasenadi, and was a park covered with flowers and fruits. [The phrase means] in that Mallikā’s Monastery, which has a single hall, a row of Tinduka trees, and is a place for discussing doctrines.

"Paṭivasati" means he dwells for the sake of comfortable living. "Divā divassa" refers to the time after the midday of the day has passed. It means he came out just after midday, which is the daytime of the day. "Paṭisallīno" means he is withdrawn, having pulled back the mind from various sense objects such as forms, and has attained solitude by way of practicing delight in meditation (jhāna). "Manobhāvanīyānaṃ" refers to the monks who develop the mind; for one who reflects and attends to them, the mind becomes free from hindrances, uplifted, and developed. "Yāvatā" means as many as. "Ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataro" means this person is one of the disciples within that group. "Appeva nāma" is said by one desiring to approach him. The reason for desiring to approach has already been stated in the Sandaka Sutta.

"Etadavoca": The householder [Pañcakaṅga], thinking "This person is of dull wisdom; I will win him over with a Dhamma talk and make him my disciple," said these words beginning with "Catuhi kho." In that context, "Panyapemi" means I show or establish. "Sampannakusala" means one possessed of complete wholesomeness. "Paramakusala" means one of supreme wholesomeness. "Ayojjha" means unshakeable, immovable, and firm, such that one cannot be moved by being fought in a debate.
184:
"Not doing" (na karoti) means mere non-action. Here, it does not mean abandonment through restraint (saṃvarappahāna) or abandonment through use (paṭisevanappahāna). The same method applies to the remaining terms.

"Neither delighted" (neva abhinandi) means he did not delight (did not accept), considering that wanderers, whether they know or not, speak whatever they please. "Nor rejected" (na paṭikkosi) means he did not prohibit it, considering that he speaks as if in accordance with the Dispensation (Sāsana) or as if showing faith in the Dispensation.

According to the words of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, an infant who can only lie on its back would be an invincible ascetic, a firm ascetic. However, we [the Buddha] do not say so. "No sense of body" means there is no specific knowledge such as "my body" or "another's body." "Except for mere movement" means there is only the mere movement of the body due to contact with the folds of the bedding or being bitten by bedbugs. Apart from that movement, there is no action performed by the body. And even that movement occurs only with a mind associated with defilements (kilesa). "No sense of speech" means there is no distinction between wrong speech and right speech. "Mere crying" means there is only mere crying for an infant oppressed by hunger and thirst. That crying also occurs only with a mind associated with defilements. "Thought" also means there is no distinction between wrong thought and right thought. "Mere sound" (vikūjita) means there is only mere crying or laughing. The minds of young infants occur with past objects; those who come from hell cry remembering the suffering of hell, and those who come from the deva world laugh [remembering it]. That crying and laughing also occur only with a mind associated with defilements. "Livelihood" also means there is no distinction between wrong livelihood and right livelihood. "Except for the mother's milk" refers to children known as "milk-thieves" who, while the mother is nursing, do not drink but come from behind and drink the milk when her attention is elsewhere. Apart from this, there is no other wrong livelihood. It is shown that this also occurs only with a mind associated with defilements.

Having thus rejected the wanderer's doctrine, now wishing to establish the outline (mātikā) in the stage of a trainee (sekkhabhūmi), he said "Catuhi kho ahaṃ," etc. In that context, "Samadhigayha tiṭṭhati" means standing pre-eminently. In the phrases "Na kāyena pāpa kammaṃ," etc., it is not just mere non-action; the Blessed One here prescribes restraint, abandonment, and reflection (paṭisaṅkhā).
185:
With reference to that, He said this. The words beginning with "Na ceva sampannakusalaṃ" (Not indeed one who has attained the wholesome), however, were spoken with reference to an Arahant.

Now, wishing to establish the matrix (mātikā) for the stage of one beyond training (asekha), He spoke the words beginning with "Dasa-hi kho ahaṃ" (By ten [qualities], I [declare]...). In that Pali text, the Buddha established the first two tetrads based on three terms, and the last two tetrads based on one term. This is the matrix mentioned regarding the stage of training (sekkhabhūmi).

Now, wishing to analyze that matrix, He spoke the words beginning with "Katame ca thapati akusalasīlā" (And what, Thapati, are unwholesome conducts?). In that Pali text, "sarāgaṃ" (with lust) refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. "Sadosaṃ" (with hate) refers to the two types of consciousness associated with aversion. "Samohaṃ" (with delusion) is appropriate for both the two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness, as well as all unwholesome consciousness. This is because it is said that delusion arises in all unwholesome consciousness. "Ito-samuṭṭhānā" (originating from this) means they are called "ito-samuṭṭhāna" because the arising of these unwholesome states is from these types of consciousness such as those with lust.

"Kuhiṃ" (where) means having reached which place do they cease without remainder? "Etthete" (here these) is in the locative case meaning "in the fruit of Stream-entry" (sotāpattiphala). Indeed, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla) becomes fulfilled in the fruit of Stream-entry; upon reaching that fruit of Stream-entry, unwholesome conduct ceases without remainder. It should also be understood that "akusala-sīla" (unwholesome conduct) is a designation for an immoral person (dussīla).

In the Pali "akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno" (one practicing for the cessation of unwholesome conducts), one is called "practicing for cessation" up until the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga); however, upon reaching the fruit, they are called "those for whom [unwholesome conducts] have ceased."

By the words beginning with "vītarāgaṃ" (faded away is lust), only the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness are spoken of. This is because wholesome conduct arises due to this sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.

"Sīlavā hoti" (he is virtuous) means he is endowed with virtue and endowed with good qualities. "No ca sīlamayo" (but not made of virtue) means one is not "sīlamayo" in the sense of thinking, "This much virtue is enough; there is nothing further to be done beyond this virtue." "Yatthassa te" (where these of his) is in the locative case meaning "in the fruit of Arahantship" (arahattaphala). Indeed, upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, unwholesome conduct ceases without remainder.

In the Pali "nirodhāya paṭipanno" (one practicing for cessation), one is called "practicing for cessation" up until the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga); however, upon reaching the fruit, they are called "those for whom [unwholesome conducts] have ceased."

Among the perceptions of sensual desire (kāma-saññā) and so on, "kāma-saññā" arises together with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed; the remaining two perceptions arise together with the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa).
186:
"First Jhāna" means the first Jhāna associated with the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). In the phrase "here these [states]," "here" is in the locative case meaning "in the fruit of Non-returning." Indeed, upon reaching the fruit of Non-returning, unwholesome intentions (akusala-saṅkappa) cease without remainder. In the phrase "practicing for cessation," one is called "practicing for cessation" up until the path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga); however, upon reaching the fruit, those states are called "ceased." The three perceptions beginning with the perception of renunciation (nekkhamma-saññā) are only those perceptions that arise together with the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.

In the phrase "here these [states]," "here" is in the locative case meaning "in the fruit of Arahantship" (arahattaphala). Indeed, upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship associated with the second Jhāna, wholesome intentions (kusala-saṅkappa) cease without remainder. In the phrase "practicing for cessation," one is called "practicing for cessation" up until the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga); however, upon reaching the fruit, those states are called "ceased." The remaining passages are clear in every respect.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta
The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard) is the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta. In that sutta, the words "Venerable Sir, at whatever time the Blessed One..." were spoken by the wanderer Sakuludāyi, who wished to hear a Dhamma talk and wanted to show his devotion and delight in the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching.

"Let only that matter appear here" means if you wish to hear the Dhamma, let only one question, one reason, appear in your mind. "As it would appear to me" means the reason by which My Dhamma teaching would appear; it shows that when a conversation arises because of this reason, the Dhamma can be taught easily. In the phrase "Venerable Sir, to that me," it is said that the wanderer, seeing that, thought: "If the Blessed One were here, He would make the meaning of this statement clear to me today, as if lighting a thousand lamps." Thus, he recollected only the Buddha, the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala). Therefore, he spoke the words beginning with "Venerable Sir, to that me." In that passage, "Aho nūna" (O that...) are two particles used in the sense of recollection. By those particles, to that wanderer recollecting the Blessed One, this thought occurred: "How wonderful is the Blessed One! How wonderful is the Sugata!" "He who [is skilled] in these teachings" means he who, among these teachings... Very skillful...
187:
The Blessed One is exceedingly skilled, subtle, and wise. If the Blessed One were to teach, oh, how good it would be! If the Sugata were to teach, oh, how good it would be! For to the Blessed One’s knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa), many thousands of crores of aeons appear as clearly as a single courtyard; this is the meaning here.

Regarding "I, concerning the past extremity": One who has attained the higher knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-abhiññā), when told, "In the past, you were a king, you were a brahmin," understands and listens respectfully. However, one who has not attained it, when told, "It will be like this, it will be like that," merely shows a nod of the head. Therefore, He said, "I, concerning the past extremity, would satisfy the mind by answering the question."

Regarding "Or he, concerning me, the future extremity": For one who has attained the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) is perfected; hence He spoke thus. The rest is as previously explained.

Regarding "I will teach you the Dhamma": It is said that this Sakuludāyi the wanderer would not understand even if the past Dhamma were taught, nor would he understand if the future Dhamma were taught. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to teach him the subtle and profound Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), spoke thus. If asked, "Will he understand it?", the answer is: "How could he understand this? He will not." However, seeing that it would serve as a supporting condition (vāsanā) in a future life, the Blessed One spoke thus.

Regarding "Pamsu-pisāca" (earth-ghost): This refers to a ghost born in an impure place. If such a ghost holds a certain medicinal root, it can remain invisible. In this regard, there is this story: A certain yakkhiṇī (ogress) left two children sitting at the gate of the Thūpārāma and went into the city to search for food. Seeing an alms-collecting elder, the children said, "Venerable sir, our mother has entered the city; please tell her, 'Whatever you have obtained, take it and come quickly; the children can no longer endure their hunger.'" The elder asked, "How shall I see her?" They gave him a piece of a medicinal root, saying, "Venerable sir, take this." Thousands of yakkhas became visible to the elder. By the sign given by the children, he saw that yakkhiṇī, who was ugly and loathsome, merely waiting for the impurities of a womb on the street. Having seen her, he told her the matter. When she asked, "How do you see me?", he showed the medicinal root. She snatched it away. Thus, pamsu-pisācas can remain invisible when holding a medicinal root. With reference to that...
188:
He said, "I do not even see a pamsu-pisāca." "Does not appear" means it is not seen, not present to the senses.

Regarding "Udāyi, this [speech] of yours is long": The meaning is, "Udāyi, these words of yours might be long; even if one spoke like this for a hundred or a thousand years, it would not clarify the meaning." "Appāṭihīrakata" means it becomes a speech that is ineffectual, unfounded, and useless.

Now, showing that beauty, he said, "Venerable sir, just as..." and so on. There, "placed on a pale-yellow blanket (paṇḍukambala)" refers to a gem placed on a red blanket of a contrasting color. "The self is of such a color": Sakuludāyi the wanderer says this with reference to the aggregates (khandhas) born in the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm, meaning, "At the time of our death, the self shines like the aggregates in the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm."

Regarding "This is of these two...": It is said that while the radiance of a gem does not go outside, the radiance of a firefly (khajjopanaka) extends for one, two, or four finger-breadths. The radiance of a large firefly even extends to the size of a threshing floor; hence he spoke thus.

"Viddhe" means high up, distant due to the absence of clouds. "Vigata-valāhake" means free from clouds. "Deve" means in the sky. "Osadhi-tārakā" is the star Venus (the morning star). Because people take or drink medicines using that star as a sign from the time it rises, it is called the "medicine star" (osadhi-tārakā). By the phrase "at the time of midnight (abhido aḍḍharattasamayaṃ)", he shows the moon situated in the middle of the sky. The same method applies to the time of midday.

Regarding "Ato kho": It means there are many more than those who experience (the light of the sun and moon); they are both many and much more. "They do not experience the radiance" means they do not use the light of the sun and moon, but live pervading the area with light through the radiance of their own bodies.

Now, although Sakuludāyi sat down thinking, "I will ask about the world of absolute happiness (ekantasukha loka)," he became confused in his questioning. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to remind him of that question, said, "But Udāyi, is there a world of absolute happiness?" and so on.
189:
In that Pali, "ākāravatī" means a practice that has a cause. By the phrase "aññataraṃ vā pana tapoguṇaṃ", it refers to the Acelaka-pāḷi, meaning abstinence from drinking intoxicants.

Why does he ask, "Venerable Sir, what is that ākāravatī practice for absolute happiness?" It is said that Sakuludāyī the wanderer thought: "We speak of absolute happiness for beings, but as for the practice, we speak of it as sometimes happy and sometimes painful. The practice for a world of absolute happiness should itself be absolutely happy. Our words do not lead out [of Saṃsāra]; only the words of the Teacher lead out." Therefore, thinking he would now ask the Teacher to know the truth, he asked the question.

In the phrase "We are ruined in this matter," it means "we are ruined because of that reason." Why did they say this? It is said that in the past, his followers, established in the five dhammas, performed kasiṇa preliminary work, attained the third jhāna, and having died with the jhāna intact, were reborn in the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm. However, as time went by, they no longer knew the kasiṇa preliminary work and were unable to attain the third jhāna. Yet, they had learned the five preliminary dhammas as the "ākāravatī paṭipadā" and the third jhāna as the "ekantasukho loko" (world of absolute happiness). That is why they spoke thus. "Uttaritaraṃ" means they do not know a practice superior to these five dhammas or a world of absolute happiness superior to the third jhāna. "Appasadde katvā" means making the audience silent when they had started making a great noise all at once.

In this Pali, "sacchikiriyāhetu" (for the sake of realization), there are two kinds of realization: realization by attainment (paṭilābha-sacchikiriyā) and realization by direct vision (paccakkha-sacchikiriyā). Among these, attaining the third jhāna and, dying with the jhāna intact, being reborn in the Subhakiṇha world with a lifespan and appearance similar to those devas is called realization by attainment. Attaining the fourth jhāna and going to the Subhakiṇha world through psychic power, standing with those devas, conversing, and engaging in discussion is called realization by direct vision. For both types of realization, the third jhāna is called the ākāravatī paṭipadā (the practice with a cause). This is because without producing that third jhāna, it is impossible to be reborn in the Subhakiṇha world, nor is it possible to produce the fourth jhāna. Thus, referring to these two kinds of realization, he said, "Venerable Sir, for the sake of realizing that world of absolute happiness."
190:
"Udañcanika" refers to a small water pot. "Created an obstacle" means causing harm so that he could not obtain ordination, or causing the destruction of his supporting conditions (upanissaya).

It is said that this Sakuludāyī had ordained and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse during the time of Kassapa Buddha. At that time, a friend of his, a monk who was dissatisfied with the Dispensation, informed him, "Friend, I will disrobe." Sakuludāyī, feeling greed for that monk's bowl and robes, spoke in praise of the lay life. The other monk gave him the bowl and robes and disrobed. Due to that unwholesome kamma, an obstacle to obtaining ordination in the presence of the Blessed One has now arisen.

The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma through the previous sutta and this sutta, which are about one bhāṇavāra (recitation section) in length. Although he did not attain the paths and fruits through this single teaching, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma seeing that it would become a supporting condition for him in the future. Seeing that he would have future benefits, the Blessed One, while still alive, did not appoint any other monk to the foremost position (etadagga) of those who dwell in loving-kindness (mettāvihārī). This is because the Blessed One saw: "In the future, this man will ordain in my Dispensation and become the foremost among those who dwell in loving-kindness."

After the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, during the time of King Dhammāsoka, he was reborn in Pāṭaliputta, ordained, and attained Arahantship, becoming the elder named Assagutta, the foremost among those who dwell in loving-kindness. Due to the power of the elder's loving-kindness, even animals developed minds of loving-kindness. The elder became the instructor (ovādācariya) for the Saṅgha of monks throughout the whole of Jambudīpa and resided at the Vattaniya-senāsana monastery. A forest about thirty yojanas in size became a single meditation hall for him. The elder would spread a leather rug in the air and, sitting there, teach meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). As time went by, he no longer went for alms but stayed in the monastery to teach meditation, and people came to the monastery to offer alms. King Dhammāsoka, hearing of the elder's virtues and wishing to see him, sent for him three times. However, the elder did not go even once, saying, "I am giving instructions to the Saṅgha of monks."

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya in the Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta is finished.
191:
## 10. Commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Vekhanasa Sutta. In this sutta, it is said that Vekhanasa was the teacher of this wanderer Sakuludāyī. When the wanderer Vekhanasa heard that "the wanderer Sakuludāyī was defeated regarding the question of the supreme beauty (parama-vaṇṇa)," he thought: "I taught that Sakuludāyī well, and he also learned it well; why then was he defeated? Now, I will go myself and question the ascetic Gotama about the supreme beauty to find out." Thus, he traveled from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī, forty-five yojanas away, and approached the Blessed One. After approaching, while standing near the Blessed One, he uttered an inspired exclamation (udāna). The meaning of that inspired exclamation should be understood in the same way as stated in the previous sutta.

Why did He begin the teaching with the words "Pañca kho ime" (These five)? Some laypeople are focused on sensual pleasures and are inclined toward them, while others are focused on renunciation (nekkhamma) and are inclined toward it. Similarly, some monks are focused on sensual pleasures and are inclined toward them, while others are focused on renunciation and are inclined toward it. This wanderer Vekhanasa, however, was one who was focused on and inclined toward sensual pleasures. The Blessed One began this teaching with the thought: "When this discourse is spoken, he will notice his own inclination toward sensual pleasures; if he notices this, this teaching will be suitable for him." By the term "kāmagga-sukha" (the highest sensual bliss), Nibbāna is intended.

"Pāpito bhavisatti" means he will be led to a state of not knowing (ignorance). "Nāmakam-eva sampajjati" means it becomes merely a useless word. The statement "Let the past discourse stand, let the future discourse stand" was said because you do not have the appropriate knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) for a discourse on the past, nor the appropriate divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) for a discourse on the future; therefore, let both of these be. "Sutta-bandhanehi" means by bonds made of thread. To protect a young child, small threads are tied around their hands, feet, and neck. This was said in reference to those threads. When that child grows up, those threads either rot and fall off on their own, or they are cut and removed.

By the words "Evam-eva kho," He intends to show this meaning: Just as a young child does not know about the threads tied to him, the preceding end (beginning) of ignorance (avijjā) cannot be known. It is impossible to know the first point of ignorance. Just as one knows when the threads are released...
192: He strives. By the word 'kāmaggasukha', Nibbāna is intended. 'Pāpito bhavissati' means it will be made to reach the state of not knowing. 'Nāmakaṃyeva sampajjati' means it is merely a useless statement. 'Let the former end remain, let the latter end remain' means that because you, the wanderer Vekhanassa, do not have the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) suitable for talk concerning the past, nor the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) suitable for talk concerning the future, let both those talks of the past and future remain as they are—this is what was said. 'Suttabandhanehi' means by bindings made of thread. Indeed, for the sake of protecting a child, they tie small threads on the hands, feet, and neck. Referring to those small threads, He said 'suttabandhanehi'. When that child grows up, those small threads either rot and fall off by themselves or are cut and thrown away. By the words 'evameva kho', He shows the following meaning: Just as when one does not know the small threads tied to a very young boy, so should the non-knowing of the first end of ignorance (avijjā) be understood. Indeed, the first end of ignorance... However, it is the knowledge that 'liberation from the bond of ignorance has occurred through the Path of Arahantship'. The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all places. ## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī, ## the Explanation of the Vekhanassa Sutta is finished. ## The Explanation of the Third Division (Vagga) is finished.
193:
## 4. Rāja Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta. In that Ghaṭīkāra Sutta, "sitaṃ pātvākāsi" means that while traveling on the main road, He looked at a certain spot of ground and reflected: "Have I, who practiced the conduct that is the precursor to omniscience, ever lived in this place before?" Upon reflecting, He saw: "In the time of Kassapa Buddha, there was a village-market named Vigaḷinga in this place. At that time, I was a youth named Jotipāla. My friend was a potter named Ghaṭīkāra. Together with him, I performed a good deed in this place. That event is not well-known to the Sangha of monks; it is hidden. Now, I shall make it known to the Sangha of monks." Having so thought, He stepped off the path, and while standing in a certain spot, He manifested a smile, showing the tips of His teeth and smiling slightly.

Worldly people laugh by beating their chests and making the sound "kuhaṃ kuhaṃ," but Buddhas do not laugh in that way. In fact, the smile of the Buddhas is merely a joyful manner.

What is called smiling occurs through thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata-citta). Among those thirteen, the worldly masses laugh with eight types of consciousness: four unwholesome and four wholesome belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). Trainees (sekha) laugh with six types of consciousness, having removed the two unwholesome types associated with wrong view. Arahants (khīṇāsava) smile with five types of consciousness: four functional consciousnesses with roots (sahetuka-kiriya) and one functional consciousness without roots (ahetuka-kiriya). Among those five, when a strong object enters the range of the senses, they smile with the two types of consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta). When a weak object appears, they smile with the three types of consciousness: the two types with two roots (duhetuka) and the one rootless type. In this particular case, the functional rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (hasituppāda-citta) produced the Blessed One's smile, which was merely a joyful manner.

That smile, although so slight, was clear to the Elder Ānanda. How was it clear? At the time of such a smile, from the four canine teeth of the Tathāgata, bundles of rays the size of palm trunks emerged, shining like hundreds of streaks of lightning from the face of a great rain cloud over the four continents. These rays circled the noble head three times clockwise and...
194:
Arahants smile with five types of consciousness: four types of functional consciousness accompanied by joy with roots (sahetuka-kiriya-somanassa-sahagata-citta) and one type of rootless functional consciousness producing a smile (ahetuka-kiriya-hasituppāda-citta). Among these five types of consciousness, when an extensive object appears, they smile with two types of great functional consciousness associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy (mahā-kiriya-ñāṇasampayutta-somanassa-sahagata-citta). When an object that is not extensive appears, they smile with three types of consciousness: two types of functional consciousness with two roots and one type of rootless functional consciousness producing a smile. In this context, the rootless functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (hasituppāda-citta) caused the Blessed One's smile, which was merely a cheerful expression. Although that smile was subtle, it was clearly perceived by the Venerable Ānanda. How was it clear? When the Blessed One smiled, from his four canine teeth, clusters of rays as bright as numerous lightning bolts emerging from a cloud bank over the four continents, and as thick as palm trunks, came forth. They circled the noble head three times clockwise and disappeared into the tips of the canine teeth themselves. By that sign, the Venerable Ānanda, even while walking behind the Blessed One, knew that he had smiled.

Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "In this place, the Blessed One Kassapa once exhorted the Saṅgha of monks and proclaimed the Four Noble Truths. Our Blessed One will also likely wish to reside in this place. If so, this site will be a place used by two Buddhas. Many people, by making offerings of flowers and scents and establishing a shrine (cetiya) to pay respects, will be headed for the heavenly realms." Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with "Te na hi, bhante."

"Muṇḍakena samaṇakena" means it is indeed appropriate to call a shaven-headed person "shaveling" and an ascetic "ascetic." However, this young man Jotipāla, having immature wisdom, spoke thus with a desire to insult, according to the terminology learned in his brahmin lineage. "Sottisinānaṃ" refers to a bundle or ball made for bathing. "Sotti" refers to balls made by binding the powder of Kuruvinda stones with lac. Referring to this, it was said: "At that time, the Chabbaggiya monks bathed with Kuruvinda-sotti." One must hold that ball from both ends and rub the body. "Evaṃ samma" means—just as when people of today are told, "Let's go to worship the shrine" or "Let's go to hear the Dhamma," they show no enthusiasm, but when told, "Let's go to see a play or a festival," they agree at once—similarly, Jotipāla spoke thus because he wanted to agree at once when told, "Let's go for a bath."

"Jotipālaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesi" means—after Ghaṭīkāra had first bathed and come up from the water according to the custom of the noble ones (ariyas), he waited for the conclusion of the bath of the young man Jotipāla, who was bathing with great lordly attendants. He addressed him while Jotipāla was changing clothes and drying the water from his hair. The word "ayaṃ" (this) is used to point him out because he was nearby. "Ovaṭṭikaṃ vinivaṭṭhetvā" means the Bodhisatta, who possessed the strength of an elephant, said, "Friend, move aside," and with just a slight turn, caused Jotipāla to release his grip. "Kesesu parāmasitvā etadavoca" means—he thought, "This Jotipāla is wise. If he gets to see the Tathāgata even once, he will gain faith in the sight of him and also in his Dhamma discourse. Once he has faith, he will be able to act according to that faith. Friends exist for such a purpose; whatever it takes, I will take my friend to the presence of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala)." Thinking thus, he spoke while holding him by the hair.
195:
"Ittarajacco" means of another birth, not of the same birth as me, of low birth. "Na vatidaṃ" means this going of ours will certainly not be low, it will not be small; it will be great. Because this Ghaṭīkāra did not grasp by his own power but by the power of the Teacher, he reached a firm decision at the very moment of grasping. In the phrase "yāvatādohipi," the syllables do-hi-pi are particles (nipāta), meaning "up to as much as." This is what is said: "Surpassing the verbal invitation and the grasping of the waist-band, an effort must be made to go to that place even by grasping the hair."

"Dhammiyā kathāyā" means in this context, a Dhamma talk connected with past lives should be understood for the purpose of regaining mindfulness. To that Jotipāla, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma for the purpose of regaining mindfulness in this manner: "Jotipāla, you are not a being who has descended into a low place; rather, you have descended having aspired for Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the throne of Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi-pallaṅka). For such a person, living in negligence is not proper." However, the elders of the Parasamuddavāsī (Overseas Dwellers) say: "Jotipāla, just as I, having fulfilled the ten perfections, realized Omniscience and now wander the world surrounded by twenty thousand monks, so too will you, having fulfilled the ten perfections, realize Omniscience and wander the world surrounded by a group of ascetics. It is not proper for such a person as you to fall into negligence." When he preached thus, Jotipāla's mind inclined towards ordination, and so the Buddha preached on the disadvantages of sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma).

"Alattha kho Ānanda... pabbajjaṃ alattha upasampadaṃ"—what did he do after ordaining? He did what is to be done by Bodhisattas. For Bodhisattas ordain in the presence of Buddhas. After ordaining, they do not become like low beings who are like bulls with broken horns; instead, being well-established in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla), they learn the Tipiṭaka Buddha-word, undertake the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), enter the forest, and while fulfilling the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgata-vatta) and performing the duties of a recluse, they develop insight (vipassanā) and remain having reached up to conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa). They do not make an effort for the paths and fruits (magga-phala). Jotipāla did the same.

"Aḍḍhamāsupasampanne" means when the Blessed One departed not even half a month after the son of a good family had been ordained, the grief of the parents had not yet subsided, and he too...
196:
(A new monk) does not yet know how to handle the alms-bowl and robes, is not yet familiar with the young monks and novices, and has not yet established affection and intimacy with the senior elders; thus, dissatisfaction arises in whatever place he reaches. However, if he resides for such a period, his parents have the opportunity to see (their son), and thus their grief and anxiety are diminished. (The new monk) also comes to know how to handle the alms-bowl and robes, becomes familiar with the novices and young monks, establishes affection and intimacy with the senior elders, and finds delight in whatever place he reaches, no longer feeling weary. Therefore, (reflecting) that it is proper to reside for such a duration, he stays for about half a month before departing.

'Paṇḍupuṭakassa sālino' refers to red sāli rice that has been placed in bundles and dried. The method of preparation from the time of sowing that sāli rice is as follows: After the fields have been well prepared, the seeds are sown and sprinkled with scented water. At the time of sowing, a cloth mat is fastened above like a canopy (for protection). When ripe, the ears of grain are reaped, made into small bundles about a handful in size, tied with string, and dried in the open air. Then, scented powders are scattered over them, and they are filled into granaries, to be opened and taken out only after three years. Taking the grains of this fragrant red sāli rice, which has been stored for three years and is extremely pure and free from dark spots, they prepare various kinds of snacks and alms-food. With reference to such preparation, it is said: "Exquisite food and snacks... he announced that it was time."

With reference to what does he say, "He has resided the rains retreat with me"? He says this with reference to the fact that Ghaṭīkāra obtained a promise (from the Buddha) to observe the rains retreat near him when departing from the village of Vegalinga. "There was a change in the state of mind, there was unhappiness" means that because of the lack of opportunity (alābha) to give alms, hear the Dhamma, and serve twenty thousand monks in this manner for the three months of the rains retreat, there was a change in mind and mental unhappiness; it was not because of the Tathāgata. Why? Because he was a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). That King Kikī was formerly a devotee of Brahmins. On one occasion, while going to suppress a rebellion in the border regions, he instructed his daughter named Uracchadā: "Dear daughter, do not neglect our gods (the Brahmins)." When the Brahmins saw the princess, they became infatuated. When asked, "Who are these?" they replied, "They are your ladyship's earthly gods." Thinking with disgust, "Are earthly gods like this?" she ascended to the palace. One day, while looking out at the street, she saw the Chief Disciple of the Blessed One Kassapa...
197:
(The princess) had (the Chief Disciple) invited and offered alms-food; while listening to the words of appreciation (anumodanā), she became a Stream-enterer. She asked, "Are there other monks as well?" Hearing that "The Teacher is residing at Isipatana with twenty thousand monks," she invited them and offered alms.

King Kikī returned after pacifying the border regions. Then, the Brahmins came to the King first and slandered the daughter to cause a rift. However, the King had granted a boon to the daughter at the time of her birth. For her sake, the relatives took the boon, saying, "The kingdom must be given (to her) for seven days." Then the King handed over the kingdom to his daughter for seven days. While that princess was feeding the Teacher, she had the King invited and made him sit outside a curtain. Just by hearing the Teacher's words of appreciation, the King became a Stream-enterer. A Stream-enterer has no ill will toward the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said: "Not because of the Tathāgata."

"Let him take what he desires" means that Ghaṭīkāra, after firing the pots, does not engage in buying and selling himself; instead, saying this, he goes to the forest for firewood, clay, or straw. When the people hear that "Ghaṭīkāra has fired the pots," they come bringing pure rice, salt, ghee, oil, molasses, and so on. If a pot is of high value and the price brought is small, they do not take that pot with the thought, "We will take it by giving this or that." Thinking, "This person is a righteous trader; he supports his parents and serves the Perfectly Enlightened One; it would be a great demerit for us," they go back and bring the (full) price. If, however, a pot is of low value and the price brought is large, thinking, "He is a righteous trader; it will be a merit for us," they store the price they brought well, like householders, and then depart. To the question of why one endowed with such virtues does not ordain, the Blessed One, wishing to interrupt the King's flow of speech, said, "Because he supports his blind and aged parents."

"Who is it?" means "Where has he gone?" "From the pot" means from the rice pot. "From the vessel" means from the curry vessel. "Please partake" means please eat. Why do they speak thus? It is because Ghaṭīkāra, after cooking the rice and preparing the curry, feeds his parents, eats himself, and then sets aside the rice and curry for the Blessed One, prepares a seat, sets out a stand and water, gives a signal to his parents, and then goes to the forest. That is why they speak in this manner.
198:
Abhivissattha means being very intimate. 'Does not abandon the bliss of rapture' (pītisukhaṃ na vijahati) does not mean that he never leaves it; rather, it means that at whatever moment—whether at night or during the day, in the village or in the forest—he reflects, “The Supreme Person in the world including the devas entered my house, took the food with his own hands, and consumed it; what a great gain for me!” at that moment, the fivefold rapture arises. It is in reference to this rapture that this was said.

Kaḷopiya means a basket. Why did the Blessed One act in this way (taking the food without it being formally offered)? It was because the cause was righteous, and it was similar to the food already in the monks' alms-bowls; therefore, he acted thus. Furthermore, the prescription of training rules (sikkhāpada) is only for the disciples; for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a limit of training rules. For example, in a king's garden, there are flowers and fruits; while others who pick those fruits and flowers are punished, the king may enjoy them as he pleases. This is a similar case. However, the Great Elders living across the ocean say, “It is said that the deities took the food (from the pot) and offered it.”

“Take it, venerable sirs, take it, good sirs,” they said because when their son was asked, “Where have you gone?” he would usually say, “To the presence of the One of Ten Powers (Kassapa Buddha).” Thinking, “Where could my son be going? He does not even know that the Teacher’s dwelling place is leaking,” and considering their son to be at fault, the parents spoke thus with joyful hearts upon the taking of the grass (for the roof).

“For three months it remained with the sky as its roof” means that the Blessed One had the grass brought after one month of the four months of the rainy season had passed; therefore, it was said thus. The meaning of the term here is: it is called “ākāsacchadana” because the sky alone was its roof. “It did not rain” means not only that it did not get wet, but just as not a single drop of water falls inside the eaves-less area where water normally falls from that house, and just as wind and heat cannot cause affliction inside a house with a thick roof, so too the wind and heat did not cause affliction, and there was only a natural balance of the seasons. Even later, when that town was abandoned, that place remained leak-proof. When people were working and it rained, they would place their clothes there and continue working. Until the end of the eon, that place will remain like that. This happened not by the psychic power of the Tathāgata, but only by the perfection of the virtues of those parents. For those parents, the thought, “Where would the Perfectly Enlightened One not obtain (almsfood)? He has had the grass removed from the house of us two blind people,” did not cause any displeasure (domanassa) because of that; instead, (they thought) “The Supreme Person in the world including the devas...”
199:
“...has had the grass taken from our house to roof the Perfumed Chamber,” and thus a great and powerful joy (somanassa) arose in those parents. Thus, it should be understood that this miracle occurred only due to the perfection of their virtues.

In the phrase “taṇḍulavāhasatāni,” it should be understood that two carts equal one vāha. “Tadupiyañca sūpeyyaṃ” refers to oil, molasses, and so on, which are suitable for the rice to make a meal. The King sent this much offering with the thought that it would serve as food for twenty thousand monks for the three months of the rains retreat. Why did he (Ghaṭīkāra) reject it, saying, “It is not necessary for me; let it be for the King alone”? It was because of his quality of fewness of wishes (appicchatā) which he had attained.
