It is said that Ghaṭīkāra had this thought: “The King has never seen me before; for what reason did he send this?” Then he thought, “The Teacher has gone to Bārāṇasī; surely, when the King requested him to spend the rains retreat, he must have informed him of my promise and spoken words of praise about my virtues. A gain obtained through words of praise is like a gain obtained by a dancer through dancing or a singer through singing. What benefit is there for me in this gain? It is only with the gain produced by my own work that I should support my parents and the Perfectly Enlightened One.” The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all places.

## The Explanation of the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta
## in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary known as Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## 2. Raṭṭhapāla Sutta Vaṇṇanā

“Evaṃ me sutaṃ” and so forth is the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta. In that sutta, “Thullakoṭṭhikaṃ” is so called because it had full granaries and prosperous storehouses. It is said that the district was always fertile with crops, and seeds were constantly going out while grain from the threshing floor was constantly coming in. Therefore, in that town, the granaries were always full. Thus, it came to be known as “Thullakoṭṭhika.”

Why is he called “Raṭṭhapāla”? He is called Raṭṭhapāla because he was capable of supporting and protecting (pāletuṃ) a broken kingdom (raṭṭha). When did this name arise for him? It was during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Padumuttara. Counting back from this eon, one hundred thousand eons ago, during the time of humans with a lifespan of one hundred thousand years, the Teacher named Padumuttara appeared and...
200:
The Blessed One Padumuttara, accompanied by a hundred thousand monks, wandered for the benefit of the world. In reference to that Buddha, it was said:

"In the city named Haṃsavatī, the Khattiya king named Ānanda was the father;
Sujātā was the mother of the Teacher Padumuttara."

Even before the appearance of Padumuttara Buddha, two faithful and devoted householders in the city of Haṃsavatī began giving alms to the poor, travelers, beggars, and so on. At that time, five hundred ascetics living in the mountains arrived at Haṃsavatī, and those two men divided the group of ascetics between them to serve them. After staying for some time, the ascetics returned to the foot of the mountains, but two senior ascetics remained behind, and those men served them for the rest of their lives. While the ascetics were giving thanks (anumodanā) after their meal, one described the celestial mansion of Sakka, and the other described the mansion of the Naga King Bhūmindhara.

Of the two householders, one aspired to the mansion of Sakka and was reborn as Sakka. The other was reborn in the Naga realm as the Naga King named Pālita. When Sakka saw that Naga King coming to pay him respects, he asked, "Do you delight in the Naga birth?" The Naga King replied, "I do not." Then Sakka said, "If so, give alms to the Blessed One Padumuttara and make an aspiration in this life; we shall both live happily."

The Naga King invited the Teacher and, while giving a great alms-offering for seven days to the Blessed One accompanied by a hundred thousand monks, he saw the novice named Uparevata, the son of the Ten-Powered Padumuttara. On the seventh day, having offered divine robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he aspired to the special position of that novice. The Blessed One, looking into the future, saw, "In the future, he will be the youth Rāhula, the son of the Buddha named Gotama," and said, "Your aspiration will be fulfilled." The Naga King told this matter to Sakka. Upon hearing the Naga King's words, Sakka likewise gave alms for seven days. Having seen a noble youth named Raṭṭhapāla, who was born into a family capable of sustaining and protecting a broken kingdom and who had ordained out of faith, he made an aspiration: "In the future, when Buddhas like you appear in the world, may I also be born into a family capable of sustaining and protecting a broken kingdom, and like this noble youth, may I be one named Raṭṭhapāla who ordains out of faith." Knowing that the aspiration would be fulfilled, the Teacher spoke this verse:
201:
## "This person will be born in the family named Raṭṭhapāla, who is capable of supporting the four castes along with the king."
Thus, it should be understood that this name arose for him during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. "Etadahosi" (this thought occurred): what kind of thought was it? It refers to "yathā yathā kho" and so on. The summary of that statement is: "In whatever ways I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as I investigate and reflect through those ways, this thought occurs: 'This holy life of the threefold training (sikkhattaya-brahmacariya) should be practiced in absolute perfection, reaching the final consciousness without breaking it for even a single day. It should be practiced in absolute purity, reaching the final consciousness without being stained by the defilements for even a single day, making it like a polished conch shell or a well-rubbed conch shell. It is not easy for one living in a house, residing in the midst of a home, to practice this in absolute perfection... I should shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron-dyed robes, go forth from the home life into homelessness, and practice the holy life.'"

When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita had departed not long ago, Raṭṭhapāla approached the Blessed One. While they had not yet left, Raṭṭhapāla did not ask the Blessed One for ordination (pabbajjā). Why? Because in that assembly, there were many of his relatives, kinsmen, and friends. They might say, "You are the only son of your parents; it is not proper for you to go forth," and might even grab him by the arm and pull him back. Thinking that this would be an obstacle to his ordination, he rose with the assembly, went a short distance, and then returned under the pretext of some bodily business. He then approached the Blessed One and asked for ordination. Therefore, it was said: "Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, when the people of Thullakoṭṭhita had departed not long ago... may the Blessed One grant me ordination."

The Blessed One, because He does not ordain a son who is not permitted by his parents since the time Prince Rāhula was ordained, asked him, "Raṭṭhapāla, have you received permission from your parents... for ordination?"

In the word "ammatātā", "amma" addresses the mother and "tāta" addresses the father. "Ekaputtako" means the only son; there is no other elder or younger brother. Here, instead of saying "ekaputta", the term "ekaputtako" is used out of compassion (endearment). "Piyo" means dear (one who causes joy). "Manāpo" means pleasing (one who increases the mind's delight).
202:
‘Sukhedhita’ means one who has grown up in happiness, or one who has been raised in comfort. ‘Sukhaparibhata’ means one who has been nurtured in happiness. It means that from the time of birth, nurses carried him from one embrace to another, let him play with children's toys such as toy horses and chariots, fed him delicious and flavorful food, and thus he was nurtured in comfort. “Dear Raṭṭhapāla, you have never known nor experienced even a small portion of suffering” means: Dear Raṭṭhapāla, you do not know and do not remember even a tiny fraction of suffering.

“Even if you were to die while we, your parents, are still alive, we would have to be separated from you against our will and not by our own choice” means: Even if your death were to occur while we are still living, because of that death, we would be separated from you against our will and not by our own choice; we would come to be parted from you. “Kiṃ pana mayaṃ taṃ” means: If we must be separated even by such a death against our will, for what reason should we give you permission while you are still alive? Or, for what reason should we allow you to ordain while you are living? This is how the meaning should be understood here.

“Tattheva” means in that very place where he remained when his parents did not give him permission. “Anantarahitāya” means because of lying on the bare ground that was not covered by any kind of mat or rug. “Paricārehi” means: Having the female attendants and dancers present, enjoy the sensory pleasures as you wish with your companions; it means to move them here and there. Alternatively, “paricārehi” means: Having the female attendants and dancers present, be merry, be very merry, delight, and play with your companions. “Kāme paribhuñjanto” means enjoying the pleasures of wealth together with one's wife and children. “Puññāni karonto” means performing meritorious deeds that clear the path to the happy realms, such as giving various alms in relation to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. “Tuṇhī ahosi” means he remained silent without any conversational response in order to cut off the continuity of the talk.

Then, although Raṭṭhapāla's parents spoke to him three times, they received no reply. So they summoned his companions and said, “This friend of yours wishes to ordain; please dissuade him.” Those companions also approached him and spoke three times, but he remained silent. Therefore, it is said: “Then the companions of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla... remained silent.” Then, after the companions had spoken three times, the thought occurred to them: “If this Raṭṭhapāla does not obtain the going-forth, he will die; no one...”
203:
(If this Raṭṭhapāla dies without obtaining ordination,) no virtue or benefit will be gained. However, if he becomes a monk, his parents will see him from time to time, and we will see him too. This state of being a monk is also very burdensome; one must wander for alms every day carrying a clay bowl. Living the holy life by sleeping alone and eating only one meal a day is extremely difficult to do. This Raṭṭhapāla is very delicate and is a youth bred in the city. When he is unable to practice that way of life, he will surely return to this house again. Come, let us persuade Raṭṭhapāla's parents to give their permission (the friends planned).

Those friends acted according to their plan. The parents also gave their permission after making this agreement: "Even after you have ordained, you must come and show yourself to your parents." Therefore, it is said, "Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to the parents of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla... (pe)... You have received permission from your parents... (pe)... you must show yourself." In that passage, "uddassetabbā" means he should show himself; it means he should come and show himself so that his parents can see him regularly.

"balaṃ gahetvā" means eating suitable food and taking care of the body through bathing and other means to gain physical strength, then paying respects to his parents and leaving his weeping relatives to approach the Blessed One... (pe)... "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One grant me ordination." The Blessed One addressed a certain monk standing nearby, "In that case, monk, ordain Raṭṭhapāla and give him the full admission (upasampadā)." That monk replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and accepting the clansman Raṭṭhapāla as a disciple (saddhivihārika) granted by the Blessed One, he performed the novice ordination and the full ordination. Therefore, it is said, "The clansman Raṭṭhapāla obtained the initial ordination in the presence of the Blessed One, and he obtained the full admission."

"pahitatto viharanto" means living in this manner for twelve years. Because this venerable one was a person to be led (neyya-puggala), although he was one with merit and possessed of great aspirations, and although he practiced the recluse's Dhamma thinking "I shall become an Arahant this very day," he only attained Arahantship in his twelfth year.

"He approached where the Blessed One was" means—when my parents gave permission to ordain, they did so saying, "You must come from time to time and let us see you." Parents are indeed those to whom it is difficult to repay gratitude. I have also reached the pinnacle of the purpose for which I ordained. Now, having asked permission from the Blessed One...
204:
Thinking, "I will show myself to my parents," he approached, wishing to ask for permission. *Manasākāsī* means he pondered in his mind, "Will any danger befall Raṭṭhapāla when he goes?" Then, knowing that "it will happen," he considered, "Will Raṭṭhapāla be able to overcome that danger?" and seeing that he had attained the fruit of Arahantship, he knew, "He will be able to." Therefore, it was said, "As the Blessed One knew... [pe]... know the time."

*Migacīre* refers to the garden of this name. The King had already donated this garden, saying, "Let the monks who arrive at an improper time use it as they please." Therefore, the Elder entered the garden without even the thought, "If I inform my parents of my arrival, they will send me water for washing my feet, hot water, foot-anointing oil, and so on." *Piṇḍāya pāvisi* means he entered for alms on the second day.

*Majjhimāyā* means at the middle gatehouse of the house which has seven gatehouses. *Ullikhāpeti* means having his hair cut by a barber. *Etadavoca* means he thought, "These wretched recluses made my dear young son ordain and, as if placing him in the hands of thieves, do not let me see him even for a single day; such cruel people think they should come to this place again; they should be driven away from here," and so he spoke the words beginning with "By these shavelings." *Ñātidāsī* means a slave-woman of the relatives. *Ābhidosikaṃ* means something that has become putrid after passing one night. The meaning of that term is: it is called *abhidosa* because it is overcome by the fault of putridity; *abhidosa* itself is *ābhidosika*. This is a name for something that has passed one night; that is *ābhidosika*. *Kummāsaṃ* means barley bread.

*Chaḍḍetukāmā* means wishing to throw it away like rubbish because even slaves, laborers, and cattle would not eat it at the very least. *Sacetam* is *sace etam*. *Bhaginī* (Sister) is the term used by the Ariyas to address the family slave-woman who was his nurse. *Chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ* means something that is of a nature to be thrown away. The meaning is: "Sister, if this is something to be thrown away, something whose ownership has been relinquished, pour it into my bowl." Is it permissible to speak like this? Is it not *viññatti* (intimation) or *payuttavācā* (indirect speech)? It is not. Why? Because ownership has been relinquished. Regarding anything that is to be thrown away and whose ownership has been relinquished, where the owners have no attachment, one can say, "Give it."
205:
"Bring it, pour it"—it is appropriate to say this. That is why this Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, even though he was one who practiced the noble lineage of the Ariyas (*ariyavaṃsa*), spoke in this way.

*Hatthānaṃ* refers to both hands from the wrist onwards as he was holding out the bowl to receive alms. *Pādānaṃ* refers to both feet from the hem of the inner robe onwards. *Sarassa* refers to the voice if he uttered the word "Sister" to that person. *Nimittaṃ aggahesi* means that slave-woman, looking at the backs of his hands and so on, took the signs, knew, and remembered the appearance she had previously noted when he was a layman, thinking, "These backs of the hands and feet are like the backs of golden tortoises, just like my son Raṭṭhapāla's; these fingers are well-rounded like sticks of yellow orpiment; there is a sweet voice." Because that Venerable one had been living in the forest for twelve years and eating only food received from alms, his bodily complexion had changed. Therefore, that family slave-woman did not recognize him just by seeing him, but she did take note of the signs (*nimitta*).

*Raṭṭhapālassa mātaraṃ etadavoca* means that although she was the nurse who had tended to the Elder's limbs and nursed him with milk, she did not dare to say to the master's son, who had ordained and reached the state of a Great Arahant (*mahākhīṇāsava*), words such as "Venerable sir, are you not my son Raṭṭhapāla?" and so she quickly entered the house and said these words to Raṭṭhapāla's mother. *Yagghe* is a particle in the sense of informing. In the phrase *sace je saccaṃ*, *je* is a particle in the sense of address. In that region, they used to address slave-women in this way. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as, "O slave-woman, if you are speaking the truth."

*Upasaṅkami*—why did she approach? In noble families, women incur blame if they go outside. And this was an urgent matter. She thought, "I will inform the merchant of this matter." Therefore, she approached. *Aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlaṃ* means that in that region, there are rest-houses (*sālā*) in the houses of donors. In those rest-houses, seats are prepared and sour rice-gruel (*udakakañjiya*) is provided. There, recluses sit and eat after wandering for alms. If they wish, they also take what belongs to the donors. Therefore, that place should be understood as the foot of a wall in such a rest-house of a certain family. This is because recluses do not usually sit and eat in unsuitable places like poor people.
206:
In the phrase “Atthi nāma tāta,” the word “atthi” is used in the sense of existence, and the word “nāma” is a particle used in the sense of questioning or reflection. The intended meaning is this: “Dear Raṭṭhapāla, do we indeed still have wealth? Should we be called poor, that you, our son, should sit in such a place and eat stale barley gruel from the previous evening?” Likewise, “Dear Raṭṭhapāla, do we indeed still have life? Should we be called dead, that you, our son, should sit in such a place and eat stale barley gruel from the previous evening?” Likewise, “Dear Raṭṭhapāla, I think there is the virtue of a recluse (samaṇaguṇa) attained within you by depending on the Dispensation, since you, though raised on the taste of excellent food, eat this loathsome stale barley gruel without any change in demeanor, as if it were nectar.”

That householder, being oppressed by the sorrow of suffering, was unable to state this meaning in full and said only this much: “Is it true, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you will eat stale barley gruel?” Grammarians, however, state this rule here: due to the sense of disbelief and intolerance, when the word “atthi” is near, the future tense “pari-bhuñjissasī” is used. Its meaning is: “Is it true... that you will eat... even though I see this with my own eyes, I do not believe it and I cannot bear it.” The householder said this much while standing and holding the rim of the Elder’s bowl.

The Elder, while his father was still standing and holding the rim of the bowl, ate that foul barley gruel, which was like dog vomit and smelled putrid like a rotten chicken egg cracked in a certain spot. It is said that an ordinary person (puthujjana) would not be able to eat such barley gruel. But the Elder, established in the power of the Noble Ones (ariyiddhi), ate it as if he were consuming the divine essence of nectar. After eating, he took water with a water-filter (dhammakaraṇa), washed and wiped the bowl, his mouth, hands, and feet, and then said, “Householder, from where would we (receive alms)?” and so on.

In that speech, “Kuto no” means “From where indeed?” “Neva dānaṃ” means we did not even receive a gift in the form of alms-food. “Na paccakkhānaṃ” means we did not even receive a refusal through polite words such as, “Dear Raṭṭhapāla, are you well? Have you arrived without much fatigue? Dear, the meal is not yet prepared in the house.” Why did the Elder speak in this way? It was because he wished to favor his father. For this thought occurred to him: “Just as this householder speaks to me, he might speak to other monks as well. And in the Buddha’s Dispensation, there are those who are like a lotus inside a bowl, like fire covered by ashes, like sandalwood heartwood covered by sapwood, like a pearl gem covered by a shell, like the moon covered by clouds...”
207:
"...there is no end to monks like me who hide their virtues; he will not speak such (harsh) words to them but will remain in restraint." He said this with a mind wishing to favor [his father].

"Come, dear," he said, "let it not be that there is no house for you; come, let us go to the house." The Elder, having the pre-eminent practice of eating in one session (ukkaṭṭha ekāsanika), rejected it, saying, "Enough." "He accepted" means that although the Elder, by nature, had the pre-eminent practice of uninterrupted alms-round (ukkaṭṭha sapadānacārika) and usually did not accept invitations for the next day's meal, he accepted it out of a desire to favor his mother. It is said that a great sorrow arose in his mother as she remembered the Elder, and her eyes became red as if cooked from so much weeping. Therefore, the Elder accepted with a mind of favor, thinking, "If I go without seeing her, her heart might break." "Having had it made" means having two heaps made—one of coins (hirañña) and one of gold (suvaṇṇa). How large were those heaps? They were so large that a man standing on this side could not see a man of medium height standing on the other side.

"Dear, this is your wealth," he said, showing the heap of coins and the heap of gold. "Wealth coming from the mother's side" means wealth inherited from the mother; the meaning is that this is the wealth given by your maternal grandmother to your mother for perfumes, flowers, etc., when she came to this house. "Other wealth from the father's side, other wealth from the grandfather's side" means the wealth belonging to your father and grandfathers is separate, and the buried wealth and wealth put out for interest are also very much. Here, it should be understood that in the word "pitāmaha," the derivative suffix is dropped. Alternatively, there is a reading "petāmaha." "It could be because of that wealth" means because of the wealth, due to the wealth. He said this referring to the sorrow, etc., that arises in someone because of guarding various wealth or because of the destruction of wealth due to kings, etc.

When this was said, the great merchant thought, "I brought him here thinking I would make him disrobe, but now he has started to give me a Dhamma talk; he will not listen to my words." He stood up, went and had the door of his harem opened, and sent them out, saying, "This is your master; go and strive to capture him by any means." The well-adorned dancing women came out and to the Elder...
208:
(The concubines) surrounded him. Regarding the two senior former wives among those women, it is said, "Purāṇadutiyikā," and so forth. "Paccekaṃ pādesu gahetvā" means grasping each of his feet.

"O prince, what are those celestial nymphs like?" Why did they ask this? At that time, many princes, brahmins, and merchant sons were seen renouncing great wealth to ordain. Not knowing the benefits of ordination, people asked, "Why do these men ordain?" Then some said, "They ordain for the sake of celestial nymphs and divine dancers." That talk spread widely. Based on that rumor, all the former wives asked in that way. Then the Elder, rejecting it, said, "Sisters, we (do not ordain for celestial nymphs)," and so forth. "Samudācarati" means to address or speak. Seeing him address them as "sisters," they fainted and fell right there. Thinking, "Our lord will come today, he will come today," they had not gone outside for twelve years. Yet, relying on him, they did not obtain children who would be their support. They had declined from the wealth to be enjoyed in this family and from the wealth to be enjoyed in another family. Thinking that this world only looks after its own interests, they thought only of their own situation, "Now we have become helpless." Thinking, "This lord no longer desires us; though we are his wives, he regards us like sisters who lay in the same mother's womb," intense grief arose, and they fainted and fell on that very spot. "Patitā" means fallen.

"Do not harass us" means do not harass us by showing wealth or by tempting us with women; this means it is a harassment to monks. Why did he say this? Out of a desire to favor his parents. That merchant thought, "The monk's appearance is indeed soiled; let him give up the monk's garb, bathe, and let the three of us—mother, father, and son—eat together," and so he did not offer alms to the Elder. The Elder thought, "By creating an obstacle to the meal of an Arahant like me, these parents will accumulate much demerit." Out of compassion for them, he said, "Do not harass us."

"He spoke the verse" means he uttered the verses. In that verse, "Passa" (Look) is said referring to the people standing nearby. "Cittaṃ" means variegatedly adorned. "Bimbaṃ" means the physical body. "Arukāyaṃ" means a body of sores by way of the nine openings. "Samussitaṃ" means erected by binding three hundred bones with nine hundred sinews, and smearing them with nine hundred pieces of flesh. "Āturaṃ" means constantly afflicted by old age, sickness, and defilements. "Bahusaṅkappaṃ" means much-fancied by the desires and thoughts of others...
209:
...a body of many fancies. In the bodies of women, the fancies (lust) of men arise; in the bodies of men, the fancies of women arise. Even this body, when it has become a bloated corpse cast away in a cemetery, is desired by crows, vultures, and the like; therefore, it is called "bahusaṅkappa." "Which has no permanent stability" means that for this body, there is no such thing as permanent stability, just like a magic trick, a mirage, a mass of foam, or a water bubble; its nature of breaking apart is certain.

"Bound by skin" means bound all around with moist human skin. "Beautiful only with clothes" means the form, even if exquisitely prepared with scents, jewels, and earrings, is beautiful only with clothes; without clothes, it is loathsome and unbearable to look at.

"Stained with lac" means (nails) dyed red with lac. "Smeared with powder" means they remove facial pimples and the like with mustard paste, clear away bad blood with fine clay, brighten the blood with sesame powder, complete the complexion with turmeric, and rub the face with a bundle of scented powder; because of this, the face shines exceedingly. Referring to such preparation, this is said.

"Styled in a checkered pattern" means the hair is smeared with resin and styled at the edge of the forehead with forward and circular curls in an aṭṭhāpadaka (checkered) design. "Añjanī" means a collyrium tube.

"Placed" means set down. "Pāsaṃ" means a snare or net. "Did not stick" means did not touch or get caught. "Nivāpaṃ" means the fodder-like food mentioned in the Nivāpa Sutta (set to trap deer). "While wailing" means at the time of crying and lamenting. With this verse, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla showed his parents as hunters, the remaining relatives as the hunter's retinue, the gold and silver as the snare, the food he consumed as the bait-grass, and himself as a great deer. Just as a great deer, having eaten as much bait-grass as it wants and drunk water, lifts its neck, looks around the directions, and thinks, "Safety will be for one who goes to such a place," and then, while the hunters are wailing, leaps up without touching the snare, enters the forest, and stands under a thicket with shade as dense as an umbrella, being fanned by a gentle breeze and looking back at the path it came; even so, the Elder, having spoken these verses, went through the air and stood in the Migacīra Park.

Why did the Elder go through the air? It is said that his father, the merchant, had the bars fastened on the seven gateway towers and ordered wrestlers, "If..."
210:
(The wealthy man) ordered, "If (my son) leaves the house and goes away, seize that Raṭṭhapāla by his hands and feet, remove the saffron-dyed robes, and make him wear lay clothes." Therefore, the Elder thought, "Let these people not accumulate demerit by seizing a great Arahant like me by the hands or feet; let that demerit not happen to them," and he traveled through the air. In the tradition of the Elders living on the other side of the ocean, however, it is said: "While standing, he recited these verses, then rose into the air and arrived at King Koravya's Migacīra Garden." This is the traditional reading.

Migavo is the name of that park keeper. Sodhento means preparing the path to the garden to be level, having the places that need planing planed, having the places that need sweeping swept, and performing tasks such as scattering sand, scattering flowers, setting up full water pots, and erecting banana trunks.

"He approached where King Koravya was" means: "Our lord the King always speaks of the virtues of this noble son Raṭṭhapāla; he greatly desires to see him but does not yet know of his arrival. This news is a great gift; I will go and inform the King," and so he approached King Koravya.

"He was praising" (Kittayamāno ahosi) means: That King, remembering the Elder, would speak of his virtues in the midst of the army and the dancers, saying, "This noble son has done what is difficult to do, renouncing such great wealth to become a monk and not looking back or returning to the lay life without regard." Based on those words, the park keeper spoke thus.

"Having said, 'Release/Distribute them'" (Vissajjethāti vatvā) means: Having ordered to give whatever gift is appropriate to whoever it is suitable for among the ladies of the court, ministers, and the army.

"With a distinguished [assembly]" (Ussaṭāya ussaṭāya) means: Approaching with a distinguished assembly composed of great ministers and citizens who are prominent in terms of lineage, wealth, retinue, and wisdom.

"Let the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sit on this rug" means: Because that rug is a noble seat, soft and made thick with flowers, he thought it inappropriate to sit there without asking permission, and thus he spoke.

Pārijuññāni means ruin or exhaustion. Jiṇṇo means worn out by old age. Vuḍḍho means advanced in years. Mahallako means old by birth. Addhagato means having passed through the stages of life. Vayoanuppatto means having reached the final stage of life. Pabbajati means going to the monastery, bowing to the monks, and saying, "Venerable Sirs, I..." (and thus becoming a monk).
211:
"...in my youth I performed many meritorious deeds, now I am old. This is the renunciation of an old man; I will live by sweeping the courtyard of the shrine and keeping it free of grass. Venerable Sirs, please ordain me," he pleads piteously. The Elders ordain him out of compassion. This is said in reference to such ordination. The same applies to the second time.

Appābādho means being free from illness. Appātaṅko means being free from affliction. Samavepākiniyā means digesting food well. Gahaṇiyā means the kamma-born fire element. In that regard, for one whose food is digested, or for one whose food remains just as it was like a packed bundle of rice—neither of these is endowed with samavepākinī gahaṇī. Only for one in whom the desire for food truly arises when it is time to eat, is he endowed with samavepākinī gahaṇī. For that very reason, he is endowed with the kamma-born fire element that is neither too cold nor too hot.

Anupubbena means in the sequence starting with "Kings carry away," etc. In the second instance, it refers to the sequence of danger from kings, danger from thieves, danger from famine, etc.

"The Dhamma summaries have been pointed out" (Dhammuddesā uddiṭṭhā) means the detailed explanations of the Dhamma (dhammaniddesa) have been pointed out. Upaniyyati means approaching old age and death, or reaching old age and death through the exhaustion of life. Adduvo means being devoid of a permanent state. Atāṇo means having no one capable of protecting. Anabhissaro means having no refuge, being devoid of someone capable of approaching and providing comfort. Assako means not being one's own, being devoid of personal property. "All must be abandoned and gone" (Sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ) means that all beings must go to the next world, abandoning everything they regarded as their own property. Taṇhādāso means being a slave to craving.

"In the elephant" (Hatthismiṃ) means in the art of elephantry. Katāvī means one who has done what was to be done, who has learned the art, and who is proficient in the art. This applies to all such terms. Ūrubalī means being endowed with the strength of the thighs. Indeed, one who, taking a shield and a weapon, enters the enemy's army, destroys the unbroken enemy forces, reorganizes his own broken forces, and has the thigh-strength to reclaim a kingdom that has fallen into others' hands, is called ūrubalī. Bāhubalī means being endowed with the strength of the arms. The rest is the same as before. Alamatto means having a capable body.

"They will live having overcome" (Pariyodhāya vattissanti) means they were brought along with the thought, "We shall live by suppressing and overcoming the dangers that have arisen."
212:
“Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, there is much gold and silver in this royal family.” The king said this because he wished to bring out the reason for the summary of the Dhamma (dhammuddesa) mentioned above.

Then, he spoke the supplementary verses (anugīti) of the four summaries of the Dhamma in the manner beginning with, “I see (beings) in the world.”

In those verses, “bhiyyo va kāme abhipatthayanti” means that if they obtain one, they desire two; if they obtain two, they desire four. In this way, they continue to desire the objects of sensuality (vatthukāma) and the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma) more and more.

“Pasayha” means by overpowering the host of enemies. “Sasāgarantaṃ” means together with the ocean as the boundary. “Oraṃ samuddassa” means one who is of a nature that cannot be satisfied with his own kingdom on this side of the ocean. In the phrase “na hatthi,” it should be split as “na hi atthi.”

“Aho vatā no” means “aho vata nu,” or even if the text remains as it is, “amarā cāhu” should be split as “amaraṃ iti ca āhu.” The meaning is: relatives surround the deceased and wail, saying, “Alas, our brother is dead, our son is dead,” and so forth.

“Phusanti” means they experience the touch of death. “Tatheva phuṭṭho” means that just like the fool, the wise man also experiences the touch of death in the same way. There is no one who does not experience death. However, the distinction here is: the fool, due to his foolishness, when he encounters the touch of death, lies down (dies) in great distress. He trembles, is shaken, and is agitated by the power of remorse, thinking, “Alas, I have not performed any good deeds.” The wise man, however, does not tremble or become agitated because he sees the sign of a happy destination (sugatinimitta).

“Yāya vosānaṃ idhādhigacchati” means that by which wisdom one attains the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), which is the conclusion of all tasks in this world; that wisdom alone is superior to material wealth. “Abyositattā” means because of not yet reaching the fruit of Arahantship (because it is not yet finished). “Bhavābhavesu” means in low and high states of existence.

“Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ” means that those beings who commit such unwholesome and evil deeds wander through the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) in succession and reach the womb as well as the next world. “Tassappapañño” refers to another person of little wisdom believing in such a person of little wisdom.
213:
“Sakammunā hañyati” means being oppressed by punishments (kammakaraṇa) such as “beating with whips” due to the power of the kamma performed by oneself. “Pecca paramhi loke” means going from this life to the world of misery (apāya) in the hereafter.

“Virūparūpena” means in various forms, or with various natures. “Kāmaguṇesu” means having seen the danger in all five cords of sensual pleasure in both the present life and the future life (and thus renouncing). “Daharā” refers to young ones, starting from the time of the embryonic stage (kalala). “Vuḍḍhā” refers to those who are over a hundred years old. “Apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo” means considering that the state of a monk (sāmañña), which is non-contradictory, not double-edged, and definitely leads out of suffering, is “excellent, especially superior and noble,” (he says) “Great King, I have gone forth.” Therefore, regarding the reason for your question, “Seeing or hearing what did you go forth?”, he concluded the teaching by saying, “Understand me as one who has gone forth having seen and heard these things.”

## The Commentary on the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta
## in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## 3. Commentary on the Makhādeva Sutta

The sutta beginning with “Evaṃ me sutaṃ” is the Makhādeva Sutta. In that sutta, “Makhādevambavane” means that in ancient times, a king named Makhādeva planted that mango grove. When those trees perished, other kings later replanted them. However, it was known as “Makhādeva’s Mango Grove” according to the original designation. “Sitaṃ pātu-akāsi” (He smiled) means that while walking around the monastery in the evening, seeing a pleasant spot of ground, he reflected, “Did I live in this place before?” and thought, “In the past, I was a king named Makhādeva and planted this mango grove. Having gone forth right here and developed the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra), I was reborn in the Brahma world. This matter is not yet known to the Saṅgha of monks; I shall make it known.” Thus, showing the tips of his teeth, he smiled.

Because he possesses Dhamma, he is called “Dhammika.” Because he became king by Dhamma, he is called “Dhammarājā.” Because he stands in Dhamma (stands in the ten courses of wholesome action), he is called “Dhamme ṭhito.” Because he practices Dhamma (practices consistently), he is called...
214:
He practices. In the phrase "among Brahmins and householders" (*brāhmaṇagahapatikesu*), there were certain honors and privileges granted to Brahmins by former kings; he continued to grant those without reduction, according to the established custom. He did the same for the householders. It is in reference to this granting that the words "among Brahmins and householders" are spoken. By the word "of the fortnight" (*pakkhassa*), the period of the extraordinary Uposatha (*pāṭihārika-uposatha*) is also included. Indeed, the seventh and ninth days, by virtue of preceding and following the eighth-day Uposatha, and the thirteenth and the first day of the [next] fortnight, by virtue of preceding and following the fourteenth and fifteenth-day Uposathas—these days should be known as the extraordinary fortnight (*pāṭihārika-pakkha*). On those days as well, he observed the Uposatha.

"Divine messengers" (*devadūtā*): "Deva" means Death; because they are the messengers of Death, they are called "devadūtā" (divine messengers). Indeed, when grey hairs appear on the head, one stands as if in the presence of the King of Death; therefore, grey hairs are called the messengers of the god of death. They are also called "devadūtā" because they are messengers like gods. Just as when a deity, adorned and prepared, stands in the sky and says, "He will die on such and such a day," and that word comes true exactly as spoken, so too, when grey hairs appear on the head, it is just like the prophecy of the gods. Therefore, grey hairs are called messengers who are like gods. They are also called "devadūtā" because they are messengers of the gods by purity (*visuddhideva*). For all Bodhisattas, upon seeing an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and an ascetic, are moved by spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), go forth, and renounce. As it is said:

Seeing the aged, the sick in pain,
Seeing the dead whose life is spent,
Seeing the ascetic in saffron robes,
Therefore, O King, I have gone forth.

For this reason, grey hairs are called "devadūtā" because they are the messengers of the gods by purity.

"Giving a choice village to the barber" means giving a head village that yields a revenue of one hundred thousand. Why did he give it? Because of his state of mind being moved by spiritual urgency. For upon merely seeing the grey hairs placed in his palms, spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arose. Although there were another eighty-four thousand years of life remaining, even though this was so, he considered himself as if standing in the presence of the King of Death, and being moved by spiritual urgency, he delighted in renunciation. Therefore, it is said:
215:
The wise Maghadeva, lord of the regions, seeing a grey hair on his head, attained spiritual urgency and delighted in renunciation.

It is also said in another verse: "These [hairs] grown on my head are stealers of my youth; the divine messengers have appeared; it is time for my renunciation."

"In a pair of men" (*purisayuge*) refers to the men born in the lineage. "Having shaved hair and beard" means that even those who renounce as hermits first shave their hair and beard to go forth. From then on, they wander as matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭā-kalāpa*), binding the hair that has grown long. The Bodhisatta also renounced as a hermit. After renouncing, without engaging in improper search, he subsisted on alms brought from the city of Rājagaha and developed the Divine Abidings (*brahmavihāra*). Therefore, it is said, "That person, with [a mind] accompanied by loving-kindness..." and so forth.

"He plays with child's play" means he played while being carried from one lap to another. They wandered about carrying that young prince like a bouquet of flowers. On the day King Maghadeva's son renounced, five auspicious events occurred simultaneously. They were: the offering of alms for the dead (*matakabhatta*) for King Maghadeva, the auspicious ceremony of the King's renunciation, the auspicious ceremony of raising the white umbrella for his son, the auspicious ceremony of appointing his son's son as viceroy, and the auspicious ceremony of naming his [son's son's] son. Thus, at one and the same time, five auspicious events occurred, and there was an extraordinary festival throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa.

"Lineage of sons and grandsons" refers to the succession of that king consisting of sons and sons of sons. He was the last of the kings who renounced. It is said that while the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Brahma realm, he reflected, "Does the noble practice established by me in the human world still persist?" and he saw, "It has persisted for this long, but now it will no longer continue." Thinking, "I cannot allow my lineage to be cut off," he took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the king born in his own lineage. Because he appeared as if joining the rim (*nemi*) of his own lineage, he was named "Nimi". Thus, that renounced...
216: Among the kings who went forth, he was the last to do so, and thus he was the final one in terms of renunciation. However, he was exceptionally superior in virtues. King Nimi possessed two qualities that were far more excellent than those of all other kings: he gave daily alms by spending one hundred thousand at each of the four gates, and he prohibited those who did not observe the Uposatha from seeing him. When those who did not observe the Uposatha went saying, "We shall see the King," the gatekeeper would ask, "Are you observers of the Uposatha or not?" He would bar those who were not observers of the Uposatha, saying, "The King does not grant an audience to those who do not observe the Uposatha." There was no opportunity to say, "We are residents of the countryside; where can we get food at this time?" regarding the non-observance of the Uposatha. This is because thousands of large pots of rice were already prepared at the four gates and in the palace courtyard. Therefore, the people would groom their beards and whiskers at their desired places, bathe, change their clothes, eat their preferred food, undertake the factors of the Uposatha, and then go to the palace gate. When asked by the gatekeeper, "Are you observers of the Uposatha?" they would reply, "Yes, yes." Then, saying, "In that case, come," the gatekeeper would let them in and allow them to see the King. Thus, he was a king who was exceptionally superior due to these two qualities. ## "Devānaṃ Tāvatiṃsānaṃ" refers to the devas born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It is said that while those devas lived in the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, they remained established in the King's admonition, observed the five precepts, and performed Uposatha duties, and because they were born in that deva realm, they spoke words of praise for the King's virtues. Referring to those devas, it was said, "Devānaṃ Tāvatiṃsānaṃ." ## "Nisinno hoti" means sitting while contemplating almsgiving and virtue, staying atop the noble palace. It is said that this thought occurred to him: "Is almsgiving more noble, or is virtue more noble? If almsgiving is more noble, I shall give alms predominantly. If virtue is more noble, I shall fulfill virtue predominantly." While he was unable to decide, "This is noble, this is noble," Sakka came and appeared before him. Therefore, it was said, "Atha kho Ānanda... sammukhe pāturahosi." It is said that this thought occurred to Sakka: "Doubt has arisen in the King; I shall answer his question to cut off that doubt, and I shall also take his promise to come to this deva realm." Therefore, he went and appeared before him. The King, seeing a form he had never seen before, was frightened and terrified, and his hair stood on end. Then Sakka said to him, "Do not be afraid, Great King; ask your question boldly, and I shall dispel your doubt."
217: The King, while staying in his noble palace, contemplated on almsgiving and virtue. This thought occurred to the King: "Is almsgiving more noble, or is virtue more noble?" He thought, "If almsgiving is more noble, I shall give alms predominantly. If virtue is more noble, I shall fulfill virtue predominantly." While he was unable to decide, "This merit is noble, that merit is noble," Sakka, the King of Devas, came to the human world and appeared clearly before the King. ## Sakka thought, "Doubt has arisen in the King; I shall dispel the King's doubt and answer the question, and I shall also take his promise to come to our abode, the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm." Thus, he appeared clearly before the King. The King, seeing the body of Sakka which he had never seen before, had his hair standing on end. Then Sakka said, "Great King, do not be afraid; ask your question. I shall dispel your doubt." ## The King asked the question: "O noble Sakka, ruler of all beings, I ask you. Both almsgiving and the holy life are beneficial; of these two, which practice is of greater fruit?" Sakka replied, "What is there to say about almsgiving? Virtue alone is much more noble because of its distinguished quality. Great King, in the past, although I gave alms to ten thousand ascetics for ten thousand years, I was not freed from the realm of hungry ghosts. However, those who possessed virtue, after enjoying my alms, were born in the Brahma realm." He then uttered these verses: ## "By a lowly holy life, one is born into a royal family. By a middling holy life, one attains devaship. By a supreme holy life, one is purified from defilements. These Brahma realms are not easily obtained by any merit associated with offerings. Only those ascetics who have renounced the world and practice austerities are born in the Brahma realm." ## After dispelling the King's doubt in this way, in order to take his promise to visit the deva realm, he said, "Great King, you are fortunate," and so on. In that passage, 'avikampamāno' means without fear. The King accepted, thinking, "I shall establish the people in merit. If I see the deva realm, which is the dwelling place of the meritorious, it will be easy to speak of the benefits of merit when I return to the human world." He said, "Very well, the words of the noble Sakka are excellent; let it be so." ## Then Sakka harnessed a thousand thoroughbred horses to a single yoke and sent them. There was no need to harness those thoroughbred horses individually; they were joined to the yoke merely by the thought of the deity Mātali. That divine chariot was one hundred and fifty yojanas long. The front of the chariot was fifty yojanas, the middle axle part was fifty yojanas, and the rear part was fifty yojanas; the entire chariot was made of the seven kinds of jewels. Since the deva realm is above and the human world is below, it should not be understood that the chariot was sent facing downwards. Just as one sends it along a normal path, he sent it together with the moon when the people had finished their evening meal, and it appeared as if two moons were rising. When the people saw it, they said, "Two moons have appeared." As the chariot drew near, they realized, "It is not two moons, it is a celestial mansion; it is not a celestial mansion, it is a chariot."
218:
When the divine chariot arrived, it was the size of an ordinary chariot, and the horses were also the size of ordinary horses. Having brought the chariot in this manner, Matali drove it clockwise around the King's palace, turned it at the eastern lion-window (sīhapañjara), facing the direction from which he had come, and stopped it right at the window, ready for the King to ascend.

"O Great King, please ascend," said Matali. Although the King thought, "I have obtained a divine vehicle," he did not ascend immediately but gave an exhortation to the citizens. "Friends, look! Sakka, the king of gods, has sent a divine chariot to me. This was not sent because of my birth, lineage, or family status, but because he was pleased with my virtue (sīla) and conduct (ācāra). If you also observe virtue, he will send it to you as well. Therefore, it is truly fitting to observe this virtue. Even though I am going to the celestial realm, I will not stay for long. Be diligent!" Having thus exhorted the multitude and established them in the five precepts, he ascended the chariot. Then, Matali the charioteer, thinking, "I shall also do what is worthy of the Great King," showed two paths in the sky and said, "O Great King," and so forth.

In that context, "By which path?" means, "O Great King, of these two paths, one goes to hell and one goes to the celestial realm. By which of these shall I lead you?" "By which [path]" means the path by which those who have done evil go to the place where they experience the results of their wicked unwholesome deeds; the meaning is that it is possible to see that place. The same method applies to the second phrase. In the Jātaka also:

"By which path shall I lead you,
O best of kings, lord of the quarters?
By which path do those of evil deeds go,
And by which those of meritorious deeds?"

The meaning of this verse is the same as what has been said. Therefore, it is said:

"I wish to see first the hell,
The abode of evil-doers,
The places of those of cruel deeds,
And the destination of the immoral."

"Matali, lead me by both paths; I wish to see hell and also the celestial realm," the King said. When asked, "By which shall I lead you first?", he replied, "Lead me by the path to hell first." Then, Matali, by his own supernatural power, showed the King the fifteen great hells. The detailed account here is as follows:
219:
Matali showed the King the difficult Vetaraṇī river, boiling and mixed with brine, like a flaming fire. This matter should be understood as preached in the Nimi Jātaka. After showing hell, he turned the chariot and headed towards the celestial realm, leading the King to heaven while showing the mansions (vimānas) of the goddess Bīraṇī, the deity Soṇadinna, and the Gana deities. There too, the detailed account is:

'If you have heard of the goddess named Bīraṇī in the world of the living, she was once a maidservant of a brahmin. When the time for offering food arrived, upon seeing a guest, she would welcome him with great joy, just as a mother welcomes her son returning from afar. Due to her self-restraint and her sharing of gifts, she now rejoices in a celestial mansion.'

This matter should also be understood as preached in the Jātaka. As they were traveling, the moment the rim of Matali's chariot wheel struck the threshold of the Cittakūṭa gateway, a great commotion arose in the city of the gods. The host of gods, leaving Sakka the king of gods alone, went out to welcome the Great Being, King Nimi. Seeing such respect from the gods, Sakka was unable to restrain his mind (and felt envious), saying, "O Great King, enjoy yourself in the celestial realm through the power of the gods." It is said that this thought occurred to Sakka: "This king has arrived only today, yet in a single day he has won over the host of gods to his side. If he stays for a day or two, the gods will not even look at me." Being envious, he spoke with this intention: "Great King, you have no merit of your own to live in this celestial realm; live here by relying on the merit of others." The Bodhisatta King Nimi, thinking, "The old Sakka could not restrain his mind; that which is obtained by relying on others is like a borrowed item," rejected the offer, saying, "Enough, my friend," and so forth. In the Jātaka also, it is preached:

'Just as a borrowed vehicle, just as borrowed wealth,
Such is the prosperity that comes from the charity of others.
I do not desire that which comes from the charity of others.'
220:
This whole story should be told. The Bodhisatta, in human form, had reached the celestial realm four times. These were: during the time of King Mandhātu, during the time of King Sādhina, during the time of Guttila the lute player, and during the time of King Nimi. During the time of Mandhātu, the Bodhisatta lived in the celestial realm for an incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya); while he was living there, thirty-six Sakkas passed away. During the time of King Sādhina, he lived there for seven days by celestial reckoning, which amounts to seven hundred years by human reckoning. During the times of Guttila the lute player and King Nimi, he lived there for only a moment, yet it amounted to seven days by human reckoning.

From that celestial realm, he was brought back to the city of Mithilā and placed in his original magnificent chamber.

Kaḷārajanaka was the name of that king. He was called Kaḷārajanaka because of his jagged (or sparse) teeth. That king did not perform only one thing—transitioning from the household life to the homeless life as a monk—but he practiced all other traditional customs of the ancient good kings as usual.

In the phrase "samucchedo hoti" (there is a cutting off), one should understand the distinction: who cuts off the good practice, by whom is it cut off, who continues it, and by whom is it continued? In this regard, a virtuous monk who does not strive, thinking "I can no longer attain Arahatship," is the one who cuts off the practice. By an immoral person, the practice is said to be cut off. The seven types of learners (sekhas) continue the practice. By an Arahant, the practice is said to be continued. The meaning of the remaining words is quite clear.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Maghadevasutta is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Madhurasutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Madhurasutta. In that sutta, the Elder Mahākaccāna was the son of the chaplain to the King of Ujjenī during his lay life; he was very handsome, pleasant to look at, inspiring, and had a golden complexion. In the city of Madhurā... in the Gundāvana forest...
221:
In the Kaṇhakagundāvana forest (while staying there). Avantiputta refers to the son of the daughter of the King of the Avanti country. "He is both old and an Arahant" means that people do not honor a young Arahant in the same way they honor an elderly person; however, the Elder was both old and an Arahant. In saying "O Kaccāna, the Brahmins...", it is because that king was a follower of the Brahmin faith that he spoke thus.

With the words "Only the Brahmin caste is the best" and so forth, he shows that only Brahmins are superior in the context of designating birth, lineage, etc. "Other castes are low" means that the remaining three castes are inferior and base. "Sukka" means one with a white (pure) complexion. "Kaṇha" means one with a black (dark) complexion. "They are purified" means they are purified in the context of designating birth, lineage, and so on. "Sons of Brahmā" means the sons of Mahābrahmā. "Born from the breast, from the mouth" means those who, having stayed in the breast, came out of the mouth, or they are called "orasa" (breast-born) because they were raised in the lap. "Brahmāja" means those born from Brahmā. "Brahmanimmita" means those created by Brahmā. "Brahmadāyāda" means the heirs of Brahmā. "This speech is just a sound" means it is merely a conventional designation.

"Would prosper" means it would be successful; it means that whatever wealth and so on one might desire, his wish would be fulfilled with that much. "A Khattiya would also be his [servant]" means that even a person of the Khattiya (warrior/noble) caste would be one who rises first to serve that person who is endowed with wealth and power. "Nothing [is different] for them here" means that in such service, there is no difference among the four castes.

"They would also invite him with a seat" means dusting the sitting place and saying, "Please sit here." "They would also invite him by bringing [requisites] forward" means going to him and inviting him. Such invitation by bringing forward is of two kinds: by speech and by body. One who says, "Venerable sir, at any time you wish, please tell me what you need in terms of robes and other requisites," is said to invite by bringing forward through speech. One who, noticing a lack of robes and so on, says "Please accept this" and gives them, is said to invite by bringing forward through the body. Referring to both, it is said, "They would also invite him by bringing [requisites] forward." "Protection, defense, and guarding" refers to guarding characterized by protection and defense. Guarding by stationing armed men is not called righteous management. However, managing so that wood-gatherers, leaf-gatherers, and others do not enter the monastery at improper times, and so that hunters and others do not catch animals or fish within the monastery boundaries—this is called righteous management. Referring to such guarding, it is said "righteously."
222: This being so, when those who have gone forth from the four castes are equal in the honor and respect due to monastics, the meaning of the remaining words is clear in all places. ## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī, ## the Explanation of the Madhura Sutta is finished. ## 5. The Explanation of the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta. 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta. There, 'Kokanada' refers to the red lotus. Because that auspicious palace was built in the appearance of a sightly red lotus, it received the name 'Kokanada'. In the phrase 'yāva pacchimasopānakalevarā', by the word 'pacchimasopānakalevara', the first step of the stairs is meant. 'Addasā kho' means Prince Bodhi, standing at the gatehouse just for the sake of looking, saw [the Buddha]. The Blessed One remained silent means that while reflecting, 'For what purpose has the Prince prepared this great honor?', He knew it was done out of a desire for a son. For that Prince Bodhi was childless, and he had heard, 'It is said that by making a special offering to the Buddhas and making a mental wish, one obtains what is desired.' He thought, 'If I am to obtain a son, the Fully Enlightened One will step on my cloth. If I am not to obtain one, He will not step on it,' and having made this prayer, he had the cloth spread out. Then the Blessed One, reflecting 'Will a son be born to him?', saw that 'He will not be born.' It is said that in the past, while living on an island, he and his like-minded wife ate young birds. If his wife had been someone else (who did not agree), he might have obtained a son. But because the evil deed was done by both being of the same mind, He knew that his son would not be born. If He were to step on the cloth, [the Prince] might hold a wrong view, thinking, 'There is a tradition in the world that by making an offering to the Buddhas, one obtains whatever is wished for; and though I have made a great effort, I do not obtain a son; this word is empty.' Even the ascetics of other sects [might say], 'There is nothing that these contemplatives will not do; they wander about treading on cloths'...
223:
...they would criticize. At the present time, when [the cloth] is stepped upon, there are many monks who are knowers of others' minds; those monks, knowing the cause (that a son would be born), would step on it, and knowing the lack of cause (that no son would be born), they would not step on it. In the future, however, the supporting conditions (upanissaya) will be weak, and they will not know the future. If those monks who do not know were to step on it, it would be well if the desired benefit were fulfilled. But if it were not fulfilled, people would become remorseful, thinking: "In the past, people made offerings to the Saṅgha of monks and obtained whatever they wished for; now they do not obtain it. Only those monks of old must have been fulfillers of the practice; these current monks are unable to fulfill the practice." For these reasons, the Blessed One, not wishing to step on it, remained silent. He then laid down a training rule: "Monks, one should not step upon a cloth" (Cullavagga 268). When monks did not step on cloth spread for the sake of a blessing, he laid down a supplementary regulation for the purpose of stepping: "Monks, laypeople desire blessings. Monks, I allow [stepping] for the sake of the laypeople's blessing" (Cullavagga 268).

"The Tathāgata has compassion for the later generations"—the Elder Ānanda said this with reference to the third of the three reasons mentioned. Why did the Prince say, "Happiness is not to be gained through happiness"? Prince Bodhi, perceiving that the Fully Enlightened One did not step on the cloth because he was one who avoids devotion to sensual pleasures, thought, "I too shall be of the same desire as the Teacher," and thus spoke in this way.

The passage beginning with "So kho ahaṃ" up to the words "until the last watch of the night" should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāsaccaka Sutta. Beyond that, up to the exhaustion of the taints (āsavakkhaya) of the group of five monks, it should be understood according to the method stated in the Pāsarāsi Sutta.

"Aṅkusagayhe sippe" means in the art of wielding the elephant hook. "Kusalo ahaṃ" means "I am skilled." From whom did this prince learn this art? He learned it from his father; his father also learned it only from his own father. It is said that in Kosambī, a king named Parantapa reigned. His queen, being heavy with child, was sitting with the king in the open air basking in the morning sun, wrapped in a red woolen blanket. A hatthilinga bird, mistaking her for a piece of meat, seized her and soared into the sky. She remained silent out of fear that the bird might drop her. The bird placed her in the fork of a tree at the foot of a mountain. Only then did the queen make a loud noise by clapping her hands.
224:
The elephant-bird flew away, and the Queen gave birth (emerged from pregnancy) right there at that tree. While it rained throughout the three watches of the night, she sat wrapped in a red woolen blanket. An ascetic lived not far from that place. Hearing the Queen's voice, he came to the foot of the tree at dawn, inquired about her lineage, constructed a ladder, brought her down from the tree, took her to his dwelling, and fed her gruel. He named the boy "Udena" because he was born during the rainy season (megha-utu) and the mountain season (pabbata-utu). The ascetic gathered various fruits and supported both of them.

One day, when the ascetic returned, the Queen went out to meet him, displayed feminine charms, and caused the ascetic to break his virtue. While they were living together and time had passed, King Parantapa passed away. The ascetic, observing the stars at night, knew the King had died and asked, "Your King has died; does your son wish to stay here, or does he wish to raise the umbrella of sovereignty in his father's kingdom?" The Queen told her son everything from the beginning, and knowing her son's desire to raise the umbrella, she informed the ascetic. The ascetic also knew the elephant-lore (Hatthigandha-sippa). How did he obtain it? He received it from Sakka, the King of Devas. Formerly, when Sakka came to serve the ascetic, he asked, "Why are you weary?" The ascetic replied, "There is danger from elephants." Sakka gave the ascetic the elephant-lore and a lute, saying, "When you wish to make the elephants flee, strike this string and recite this verse; when you wish to summon them, recite this verse." The ascetic taught this craft to the youth. The youth climbed a banyan tree, and when the elephants came, he struck the string and recited the verse; the elephants fled in fear.

Knowing the power of the craft, the next day he employed the summoning craft. The leader of the elephants came and offered its shoulder. The youth mounted the elephant's back, selected young elephants capable of battle, took the blanket and the signet ring, paid respects to his parents, and departed. Entering various villages in succession, he rallied the people, saying, "I am the King's son; let those who desire prosperity come," and surrounded the city. When he said, "I am the King's son; hand over the umbrella to me," he showed the blanket and the signet ring to those who did not believe him and was consecrated as King. Being one who greatly delighted in elephants, whenever he heard that there was a fine elephant in a certain place, he would go and capture it himself.
225:
King Caṇḍapajjota thought, "I will learn the elephant-lore from King Udena." He had a wooden elephant made, placed soldiers inside, and captured King Udena when he came to take the elephant. He then sent his daughter to learn the craft from him. King Udena cohabited with the princess and, taking her with him, returned to his own city. This Prince Bodhi, who was conceived in the princess's womb, learned the elephant-lore from his father, King Udena.

"Padhāniyaṅgāni": The word "padhāna" refers to the state of one who exerts effort or strives; one who possesses such effort is called "padhāniya". Because these are the factors of a bhikkhu who possesses such effort, they are called "padhāniyaṅgāni" (Factors of Striving). "Saddho" means being endowed with faith (saddhā). That faith is of four kinds: āgamana-saddhā, adhigama-saddhā, okappana-saddhā, and pasāda-saddhā. Among these four, the faith of the Omniscient Bodhisattas, which has been present since they made the aspiration for Buddhahood, is called "āgamana-saddhā". The faith of the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka), which is attained through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, is called "adhigama-saddhā". The unwavering confidence and trust when "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha" are mentioned is called "okappana-saddhā". The arising of devotion is called "pasāda-saddhā". In this context, however, "okappana-saddhā" is intended. "Bodhi" refers to the knowledge of the four paths (magga-ñāṇa). One believes that the Blessed One has perfectly penetrated that path-knowledge. Although this is only the beginning of the teaching, by this factor, faith in the Three Jewels is intended. For one whose devotion to the Buddha and so forth is strong, their effort and striving will succeed.

"Appābādha" means being free from illness. "Appātaṅka" means being free from affliction. "Samavepākiniyā" means being endowed with the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) that digests food evenly. "Nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya": One with a very cold digestive fire fears the cold; one with a very hot digestive fire fears the heat. For such persons, effort and striving cannot succeed. It can only succeed for one with a moderate digestive fire. Therefore, it is said, "majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya" (having a moderate digestive fire capable of enduring striving). "Yathābhūtaṃ attānaṃ āvikattā" means revealing one's faults as they truly are. "Udayatthagāminiyā" refers to the wisdom capable of discerning the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. By this phrase, the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), which encompasses the fifty characteristics, is taught. "Ariyāya" means pure wisdom. "Nibbedhikāya" means wisdom capable of penetrating the mass of greed and so forth that have not been penetrated before. "Sammādukkhakkhayagāminiyā" means being endowed with insight wisdom that leads to the end of suffering, which is Nibbāna, because defilements are abandoned through the abandonment of individual factors (tadaṅga-pahāna). Thus, by all these terms, only insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is spoken of. For one who lacks wisdom, effort and striving cannot succeed. These five factors of striving should be understood as mundane (lokiya) states.
226: "One who is instructed in the evening will attain distinction in the morning" means that one who is instructed at sunset will attain distinction at dawn. "One who is instructed in the morning [will attain distinction] in the evening" means that one who is instructed at dawn will attain distinction at sunset. This teaching was spoken with reference to a person who is to be led (neyya-puggala). Indeed, a neyya person of dull wisdom attains Arahantship in seven days; one of sharp wisdom attains it in one day; and attainment on the remaining days should be understood according to the capacity of one with medium wisdom. "How wonderful is the Buddha! How wonderful is the Dhamma! How wonderful is the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma!"—because of the loftiness of the Buddha and the Dhamma, and because of the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, having been taught the meditation subject in the morning and attaining Arahantship in the evening, Prince Bodhi, wishing to praise, spoke thus. "Yatra hi nāma" is a particle used in the sense of wonder. "Kucchimatī" refers to a pregnant woman. When asked, "Venerable Sir, this child in my womb...", does taking refuge in this way establish the refuges? The answer is: it does not. There is no such thing as taking refuge without consciousness. However, protection is established for that child. Later, when the child has grown up, the parents remind him, "Dear son, we had you take refuge even while you were in the womb," and when he realizes this and gives rise to the mindfulness, "I am a lay follower who has gone for refuge," only then is it called taking refuge. The remaining words are clear everywhere. ## The Commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 6. Commentary on the Angulimāla Sutta "Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Angulimāla Sutta. In that sutta, regarding the phrase "he wears a garland of fingers," why did he wear it? He wore it because of his teacher's words. In this regard, the sequential story is as follows: This Angulimāla took conception in the womb of a brahmin woman named Mantāṇī, the wife of King Kosala's chaplain. The birth occurred when the brahmin woman's pregnancy reached maturity during the night. When that child came out of his mother's womb, weapons all over the city blazed; the King's auspicious bird, as well as [the weapons] placed on the auspicious bed...
227:
...the small sword also glowed brilliantly. The Brahmin chaplain went out and observed the stars, and knowing that the child was born under the thief constellation (coranakkhatta), he went to the King and asked if he had slept well.

The King said, "Teacher, how could I have a pleasant sleep? My auspicious weapon glowed; I think there will be danger to the kingdom or to my life." "Do not fear, Great King. A son was born in my house. By his power, weapons glowed not only in your residence but throughout the entire city," he replied. When asked, "Teacher, what will happen?", he answered, "Great King, he will be a thief." "A lone thief, or a thief who destroys the kingdom?" the King asked. "A lone thief, Your Majesty," he replied. Having said this, and wishing to win the King's favor, he said, "Your Majesty, kill him." "If he is a lone thief, what can he do? He is like a single stalk of rice in a field of a thousand units. Just nourish and care for him," the King commanded. When they named the child, because the auspicious sword on the bed, the arrows on the roof, and the small knife in the cotton-wool box glowed but did not harm anyone, they named him 'Ahiṃsaka' (Harmless). When the time came for him to learn the arts, they sent him to Takkasilā.

He became a resident pupil (dhammantevāsika) and began his studies. He was perfect in his duties, constantly asking what task he should perform, behaving pleasingly, and speaking endearingly. The other pupils were sidelined. Those pupils sat and consulted: "Since the youth Ahiṃsaka arrived, we are no longer prominent. How can we cause a rift?" They thought, "He is wiser than all, so we cannot say he lacks wisdom. He is perfect in his duties, so we cannot say he is undisciplined. He is of noble birth, so we cannot say he is low-born. What shall we do?" Then they devised a harsh plan: "We will cause a rift between him and the teacher." Dividing into three groups, the first group went to the teacher, paid homage, and stood there. "What is it, dear sons?" the teacher asked. "A certain talk is heard in this house," they said. "What talk?" "We think the youth Ahiṃsaka is betraying you," they replied. The teacher rebuked them, saying, "Go away, you outcasts (vasala)! Do not divide my son and me," and drove them out. Then the other groups also came and spoke in the same way, saying, "If you do not believe us, investigate and see for yourself."
228:
Seeing the disciples speaking with affection, the teacher felt a sense of discord, thinking, "It seems they have a close intimacy with me," and plotted, "I shall kill him." Then he thought, "If I were to kill him myself, people would say, 'The world-renowned Disāpāmokkha teacher seeks out faults in the youths who come to him to learn the arts and deprives them of life.' Then, no one else would come to learn the arts, and thus my gains would decline. Therefore, I shall tell him, 'The concluding rite (upacāra) for your education is not yet complete; kill a thousand wayfarers.' Surely, one among those travelers will rise up and kill him."

Then he said to the youth, "Come, dear son, kill a thousand wayfarers. By doing so, the concluding rite for your education will be accomplished." The youth replied, "Teacher, we are born into a family that does not harm others; it is not possible for me to do this." The teacher said, "Dear son, the art for which the concluding rite is not obtained cannot yield its fruit." That youth Ahimsaka, taking up five kinds of weapons and paying homage to his teacher, entered the forest. He stayed at the entrance to the forest, in the middle of the forest, and at the exit of the forest, killing wayfarers. He took neither their clothes nor their turbans. He went along merely keeping count, saying, "I have one, I have two," but he had never learned the art of counting. Although he was naturally wise, the mind of one who takes the lives of others does not remain steady. Therefore, he could not even keep track of the count in order, so he cut off a finger from each person and kept it. At the place where he kept them, the fingers would rot or be lost. Therefore, he pierced the fingers and made a garland to wear. Because of that, the name "Aṅgulimāla" (Finger-garland) became famous for him. That Aṅgulimāla made the entire forest devoid of human traffic; there was no one who dared to go to the forest even for wood and such.

At night, he would even come into the villages, kick open the doors, and kill those who were sleeping, taking them one by one. As the villagers fled, the villages became deserted and the people moved to the market towns; the market towns became deserted and they moved to the city. People from as far as three yojanas away abandoned their homes, took their children by the hand, and came to Sāvatthī. Surrounding Sāvatthī, they set up camp, gathered at the royal courtyard, and cried out, saying, "Your Majesty, there is a thief named Aṅgulimāla in your kingdom," and so on. The Brahmin Bhaggava, knowing "He must be my son," said to his wife, "My lady, a thief named Aṅgulimāla has appeared. He is none other than your son, the youth Ahimsaka. Now the King will set out to capture him. What shall we do?"
229:
"My lord, go and bring back my son," she said. "My lady, I do not dare to go. For there is no trust to be placed in four kinds of people: a thief is not to be trusted even if he is an old friend; a tree branch is not to be trusted even if it is a place one has spread a mat before; a king is not to be trusted even if he honors one; and a woman is not to be trusted even if she has come under one's influence (and lives with one constantly)," he replied. But a mother's heart is truly soft. Therefore, thinking, "I shall go and bring my son back," she set out.

On that day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world, saw Aṅgulimāla and thought, "If I go, there will be well-being for this man. While staying in the village-less forest, upon hearing a four-line verse, he will go forth in my presence and realize the six higher powers (abhiññā). If I do not go, he will wrong his mother and become one who cannot be pulled out from the mire of Saṃsāra. I shall show him favor." In the morning, having adjusted his under-robe and entered for alms, and after finishing his meal, he departed from the monastery desiring to favor him. To show this matter, the passage beginning with "Atha kho Bhagavā" was spoken. "Saṅkaritvā saṅkaritvā" means having made an appointment and forming groups. "Hatthatthaṃ gacchanti" means they fall into his hands and meet their destruction. Did those people say this knowing the Blessed One, or without knowing? They said it without knowing. For the Blessed One went alone in an unrecognizable form. At that time, the thief was also weary from long-term poor food and poor sleep. How many people had he killed? One less than a thousand (999). He now had the thought that if he got one more, the thousand would be complete, thinking, "Whomever I see first, I shall kill him to complete the count, perform the concluding rite of the art, shave my hair and beard, bathe, change into new clothes, and go to see my parents." Coming out from the middle of the forest to the forest entrance, he saw the Blessed One while standing at a certain place. To show this matter, the passage beginning with "Addasā kho" was spoken. "Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi" means that by causing the great earth to fold like rising waves, as he stepped on the back part, folds appeared in the front part. Aṅgulimāla followed from a distance of about an arrow's flight. The Blessed One displayed a great open space in front and was himself in the middle, while the thief was at the edge. That thief ran with all his strength, thinking, "Now I shall catch up and seize him." The Blessed One, on the open space...
230:
The Blessed One was at the other end of the plain, and the robber was in the middle. The robber thought, "I will catch up to and seize this monk here," and ran swiftly. The Blessed One manifested a ditch or high ground in front of the robber. In this way, He led him for three leagues.
