The robber became exhausted; his mouth became parched, and sweat poured from his armpits. Then the robber thought, "Indeed, it is wonderful!"

Regarding "Migampi": Why does he catch a deer? He catches it for food when he is hungry. It is said that Angulimāla would strike a bush to make the deer come out. Then, he would chase, catch, cook, and eat the deer of his choice. "Puccheyyaṃ" means: "Why does this monk say he is 'standing' while he is actually walking? And why do I say I am 'not standing' while I am standing? I shall ask this monk the reason for that."

"Nidhāya" means: Having laid down and abandoned the stick or weapon that should be used for harming beings, I am one who is established in loving-kindness (mettā), patience (khanti), reflection (paṭisaṅkhā), non-violence (avihiṃsā), and the qualities of formal courtesy (sāraṇīyadhamma). "Tuvamaṭṭhitosi" means: For you, who are unrestrained towards living beings and are killing so many thousands of beings, there is no loving-kindness, patience, reflection, non-violence, or formal courtesy. Therefore, you are one who is "not standing" (unstable). It means that although you are currently standing in terms of physical posture, you will still be running in hell, in the animal realm, in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), or in the host of asuras.

Then the robber thought, "This roar is great like a lion's roar; it is a great thunder. This cannot be the roar of anyone else; it must be the roar of the Ascetic King Siddhattha, the son of Queen Mahāmāyā. I suppose I have been seen by the All-Enlightened One who has keen vision. The Blessed One has come to favor me." Thinking thus, he spoke the verse beginning with "Cirassaṃ vata me." In that context, "Mahitā" means one who is honored by devas and humans with the four requisites. "Paccupādi" means that after a long time, He has come to this great forest to favor me. "Pahāya pāpaṃ" means having abandoned evil.

"Itveva" means having spoken just so. "Āvudhaṃ" refers to the five kinds of weapons. "Sobbhe" refers to a place that is cut off all around (a pit). "Papāte" refers to a place that is cut off on one side (a precipice). "Narake" refers to a place that is cracked (a cleft). Here, however, all three of these words refer only to the forest. "Akirī" means he threw them down or discarded them.
231:
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Come, monk." In ordaining this person, the Blessed One had no need to search for where to get a razor or where to get a bowl and robes; He only looked at his (past) karma. Knowing that this person had previously offered the eight requisites to virtuous ones in the past, He stretched out His right hand and said, "Come, monk; the Dhamma is well-expounded. Lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering." Simultaneously with those words, he received a bowl and robes created by psychic power. At that very moment, his lay appearance vanished, and the appearance of a monk became manifest.

"Three robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a belt, and a water-filter—these eight requisites are suitable for a monk devoted to meditation." These eight requisites appeared as if they were attached to his body. This "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monk) status itself was his higher ordination (upasampadā) as a monk. Indeed, for "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks, there is no separate higher ordination.

"Pacchāsamaṇena" means with an attendant monk who carries the bowl and robes. He proceeded with Angulimāla himself carrying his own bowl and robes, making him His attendant monk. His mother was also nearby, separated by a distance of about eight usabhas. She wandered around searching, saying, "Dear son Ahiṃsaka, where are you standing? Where are you sitting? Where have you gone? Won't you speak with your mother, dear son?" But not seeing him, she went away from that place.

"With about five hundred horses" means he set out with a light force, thinking, "If the robber is defeated, I will pursue and capture him. If I am defeated, I will flee swiftly." Why did he go to the monastery? It is said that the King was afraid of the robber; though he wanted to go in his mind, he did not go (out of fear), but he eventually set out for fear of being blamed (by the public). The King thought: "I will pay homage to the All-Enlightened One and sit down. The Blessed One will ask, 'Why have you come out with an army?' Then I will inform Him. The Blessed One favors me not only for my welfare in the future life but also for my welfare in the present life. If I am to be victorious, He will remain silent (accepting it). If I am to be defeated, He will say, 'Great King, what is the use of going for the sake of a single robber?'"
232:
Then the people will know me thus: 'The King went out to capture the thief, but was turned back by the Blessed One.' Seeing this as an escape from blame, he went [to the monastery].

Why did he say, 'Whence then for him' (Kuto panassa)? He said this to investigate the Blessed One's intention, wondering if the Blessed One, having seen the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of Angulimala, had brought him and ordained him. 'To the King' (Rañño) means that it was not only the King who was afraid; the rest of the people were also terrified, and throwing away their shields and weapons, they fled in all directions. They entered the city, closed the gates, and stood looking out from the watchtowers. They also spoke thus: 'Angulimala, knowing that the King was coming to him, arrived first and is sitting in the Jetavana monastery; the King has been captured by him, but we have fled and escaped.' 'There is no danger to you from him' means that this Angulimala now does not even take the life of a small ant; therefore, it means there is no danger to you from this person.

Why did he ask, 'What is your lineage?' (Kathaṃ gotto)? He asked because he thought it was inappropriate to address an ordained person by a name that arose from a cruel deed, and he wished to address him by the clan name of his parents. 'For the requisites' (Parikkhārānaṃ) means 'I will make an effort for those requisites.' Even while speaking, he removed the cloth tied around his waist and offered it at the feet of the Elder.

The four ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) beginning with 'forest-dweller' (āraññika) appear in the Pali text. However, since the Elder had already undertaken all thirteen ascetic practices, he said, 'Enough.' What was intended by the words, 'Venerable Sir, we [could catch even a running elephant]'? As it was said that he could pursue and catch even a running elephant, the King had previously sent elephant-riders and others, and Angulimala had captured them in this way. The King also sent many elephant-riders, horsemen, and charioteers multiple times, saying, 'Surround and capture him with elephants, with horses, and with chariots.' When they went, as soon as he stood up and shouted, 'Hey, I am Angulimala!', not a single person could move their weapon, and he struck and killed them all. The elephants became wild forest elephants, the horses became wild forest horses, and the chariots were destroyed right there; it was with reference to this that the King spoke thus.

'He entered for alms' (Piṇḍāya pāvisi) does not mean this was the first time he entered. This was said with reference to the day he saw the woman [in difficult labor]. Although he entered for alms every day, people would be terrified upon seeing him, flee, and close their doors. Some, upon merely hearing the name 'Angulimala,' would flee into the forest or enter their houses and lock the doors.
233:
Those who were unable to flee stood with their backs turned. The Elder did not receive even a ladleful of gruel or a ladleful of rice, and he suffered from a lack of almsfood. Not receiving anything outside, he entered the city, thinking that the city is common to all. Through whichever gate he entered, the cry 'Angulimala has come!' became the cause for the breaking of thousands of pots. 'This thought occurred' (Etadahosi) means it occurred due to the arising of compassion. How did compassion arise in one who had killed nearly a thousand people, lacking even a single day of compassion, merely by seeing a woman in difficult labor? It was through the power of his ordination (pabbajjā-bala); indeed, this was the power of ordination.

'Therefore' (Tena hi) means 'because compassion has arisen in you.' Regarding 'by the Noble Birth' (Ariyāya jātiyā): 'Angulimala, do not take that [past life of killing]; that is not your birth. That was the time of a layman; laypeople indeed kill living beings and commit theft and so on. But now, your birth is called the Noble Birth.' Therefore, the Buddha sent him, saying, 'If you are afraid of lying by saying, "Sister, since I was born...", then speak specifically thus: "by the Noble Birth."' 

'He said this to that woman' (Taṃ itthiṃ etadavoca) means that it is not appropriate for men to approach the place where women give birth. What did the Elder do? He sent word that 'Elder Angulimala has come to perform an Act of Truth (saccakiriya) for the sake of safety.' Then the people surrounded the area with a curtain and prepared a seat for the Elder outside the curtain. The Elder sat there and performed the Act of Truth: 'Sister, since I was born in the Noble Birth of the Omniscient Buddha...' Along with the words of truth, the child came out immediately like water released from a water-strainer. Both mother and son were safe. It is said that this protection (paritta) does not fail to crush any danger; this is called a Great Protection (Mahāparitta). They kept the seat where the Elder sat and performed the Act of Truth. Even animals in difficult labor were brought there and made to sit, and they would give birth happily and immediately. For a woman who was too weak to be brought, they would take the water used to wash that seat and sprinkle it on her head, and she would give birth in that very instant; it also calms other diseases. It is said that this is a miracle (pāṭihāriya) that lasts as long as the aeon (kappa).

Did the Blessed One make the Elder perform medical work? He did not. People would flee in fear upon seeing the Elder. The Elder suffered from a lack of almsfood and was unable to develop his recluse-dharma (samaṇadhamma). Out of compassion for him, the Buddha had him perform the Act of Truth. It is said that the Buddha thought, 'Now, the Elder Angulimala...'
234:
Thinking, "By attaining a mind of loving-kindness and performing an Act of Truth, the Elder Aṅgulimāla brings safety and happiness to people," people will consider the Elder worthy of approaching. From then on, he will be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse without being fatigued by the search for alms food. With this intention of supporting him, the Blessed One had him perform the Act of Truth. Indeed, an Act of Truth is not a medical treatment. Even though the Elder took up his original meditation subject, thinking, "I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse," and sat in his night-quarters and day-quarters, his mind did not turn towards the meditation subject. Instead, the places in the forest where he had killed people appeared clearly in his mind. When the words of those fearing death—"Lord, I am poor, I have a young son, please give me my life"—and their trembling hands and feet appeared in his mind, the Elder became remorseful (vippatisāra) and would get up from that place and leave. Then, the Blessed One, considering, "I will make his original birth (as a killer) unmentionable, and by making him develop insight, I will have him attain the fruit of Arahantship," had him perform the Act of Truth by means of his Noble Birth. The passage beginning with "Eko vūpakaṭṭho" is explained in detail in the Vattha Sutta.

"A stone thrown by another" means a stone thrown from any direction within a range of about an arrow's flight to drive away crows, dogs, pigs, etc., which comes and falls only on the Elder's body. In what kind of place does this happen? It happens from the time he puts on his waist-tie and wanders for alms until he returns and reaches the place where he removes the waist-tie. "With a broken head" means the thick skin was cut and broken down to the bone.

By the word "Brāhmaṇa," he refers to the state of an Arahant. The words "Brāhmaṇa, because of the result of that karma which you..." were said in reference to the corresponding karma to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma). Karma being performed fills three portions. Among the seven impulsion consciousnesses (javana-citta), whether wholesome or unwholesome, the first impulsion intention is called karma to be experienced in this very life. It gives its result in this very existence. If it is unable to do so, it becomes lapsed karma (ahosikamma) according to the triad: "the result of karma did not exist, will not exist, and does not exist." The seventh impulsion intention, which accomplishes the result, is called karma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya-kamma). It gives its result in the immediately following existence. If it is unable to do so, it becomes lapsed karma in the same manner mentioned. The five impulsion intentions between these two are called karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya-kamma). When it finds an opportunity in the future...
235:
...at that time, it gives its result. As long as the continuation of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) exists, there is no such thing as lapsed karma (ahosikamma) for this type. However, for the Elder Aṅgulimāla, these two types of karma—karma to be experienced in the next life and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives—were eradicated by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), which brings an end to karma. But the karma to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma) still remains. That karma indeed gives its result even to one who has attained the fruit of Arahantship. Referring to this, the Blessed One said the words beginning with "Yassa kho tvaṃ." Therefore, in this context, the meaning of "Yassa kho" should be understood as: "Brāhmaṇa, because of the result of such karma which you [performed]..."

The phrase "Abbhā mutta" (freed from clouds) is just the beginning of the teaching. In fact, the moon freed from these defilements—clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu—is intended here. Just as the moon, free from defilements, illuminates the world, so too a diligent monk, freed from the defilement of negligence, illuminates this world of his own aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), and destroys the darkness of defilements.

"Kusalena pidhīyati" (covered by the wholesome) means it is blocked by the Path-wholesome; it is made so that there is no further rebirth. "Yuñjati buddhasāsane" (engages in the Buddha's teaching) means he dwells being intensely devoted to the Buddha's teaching through body, speech, and mind. These three verses are known as the Elder's verses of inspiration (udāna-gāthā).

The Elder said the words "Disā hi me" (my enemies) with the desire to perform an act of self-protection. In those words, "Disā hi me" means "they are my enemies." Those who revile and curse me, saying, "Just as we suffer because of our relatives killed by Aṅgulimāla, may Aṅgulimāla also suffer," may those enemies of mine hear the discourse on the Four Noble Truths. This is the meaning. "Yuñjantu" means may they dwell being intensely devoted through body, speech, and mind. "Ye dhammam evādapayanti santo" means those peaceful ones, the virtuous people (sappurisa), who establish, encourage, and make others take up only the Dhamma—may my enemies associate with, serve, and attend upon those virtuous people. This is the meaning.

In the term "Avirodhappasaṃsīnaṃ," "avirodha" refers to loving-kindness (mettā); it means "of those who praise loving-kindness." "Suṇantu dhammaṃ kālena" means may they hear the Dhamma of conciliation (sāranīyadhamma) associated with patience and loving-kindness at all times. "Tañca anuvidhīyantu" means may they also follow and fulfill that Dhamma.

"Na hi jātu so mamaṃ hiṃse" means may that enemy of mine certainly not harm me. "Aññaṃ vā pana kiñci naṃ" means not only me, but also any other person...
236:
Indeed, let them not harm any person; let them not harass anyone. Having reached the supreme peace, Nibbāna, in the phrase 'one should protect the trembling and the firm,' 'the trembling' (tasa) refers to those with craving, and 'the firm' (thāvara) refers to those without craving. The meaning is this: whoever reaches Nibbāna is able to protect all, both the trembling and the firm. Therefore, may my enemies also reach Nibbāna; if they reach it, they will certainly not harm me. These three verses were spoken to create a protection (paritta) for himself.

Now, wishing to show his own practice, he said, 'Conduit-makers lead the water,' and so on. In that context, 'conduit-makers' (nettikā) refers to those who clear the channels, and after damming them at the appropriate places, lead the water where they desire. 'Fletchers' (usukārā) are arrow-makers. 'They straighten' (namayanti) means that after coating the arrows with oil and sour gruel and heating them in hot ashes, they bend the high parts to make them straight. 'Tejana' refers to the arrow shaft. Because an archer can make that arrow sharp and can threaten (tajjeti) others with it, it is called 'tejana.' 'They tame themselves' means that just as conduit-makers lead water by a straight path, fletchers straighten arrows, and carpenters straighten wood, even so, the wise tame themselves, make themselves upright, and make themselves free from faults.

'By the Such One' (tādinā) refers to the Teacher, the Blessed One, who is unshakable by the desirable and the undesirable, and who is endowed with the fivefold quality of 'Suchness.' The Blessed One is called 'Tādi' (the Such One) for five reasons: being 'Such' in the face of the desirable and the undesirable, having vomited out defilements, having abandoned defilements, having crossed over the ocean of existence, and being described by these qualities. Such a Teacher, endowed with the characteristics of 'Suchness,' has cut the 'conduit to existence' (bhavanetti). 'Bhavanetti' is a name for craving (taṇhā), which is the rope of existence. Just as cattle are led by a rope around their necks, craving binds beings at the heart and leads them to various existences; therefore, it is called 'bhavanetti.'

'Touched by the result of action' (phuṭṭho kammavipākena) means touched by the volition of the Path (maggacetanā). Because Path-volition causes kamma to ripen, to ripen fully, to burn away, and to reach exhaustion, that Path-volition is called 'kammavipāka.' Being touched by that Path-volition, this person has become 'debtless' (aṇana) and free from defilements; he is not debtless because of painful feeling. In the word 'I consume' (bhuñjāmi), it should be understood that there are four types of consumption (paribhoga): consumption by theft (theyyaparibhoga), consumption by debt (iṇaparibhoga), consumption by inheritance (dāyajjaparibhoga), and consumption by ownership (sāmiparibhoga). Among these, the consumption by one who lacks virtue is called 'consumption by theft.' He consumes the four requisites by stealing them. Thus it was said: 'Monks, the country's alms-food was consumed by you as a theft.' The consumption by a virtuous person without reflection is called 'consumption by debt.' The consumption by the seven types of noble learners (sekha) is called 'consumption by inheritance.' The consumption by an Arahant...
237:
...is called 'consumption by ownership' (sāmiparibhoga). Here, the word 'debtless' (aṇana) is used with reference to the absence of the debts of defilements. There is also a variant reading 'aniṇa.' The phrase 'I consume food' is said with reference to consumption by ownership.

'Intimacy of delight in sensual pleasures' (kāmaratisanthava) means do not practice or engage in the intimacy of delight through craving in the two types of sensual pleasures. 'This thought of mine was not ill-conceived' means that the thought 'I will see the Fully Enlightened One and ordain' was a well-conceived thought, not an ill-conceived one. 'Among the shared Dhammas' means that among the Dhammas shared by the Buddhas who have appeared in the world—of which I am the Teacher—I have reached Nibbāna, which is the most excellent. Therefore, this coming of mine is 'well-come' (svāgata).

'The three knowledges' (tisso vijjā) are the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of taints. 'Done is the Buddha's bidding' means that whatever task was to be done in the Buddha's dispensation, I have done it all. He brought the teaching to its climax with the three knowledges and the nine supramundane states.

## The Explanation of the Angulimāla Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Piyajātika Sutta

'Thus have I heard' and so on is the Piyajātika Sutta. In that sutta, 'work does not appear' means it does not fail to appear entirely, but it does not appear in its normal state. The same method applies to the second phrase. Here, 'does not appear' (na paṭibhāti) means 'does not please.' 'Cemetery' (āḷāhana) means the charnel ground. 'Alteration' (aññathatta) means becoming otherwise due to discoloration. 'Faculties' (indriyāni) refers to states cognizable by the mind, but this is said with reference to their physical base. 'Born of the beloved' (piyajātika) means they are born from what is dear. 'Originating from the beloved' (piyappabhāvika) means they have what is dear as their source.

'If that is so, Great King' means that although she did not fully grasp the meaning of those words, she spoke thus out of faith in the Teacher. 'Go away, you wretch' (cara pire) means 'go away, you who are an outsider to us' (unrelated to us). Alternatively, 'cara pire' means 'go further away, do not stay here.'
238:
"Dvidhā chetvā" means cutting into two parts with a sword. "Attānaṃ upphālesi" means splitting his own belly with that same sword. If that woman were not dear to that man, he would not have killed himself, thinking, "Now I will take another woman." Because that woman was dear to him, he did this, wishing to be united with her even in the next world.

Regarding the phrase "Piyā te Vajirီ" (Is Vajirī dear to you?), it is said that Queen Mallikā had this thought: "If I were to tell a story like 'Great King, formerly in this very Sāvatthī, a certain woman...', he might stop me saying, 'Who did this to you? Go away, there is no such thing.' I will make the King understand using a present event." Thus she spoke. In the phrase "Vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā," vipariṇāma (change) should be understood as change due to death, and aññathābhāva (alteration) as becoming otherwise due to running away with someone.

"Vāsabhāyā" refers to a queen of the King named Vāsabhā.

Why did she ask "Piyā te ahaṃ" (Am I dear to you?) last of all? It is said Queen Mallikā had this thought: "This King is angry with me. If I ask 'Am I dear to you?' first of all, he might say 'You are not dear to me, go away.' If so, the conversation will find no footing." Thus she asked last to establish the conversation. Vipariṇāma is understood as change due to the abandonment of the Kāsī and Kosala kingdoms, and aññathābhāva as alteration due to falling into the hands of rival kings.

"Ācamehi" means "Give rinsing water." He said this because he wished to pay homage to the Teacher after washing his hands and feet and rinsing his mouth. The rest of the words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the explanation of the Piyajātika Sutta is finished.
## 8. Bāhitikasutta-vaṇṇanā
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" etc. is the Bāhitika Sutta. In that sutta, "Ekapuṇḍarīkaṃ nāgaṃ" refers to an elephant of that name. On the ribs of that elephant, there were white spots the size of palm fruits...
239:
(On the ribs of that elephant, there was a bone fifteen cubits long); therefore, they named that elephant Ekapuṇḍarīka. "Sirivaḍḍhaṃ mahāmattaṃ" refers to the high official named Sirivaḍḍha who went along, riding a separate elephant, for the sake of pleasant conversation. In the word "Āyasmanto," the syllable 'no' is an interrogative particle. The high official, observing the manner in which the Elder Ānanda carried his double-robe and bowl, said, "It is so, Great King."

"Opārambho" means deserving of blame or reproach. "What shall I ask?" the King asked. This sutta arose in the context of the Sundarī incident; "I will ask about that," he said. "Venerable Sir, the reason we were unable to complete the question by taking the word 'viññūhi' (by the wise), that reason has been fulfilled by the Venerable Ānanda speaking thus."

"Akusalo" (Unwholesome) means a state arising from lack of skill. "Sāvajjo" (Blameworthy) means a state with fault. "Sabyābajjho" (Afflictive) means a state with suffering. "Dukkhavipāko" (Resulting in suffering) refers to the result that flows on in this very life. "Tassa" refers to that person who has such bodily conduct leading to his own affliction and so on.

"Great King, the Tathāgata has abandoned all unwholesome states and is endowed with wholesome states." In this passage, it means he praises the abandonment of all unwholesome states. When he answers "Yes, he praises it," the meaning is stated according to the question. Answering in this way is not difficult. Even one who has not abandoned unwholesome states can praise their abandonment. However, the Buddha answered thus to show that because he has abandoned unwholesome states, he acts as he speaks (yathākārī tathāvādī). The same method should be understood for the wholesome side.

"Bāhitikā" is the name of a cloth produced in the Bāhitika country. It is sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width.

He offered it to the Blessed One. After offering it, he made it into a canopy and fastened it in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). From that time on, the Fragrant Chamber became even more...
240:
(From the time the canopy was made and tied,) the Gandhakuti is exceedingly beautiful. The remaining words are clear in all places. This teaching is concluded by the power of the person to be guided (neyya-puggala).

## In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī,
## the explanation of the Bāhitika Sutta is finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Dhammacetiya Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Dhammacetiya Sutta. In that sutta, "Medāḷupa" is the name of that market town (nigama). In that town, it is said that stones with the color of fat (meda) were abundant; therefore, it came to be called "Medāḷupa." In this context, the lodging (senāsana) is not specifically mentioned; therefore, it was not spoken of. "Nagaraka" is the market town of the Sakyans of that name.

"Due to some business to be done" means not for any other reason, but because King Kosala had given the order, "Seize (and kill) General Bandhula along with his thirty-two sons in a single day." On the day (Bandhula was killed), his wife Mallikā had invited the Blessed One along with five hundred monks. While the community of monks headed by the Buddha had arrived at the house and were seated, people brought the news, "The General has passed away," and gave it to Mallikā. Mallikā took the letter and asked for the verbal message. They informed her, "Lady, the King has had the General seized and killed along with his thirty-two sons all at once." Mallikā instructed, "Do not let this news spread to the public," and placing the letter in her lap, she continued to serve the community of monks. At that time, a jar of ghee was being brought out; it struck the threshold and broke. Mallikā had the broken jar removed, another one brought, and continued to serve the community of monks.

When the meal was finished, the Teacher, in order to start a conversation, said, "Do not worry about the breaking of the ghee jar." Then Mallikā took out the letter, placed it before the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, this letter is the news of the death of the General along with his thirty-two sons. I do not worry even for such a great death; why should I worry about the breaking of a ghee jar?" The Blessed One said, "Mallikā, do not worry; for beings wandering in the beginningless cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), such destruction is a natural occurrence," and having given a Dhamma talk related to impermanence (anicca) and so forth, He departed. Mallikā also called her thirty-two daughters-in-law and gave them advice. The King summoned Mallikā and said, "Regarding our General..."
241:
...is there any fault of offense within him or not?" Mallikā replied, "There is none, my Lord." Through her words, the King realized the General's innocence and felt remorse, giving rise to strong distress. He thought, "I have destroyed such a friend who came to me with respect and without fault." From then on, he found no delight in the palace, among the dancers, or in royal pleasures, and began to wander here and there. This distress became the King's constant preoccupation. Referring to this, it is said, "Due to some business to be done" (kenacid-eva karaṇīyena).

"Dīgha Kārāyana" is the nephew of General Bandhula. Although he thought, "The King has killed my uncle, the innocent General Bandhula, without cause," the King appointed him to the position of General. Referring to him, this was said. "With great royal majesty" (mahatā rājānubhāvena) means with a great army of beautiful appearance, as if splitting the earth or turning the ocean. "Pāsādikāni" means places that are delightful and pleasing just by seeing them. "Pasādanīyāni" is a synonym for that same term. Alternatively, "pāsādikāni" means places that inspire faith. "Appasaddāni" means without noise. "Appanigghosāni" means free from loud shouts of indistinct meaning. "Vijanavātāni" means free from the breeze of people's movement. "Manussarāhasseyyakāni" means suitable for doing things away from people's ears, appropriate for those holding secret consultations. "Paṭisallānasāruppāni" means suitable for staying alone in seclusion. In the phrase "where we (used to visit)," although the King had not visited the Blessed One in that particular place before, he had visited Him in other similar places; therefore, it means "in such places (where we shall visit)."

In the phrase "There is, Great King," General Dīgha Kārāyana, being a wise man, knew, "Our Lord the King is very fond of the Blessed One." He thought, "If the King asks me where the Blessed One is, it is proper to be able to inform him without delay." Thus, he sent spies and already knew the place where the Blessed One was staying. Therefore, he spoke thus. "Entered the park" (ārāmaṃ pāvisi) means having established a camp outside the market town, he entered with Dīgha Kārāyana.

"Vihāro" refers to the Gandhakuti, as the commentators say. "Āḷinda" is the front of the monastery (porch). "Ukkāsitvā" means making the sound of clearing the throat. "Aggaḷa" is the door-leaf. "Ākoṭehi" means "knock slightly with the tip of the fingernail near the keyhole." It is said that non-humans (amanussa) usually knock at a very high place on the Gandhakuti door, and creatures like snakes knock at a very low place. Likewise...
242:
One should not knock on the door too high up, but in the middle, near the bolt hole. The commentators, wishing to show that this is the proper conduct for knocking on a door, say this. "Tattheva" means only at the place mentioned by the monks. "Khaggañca uṇhīsañca" is merely a teaching. In fact:

The yak-tail fan, the turban, the sword, the parasol, and the sandals—
These five royal regalia the King, having descended from his vehicle,
Left behind as protection (and handed them over).

He handed over the five royal regalia that were brought. Why did he hand them over? Because it is not proper to approach the most venerable Fully Enlightened One in an exalted manner, and because he wished to approach alone and converse joyfully according to his own desire. Indeed, when the five royal regalia are turned back, there is no need to say, "You all turn back," for all the troops turn back of their own accord. Thus, he handed them over for these two reasons. "Rahāyati" means he performs a secret act, he hides it. This was the intention of Dīgha Kārāyana. It is said that he thought: "Previously, this King consulted with the ascetic Gotama in private and had my uncle Bandhula the General arrested and killed along with his thirty-two sons. Now he wishes to consult in private again; will he have me arrested too?" Thus, this thought arose in him through the power of anger.

"The Blessed One opened the door" does not mean the Blessed One stood up and opened the door himself, but thinking "Let it open," he extended his hand. Then, as if saying, "Venerable Blessed One, you who have given gifts for countless billions of aeons should not perform the act of opening a door with your own hand," the door opened by itself. Since that door opened because of the Blessed One's mind, it is appropriate to say, "The Blessed One opened the door." "Having entered the monastery" means entering the Gandhakuṭi. As soon as he had entered, Dīgha Kārāyana took the five royal regalia, went to the camp, and said to Viṭaṭūbha, "Friend, raise the white parasol." Viṭaṭūbha asked, "Where has my father gone?" "Do not ask about your father; if you do not raise it, I will take it and raise it myself." Thus, he consented, saying, "Friend, I will raise it." Dīgha Kārāyana left only one horse and one female servant for the King and said, "If the King wishes to live, let him not come," and having Viṭaṭūbha raise the white parasol, he took him and returned to Sāvatthī.
243:
Dhammanvaya means knowing the Dhamma, which is called direct knowledge, through following, reflecting, and special suitability. Now, to show how this Dhammanvaya (inference of the Dhamma) such as "The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One" arose in King Kosala, he spoke the words beginning with "Idha panāhaṃ, bhante."

In those words, "āpāṇakoṭikaṃ": pāṇa means life; making that life the limit and practicing even at the time of death, not transgressing that practice. There is also a variant reading "apāṇakoṭikaṃ," which means until the end of life. While some people transgress the precepts for the sake of survival, these people do not do so, but practice even at the cost of their lives. "Ayampi kho me, bhante" means that this reflection arose because of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's being well-expounded, and the Saṅgha's good practice. He shows, "Venerable Sir, such is my Dhammanvaya (inference of the Dhamma) regarding the Blessed One." This method should be understood in all sentences.

"Na viya manye cakkhuṃ bandhante" means as if they do not captivate the eye. When one sees someone who is not inspiring, there is no further need to look, therefore that person is said not to captivate the eye. When one sees someone who is inspiring, the need to look again and again arises, therefore that person is said to captivate the eye. Since these people are not inspiring, he spoke thus. "Bandhukarogo no" means a family disease (hereditary disease). It means, "Those born in our family tend to have such a disease." "Uḷāraṃ" means having great power. "Pubbenāparaṃ" means a distinction following a previous distinction. Here, one who performs the preliminary work for a kasiṇa and attains meditative absorption (samāpatti) is said to know a great initial distinction. One who, based on that absorption, develops insight (vipassanā) and attains Arahantship is said to know a distinction further than the initial insight, namely Arahantship.

"Ghātetāyaṃ vā ghātetuṃ" means to execute one who deserves to be executed. "Jāpetāyaṃ vā jāpetuṃ" means to fine one who deserves to be fined with wealth, or to make them destitute. "Pabbājetāyaṃ vā pabbājetuṃ" means to banish one who deserves to be banished from the country.

"Isidattapurāṇā" refers to Isidatta and Purāṇa. Among them, one was a celibate (brahmacārī) and one was content with his own wife (sadārasantuṭṭha). "Mamabhattā" means my servants or my subordinates.
244:
"Mama-bhattā" means that these people have rice that is my property. "Mama-yānā" means that these people have a vehicle that is my property. "Jīvikāya dātā" means one who gives the means of livelihood. "Vīmaṃsamāno" means while investigating and reflecting. At that time, it is said that King Kosala lay down, not yet fallen into a deep sleep, but as if he were asleep. While he was lying thus, those two carpenters asked, "In which direction is the Blessed One staying?" and having heard, "He is in such and such a place," they consulted each other: "If we place our heads towards where the Perfectly Enlightened One is, our lord King Kosala will be at our feet. If we place our heads towards where King Kosala is, the Teacher will be at our feet. What shall we do?" Then it occurred to them: "If our lord King Kosala gets angry, he might take back the gifts he has given us. However, we cannot knowingly place the Teacher at our feet." Thus, they lay down with their feet towards King Kosala. It was with reference to this that the King spoke in this way.

"Pakkāmi" means that King Kosala, having left the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), went to the place where Dīgha Kārāyana was stationed, but not finding him there, he went to the site of the encampment. Finding no one else there either, he questioned that young woman. She reported the whole sequence of events. The King thought, "Now I should not go to Sāvatthī alone. I will go to Rājagaha, and after returning with my nephew, King Ajātasattu, I will retake my throne." While traveling to Rājagaha, he ate broken rice and drank thick, turbid water along the way. For the King, who was of a delicate nature, that food did not digest well. Even when he reached Rājagaha, he arrived at a late hour when the city gates were closed. Thinking, "I will sleep in the rest house today and see my nephew, King Ajātasattu, tomorrow," he lay down in a rest house outside the city. During the night, he had to go outside several times, and eventually, being unable to walk on foot, he lay in the woman's lap and passed away at the break of dawn. Realizing he was dead, the young woman began to lament loudly, saying, "My lord, King Kosala, who ruled over two kingdoms, has now died a helpless death in another's rest house outside the city and lies here alone," and so on. People heard the sound and informed King Ajātasattu. The King came, saw, and recognized him. Having learned the reason for his coming, he performed the funeral rites with great ceremony. Then, thinking "I will capture Viṭaṭūbha," he had the drums beaten and assembled his army. The ministers bowed at his feet and pleaded, "Great King, if your maternal uncle were healthy, it would be appropriate for you to go. But now, Viṭaṭūbha also..."
245: Having informed [King Ajātasattu] that 'Viṭūḍabha is indeed worthy of having the parasol raised by depending on Your Majesty,' they prevented him. 'Dhammacetiyāni' refers to words of respect for the Dhamma. For when respect is shown to any one of the Three Jewels, it is considered shown to all; therefore, when respect is shown to the Blessed One, it is also shown to the Dhamma, and thus the Blessed One said 'Dhammacetiyāni'. 'Ādibrahmacariyakāni' means those practices that are the beginning of the Path-holy-life, the practices of the preliminary stage. The meaning of the remaining words is very clear in all places. ## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī, ## the Explanation of the Dhammacetiya Sutta is finished. ## 10. The Explanation of the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta. 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta. There, 'Uruññāyaṃ' is the name of both that country and that city. The Blessed One was staying in dependence on the city of Uruññā. 'Kaṇṇakatthale migadāye' means that not far from that city, there is a delightful piece of ground named Kaṇṇakatthala. Because that place was given for the safety of deer, it is called a Deer Park (Migadāya). It was in that Kaṇṇakatthala Deer Park. 'Kenacideva karaṇīyena' means not for any other reason, but for the very reason mentioned in the preceding Dhammacetiya Sutta. 'Somā ca bhaginī sakulā ca bhaginī' means these two sisters were the King's queens. 'Bhattābhihāre' means at the place where the meal is served. To the place where the King takes his meal, all the harem women go to serve the King, carrying ladles and so forth. Somā and Sakulā also went in the same way. Why did the Blessed One say, 'Great King, how is it?' It was for the sake of freeing the King from reproach. For otherwise, the assembly might think, 'As soon as this King arrives, he reports the message of the women. We thought he came to see the Blessed One of his own accord, but he has come bringing the message of women; he seems to be a slave to women. Perhaps he came for this very reason before too.' But when questioned, he will state the reason for his own coming; thus He spoke in this way to free him from reproach, so that this reproach would not arise.
246:
'Abbhudāhāsi' means he spoke. "He will know all, he will see all at once" means there is no one who, with a single advertence or a single thought, can know or see all of the past, future, and present. For even if one adverts, "I will know all of the past with one thought," one cannot know all of the past; one knows only a portion. With that same thought, one cannot know all of the future and present entirely. This same method applies to the others. Thus, this question was answered in terms of a single thought. 'Heturūpa' means the nature of cause, or having a causal nature. 'Saheturūpa' means having a nature together with a cause. "Venerable sir, I ask about the qualities pertaining to the next life (samparāyika)."

'Pañcimāni' means that in this sutta, the five factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga) mixed with the supramundane are taught. However, when Elder Cūḷasamudda, who lived at Kaṭhinaṅgaṇa, was asked, "Venerable sir, what do you prefer?" he said, "I prefer only the supramundane." 'Padhānavemattatā' means the variation in striving. For the striving of a worldling is of one kind, that of a Sotāpanna is another, that of a Sakadāgāmī another, that of an Anāgāmī another, that of an Arahant another, that of the eighty Great Disciples another, that of the two Chief Disciples another, that of the Paccekabuddhas another, and that of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas is of yet another kind. The striving of a worldling does not reach the striving of a Sotāpanna... the striving of a Paccekabuddha does not reach the striving of a Fully Enlightened Buddha. Referring to this meaning, he said, "I speak of the variation in striving." "They would reach the state of discipline" (dantakāraṇaṃ gaccheyyuṃ) means they would reach that cause seen in disciplined animals, such as not being crooked, not breaking away, and not throwing off the yoke. 'Dantabhūmi' means the ground to be reached by the disciplined.

In the words "faithless" (assaddho) and so on, even the four types of persons—the worldling, the Sotāpanna, the Sakadāgāmī, and the Anāgāmī—are called "faithless." Because a worldling has not reached the faith of a Sotāpanna, he is "faithless"; a Sotāpanna [is faithless] compared to a Sakadāgāmī, a Sakadāgāmī to an Anāgāmī, and an Anāgāmī is "faithless" because he has not reached the faith of an Arahant. Since illness can also occur to an Arahant, all five are called "those of much illness." But for a noble disciple, the names "deceitful" (saṭha) and "hypocritical" (māyāvī) do not exist. That is why the Elder said, "I prefer that the five factors of striving are taught as supramundane." However, in the Assakhaluṅka Sutta, where it says, "Bhikkhus, I will teach the three types of horse-colts and the three types of man-colts," the name "Enlightenment" (sambodhi) for the noble disciple...
247:
...is mentioned; by the power of that striving, it is said that the things mixed with the supramundane are taught. A worldling, not having reached the energy associated with the path of stream-entry... (and so on) ...a non-returner, not having reached the energy associated with the path of arahantship, is called 'lazy' (kusīta), and like the 'faithless,' there are only four such persons; likewise, there are only four 'unwise' (duppañña) persons.

The comparison between the simile and the thing illustrated should be understood thus: A person devoid of striving associated with the path is like an untamed elephant, etc. A person possessing striving associated with the path is like a tamed elephant, etc. Just as untamed elephants, etc., without acting without deceit, without breaking the bond, and without dropping the burden, are unable to walk in a tamed manner or reach the ground reached by tamed elephants and horses; even so, a person devoid of striving associated with the path is unable to reach the quality to be reached or produce the quality to be produced by one possessing striving associated with the path. Just as tamed elephants, etc., without acting with deceit, without breaking the bond, and without dropping the burden, are able to walk in a tamed manner or reach the ground reached by tamed elephants and horses; even so, a person possessing striving associated with the path is able to reach the quality to be reached or produce the quality to be produced by one possessing striving associated with the path. This is what is meant: 'A person possessing striving associated with the path of stream-entry is able to reach the state and produce the quality to be reached and produced by one possessing striving associated with the path of stream-entry... (and so on) ...a person possessing striving associated with the path of arahantship is able to reach the state and produce the quality to be reached and produced by one possessing striving associated with the path of arahantship.'

Sammappadhānā means having equal striving by way of striving associated with the path. 'I do not speak of any difference, that is, in terms of liberation' means that I do not speak of any distinction to be made regarding the liberation of fruition of one person compared to the liberation of fruition of another. 'Acciyā vā acci' means from one flame or in one flame. In the remaining two phrases, the method is the same; here the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. 'Great King, what do you think? "There are the gods of the Four Great Kings, there are the Tāvatiṃsa gods... (and so on) ...there are the Paranimmitavasavatti gods, there are gods beyond that"—do you not know the existence of gods in this way, that you speak thus?' Then, [the King replied], 'I know the existence of gods, but do they come to the human world or not?' Wishing to ask this, he said, 'Venerable sir, those gods...' and so on. Sabyābajjha means those with suffering, having mental suffering not yet abandoned by the abandonment of eradication. Āgantāro means those who come by way of rebirth. Abyābajjha means those who have completely eradicated suffering. Anāgantāro means those who do not return by way of rebirth.
248:
"Pahoti" means "is able." To explain in detail, a king can displace even a person of merit and wealth from their position by making it so that no one dares to approach them. He can also change the condition of a person without merit, who cannot even get enough food to survive despite wandering through the whole village, by making them endowed with gain and honor. He can displace a person of holy life from their position by causing them to associate with women and destroy their virtue, or by forcibly making them disrobe. He can displace a minister endowed with sensual pleasures from the enjoyment of those pleasures by putting them in prison and not allowing them to see even the face of a woman. He can also banish whomever he wishes from the country.

"Dassanāyapi nappahontīti" means that, first of all, in the sense-sphere, devas who are subject to suffering (worldlings and learners) are not able to see devas who are free from suffering (Non-returners and Arahants) even with eye-consciousness. Why? Because Arahants do not reside in that sense-sphere. In the fine-material sphere, however, they stand and sit together in the same mansion, so they can see with eye-consciousness; yet they are unable to see, note, or penetrate with the eye of wisdom the characteristics that those [noble ones] have seen, noted, and penetrated. They are also unable to see devas of higher realms with eye-consciousness.

"Venerable sir, what is the name of this venerable one?" The King asks the Elder as if he does not know, even though he does. Why? Because of a desire to praise him. "Ānandarūpo" means having a pleasing nature. The questions of the Brahmas should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. "Then a certain man" refers to the fact that those words were actually spoken by Viṭaṭūbha. It is said that the royal messenger said this to prevent a quarrel, lest they should get angry with one another at that very spot, saying "You said it, you said it," and rouse their respective armies. The remaining words are clear. This teaching is concluded by way of a person who is to be led (neyyapuggala).

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Fourth Division is finished.
249:
## 5. Brāhmaṇavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta
This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Brahmāyu Sutta. Therein, in the phrase "mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ," "mahatā" means great both because of the greatness of virtues and because of the greatness of number. That assembly of monks was great in virtue because they were endowed with virtues such as fewness of wishes, and great in number because they numbered five hundred. "Bhikkhusaṅghena" refers to the group of samanas who are united by the commonality of view and virtue. "Saddhiṃ" means together. "Pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi" means together with monks who are five hundred in measure. The word "mattā" means measure (pamāṇa). Therefore, just as in the phrase "bhojane mattaññū" it means knowing the measure in food, here too the meaning should be understood as the number of those monks being five hundred in measure. Hundreds of monks are called "bhikkhusatāni." It is together with those five hundred monks.

"Vīsavassasatiko" means one who is one hundred and twenty years old (twenty years in excess of a hundred). "Tiṇṇံ vedānaṃ" refers to the three Vedas: Iruveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. He is called a "pāragū" (master) because he has reached the other shore [of knowledge] merely by the contact of lips and vocal organs. He is called "sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ" because he is proficient in the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha. "Nighaṇḍu" is the lexical text that explains synonyms for trees and so on. "Keṭubha" is the text concerning the variety of ritual acts and poetic techniques for the benefit of poets. He is called "sakkharapabbhedānaṃ" because he is proficient in the differentiation of letters. "Akkharapabbheda" refers to the science of phonology (Sikkhā) and etymology (Nirutti). "Itihāsapañcamānaṃ" means those Vedas of which Itihāsa is the fifth, making the Athabbaṇaveda the fourth; Itihāsa refers to ancient legends connected with such words as "Thus it has been." He is called "padaka" and "veyyākaraṇa" because he has studied and can proclaim the words and the remaining science of grammar. "Lokāyata" refers to the science of sophistry (Vitaṇḍavāda). "Mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ" is the science that illustrates the marks of Great Men such as the Buddhas, consisting of twelve thousand texts. In that science, there were the "Buddhamantas" (Buddha-mantras) amounting to sixteen thousand verses. By means of those, one can distinguish: "One endowed with this mark is a Buddha; one endowed with this mark is a Paccekabuddha; these are the two Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, the chief attendant, the chief female attendant, and the Cakkavatti King."
250:
Through these texts, this distinction is known. 'Anavaya' means one who is not deficient but complete in these Lokāyata and Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa texts; it means he is not 'avaya' (incomplete). One who is unable to master these texts in both meaning and phrasing is called 'avaya.' Regarding the passage beginning with 'Assosi kho,' what should be said has already been explained in the Sāleyyaka Sutta.

'Ayaṃ tāta' refers to the Brahmin Brahmāyu, who, being unable to go himself due to old age, addressed the youth Uttara and spoke thus. Alternatively, that Brahmin thought: 'In this world, many people wander about taking the famous name, saying "I am the Buddha, I am the Buddha." Therefore, it is not proper for me to approach him merely on hearsay. For some, after approaching, it is difficult to leave, and harm may arise. What if I send my pupil, the youth Uttara, to find out whether he is indeed the Buddha or not, and then approach him?' Thus, he addressed the youth and said 'Ayaṃ tāta,' etc. 'Taṃ bhavantaṃ' refers to that Venerable Gotama. 'Tathā santamyeva' means 'being just so.' Here, the word 'taṃ bhavantaṃ' uses the second case (accusative) in the sense of itthambhūtākhyāna (description of a state). It means: 'Teacher, how shall I know that Venerable Gotama as the Buddha? If there is a way to know him, please tell me that way.' Alternatively, 'yathā' is merely a particle. 'Kathaṃ' is an inquiry into the manner, meaning: 'In what manner shall I know the Venerable Gotama as the Buddha?'

When this was said, his teacher, the Brahmin Brahmāyu, said: 'Dear boy, why do you speak as if standing on the earth and saying "I do not see the earth," or as if standing in the light of the moon and sun and saying "I do not see the moon and sun"?' To show the manner of knowing, he said 'Āgatāni kho tāta,' etc. In that context, 'mantesu' means in the Vedas. It is said that the Suddhāvāsa deities, knowing in advance that a Tathāgata would arise, inserted the marks into the Vedas and, appearing in the guise of Brahmins, taught the Vedas, saying, 'These are the Buddha-mantras.' They intended that 'based on those [Vedas], noble beings will recognize the Tathāgata.' Therefore, in ancient times, the marks of a Great Man appeared in the Vedas. However, after the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, those marks gradually disappeared, and thus they do not exist now. 'Mahāpurisassa' refers to a man who is great due to qualities such as resolution (paṇidhi), undertaking (samādāna), wisdom (ñāṇa), and compassion (karuṇā). 'Dve yeva gatiyo' means there are only two final destinations. Indeed, this word gati [is used in the sense of] 'Five, O...'
251:
'Sāriputta, these five are the destinies (gatiyo)'—in such passages (M. Ni. 1.153), the word gati refers to the distinction of births. 'The destiny (resort) of beasts is the forest'—in such passages (Pari. 339), it refers to a place of residence. 'Thus, the Venerable Ānanda, who possesses supreme wisdom (gatimanto)'—in such passages (M. Ni. 1.161), it refers to wisdom. In phrases like 'attained to diffusion (gatigata),' it refers to the state of being diffused. Here, however, it should be understood as referring to the finality (niṭṭhā).

Among those [marks], although one endowed with them becomes a king, he does not become a Buddha merely by being endowed with them; yet, because the marks are identical, they are called the same. Therefore, it was said: 'For one endowed with those [marks]...'

'If he lives the household life' means if he dwells in a house, he becomes a Wheel-turning King. He is called 'Rājā' (King) because he delights the world with the four wonderful qualities and the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He is called 'Cakkavatti' because he turns the Wheel-jewel, or because he turns [the world] with the four wheels of prosperity, or because he causes others to turn by means of them, or because he possesses the turning of the wheels of postures for the benefit of others. Here, 'Rājā' is a general term, and 'Cakkavatti' is a specific qualification.

He is 'Dhammika' because he practices according to the Dhamma, meaning he proceeds rightly and evenly. He is 'Dhammarājā' because he becomes king after obtaining kingship through Dhamma. Or, he is 'Dhammika' by performing deeds for the benefit of others, and 'Dhammarājā' by performing deeds for his own benefit. He is 'Cāturanta' because he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans; it means the lord of the earth adorned with the four great islands and bounded by the four oceans. He is 'Vijitāvī' (Victorious) because he has conquered internal enemies such as anger within himself and all external kings.

He is 'Janapadatthāvariyappatta' because he has attained stability and permanence in the country, such that no one can shake him. Alternatively, it means the country-folk have attained stability under him, being free from anxiety, devoted to their own work, unshakable, and undisturbed. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle meaning 'What are those [seven jewels]?' In the word 'Cakkaratanaṃ' and others, it is called 'Cakkaratana' because it is both a wheel (cakka) and a jewel (ratana) in the sense of producing delight. The same method applies to the other terms.

Among these jewels, the Wheel-turning King conquers the unconquered territory with the Wheel-jewel. He travels at will through the conquered territory with the Elephant-jewel and Horse-jewel. He protects the conquered territory with the Counselor-jewel (pariṇāyakaratana). With the remaining jewels, he enjoys the pleasures of use. With the first, the Wheel-jewel, his power of effort (ussāhasatti) is complete. With the Elephant, Horse, and Householder jewels, his power of majesty (pabhusatti) is complete. With the last, the Counselor-jewel, his power of counsel (mantasatti) is fully perfected. Through the Woman-jewel and Gem-jewel, he obtains the fruits of the three powers. That king enjoys the pleasure of wealth through the Woman-jewel and Gem-jewel.
252:
He enjoys the bliss of sovereignty through the remaining five treasures. Specifically, the first three treasures of that Universal Monarch—the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, and the horse-treasure—are perfected through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa). The middle three—the woman-treasure, the gem-treasure, and the householder-treasure—are perfected through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha). The final one, the counselor-treasure (the eldest son), is perfected through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha). This explanation in this commentary is just a summary. The detailed version should be taken from the instructions of the Ratana Sutta in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta. Furthermore, in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta, the detailed explanation along with the order of appearance of these seven treasures will be found.

'Parosahassaṃ' means more than a thousand. 'Sūrā' means they are of a fearless nature. 'Vīraṅgarūpā': some teachers first explain it as having bodies like those of young devas. However, the natural meaning here is: 'Vīrā' refers to those who are noble and brave. The cause of those brave ones is energy (vīriya), which is called 'vīraṅga'. Because they have bodies made of that energy, they are called 'vīraṅgarūpā'; it means as if their bodies are composed of energy. 'Parasenappamaddanā' means that if an enemy army stands before them, they are capable of crushing that army. 'Dhammena' means by the Dhamma of the five precepts, such as "one should not kill living beings."

"The Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has appeared in the world, one who has removed the veil (vivaṭṭacchado)." In this passage: in the world of the darkness of defilements, which is covered by the seven veils of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, ignorance, and misconduct, he has removed those veils and stands having become a light that has arisen all around; thus he is called 'vivaṭṭacchado'. In that passage, the first term (Arahaṃ) expresses his worthiness of offerings. The second term (Sammāsambuddho) expresses the reason for that worthiness, because he is perfectly enlightened by himself. The third term (Vivaṭṭacchado) expresses the state of being free from all veils along with latent tendencies (vāsanā), which is the cause of Buddhahood.

Alternatively, he is free from the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and free from the veil (chada), hence 'vivaṭṭacchado'. Because of the absence of the round, he is 'Arahaṃ'; because of the absence of the veil, he is 'Sammāsambuddho'. Thus, these are the two reasons for the first two terms. Here, the first term (Arahaṃ) is accomplished through the second vesārajja-ñāṇa (knowledge of fearlessness); the second term (Sammāsambuddho) is accomplished through the first vesārajja-ñāṇa. The third term (Vivaṭṭacchado) is accomplished through the third and fourth vesārajja-ñāṇas. Furthermore, it should be understood that the first term achieves the dhamma-cakkhu (eye of Dhamma), the second the buddha-cakkhu (eye of a Buddha), and the third the samanta-cakkhu (all-seeing eye).

"You are the receiver of the mantras"—with these words, he inspires bravery in him. That person, due to those words of the teacher, became free from confusion regarding the marks, and as if a light had appeared, while looking at the Buddha-mantras, he said, "Yes, sir (bhoti)." The meaning of those words is: "Sir, I will do as you tell me." 'Samannesi' means he searched; he gathered them together while counting one, two, and so on. Addasā...
253:
In what manner did he see? Indeed, no one is able to investigate the marks of the Buddhas when they are sitting or lying down; however, they are able to do so when they are standing or walking. Therefore, seeing one who has come to seek the marks, the Buddhas rise from their seats and stand or perform the walking meditation. Thus, the young man Uttara saw the Blessed One engaged in a posture suitable for seeing the marks.

The term 'yebuyyena' means mostly; it signifies that he saw many marks but did not see a few. To explain those marks he did not see, it is said 'leaving aside two'. 'Kaṅkhati' means to give rise to the wish, "Oh, if only I could see!" 'Vicikicchati' means being exhausted in investigating those marks from here and there and being unable to see them. 'Nādhimuccati' means being unable to reach a conclusion due to that doubt. 'Na sampasīdati' means not attaining confidence in the Blessed One, thinking "This Venerable Gotama is one possessed of complete marks," because of that inability to decide. Alternatively, 'kaṅkhā' refers to weak doubt, 'vicikicchā' to moderate doubt, and 'anadhimuccanatā' to strong doubt; 'asampasāda' refers to the turbidity of the mind caused by these three states.

'Kosohita' means covered by a sheath; 'vatthaguyha' refers to the male organ. Indeed, the Blessed One has a male organ covered by a sheath like that of a noble elephant, golden in color and resembling the interior of a lotus; because that organ was covered by cloth, and because he did not notice the extensiveness of the tongue within the mouth, the young man Uttara had doubt and difficulty regarding those two marks.

Then the Blessed One thought: "If I do not show these two marks to this young man, he will not be free from doubt. If he has doubt, his teacher will also not be free from doubt. In that case, he will not come to see me; if he does not come, he will not hear the Dhamma; if he does not hear the Dhamma, he will not be able to realize the three fruits of recluseship. But if this young man is free from doubt, his teacher will also be free from doubt, and having approached me and heard the Dhamma, he will realize the three fruits of recluseship. It is for the benefit of others such as these that I have fulfilled the perfections. I shall show him those marks."

He performed such a psychic manifestation. Of what nature was it? Who else could say anything here? This was said by the Elder Nāgasena himself when questioned by King Milinda:

"Venerable Nāgasena, the Blessed One performed a difficult task," he said. "Great King, what task do you mean?" "Venerable sir, in the presence of many people, he showed the place that should be shameful to the Brahmin Brahmāyu, to the student Uttara, to the sixteen Brahmins who were students of Bāvarī, and to the Brahmin Sela and his three hundred students." "Great King, the Blessed One [did not show it openly]..."
254:
"The Blessed One did not show the secret organ itself, but showed only a reflection. Great King, the Blessed One, having manifested through psychic power, showed only a reflected image of himself wearing the undergarment fastened with a waistband and robed in the upper garment." "Venerable sir, if the reflection is seen, is it not the same as being seen?" "Great King, let alone that secret organ; if there were a being who could be enlightened by seeing the heart, the Perfectly Enlightened One would even take out and show the flesh of his heart." "Venerable Nāgasena, your words are most fitting," he said.

'Ninnāmetvā' means having put out. 'Anumasi' means he touched repeatedly, making it like a firm needle. It should be understood that by doing so, the softness of the tongue was revealed; by touching the ear-holes, its length; by touching the nostrils, its thinness; and by covering the forehead, its breadth. In the ear-holes of the Buddhas, there is no dirt or wax; they are like silver tubes that have been washed clean. Likewise in the nostrils; they are like well-crafted golden tubes or jeweled tubes. Therefore, putting out his tongue and making it like a firm needle, bringing it to the edge of his face, he inserted it into the right ear-hole, and having withdrawn it, inserted it into the left ear-hole. Then, withdrawing it, he inserted it into the right nostril, and having withdrawn it, inserted it into the left nostril. Then, putting it out again to show its breadth, he covered the entire circle of his forehead with his tongue, which was like a flash of lightning, just as a red cloud covers half the moon or as a red woolen cloth covers a gold plate.

Why did he think, "What if I... (yannūnāhaṃ)"? "I came to investigate the marks of a Great Man. If my teacher asks, 'My dear, did you see the marks of a Great Man?' I will be able to say, 'Yes, teacher.' But if he asks, 'What are the Buddha's actions and behavior like?' and I say I do not know, the teacher will be angry, saying, 'Did I not send you to know everything? Why have you returned without knowing?'" Thinking thus, he followed the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave him the opportunity to observe in all places, even in the single Perfumed Chamber, except for these four places: the place of bathing, the place of washing the face, the place of grooming the body, and the place where he sat surrounded by the harems of kings and great ministers.
255:
As time passed, it became well-known: "This is the young man named Uttara, a disciple of the Brahmin Brahmāyu. He wanders about investigating the Buddhahood of the Tathāgata, wondering whether he is truly a Buddha or not; he is known as the 'Investigator of the Buddha' (Buddha-vīmaṃsaka)." In every place where the Buddhas reside, the five duties are always performed; these duties have been shown below. Among those five duties, in the afternoon, the Blessed One would sit upon the decorated Dhamma-seat, holding an ornate ivory fan, and preach the Dhamma to the multitude; at that time, the young man Uttara would also sit nearby. When the preaching of the Dhamma concluded, people endowed with faith would invite the Blessed One for the next day's meal, and approaching the young man Uttara, they would say, "Dear friend, we have invited the Blessed One; please come along with the Blessed One and accept alms-food at our house."

On the following day, the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, would enter the village. The young man Uttara would follow closely behind, step by step, observing every single footstep. When they entered the donor's house, he would sit and observe all the Buddha's manners, starting from the receiving of the water of donation. At the conclusion of the meal, when the Blessed One sat down after placing his bowl on the ground, they would prepare the morning meal for the young man. Having sat in a suitable place and eaten, he would return and stand in the presence of the Teacher, listen to the words of appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, and then return to the monastery together with the Blessed One.

At the monastery, the Blessed One would sit in the perfumed circular pavilion (Gandhamandalamāla), waiting for the monks to finish their meal. When the monks had finished their meal, put away their bowls and robes, and approached to pay homage and announce that it was time, the Blessed One would enter the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī). The young man Uttara would also go along with the Blessed One. The Blessed One, standing at the entrance of the Gandhakuṭī, would give advice and exhortation to the Saṅgha of monks who had followed him, dismiss them, and then enter the Gandhakuṭī. The young man Uttara would also enter. The Blessed One would sit for a short while on a small couch, and the young man Uttara would sit nearby, observing him. After sitting for a moment, the Blessed One showed the sign of reclining his head. Thinking, "It must be the time for the Venerable Gotama to rest in the monastery," the young man Uttara closed the door of the Gandhakuṭī, went out, and sat in a suitable place. People, having given alms in the morning and eaten their morning meal, would undertake the Uposatha precepts, dress in clean upper robes, and carrying flowers, perfumes, and so on, would come to the monastery saying, "We shall listen to the Dhamma." At that time, the place became as crowded as the encampment of a Universal Monarch.

The Blessed One, having rested for a moment in the lion's posture (sīhaseyya), would arise and, first determining the time, enter into a meditative attainment (samāpatti). Arising from the attainment and knowing that the multitude had arrived...
256:
Knowing that the multitude had arrived, the Blessed One would emerge from the Gandhakuṭī and, surrounded by the people, go to the Gandhamandalamāla which was decorated with garlands of perfume and flowers. Having reached the noble Buddha-seat that had been prepared, he would preach the Dhamma to the assembly. The young man Uttara, sitting nearby, would investigate every syllable and every word, thinking, "Does the ascetic Gotama preach the Dhamma by exalting or disparaging the assembly based on household-related thoughts (gehassita), or does he not?" The Blessed One, without speaking any such words related to exalting or disparaging, and knowing the proper time, would conclude the discourse.

Investigating in this manner, the young man Uttara wandered together with the Blessed One for seven months, yet he did not see even the slightest fault in the Blessed One's bodily door and so on. This is not surprising, that a human being like the young man should not see any fault in one who has become a Buddha. For even the celestial Māra, while the Buddha was still a Bodhisatta for six years in the place of great exertion, could not see even a single household-related thought; and even after he became a Buddha, Māra followed him for a whole year but seeing nothing, he departed after reciting verses such as:

"For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step,
But I found no opening (fault) in the mindful Sambuddha."
(Sutta Nipāta 448)

Then the young man Uttara thought: "I have followed the Venerable Gotama for seven months, yet I see no fault. Even if I were to follow him for another seven months, or seven years, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, I would never see a fault in this Venerable One. My teacher is very old; it is impossible to know the time for him to realize the security from bondage (Yogakkhema/Arahatship). I shall inform my teacher of his Buddhahood based on the natural virtues of the Venerable Gotama." Having thus thought, he asked permission from the Blessed One, paid homage to the Saṅgha of monks, and departed.

When he reached his teacher's presence, he was asked, "Dear Uttara, is that Venerable Gotama truly as his reputation suggests?" He replied, "Teacher, what are you saying? The universe is too narrow, and the peak of existence (Bhavagga) is too low; the mass of virtues of that Venerable Gotama is as infinite as the sky. Indeed, sir, that Venerable Gotama is exactly as his reputation suggests." Saying such things, he described in order the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) that he had seen, and also described his conduct and character. Therefore, it is said: "Then the young man Uttara... the Venerable Gotama is endowed with such and such virtues, and he has even more virtues than that."
257:
## Among those [marks], 'Suppatiṭṭhitapāda' (one with well-placed feet) means: when others place their feet on the ground, either the toes, the heel, or the side of the foot touches first; otherwise, there is a gap in the middle of the sole. When lifting the foot, only one part, such as the toes, rises first. For the Blessed One, it is not so. The entire sole of the Blessed One's foot touches the ground and rises from the ground all at once, like the surface of a golden sandal. Therefore, [the youth Uttara] said, "That Venerable Gotama has well-placed feet."

Regarding the Blessed One's possession of well-placed feet, there is this [extraordinary quality]: if the Blessed One extends his foot to step over a chasm more than a hundred fathoms deep, at that very moment, the low place rises like a blacksmith's bellows filled with air and becomes level with the ground. High places also sink into the earth. When he extends his foot to step far away, even a mountain the size of Mount Sineru bends down like a steamed rattan shoot and comes near his foot. Because of this, when the Blessed One extended his foot to step on Mount Yugandhara after performing the Twin Miracle, the mountain bent down and came near his foot. Stepping on that mountain, he reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his second step. Due to the power of the wheel-mark, the place where the foot is set cannot be uneven. Stumps, thorns, pebbles, potsherds, excrement, urine, spit, snot, and so on, move away in advance, or else they sink into the earth right there. By the power of the Tathāgata's virtue, wisdom, and Dhamma, and by the influence of the ten perfections, this great earth becomes level, soft, and as if strewn with flowers. On such ground, the Tathāgata places his foot evenly, lifts it evenly, and touches the ground with the entire surface of his soles.

'Cakkāni' refers to the existence of two wheels on the two feet. Their spokes (ara), rims (nemi), and hubs (nābhi) have already been mentioned in the Pāḷi text. By the words 'sabbākāraparippūrāni' (complete in every aspect), this distinction should be understood: in the middle of the soles of those wheels, the hub is seen; the circular line delimiting the hub is seen; the band encircling the face of the hub is seen; the opening of the hub is seen; the spokes are seen; the circular lines on the spokes are seen; the rims are seen; and the jewel-like spots on the rims are seen. This much is what appears in the Pāḷi text.

However, the many other items (the 108 auspicious marks) not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text should be understood as follows: the royal spear, the Sirivacca, the Nandi, the Sovattika, the crest-garland, the Vaḍḍhamānaka, the pair of fish, the auspicious throne (Bhaddapīṭha)...
258:
...the goad, the trident, the palace, the portal, the white umbrella, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather whisk, the yak-tail fan, the diadem, the bowl, the gem, the flower garland, the blue lotus, the red lotus, the white lotus, the pink lotus, the white lily, the pot full of mustard powder and so on, the bowl full of mustard powder and so on, the ocean, the world-system (Cakkavāḷa), the Himavā mountains, Mount Sineru, the moon, the sun, the stars, the four great islands, and the two thousand small islands; and finally, beginning with the retinue of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), all these are the attendants of the wheel mark itself.

'Āyatapaṇhī' means having long heels or full heels. While for others the forefoot is long and the leg (ankle) is positioned above the heel, making it look as if the heel was carved out, it is not so for the Tathāgata. If the Tathāgata's foot is divided into four parts, two parts are the forefoot, the leg is positioned at the third part, and in the fourth part, the heel is rounded like a red woolen ball, as if turned on a lathe.

'Dīghangulī' means that while for others some fingers and toes are long and some are short, it is not so for the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata's fingers and toes are long like those of a monkey. They are thick at the base and gradually become slender at the tips, resembling medicinal sticks made of realgar rolled with sugarcane oil. Therefore, it is said 'dīghangulī'.

'Mudutalunahattapāda' means the Blessed One's hands and feet are soft like a layer of cotton wool that has been beaten a hundred times and dipped in clarified butter. Because his hands and feet are always as tender and delicate as those of a newborn infant, he is called 'mudutalunahattapāda'.

'Jālahattapāda' does not mean having the spaces between the fingers connected by skin. Such a hand would be like a frog's hand, which is a human defect, and such a person would not even be allowed to ordain. For the Tathāgata, the four fingers and five toes are of equal length. Because they are of equal length, the barley-grain marks (yavalakkhaṇa) stand touching one another. Thus, his hands and feet resemble a lattice window (jālavātapāna) designed by a skilled carpenter. Therefore, it is said 'jālahattapāda'.

He is called 'ussaṅkhapāda' because he has high-raised ankles. For others, the ankles are on the sides of the feet, making their feet stiff as if bolted, so they cannot turn them freely. When they walk, the soles of their feet...
259:
The Buddha's heels are high and set high. Because they are set high, from the navel upwards, the Buddha's upper body is as steady and motionless as a golden statue placed on a boat; only the lower body moves. The feet can turn with ease. To those standing and observing from the front, the back, or from either side, the soles of the feet are clearly visible, unlike those of elephants which can only be seen from behind.

'Eṇijaṅgho' means having calves like those of the king of deer named Eṇī, possessing calves full of flesh. It does not mean the flesh is bunched on only one side; rather, it means being endowed with calves that are surrounded by evenly distributed flesh, well-rounded, and shaped like a grain of rice.

'Anonamanto' means not bending. By this term, the Buddha's state of being neither hunched nor dwarfish is shown. Other people tend to be either hunched or dwarfish; the upper body of hunched persons is incomplete, and the lower body of dwarfish persons is incomplete. Due to such bodily incompleteness, they are unable to touch their knees without bending. The Buddha, however, being complete in both the upper and lower body, is able to touch his knees without bending.
