Because his private parts are enclosed and concealed in a sheath like those of a noble bull or a noble Gandha elephant, resembling the calyx of a golden lotus, he is called 'Kosohitavatthaguyho'. 'Vatthaguyha' refers to the organ that should be concealed by cloth.

'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo' means having a complexion like a solid gold statue that has been polished with cinnabar, rubbed with a boar's tusk to make it smooth, and treated with red chalk. By this term, the solid and delicate nature of the Buddha's body is shown, and to describe the complexion, it is said 'Kañcanasannibhattaco' (skin like gold), or it is simply a synonym for the former term.

'Rajojalla' means dust or dirt. It does not smear or stick to the Buddha's body. It rolls off like water drops on a lotus leaf. The Buddhas perform the washing of hands and feet for the sake of seasonal comfort, for the merit of the donors, and also as a matter of duty. This is because it is said that a monk entering a dwelling must wash his feet before entering.

'Uddhaggalomo' means having body hairs that grow upwards, with the tips curling at the end, standing as if they were looking up at the beauty of the face.
260:
'Brahmujugatto' means having a straight body like Brahma, a body that rises straight and tall. Generally, beings tend to bend at three places: the shoulders, the waist, and the knees. When they bend at the waist, they bend backward; when they bend at the other two places, they bend forward. Some tall people have crooked sides; some walk with their faces tilted up as if counting the stars; some, having little flesh and blood, are like a spit and walk trembling. The Buddha, however, rises straight and tall in stature, like a golden ceremonial arch (toraṇa) erected in a city of devas.

'Sattussado' means having a fullness of flesh in these seven places: the backs of the two hands, the backs of the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck. In others, the network of veins is visible on the backs of the hands and feet, and the bone ends are prominent on the shoulders and the nape; such people appear like human ghosts (peta). The Buddha is not like that. Because he has full flesh in those seven places, with the backs of the hands etc. having concealed networks of veins, and with a neck like a rounded golden drum, he appears like a stone statue or a painted image.

Because he has a torso like the front half of a lion, he is called 'Sīhapubbaddhakāyo'. Only the front part of a lion's body is full, while the back part is not. The Buddha's entire body, however, is full like the front part of a lion. His body, like a lion's, does not have an ill-formed or distorted shape with depressions or elevations here and there; rather, it is long where it should be long, and it is likewise where it should be short, thin, thick, or rounded. Thus it has been said:

'Monks, when the fruit of pleasant kamma appears, those limbs that are beautiful when long, are long. Those limbs that are beautiful when short, are short. Those limbs that are beautiful when thick, are thick. Those limbs that are beautiful when thin, are thin. Those limbs that are beautiful when rounded, are rounded.'
261:
## Thus, the physical form (attabhāva) of the Tathāgata is fashioned by various and diverse meritorious thoughts and adorned with the ten perfections. No artist or powerful being in the world is able to create even a replica of that physical form of the Tathāgata.

'Citantaraṃsa' means the interval between the two shoulder blades is called 'antaraṃsa'. For the Blessed One, that space between the two shoulders is full; therefore, he is called 'Citantaraṃsa'. For other people, that area is usually depressed, and the two shoulder blades appear separately. In the Tathāgata's body, however, starting from the waist, a layer of flesh rises up to the nape of the neck, covering the back like a golden slab set upright.

'Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala' means having a body as well-proportioned as a banyan tree. Just as a banyan tree of fifty or a hundred cubits, with its trunk and branches in proportion, is equal in height and in spread, so too the Tathāgata's body is equal in height and in his arm span (fathom). It means that his proportions are not uneven like other people whose bodies might be long in height or long in arm span. Therefore, it was said, "yāvatakvassa kāyo," and so on. In that phrase, 'yāvatakvassa' means 'yāvatako assa'.

'Samavaṭṭakkhandha' means having a well-rounded neck. Some people have necks that are long, crooked, or thick, like those of cranes, herons, or pigs; when they speak, the network of veins becomes prominent, and only a weak voice comes out. For the Blessed One, it is not so. The Tathāgata has a neck like a well-rounded small golden drum; when he speaks, the network of veins does not appear, and his voice is great like the roar of a thundercloud.

In the term 'Rasaggasaggī', they are called 'rasaggasā' because they receive taste; this is a designation for the taste-nerves. Those nerves are most excellent for the Blessed One; therefore, he is called 'Rasaggasaggī'. For the Blessed One, seven thousand taste-nerves, with their ends directed upwards, remain gathered and fixed in the throat. Even food the size of a sesame seed placed on the tip of the tongue spreads throughout the entire body. For this reason, while practicing the Great Struggle (Mahāpadhāna), he was able to sustain his body with only a single grain of rice or a handful of bean soup. For others, it is not so, and thus the essence of food (ojā) cannot spread through the whole body; therefore, they are prone to many illnesses. This mark is clearly evident through the result of being free from illness.
262:
He is called Sīhahanu because his jaw is like that of a lion king. In the term Sīhahanu, only the lower jaw of a lion king is full, not the upper jaw. However, both jaws of the Blessed One are full, like the lower jaw of a lion king; they are like the moon on the twelfth day of the waxing or waning fortnight.

In the terms such as Cattālīsadanta, he is called Cattālīsadanta because he has forty teeth, with twenty teeth set in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower jaw. Even among others who have a full set of teeth, there are only thirty-two; however, the Blessed One has forty.

Some teeth of others are high and some are low, being uneven. But the teeth of the Blessed One are even in appearance, like a layer of mother-of-pearl cut with an iron tool.

The teeth of others are widely spaced like those of crocodiles; when they eat fish, meat, etc., the gaps between the teeth become filled. But the teeth of the Blessed One are not widely spaced, like a row of diamonds set in a golden creeper; they are like teeth whose boundaries are shown as if marked by a brush.

Regarding Susukkadāṭha, in others, decayed teeth arise, and because of that, some eye-teeth (canines) are black or discolored. The Blessed One has very white eye-teeth; he possesses eye-teeth endowed with a radiance that surpasses even the brightness of the morning star (Osadhī-tāraka). Therefore, it is said, "Susukkadāṭha."

Regarding Pahūtajivha, the tongues of others may be thick, thin, short, rough, or uneven. But the tongue of the Blessed One is soft, long, broad, and perfect in color. To dispel the doubts of those who came to search for that mark, because of its softness, he rolls that tongue like a needle and touches both nostrils; because of its length, he touches both ear-holes; because of its breadth, he covers the entire forehead up to the hairline. Thus, by showing the softness, length, and breadth of his tongue, he dispels their doubts. Referring to the tongue endowed with these three characteristics, it is said, "Pahūtajivha."

Regarding Brahmassara, others may have broken voices, cracked voices, or voices like a crow's. But the Blessed One is endowed with a voice similar to that of Mahābrahmā. The voice of Mahābrahmā is pure because it is not disturbed by bile or phlegm. For the Blessed One as well, his past deeds purified the physical base of the voice; because that base is pure, the voice arising from the navel is pure and arises endowed with the eight factors. Because he speaks like a Karavika bird, he is called Karavikabhāṇī, which means one who has a sweet voice like the song of an intoxicated Karavika bird.
263:
Regarding the sweetness of the Karavika bird's voice, there is this illustrative story. It is said that when a Karavika bird strikes a sweet, ripe mango with its beak, tastes the trickling juice, flaps its wings, and sings, all four-footed creatures begin to frolic as if intoxicated. Even four-footed animals busy grazing drop the grass in their mouths and listen to that sound. Predators chasing small prey stop with their paws raised without putting them down upon hearing it. The hunted prey also stop, forgetting even the fear of death. Birds flying in the sky also stop, spreading their wings. Fish in the water also stop, flapping their gill covers while listening to that sound. In this way, Karavika birds have a melodious voice.

Queen Asandhimittā, the consort of King Dhammāsoka, asked the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, is there anyone whose voice is like the voice of the Buddha?" "There is the voice of the Karavika bird," they replied. "Venerable sirs, where are those birds?" she asked. "In the Himavanta," they said. Then the Queen said to the King, "Great King, I wish to see a Karavika bird." The King released a golden cage with the command, "Let the Karavika bird come and perch in this golden cage." The cage went and stood before a Karavika bird. The bird thought, "This cage has come by royal command; I must go," and perched inside. The cage returned and stood before the King. They could not make the Karavika bird sing. Then the King asked, "Friends, when do these birds sing?" "They sing when they see their relatives, O King," they replied. Then the King had the bird surrounded by mirrors. Seeing its own reflection and thinking, "My relatives have come," the bird flapped its wings and sang with a sweet voice, like someone blowing a jeweled flute. The people in the entire city frolicked as if intoxicated. Queen Asandhimittā thought, "If even the voice of this animal is so sweet, how much more sweet must be the voice of the Blessed One who has attained the glory of Omniscient Knowledge?" and she gave rise to joy. Without letting go of that joy, she, along with seven hundred attendants, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). In this way, the voice of the Karavika bird is very sweet. The voice of the Blessed One is a hundred times, a thousand times sweeter than that. Because there is no voice in the world sweeter than the Karavika bird's, He is called "Karavika-bhāṇī".

"Abhinīlanetto" (deep blue eyes) does not mean the entire eye is blue. It means that in the parts that should be blue, the eyes are endowed with a very pure blue color like the Umā flower. In the parts that should be yellow, they are yellow like the Kaṇikāra flower; in the parts that should be red...
264:
...in the parts that should be red, they are red like the Bandhujīvaka flower; in the parts that should be white, they are white like the Osadhī star; in the parts that should be black, they are black like a wet Ariṭṭhaka seed. They appear like jeweled lion-windows opened in a golden mansion.

In the term "Gopakhumo", by "pakhuma", the entire eye apparatus is intended. That eye apparatus is thick in a black calf and clear in a red calf. The meaning is that He has eyes like those of a red calf born that very moment. The eyes of others are incomplete; they are endowed with eyes that are protruding or deep-set, like the eyes of elephants, mice, crows, etc. The Blessed One's eyes, however, are surrounded by eyelashes that are soft, smooth, dark blue, and delicate, like polished jeweled spheres.

"Uṇṇā" refers to the hair-tuft. "Bhamukantare" means it grows between the two eyebrows, just above the bridge of the nose. Growing upwards, it stands in the middle of the forehead. "Odātā" means it has a color like the pure Osadhī star. "Mudū" means it is like a layer of cotton-wool that has been beaten a hundred times and placed in clarified butter. "Tūlasannibhā" means it is like silk-cotton or creeper-cotton. This is a simile for its whiteness. If one takes that hair-tuft by the tip and pulls it, it is about half an arm's length. When released, it curls to the right, with the tip pointing upwards. It shines with a heart-ravishing glory, like a silver bubble placed in the middle of a golden plate, or like a stream of milk flowing from a golden jar, or like the Osadhī star in the sky tinged with the glow of dawn.

"Uṇhīsasīso" is spoken with reference to two meanings: having a full forehead and having a full head. For the Blessed One, a band of flesh rises from the top of the right ear, covering and filling the entire forehead, and ends at the top of the left ear. It shines like a royal turban-band bound by kings. It is said that kings made turban-bands for themselves after knowing this mark of Bodhisattas in their final existence. This is one meaning. Other people have incomplete heads. Some have heads like a mallet, some like a fruit, some like a skull, some like a gourd, or some like a slope. The Blessed One's head, however, is perfectly full like a water bubble, as if turned on a lathe. Among these (two meanings), according to the first method...
265: He is called 'Uṇhīsasīsa' because his head appears as if wrapped with a turban-band. According to the second method, he is called 'Uṇhīsasīsa' because his head is perfectly rounded all over like a turban. These marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) are well-expounded only when these four categories—(1) action (kamma), (2) the arising in accordance with action, (3) the mark, and (4) the benefit of the mark—are shown for each individual mark. Therefore, these factors such as kamma, as taught by the Blessed One in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta, should be explained. One who is unable to determine this through the Sutta itself should adopt the method described in the commentary to that very Sutta in the Sumangalavilāsinī, the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary. 'O Teacher, the Venerable Gotama is endowed with these thirty-two marks of a Great Man. He walks like a golden gateway adorned with jewels erected in a celestial city, like a Parichattaka tree a hundred yojanas high in full bloom, like a Sāla tree in full bloom in a mountain cleft, and like the sky adorned with hosts of stars, illuminating the world with the power of his own glory.' To describe his physical and verbal conduct, the text says 'Gacchanto kho pana' and so on. 'Dakkhiṇena' means that for the Buddhas, whether starting to walk from a standing, sitting, or reclining position, the right foot always moves forward first. This is said to be a constant miracle. 'Nātidūre pādaṃ uddharati' means he walks with the intention of placing that right foot not too far away. If he steps too far, the left foot would be dragged along with the right, and the right foot would not be able to reach the far distance but would land nearby. If this happens, it is called a broken stride. When the right foot is lifted to the proper measure, the left foot is also lifted to the proper measure; when it is placed down, it is also placed down to the proper measure. Thus, it should be understood that the movement of the Tathāgata's right foot is regulated by the left, and the movement of the left foot is regulated by the right. 'Nātisīghaṃ' means he walks not too fast, like a monk going for alms during the day. 'Nātisaṇikaṃ' means he walks not too slowly, such that those following behind find no space. 'Adduvena adduvaṃ' means knee to knee...
266: ## Na satthiṃ unnāmetīti and so on. 'Na satthiṃ unnāmetīti' means he does not lift his thighs high like one walking in deep water. 'Na onāmetīti' means he does not walk dragging his feet backward like one with feet like a hooked staff used for cutting tree branches. 'Na sannāmetīti' means he does not make his feet stiff as if striking them against the upper and lower joints. 'Na vināmetīti' means there is no swaying from side to side like a mechanical puppet being played. 'Adharakāyovā' means only the lower body moves, while the upper body is as still as a golden statue placed on a boat. A person standing at a distance and looking cannot tell whether the Buddhas are standing or walking. 'Kāyabalena' means he does not walk with physical force, swinging his arms and with sweat pouring from his body. 'Sabbakāyeneva' means he does not turn his neck but turns his whole body to look, using the 'elephant-look' (nāgāpalokita) as taught in the Rāhulovāda Sutta. In the passage 'Na uddhaṃ' and so on, he does not look up as if counting the stars; he does not look down as if searching for a lost half-pice or a small coin; he does not walk looking here and there as if watching elephants, horses, and so forth. 'Yugamattaṃ' means a monk who walks with his eyes fixed on a spot about nine spans away is said to be looking a yoke's length. The Blessed One also walks looking at such a distance, like a well-trained thoroughbred horse harnessed to a yoke. 'Tato cassa uttarī' means it should not be said that he does not see beyond that yoke's length. Walls, doors, bushes, or creepers are unable to obstruct him. Indeed, to the Blessed One who possesses unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa), many thousands of world systems appear as a single courtyard. 'Antaragharaṃ' (inside the house) is to be understood as starting from the city pillar (indakhīla) according to the Mahāsakuludāyī Sutta below. In this Brahmāyu Sutta, however, it should be understood as starting from the threshold of the house. 'Na kāyaṃ' and so on is spoken to show that he enters only with his natural posture. Even when the Tathāgata enters the low house of a poor person, the roof rises or the ground sinks. The Blessed One, however, walks only with his natural gait. 'Nātidūre' means if he turns his body too far from the seat, he would have to sit down after moving one or two steps backward. 'Nāccāsanne' means if he turns too close to the seat, he would have to sit down after moving one or two steps forward. Therefore, he turns his body at the very spot where he can sit without moving forward or backward. 'Pāṇinā' means he does not sit holding the seat with his hands like one suffering from back pain. 'Pakkhipati' means like one who, having done some work, drops down while standing as if playing, or like one who, leaning on a nearby limb and rubbing it, moves to reach a distant limb...
267:
One who sits leaning on this side [of the body or seat] and rubs the seat until reaching that side, or one who sits leaning on another side and similarly rubs it until reaching this side—all such persons are said to throw the body onto the seat. The Blessed One, however, does not do so; He sits down gently as if holding a hanging rope in the middle of the seat or as if placing a tuft of cotton. Fidgeting with hands (hatthakukkucca) refers to unrestrained actions with the hands, such as placing water drops on the rim of the bowl, or cutting and tearing leaves with a fly-whisk, and so forth. Fidgeting with feet (pādakukkucca) refers to unrestrained actions such as scratching the ground with the feet.

'Na chambhati' means not being afraid. 'Na kampati' means not sinking or wavering. 'Na vedhati' means not shaking. 'Na paritassati' means not being agitated either by the agitation of fear or by the agitation of craving. Indeed, some people, having come for the purpose of a Dhamma talk and the like, when people stand and pay homage, become agitated with the agitation of fear, thinking: "Will I be able to win their hearts and preach the Dhamma, or answer if asked a question, or give a blessing (anumodanā)?" Some become agitated with the agitation of craving, thinking: "Will I get delicious gruel? Will I get delicious snacks?" Since both types of agitation do not exist in the Blessed One, He is not agitated.

Vivekāvaṭṭo means having a mind that turns towards seclusion, which is Nibbāna. There is also a reading 'vivekavatto', meaning being endowed with the duty of seclusion (vivekavatta). The duty of seclusion refers to a monk who, after finishing his meal, takes up his basic meditation subject through the power of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) during the day's abiding and sits cross-legged. For one sitting thus, the posture is peaceful.

In the words 'na pattaṃ unnāmeti' and so forth, some lift the bowl like one about to pour water from the rim of the bowl; some lower it as if placing it on the top of the foot; some hold it tightly; some shake it here and there. The Blessed One does not do so; He holds it with both hands, tilts it slightly, and receives the water. 'Na samparivattakaṃ' means not washing the outside of the bowl first by turning it over. 'Nātidūre' means not discarding [the water] far from the sitting place. 'Nāccāsanne' means not discarding it right at the feet. 'Vicchaddayamāno' means not splashing it so that the person receiving the water gets wet.
268:
"Not too little" means He does not receive only a handful to show fewness of wishes like some with evil desires; He does not do so. "Not too much" means not receiving more than what is sufficient for sustenance. "According to the measure of curry" means the measure of curry is one-fourth of the rice. Indeed, some take much rice if the rice is pleasing, or much curry if the curry is pleasing. The Teacher, however, does not take it that way. "Nor with [only] curry" means setting aside the curry one dislikes and eating only rice, or setting aside the rice and eating only curry; this is called exceeding the mouthful with curry. The Teacher takes curry with every other mouthful; thus the rice and curry finish at the same time.

"Two or three times" means the food brought to the teeth by the Tathāgata's broad tongue becomes like very fine flour after being touched by the teeth only two or three times; therefore, it is said thus. "Nothing remains in the mouth" means it slides down like a drop of water on a lotus leaf and goes directly into the throat; therefore, nothing remains. "Experiences the taste" means He knows tastes such as sweet, bitter, pungent, and so forth. For the Buddhas, even in drinking water, divine essence (ojā) is already present; thus the taste is clear in everything, but there is no greed for taste.

"Endowed with eight factors" means being endowed with the eight factors mentioned in "not for fun" and so forth. The decision on this matter is found in the Visuddhimagga and is also taught in the Sabbāsava Sutta. "When the hands are washed," what does the Teacher do? First, He washes the place where the bowl is held. Then, holding the bowl, He moves it around twice with His delicate, net-like hands. By this, the water slides off like water on a lotus leaf. "Not without concern" means He does not neglect the bowl like some who place it on a stand and do not wipe the water, ignoring the dust; He does not do so. "Not over-protecting" means He does not protect it excessively, like some who wipe the water from the bowl after eating, put it inside the folds of the robes, and hold the bowl by pressing it against the belly; He does not do so.

"Nor for the sake of Anumodanā" means some start the Anumodanā immediately after eating while children are crying for food, while people are hungry, and before everyone has arrived; thus some leave their work to come, while others have not yet arrived; this is wasting time. And whoever...
269:
When people have come and are sitting in salutation to listen to the Anumodanā, if a monk, without yet performing the Anumodanā, initiates individual worldly talk unrelated to the Anumodanā, such as "How is it, Tissa? How is it, Phussa? How is it, Sumana? How is it, Tisse? How is it, Phusse? How is it, Sumane? Are you free from illness? Are the crops abundant?" and so on, this monk is said to let the time for Anumodanā pass. A monk who performs the Anumodanā at the requested time, knowing the opportunity of the people, is said not to let the time pass. The Blessed One acts in that way (without letting the time pass).

He does not criticize the offered food by saying, "What kind of food is this? It is undercooked, it is over-boiled," and so on. A monk who performs Anumodanā with the thought, "I shall obtain food for tomorrow or the day after," is said to desire other food. Or, a monk who prolongs the Anumodanā with the thought, "I will perform Anumodanā as long as the womenfolk have not finished cooking the rice; then, at the end of my Anumodanā, they will give me a little from their own cooked rice," is also said to desire food. The Blessed One does not act in this way. "Na ca muccitukāmo" means that some monks leave quickly without taking leave of the assembly; such a monk often has to be followed in a hurry. The Blessed One, however, does not go in that way; He departs while remaining in the midst of the assembly. "Accukkaṭṭha" refers to a monk who wears the robe by pulling it up as high as the jawbone; he is said to wear it excessively high. A monk who wears the robe by letting it down as far as the ankles is also said to wear it excessively low. A monk who goes with the robe placed over both shoulders, exposing the abdomen, is also said to wear it excessively high. A monk who goes with the robe over one shoulder, exposing the breast, is also said to wear it excessively high. The Blessed One does not practice any such ways of wearing the robe.

"Allīna" means that unlike others whose robes stick to the body when wet with sweat, the Blessed One's robes do not stick to His body. "Apakaṭṭha" means that the robes do not remain detached from the body like a slipping garment. "Vāta" means that even the Veramba wind is unable to rise and move Him. "Pādamandaṇānuyoga" refers to the effort to make the feet beautiful by rubbing them with bricks and so on. "Pakkhāletvā" refers to washing the feet by rubbing one foot against the other.

When saying, "That person is not for his own harm," and so on, it is not said because of the existence of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) or the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), but it is said by inference after observing the continuity of the postures. "Dhamma" refers to the Pariyatti Dhamma. "Na ussādeti" means He does not flatter based on household status by saying, "O great official, O great householder," and so on. "Na apasādeti" means He does not disparage by saying, "O lay follower, how did you know the way to the monastery? Why do you not come out of fear? Monks do not take anything by force, do not..."
270:
...be afraid," or "What is the use of such a stingy life for you?" and so on, He does not disparage with household-based affection.

"Vissaṭṭha" refers to a voice that is smooth and not congested with phlegm or bile. "Viññeyya" refers to a voice that is intelligible and clear; because it is distinct, it makes the meaning known. "Mañjū" refers to a sweet voice. "Savanīya" refers to a voice that is pleasant to the ear; because it is sweet, it is worthy of being listened to. "Bindu" refers to a compact voice. "Avisārī" refers to a voice that is not scattered; because the voice is compact, it does not scatter. "Gambhīra" refers to a voice that originates from the depths. "Ninnādī" refers to a resonant voice; because the voice is deep, it has resonance. "Yathāparisaṃ" means it can make the entire assembly, even up to the limits of the universe, understand. "Bahiddhā" means the voice does not go even a finger's breadth outside the assembly. Why? Because it is thought, "Let such a sweet voice not perish without cause." Therefore, the Blessed One's voice circulates only over the heads of the assembly.

"Avalokayamānā" means they depart while looking at the Blessed One with hands joined at their heads, backing away and paying homage at the place where He is no longer visible. "Avijahitattā" means that if a person, after rising from hearing the Dhamma, goes away speaking of other things seen or heard, that person is said to abandon the Dhamma by nature. But if a person goes away speaking only of the virtues of the Dhamma heard, that person is said not to abandon the Dhamma; thus they depart in a manner of not abandoning the Dhamma. "Gacchantaṃ" refers to seeing the Blessed One departing like a great golden pagoda seven cubits high moving by a mechanical rope. "Ṭhitaṃ addasāma" means they saw the Blessed One standing like a towering golden mountain. "Tato ca bhiyyo" means that the young man Uttara, being unable to speak of the Blessed One's virtues in detail, summarized the remaining virtues like a bundle or like something bound with thread and replied in this way. The meaning here is: "The virtues not spoken of by me are far more numerous than the virtues spoken of. Like the great earth and the great ocean, the virtues of that Blessed One are endless, immeasurable, and as vast as the sky."

"Appaṭisaṃvidito" means the arrival is not known. If one approaches monks during the time of robe-preparation or during the time of bathing, one might have to return from that very place, and even a mere greeting does not occur. However, if permission is obtained beforehand, the monk sweeps the day-quarters, puts on his robe, and sits in a secluded place; the person who comes and sees him sitting thus...
271:
Just by seeing [him], they are inspired; conversation arises, or an answer to a question or a Dhamma talk is obtained. Therefore, the wise grant an opportunity. That Brahmāyu Brahmin was also one among those wise ones; thus, this thought occurred to him: "Why does he say 'I am old and aged' without mentioning his own fame?" The Buddhas are indeed endowed with compassion; thinking that [the Buddha] would quickly grant an opportunity upon knowing his old age, he spoke thus.

"Making way and giving an opportunity" means quickly rising and dividing into two to open the path.

"Ye me" means "those which are mine (the marks)." "Having a name like a woman" refers to a feminine name, and because he is addressed by that name, he is called "Nārīsamānasavhaya"; he speaks thus because of his skill in conventional usage, saying it should be spoken in the feminine gender. "Having a broad tongue" means having a wide tongue. "Let him show it" means "please bring that tongue out."

"Kevalī" means being endowed with all attributes.

"He replied" means he answered the eight questions asked at once. "He who knows" means he who knows the sequence of past lives (pubbenivāsa); for him, the knowledge of past lives is clear. By the phrase "He sees heaven and the states of deprivation," the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) is meant. "Reached the end of rebirth" means reaching the fruition of Arahantship. "Reached the end through higher knowledge" means knowing that fruition of Arahantship through direct knowledge (abhiññā) and reaching the end. "Muni" means being endowed with the quality of sagehood (moneyya) called the knowledge of Arahantship.

"Pure" means having a pure mind. "Free from passions" means being liberated from the passions of defilements. "Having abandoned rebirth and death" means having abandoned rebirth because of reaching the end of rebirth through Arahantship; by the very abandonment of rebirth, death is also abandoned. "Consummate in the holy life" means possessing the completeness of the holy life of the path; it means living the holy life of all four paths. "Gone to the far shore of all dhammas" means having gone to the far shore by knowing all mundane and supramundane dhammas through higher knowledge; it means standing having known all dhammas through higher knowledge. Alternatively, "Pāragū" (one who has gone to the far shore) means: a Pāragū of full understanding (pariññā) regarding the five aggregates, a Pāragū of abandoning (pahāna) regarding all defilements, a Pāragū of development (bhāvanā) regarding the four paths, a Pāragū of realization (sacchikiriyā) regarding cessation (nirodha), and a Pāragū of attainment (samāpatti) regarding all meditative attainments. Furthermore, by the phrase "of all dhammas," a Pāragū of higher knowledge (abhiññā) is meant. "Such a Buddha is called Tādī" means he is one of such a nature.
272:
He is called the Buddha because he has reached the further shore through six modes and has understood the Four Noble Truths in every aspect.

If it is asked, "Have all the questions been answered by this much of the discourse?" Yes, they have been answered. By the words, "The mind is pure and liberated from passions," the first question is answered, for he is a Brāhmaṇa because he has barred out evil. By the word "Pāragū" (one who has gone to the further shore), the second question is answered, for he is a Vedagū because he has reached the shore through the Vedas (the paths of knowledge). By the words beginning with "Pubbenivāsaṃ" (former births), the third question is answered, for he is a Tevijja because he possesses these three true knowledges. By the words, "He is entirely liberated from passions," the fourth question is answered, for he is a Sottiya because he has emerged from evil states. By the words, "He has reached the end of birth," the fifth question is answered, as this refers specifically to the Fruit of Arahantship. By the two terms "Vosito" (one who has reached the goal) and "Kevalī" (one who is complete in the holy life), the sixth question is answered. By the words, "A Muni who has reached the goal through higher knowledge (abhiññā)," the seventh question is answered. By the words, "He has reached the further shore of all phenomena; such a one is called the Buddha," the eighth question is answered.

The discussions on giving (dānakathā) and so forth have already been explained in detail in the sutta below. "Paccapādi" means he practiced. Regarding "Dhammassānudhamma" (Dhamma and what conforms to Dhamma) in this Brahmāyu Sutta, "Dhamma" refers to the Path of Arahantship, and "Anudhamma" refers to the three lower paths and the three lower fruits of recluseship. The meaning is that he attained them in due order. "Do not weary me for the sake of the Dhamma" means do not tire me out for the sake of the Dhamma, do not make me speak again and again. All the remaining words are clear in every instance. Therein, with the word "Parinibbāyī," the climax of the teaching is taken as the Fruit of Arahantship itself.

## The explanation of the Brahmāyu Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
## 2. Commentary on the Sela Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Sela Sutta. Therein, the words beginning with "among the Aṅguttarāpans" have already been explained in detail in the Potaliya Sutta. "Aḍḍhateḷasehi" means by half of the thirteenth [hundred] (i.e., twelve hundred and fifty).
273:
It means together with one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. All those monks assembled in that gathering of disciples were Arahants who had been ordained through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. Keṇiya is his name, and Jaṭila means he is an ascetic (tāpasa). Although he was a Brahmin Mahāsāla, he took up the life of an ascetic in order to protect his wealth. Having given gifts to the king and secured a portion of land, he built a hermitage and lived there. He engaged in trade with five hundred carts and was the benefactor for a thousand families. It is said that in the hermitage of that Keṇiya the ascetic, a single palm tree would drop one golden palm fruit every day. During the day, he wore saffron-dyed robes and wore his hair in mats, but at night, he enjoyed sensual pleasures.

'With a talk on Dhamma' means with a Dhamma talk related to the benefits of beverages. This Keṇiya the ascetic felt ashamed to go and see the Blessed One empty-handed. Thinking, 'Beverages are allowable even for monks who abstain from eating at the wrong time,' he had five hundred shoulder-loads of well-prepared jujube juice brought and went. The account of his going in this manner is already presented in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka of the Vinaya Pali, starting with: 'Then the thought occurred to Keṇiya the ascetic: "What should I have carried to the ascetic Gotama?"'

Why did the Blessed One refuse repeatedly, saying, 'For the second time also, the Blessed One...'? He refused in order to inspire faith in the heretics (titthiyas) regarding his refusal. This reason is not the primary cause; for the Buddhas, there is no such hypocrisy for the sake of requisites. In fact, seeing these twelve hundred and fifty monks, this Keṇiya the ascetic would prepare food only for this many monks. However, on the following day, Sela the Brahmin would ordain along with three hundred men. It would not be appropriate to send the three hundred newly ordained monks elsewhere and go only with these twelve hundred and fifty senior monks; nor would it be appropriate to send these senior monks elsewhere and go only with the new monks. Furthermore, if He were to go taking all the monks, the food would not be sufficient. Then, when the monks went around for alms, people would criticize, saying, 'After a long time, Keṇiya invited the ascetic Gotama but could not even offer enough food for sustenance,' and he himself would feel remorse. But when the refusal was made, he would think, 'The ascetic Gotama repeatedly mentions the name of the Brahmins, saying, "You are also one who has great faith in the Brahmins,"' and he would desire to invite the Brahmins as well. Then, the Brahmins separately...
274:
(Keṇiya the ascetic) will invite the Brahmins; those invited Brahmins will become monks and partake of the meal. In this way, his faith will be preserved; thinking thus, the Buddha refused repeatedly. By the words 'Kiñcāpi kho bho,' he shows this meaning: 'Venerable Gotama, what does it matter if I have great faith in the Brahmins? May the Venerable Gotama accept; I am able to give to the Brahmins and also to you.'

'Kāyaveyyāvaṭika' means physical service (kāyaveyyāvacca). 'Maṇḍalamāḷa' means a pavilion made of cloth.

'Āvāha' means taking a bride. 'Vivāha' means giving a bride. 'So me nimantito' means 'That Venerable Gotama has been invited by me.' Then, because Sela the Brahmin had mature supporting conditions (upanissaya), as soon as he heard the word 'Buddha,' he was as if sprinkled with the Deathless (amata). Expressing his devotion, he said, 'O Keṇiya, did you say "Buddha"?' Keṇiya, wishing to speak the truth, said, 'O Sela, I say "Buddha".' Then, to make it certain, Sela asked him again, and the other replied in the same way.

Then, to that Sela who saw that even the sound of the word 'Buddha' is rare even in a hundred thousand aeons, this thought 'Ghosopi kho' and so on occurred. 'Nīlavanarāji' means a row of dark green trees. 'Pade padaṃ' means placing a foot in a space the size of a footprint. Indeed, if a foot is placed too close or too far, a sound arises; wishing to prevent that sound, he spoke thus. In the phrase 'Sīhāva ekacarā' (wandering alone like lions), a lion living in a group with cubs and others falls into negligence; a lone wanderer is diligent. Thus, showing the practice of diligence, he makes a comparison with a lone-wandering lion. He spoke the words 'Mā me bhonto' and so on, wishing to teach proper conduct. The intended meaning here is: 'If you, without getting a turn to speak, insert your words in the middle of my speech, the reproach
275:
Paripuṇṇakāyo means having a complete body due to being endowed with the marks and having no deficiency in limbs. Suruci means having a beautiful bodily radiance. Sujāto means being well-formed due to the perfection of height and girth, and the perfection of shape. Cārudassano means having an appearance that is captivating and never satiates those who look at it even for a very long time. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo means having a complexion like the color of gold. Susukkadāṭho means having very white canine teeth. By the term 'Mahāpurisalakkhaṇā', the previously mentioned marks of a Great Man are concluded using different words.

Now, wishing to praise by selecting those marks that please his mind, he said 'Pasannanetto' and so on. The Blessed One has clear eyes because he is endowed with the five-colored visual sensitivity. He has a beautiful face because his face is like the full moon. He is great like Brahma because of the perfection of his height and girth. He has a straight body because it is upright like that of Brahma. He is majestic because of his bright radiance. Here, the word 'Suruci' mentioned earlier is repeated with the intention of praising him 'in the midst of the community of monks.' One with such an appearance shines in this way. The same method should be understood for the subsequent verse. Uttamavaṇṇino refers to the Buddha who is endowed with the supreme complexion. Rathesabho means the supreme charioteer. Jambusaṇḍassa means the lord of Jambudīpa. This is said to praise his sovereignty over the well-known Jambudīpa. In truth, a Cakkavattī (Universal Monarch) is the ruler of all four great islands.

Khattiyā refers to those who are kings by birth. Bhogī refers to wealthy kings. Rājāno refers to any who exercise kingship. Rājābhirājā means a king honored by kings, an overlord (Adhirājā), implying a Cakkavattī. Manujindo means the lord of men, the supreme ruler.

When this was said, the Blessed One, wishing to fulfill the desire of the Brahmin Sela—who thought, 'Those who are Worthy Ones, Fully Enlightened Buddhas, manifest themselves when their own virtues are praised'—said, 'I am a king,' and so on. The meaning is: 'Sela, do not be concerned about the matter in which you urge me, saying "You deserve to be a king"; I am indeed a king. However, regarding kingship, while other kings rule a territory of a hundred or a thousand yojanas, or even a Cakkavattī rules only as far as the four great islands, I do not have such a limited domain. I am the Unsurpassed King of Dhamma, and I discipline and rule the world systems, which are infinite horizontally, from the highest point of existence (Bhavagga) down to the Avīci hell.'
276:
Among all beings, such as those without feet or those with two feet, I am the supreme. There is no one equal to me in virtue... or in the knowledge and vision of liberation. I, being such an unsurpassed King of Dhamma, turn the wheel by means of the unsurpassed Dhamma, categorized as the four foundations of mindfulness and so on. He turns the wheel of authority (āṇācakka) by saying, 'Abandon these unwholesome states, dwell having attained these wholesome states,' or the wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) by means of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyattidhamma), such as 'Monks, this is the Noble Truth of Suffering.' 'Cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ' means a wheel that cannot be turned back by any recluse... or by anyone in the world.

Seeing the Blessed One thus manifesting himself, Sela, filled with joy and gladness, spoke two verses beginning with 'Sambuddho paṭijānāsi' for the sake of confirmation. In that verse, 'Ko nu senāpati' is an inquiry: 'Who is the general who, following your will, turns the wheel of authority that has been turned righteously by you, the Lord?'

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting on the right side of the Blessed One, shining with glory like a heap of gold. Wishing to point to the Venerable Sāriputta, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with 'Mayā pavattitaṃ'. In that verse, 'Anujāto tathāgataṃ' means one who has arisen in the Noble birth because of the Tathāgata, one who is born because of the Tathāgata. Alternatively, there are three kinds of sons: the low-born (avajāta), the following-born (anujāta), and the superior-born (atijāta). Among them, one who lacks virtue is called 'low-born'; such a person is not truly a son of the Tathāgata. One who excels his father is called 'superior-born'; such a son also does not exist for the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, there is only the 'following-born' son; wishing to point to such a son, he spoke thus.

Having thus answered the question 'Who is the general?', and wishing to remove the doubt of the Brahmin Sela regarding his statement 'Do you claim to be a Buddha?', the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with 'Abhiññeyyaṃ' to make him understand: 'I do not claim it merely by assertion; rather, I am a Buddha for this reason.' In that verse, 'Abhiññeyya' (to be known) refers to the Path and the Fruit. The truth to be developed (bhāvetabba) is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). The truth to be abandoned (pahātabba) is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). By mentioning the cause, the results are also accomplished; therefore, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) and the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), which are the results of those, are also effectively mentioned. Thus, the meaning 'that which is to be realized has been realized, that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood' is also included in this verse. In this way, wishing to show the fruit of developing the Four Noble Truths and liberation, he proves his state of Buddhahood with a fitting reason: 'Having known what is to be known, I have become a Buddha.'
277: Having thus revealed himself by way of a direct cause, the Blessed One, wishing to make Sela the Brahmin practice exceedingly for the sake of overcoming his doubts, spoke the three verses beginning with 'Vinayassa'. In those verses, 'Sallakatta' means one who has cut out the darts of lust and so forth. 'Anuttara' means that unlike a disease cured by an external physician which might recur in this very existence, the disease of defilements cured by the Buddha does not arise even in a future existence; therefore, the meaning is 'I am the unsurpassed physician'. 'Brahmabhūta' means one who has become noble. 'Atitula' means one who has transcended any comparable person, meaning one who is incomparable. 'Mārasenappamaddana' means the crusher of the army of Māra, which is described as 'Sensual pleasures are your first army'. 'Sabbāmitta' refers to all enemies known as the Māra of the aggregates (khandha), the Māra of defilements (kilesa), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), the Māra of death (maccu), and the Māra of the deity (devaputta). 'Vasīkatvā' means having brought them under one's own will. 'Akutobhaya' means one who is fearless from any direction. When this was said, Sela the Brahmin immediately gained faith in the Blessed One and, looking forward to monkhood, spoke these three verses beginning with 'Bhonto'. In those verses, 'Kaṇhābhijātika' means one born in a low caste such as the Caṇḍāla. Furthermore, those young students, also looking forward to monkhood, spoke the verse beginning with 'If this is pleasing to the Master'. Then Sela the Brahmin, with a delighted mind towards those students and wishing to show them as well, spoke the verse 'Brāhmaṇā' requesting monkhood. Furthermore, the Blessed One [granted this] because in the past, during the dispensation of Padumuttara Buddha, Sela had been the leader of a group of those same three hundred men, and together with them, he had built a monastery and performed meritorious deeds such as giving. Due to that merit, he enjoyed the bliss of devas and humans, and in his final birth, he was born as their teacher. Their merit was also ripe for the maturation of liberation and served as a supporting condition (upanissaya) for the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. Therefore, granting the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination to all of them, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Svākkhāta'. In that verse, 'Sandiṭṭhika' means the Dhamma that is to be seen by oneself, directly. 'Akālika' means that because the fruit (phala) arises immediately after the path (magga), it is not a benefit to be attained after a lapse of time. 'Yattha amoghā' means that in which noble practice of the path, the monkhood of one who practices by fulfilling the three trainings without negligence is not in vain, meaning it is fruitful. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One said, 'Come, Bhikkhus'. They all became possessors of bowls and robes, and having come through the air, they paid homage to the Blessed One, well-disciplined like elders of a hundred years. Thus, with reference to their 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination, it is said 'Sela has obtained', and so forth.
278:
"Imāhi" means with these verses that were pleasing to the mind of the ascetic Keniya. In those verses, because there is no sacrifice for Brāhmaṇas without the fire-service, it is said: "Sacrifices have the fire-offering (aggihutta) as their foremost (mukha)." The meaning is that the fire-offering is the most excellent, having the fire-sacrifice as its primary element. Because it is to be recited first by those reciting the Vedas, the Sāvitrī verse is called "the foremost of meters (chandas)." The King is called "the foremost" because he is the most excellent among humans. The ocean is called "the foremost" because it is the repository and the refuge of rivers. It is said, "The moon is the foremost of constellations," because it is the sign of recognition through its association with the lunar mansions, such as "Today is the Kattikā constellation, today is the Rohiṇī constellation," and because it provides light and is of a cool nature. The sun is called "the foremost of shining things" because it is the highest among those that blaze.

Because the Saṅgha is the most excellent among those worthy of offerings, it is said, specifically referring to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha at that time: "For those desiring merit, the Saṅgha is indeed the foremost among those to be sacrificed to." By saying this, he shows that the Saṅgha is the source and the foremost for the arising of merit.

With the phrase "Yaṃ taṃ saraṇaṃ," he spoke another verse declaring the Fruit of Arahantship. The meaning of that verse is: "O Blessed One endowed with the five eyes, we have come to you for refuge on the eighth day from now; therefore, we have become disciplined through the unsurpassed discipline in your Dispensation. Oh, how wonderful is the power of your refuge!"

After that, praising the Blessed One with two verses and requesting the act of worship with the third verse, the Brahmin Sela spoke the words beginning with "Bhikkhavo tisatā ime."

## The explanation of the Sela Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
## 3. Commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Assalāyana Sutta. Therein, "Nānāverajjakānaṃ" means those who have come from various countries such as Aṅga and Magadha; or it also means those who were born and raised in those countries. "Kenacidiva" means by some indefinite business such as the worship of sacrifices. "Cātuvaṇṇiṃ" means pertaining to all four castes. Thinking, "We say that only Brāhmaṇas are purified through purification by bathing and purification by the cultivation of mantras, yet the ascetic Gotama is doing what is improper," they thought in this way. "Vuttasiro" means one with a shaved head.
279:
"Dhammavādī" means a speaker of reality (one who speaks according to the truth of nature). "Duppaṭimantiya" means that they are difficult to be countered by those like us who are speakers of non-Dhamma (those who speak what is not the truth). It is intended to show that those called speakers of Dhamma cannot be defeated. "Paribbājaka" refers to the procedures of a wanderer. Those who become wanderers after studying the three Vedas, the mantras with which they go forth, the mantras they constantly maintain after going forth, or the conduct they practice—all that has been practiced and learned by the venerable (Assalāyana). Therefore, thinking "There will be no defeat for you, only victory," they spoke in this way.

The words beginning with "Dissanti kho pana" were spoken to destroy the views of those brahmins. In that passage, "brāhmaṇiyo" means brahmin women are seen who have been brought from other families through marriage for the purpose of obtaining sons for the brahmins. Those brahmin women, at a later time, also have their seasons; the meaning is they have the "flowering" of the menses. "Gabbhiniyo" means they become pregnant. "Vijāyamānā" means they give birth to sons and daughters. "Pāyamānā" means they are brahmin women who suckle children. "Yonijāva samānā" means although they are born from the birth canal (passāvamagga) of brahmin women, they say: "Only the brahmin caste is the highest caste... they are the heirs of Brahmā." If their words were true, the womb of brahmin women would be the chest of Great Brahmā, and the birth canal of brahmin women would be the mouth of Great Brahmā. To prevent them from being able to say "We lived in the chest of Great Brahmā and came out from his mouth," this "speech that cuts off the view of being born from the mouth" was spoken.

"Having been a master, one becomes a slave; having been a slave, one becomes a master" means if a brahmin, along with his wife, goes to the Yona kingdom or the Kamboja kingdom to trade and dies there, and if there is no grown son in that brahmin's house, the brahmin woman consorts with a slave or a laborer. When a young son is born, although that father is just a slave, the son born from that slave becomes the master who is the owner of the inheritance. He is pure from the mother's side but impure from the father's side. That person goes to the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) to trade, takes a maiden who is a pure brahmin, and obtains a son in that brahmin woman's womb. That son also is pure only from the mother's side and impure from the father's side. This was spoken to show that even within the brahmin tradition itself, there is a mixing of castes. What strength is there, what reliance is there, where...
280:
If you are all slaves, then all be slaves; if you are all masters, then all be masters. In such a case, what is your power, what is your refuge, that you say 'Only the Brahmin caste is the superior caste'? This is what is shown.

The words beginning with "Is it only the warrior caste?" (Khattiyo va nu kho) are called arguments that refute views (suttacchedakavāda).

Now, wishing to show the purity of the four castes, he said the words beginning with "In this world, a king." "Sāpānadoṇiyā" refers to a drinking trough for dogs. "Aggikaraṇīyaṃ" refers to fire-related duties such as removing cold, dispelling darkness, and cooking food. Here, "Assalāyana" refers to performing all such fire-related duties.

Now, regarding the Brahmins' claim of the "purity of the four castes," there is no such restriction to four castes in that statement. In fact, there is also a fifth class called the Pādasika. To briefly show the fault in their doctrine, he said the words beginning with "In this world, a prince." "Tatra amutra ca panesānaṃ" means "I do not see any difference between these youths even in the previous method." However, there is indeed a difference among those youths. A child born to a prince from a Brahmin woman is called a Khattiyapādasika; the other, born to a Brahmin youth from a princess, is called a Brāhmaṇapādasika. These are youths of low birth.

Having thus shown the fault in their doctrine of the "purity of the four castes" due to the existence of a fifth class, he now wished to instruct them again on the purity of the four castes and said the words beginning with "What do you think of that?" In those words, "Saddha" refers to food offered for the deceased (matakabhatta). "Thālipāka" refers to food given as a gift. "Yañña" refers to sacrificial food. "Pāhuna" refers to food prepared for guests. "Kiṃ hi" is intended to show whether it will be of great fruit or not.

"Assalāyana... once upon a time" means: "Assalāyana, in the past, when I was of much lower birth and you were superior, you were unable to answer the questions I asked about birth. Now that you are lower and I am the superior Buddha, how will you answer the questions I ask about your own doctrine of birth? There is no need to worry about this." He began this teaching to encourage the youth. In that passage, "Asita" refers to a dark-skinned person.
281:
"Devala" is his name; at that time, the Blessed One was that ascetic Devala. "Paṭaliyo" means many-layered sandals. "Patthaṇḍile" means in the precinct of the leaf-roofed hut. "Ko nu kho" means "Where indeed are they going?" "Gāmaṇḍalarūpo viya" means like the appearance of village children. "So khvāhaṃ, bho, homi" means "Friend Assalāyana, I am that Asita Devala." At that time, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) was wandering as a subduer of the untamed (Koṇḍadamaka). "Abhivādetuṃ upakkamiṃsu" means they endeavored to pay homage. From then on, even an ascetic of a hundred years would be considered untamed (koṇḍita) if he did not pay homage to the brahmin youth born on that day.

"Janikā mātā" means the mother who gave birth to you is called your birth-mother. "Janikāmātū" means the mother of the birth-mother. "Yo janako" means the one who generates is called the father. There is also a reading "Yo janiko pitā."

"Asitena" means that if the seer Asita Devala, who possessed the five superknowledges, were to ask this Gandhabba question, the brahmins would not be able to answer it fully. "Yesaṃ" means of those seven seers. "Na puṇṇo dabbigāho": Among those seven seers, there was once a servant named Puṇṇa who would take the ladle, cook the leaves, and offer them; he knew the art of handling the ladle. You, along with your teacher, are not even equal to that servant Puṇṇa of those seers; you do not even know the art of handling the ladle that Puṇṇa knew. The rest of the words are clear in meaning in every respect.

This Brahmin Assalāyana became a person of faith and devotion, and he had a shrine (cetiya) built within his own residence. To this day, the descendants of Assalāyana, when building a house, always build a shrine within the residence.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Assalāyana Sutta is finished.

## 4. Ghoṭamukhasutta-vaṇṇanā
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Ghoṭamukha Sutta. Therein, "Khemiyambavane" means in the mango grove of that name, Khemiya. "Dhammiko paribbājo" means a state of renunciation in accordance with the Dhamma. "Adassanā" means...
282:
...due to not seeing wise ones like your reverences, or due to not seeing the true nature (Dhamma) in this Dispensation. By this statement, he shows: "Our words are not the standard; the Dhamma alone is the standard." Then the Elder Utena, thinking, "There must be much work here as if in a new Uposatha hall," descended from the walkway, entered the leaf-roofed hut, and sat down. To show that sitting, the words beginning with "Evaṃ vutte" were spoken.

Regarding the words "Cattārome brāhmaṇā," it is heard that this thought occurred to the Elder: "This Ghotamukha Brahmin is saying that there is no recluse (samaṇa) or brahmin who has attained a righteous state of monkhood. I will show this brahmin the four types of persons and the two assemblies and ask, 'In which assembly is the fourth type of person mostly found?' Then, being one who understands, he will say, 'In the non-householder assembly.' In this way, I will make him admit from his own mouth that 'there is a righteous monk.'" Having planned thus, he began this discourse.

In that Pali, "Sārattarattā" means those who are very intensely lustful. "Sānuggahā vācā bhāsitā" means speech spoken with reason. Did I not say before, "Our words are not the standard; the Dhamma alone is the standard"?

With the words "Kiṃ pana te," he asked to ensure freedom from accepting unallowable things (akappiya), because householders might speak of both what is allowable and what is unallowable. "Kārāpesi" means he had it built (or created). After having the rest house built, the brahmin passed away and was reborn in heaven. It is said that in the art that this brahmin mastered, it is mentioned that one must kill one's mother and father and then kill oneself. Among those who know this art, there is no one other than this Ghotamukha Brahmin who has been reborn in heaven. However, this brahmin was reborn there because he performed meritorious deeds depending on the Elder. That deity reflected, "By what karma was I reborn here?" and saw the truth. One day, when the Saṅgha had assembled to repair the old dining hall, he came in human form and asked, "Venerable sirs, why has the Saṅgha assembled?" They replied, "To repair the dining hall." He asked, "Who had this built?" They answered, "Ghotamukha Brahmin built it." He asked, "Where is he now?" They said, "He has passed away." He asked, "Does he have any relatives left?" They said, "He has a sister." He requested, "Please call her," and the monks had her called. The deity approached his sister and said, "I am your brother, Ghotamukha. Having had this hall built, I was reborn in heaven. In such and such places, I have left..."
283:
"I have wealth buried; take that wealth and have this dining hall built, and also support the children." Having said this, he paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, ascended into the sky, and went only to the celestial realm. The remaining words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī
## The Explanation of the Ghotamukha Sutta is finished.
## 5. The Explanation of the Caṅkī Sutta

The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Caṅkī Sutta. In that sutta, "devavane sālavane" means it is heard that in that Sal forest, offerings were made to the deities; for that reason, that forest is called both Devavana and Sālavana. "Opāsādaṃ ajjhāvasati" means he resides in the Brahmin village named Opāsāda, or he resides there having overcome it; being the lord of that village, he lives according to whatever regulations one should live by in that village. Here, it should be understood that the second case (accusative) is used in the sense of the seventh case (locative) due to the power of the prefix (upasagga); because of that, it is the same in the remaining words due to their application. In that context, the characteristics should be sought from the grammar treatises.

"Sattussadaṃ" means abounding in beings, having many people, teeming with various kinds of people, and teeming with various animals such as domesticated elephants, horses, peacocks, and deer. Because that village is abundant with grass for fodder for elephants and horses and grass for roofing houses grown outside, likewise with firewood and timber for house construction, and because inside there are many ponds of circular or square shapes, and outside many large lakes adorned with aquatic flowers are always full of water, it is called "satiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ."

"Sadhanyaṃ" means being with grain; it means having a store of many kinds of grain such as legumes and others. By this much, the prosperity and wealth of the Brahmin, who lives like a king with a white parasol raised in that village, is shown. "Rājabhoggaṃ" is wealth obtained from the king. If asked who gave it, it was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala. "Rājadāyaṃ" means it is a royal inheritance. "Brahmadeyyaṃ" means being an excellent gift, to be enjoyed like a king with a white parasol raised. Alternatively, "rājabhoggaṃ" means exercising all administrative powers at ports, mountains, and so forth...
284:
...by collecting taxes, he raises a white parasol and enjoys it like a king. In that text, in the phrase "the royal gift (rājadāya) given by King Pasenadi of Kosala," it is called rājadāya because it was given by the king. To clarify the donor king, it is said "given by King Pasenadi of Kosala." Brahmadeyya means an excellent gift. It means a gift given in such a way that it is completely relinquished and cannot be taken back.

They are called Saṅgha because they are many and are united. They are called Saṅghī because they have a group or assembly, not being individuals. They are called Gaṇībhūta because they were not a group inside the village at first, but became a group upon coming outside. "Uttarenamukhā" means facing the north. "Khattaṃ āmantesi": a high official (mahamatta) capable of answering questions asked is called "Khatta"; he called that official. "Āgamentu" means "Please wait for a moment," or "Please stay."

"Nānāverajjakānaṃ" refers to those born in, residing in, or coming from various other kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala; they are called "Nānāverajjaka," and it refers to those Brahmins from various kingdoms. "Kenacidiva" means by some matter such as an irregular sacrifice or worship. Those Brahmins, hearing of the Brahmin Caṅkī's departure, thought: "This Caṅkī is a famous Brahmin; for the most part, other Brahmins have gone to the ascetic Gotama as their refuge, but this Caṅkī alone has not gone yet. If he goes there, he will surely be converted by the ascetic Gotama's enticing magic and go for refuge. Then there will no longer be a gathering of Brahmins at his door. Let us now create an obstacle to his going." Having consulted thus, they went to that Brahmin Caṅkī. Referring to their arrival, the words beginning with "Atha kho te brāhmaṇā" are spoken.

In that text, "ubhato" means from both sides, the mother's side and the father's side. "Mātito ca pītito ca" means the mother of the venerable one is a Brahmin, the mother's mother (grandmother) is a Brahmin, and her mother is also a Brahmin. The father is a Brahmin, the father's father (grandfather) is a Brahmin, and his father is also a Brahmin. Thus, the venerable one is well-born from both sides, from the mother's side and from the father's side.
285:
"Saṃsuddhagahaṇiko" means your mother's womb is pure, your mother's belly is pure. In this Pali phrase "yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā," the father's father is called "pitāmaha" (grandfather). The lifespan of a grandfather is called "pitāmahayuga." The word "yuga" refers to the extent of life. This is merely a term, but in meaning, "pitāmahayuga" refers to the two grandfathers. All ancestors prior to those two grandfathers are also included by the term "pitāmaha." Thus, one is pure from the mother's womb up to the seventh generation of men. Alternatively, it shows that one is not to be rejected or reproached based on birth. "Akkhitto" means not being rejected as inferior, as in "Cast this person away, what shall we do with him?" "Anupakkuṭṭho" means not being reproached, having never before encountered abuse or blame. For what reason is one not reproached? It is because of birth. It means not being reproached with words such as "This person is of low birth." "Imināpaṅgena" means for this reason as well.

"Aḍḍho" means being powerful. "Mahaddhano" means being endowed with great wealth. Although there is much wealth in the house of the noble Brahmin, like the dust and sand on the ground, they wish to show that the ascetic Gotama has no wealth and sustains himself only by filling his stomach through alms-round. "Mahābhogo" means having great possessions through the power of the five cords of sensual pleasure. Thus, whatever quality they mention, they speak thinking, "We shall show the lack of quality in the Blessed One through the opposite of that quality."

"Abhirūpo" means having an appearance superior to other people. "Dassanīyo" means worthy of looking at because even those looking all day long cannot be satisfied, and being inspiring because of generating mental clarity just by seeing. The word "pokkharatā" refers to the state of being good or excellent. The excellence of complexion is called "vaṇṇapokkharatā." It means the excellence of complexion or being endowed with a complexion. Ancient teachers, however, say the word "pokkhara" refers to the body and "vaṇṇa" refers to the complexion itself. According to their view, complexion and body are called "vaṇṇapokkhara," and the state of that complexion and body is "vaṇṇapokkharatā." Therefore, "paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya" means being endowed with an extremely pure complexion and with the perfection of bodily form. "Brahmavaṇṇī" means having a sublime complexion, and it means being endowed with a golden hue, which is the most excellent among pure complexions. "Brahmavacchasī" means being endowed with a body similar to the body of Mahābrahmā. "Akhuddāvakāso dassanāya" means the opportunity for viewing the body of the noble Brahmin is not small but very great. It intends to show that all your limbs and parts are worthy of viewing and are indeed great.
286:
Because that Brahmin Caṅkī possesses virtue, he is called "sīlavā." Because he has virtue that has been developed, he is called "vuddhasīlī." "Vuddhasīlena" means with developed virtue, and "samannāgato" means endowed with; this is a synonym for the term "vuddhasīlī." The Brahmins say all this referring only to the five precepts. In the terms beginning with "kalyāṇavāco," he is "kalyāṇavāco" because he has speech with good and well-rounded syllables. He is "kalyāṇavākkaraṇo" because he has a pleasant and melodious utterance. "Vākkaraṇa" refers to the sound of the utterance. He is called "porī" (urbane) because he is preceded by qualities and existed in the past, or because he was born in the city, or because he is delicate like a city woman. With such urbane speech, "vissaṭṭhāya" refers to speech that is without obstruction, free from defects such as being half-spoken or delayed. "Anelagalāya" refers to speech free from the trickling of saliva. For when some people speak, saliva trickles, or drool flows, or droplets of spit come out; such speech is called "elagalā." It means the opposite of that. "Atthassa viññāpaniyā" means speech capable of making the meaning known, having made the beginning, middle, and end clear. The remaining qualities of a Brahmin in this Caṅkī Sutta are quite obvious.

When the Brahmins spoke thus, the Brahmin Caṅkī thought, "There is no being who does not enjoy hearing their own praises. These Brahmins, thinking they will prevent me [from going to the ascetic Gotama] by speaking my praises, are mentioning my qualities such as birth. However, it is not proper for me to be attached to my own qualities. Now, I shall break their argument, make known the greatness of the ascetic Gotama, and make them go to him." Having thought thus, he said, "In that case, sirs, listen also to my words," and so on. Therein, even those qualities that are similar to his own, such as "well-born on both sides," he presents as being far superior to his own, thinking, "What am I, and what are the qualities of the ascetic Gotama, such as his perfection of birth?" As for the other qualities, he reveals them specifically to illustrate the greatness of the Blessed One. In restricting it thus, "We alone are worthy [to go to the ascetic Gotama]," he intends to show this meaning: If one should approach another because of greatness of qualities, then just as a mustard seed is small and inferior when compared to Mount Sineru, or the water in a cow's footprint when compared to the great ocean, or a dewdrop when compared to the water in the seven great lakes, even so, when compared to the qualities of the ascetic Gotama, such as his perfection of birth, our...
287:
Our virtues are few and lowly. Therefore, we alone are worthy to approach and see the Venerable Gotama. In this context, wealth situated in the ground (bhūmigata) and wealth situated in the air (vehāsaṭṭha) are defined as follows: wealth filled with the seven treasures and buried in the ground in palace courtyards or gardens is called 'bhūmigata'. Wealth stored in the rafters of palaces and such is called 'vehāsaṭṭha'. These are the types of wealth inherited through lineage. On the very day the Blessed One was born, four great treasure pots appeared: Saṅkha, Ela, Uppala, and Puṇḍarīka. Among them, the Saṅkha treasure pot was one gāvuta in size, the Ela treasure pot was half a yojana, the Uppala treasure pot was three gāvutas, and the Puṇḍarīka treasure pot was one yojana. No matter how much was taken from these treasure pots, they would always remain full. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One renounced a vast amount of gold and silver to enter the monkhood. The words beginning with 'Daharo vā' are as explained in detail below.

In the phrase 'akhuddāvākāsa', it should be understood that the opportunity to see the Blessed One is immeasurable. Regarding this, there is this story: In the city of Rājagaha, a certain Brahmin heard that 'it is impossible to measure the height of the ascetic Gotama.' When the Blessed One entered for alms, the Brahmin took a bamboo pole sixty cubits long and waited outside the city gate. When the Blessed One arrived, he stood nearby and measured with the bamboo pole, but the pole only reached the Blessed One's knees. The next day, he joined two sixty-cubit bamboo poles together and measured again. The Blessed One appeared to be the height of two bamboo poles above the poles themselves. He asked, 'Brahmin, what are you doing?' The Brahmin replied, 'I am measuring your height, Venerable Sir.' The Buddha said, 'Brahmin, even if you were to join enough bamboo poles to fill the entire universe, you would not be able to measure my height. I did not fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable periods (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa) so that others could measure me. Brahmin, the Tathāgata is incomparable and immeasurable.' After saying this, he spoke a verse from the Dhammapada. At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Dhamma (Amata).

Another story: Rāhu Asurinda is four thousand eight hundred yojanas tall. The distance between his shoulders is one thousand two hundred yojanas. The width of his palms and soles is three hundred yojanas. His finger joints...
288:
...are fifty yojanas each. The space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas. His forehead is three hundred yojanas. His head is nine hundred yojanas. This Rāhu Asurinda thought, 'I am very tall; I will not be able to look down to see the Teacher,' and so he did not go. One day, having heard of the Blessed One's virtues, he thought, 'I will see him by whatever means possible,' and he came. The Blessed One, knowing his intention, considered, 'In which of the four postures should I show myself?' and thought, 'A person who is standing, even if short, appears tall. I will show myself only while lying down.' He said, 'Ānanda, prepare a couch in the vicinity of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi),' and there he lay down in the lion's posture (sīhasayya). Rāhu arrived and, looking at the reclining Blessed One, had to crane his neck as if looking up at the full moon in the middle of the sky. When asked, 'Lord of the Asuras, why do you look up like this?' Rāhu replied, 'I stayed away thinking I would not be able to look down to see the Blessed One.' The Blessed One said, 'Lord of the Asuras, I did not fulfill the perfections with my face turned downwards; I gave gifts (dāna) only with my face turned upwards.' On that day, Rāhu Asurinda took refuge in the Triple Gem. Thus, the Blessed One has an 'unrestricted opportunity' (akhuddāvākāsa) for viewing.

He is called 'Sīlavā' (virtuous) because he is endowed with the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). Because that virtue is noble and supreme, he is called 'Ariyasīlီ' (of noble virtue). Because that same virtue is wholesome in the sense of being blameless, he is called 'Kusalasīlီ' (of wholesome virtue). 'Kusaleṇa sīlena' is a synonym for this term. 'Teacher and teacher of teachers of many' (bahūnaṃ ācariyapācariya) means that in each of the Blessed One's Dhamma teachings, eighty-four thousand beings and countless devas and humans drink the nectar of the Path and Fruition. Therefore, he is the teacher (ācariya) of many devas and humans, and the teacher of teachers (pācariya) for the disciples to be disciplined.

In the term 'khīṇakāmarāgo' (one whose lust for sensual pleasures is destroyed), although all defilements (kilesas) are destroyed in the Blessed One, the Brahmin does not know that total destruction; he speaks of the virtue only to the extent that he can understand. 'Vigatacāpallo' means being free from fickleness (cāpalya), such as decorating the bowl, decorating the robes, decorating the monastery, or grooming and primping this foul body. 'Apāpapurekkhāro' means practicing with the nine blameless supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) at the forefront. 'Brahmaññāya pajāya' refers to the Brahmin progeny/community consisting of Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others. He is the leader (purekkhāro) of this community. This community, having placed the ascetic Gotama at the forefront...
289:
It means 'he acts and practices.' Furthermore, 'apāpapurekkhāra' means one who does not place evil in front; he does not practice with evil in front, he does not act with evil in front, and he does not desire evil. To whose assembly of beings? It means that even toward the assembly of Brahmins who are hostile to him, he is not hostile but desires only their welfare and happiness.

'Tiroraṭṭhā' means from another country. 'Tirojanapadā' means from another district. 'Sampucchituṃ āgacchanti' refers to wise Khattiyas and others, as well as Brahmins and Gandhabbas, who come after preparing questions, thinking, 'We will ask.' Among them, some notice a fault in the question or their own inability to receive the answer and remain silent without asking. Some do ask. For some, the Blessed One inspires the enthusiasm to ask and then answers. Thus, the doubts of all of them break upon reaching the Blessed One, just as the waves of the great ocean break upon reaching the shore. The rest of the praise for the Tathāgata's qualities here is clear.

'Atithī no te honti' means they are our guests, newcomers, and visitors. 'Pariyāpuṇāmi' means 'I know.' 'Aparimāṇavaṇṇo' shows that if even the All-Knowing Buddha, who is of such a nature, has immeasurable qualities, what need is there to speak of someone like me? There is also this spoken word:

'Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of a Buddha,
And speak of nothing else for an entire aeon,
The long and distant aeon would come to an end,
But the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.'

Hearing this talk of qualities, those Brahmins thought, 'Just as Caṅkī speaks the praise of the ascetic Gotama, that Venerable Gotama is of supreme quality. Indeed, this Caṅkī, knowing his qualities, has waited for a very long time. Come, let us follow him.' Thinking thus, they said, 'Very well, sir,' and so on.

'Opāteti' means he introduces or causes to enter. 'Sampurekkharonti' means they go about putting even their sons and grandsons in front. 'Mantapada' means the mantras themselves are the mantapada; it means the Vedas. 'Itihitiha paramparāya' indicates that it has come down by tradition, as in 'so it is said, so it is said.'
290:
'Piṭakasampadā' means the fulfillment of the prose known as the Word (Pāvacana). It shows that it has come down fulfilled through poetic compositions such as the Sāvittī and through divisions into sections. 'Tattha ca' means in that mantapada. 'Pavattāro' means those who cause it to proceed (originators). 'Yesaṃ' means 'of whom it is the property.' 'Mantapada' refers to the mantra itself, known as the Veda. 'Gīta' means recited by the ten ancient Brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka, by virtue of the perfection of the words. 'Pavutta' means spoken or taught to others. 'Samihita' means combined, accumulated, or placed together as a collection.

'Tadanugāyanti' means that Brahmins nowadays imitate, recite, and teach those mantapadas sung by the ancient Brahmins. 'Tadanubhāsanti' means speaking in imitation of those mantapadas; it is a synonym for the previous term. 'Bhāsitamanubhāsanti' means reciting in imitation of what they recited.
