'Vācitamanuvācenti' means teaching in imitation of what they taught. 'Seyyathidaṃ' means 'who are they?' Aṭṭhaka and others are their names. It is said that those ancient sages, such as Aṭṭhaka, looked with the divine eye and, without harming others, composed the Vedas in accordance with the Word of the Blessed One Kassapa. However, later Brahmins inserted things like killing living beings, corrupted the three Vedas, and made them contrary to the Buddha's word.

'Andhaveṇī' means a lineage of blind men (andhapaveṇī). One blind man holds the end of a staff held by a sighted person; another blind man holds that blind man, and another holds him. Thus, a line of fifty or sixty blind men connected in order is called andhaveṇī. 'Paramparāsaṃsatta' means being attached to one another. It means being separated from the sighted person who leads with the staff. A rogue, seeing a group of blind men, encouraged them, saying, 'In such-and-such a village, food and snacks are easy to get.' When the blind men said, 'Master, please lead us there; we will give you such-and-such wealth,' he took the bribe. Midway, he led them off the path, circled a large thicket, made the one behind hold the waist-band of the one in front, said, 'I have some business; you go on ahead,' and fled. Those blind men traveled all day but could not find the path. Crying out, 'Where is the sighted one? Where is the path?' and not finding the way, they died right there. Referring to them, it is said, 'attached to one another' (paramparāsaṃsatta). 'Purimopi' refers to any one of the ten ancient Brahmins. 'Majjhimopi' refers to any one of the teachers and teachers' teachers in the middle. 'Pacchimopi' refers to any one of the Brahmins at the present time.
291:
“Pañca kho” means that in addition to the two qualities (faith and oral tradition) mentioned in the Pali, three other qualities of this nature (inclination, reflective thought, and acceptance of a view after deliberation) are included in the teaching. “Dvedhā-vipākā” means having a true result or an untrue result. “Nālamettha” means: “Bhāradvāja, a wise person who practices to preserve the truth should not come to a definitive conclusion in this matter, saying ‘Only this is true, everything else is false’; it is not fitting.” Thus, the way was opened for further questioning.

“Idha Bhāradvāja bhikkhu” refers to the Buddha himself, just as in the Jīvaka Sutta and the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta. “Lobhanīyesu dhammesu” means in states of greed. The same method applies to the remaining two terms (states of hatred and states of delusion).

“Saddhaṃ niveseti” means establishing faith that is convincing (okappanīya-saddhā). “Upasaṅkamati” means approaching. “Payirupāsati” means sitting close by to serve. “Sotaṃ” means lending a clear ear (pasāda-sotaṃ). “Dhammaṃ” means listening to the Dhamma as it is taught. “Dhāreti” means retaining it after mastering it. “Upaparikkhati” means investigating and reflecting on it in terms of both meaning and cause. “Nijjhānaṃ khamanti” means being able to endure the investigation; it means perceiving thus: “Here virtue is taught, here concentration is taught.” “Chando” means the wholesome desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). “Ussahati” means making an effort. “Tuleti” means judging by way of impermanence and so on. “Padahati” means exerting effort associated with the Path. “Kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ” means realizing Nibbāna with the mental body (nāmakāya) that arises together with the Path; it is seeing by making that very Cessation (nirodha-sacca) manifest while piercing the defilements with wisdom.

“Saccānubodho” means awakening to the truth through the Path. “Saccānuppattī” means the realization of the Fruit. “Tesaṃyevā” refers to the twelve factors mentioned above; in this way, it conforms to the long discourse on the Path, therefore this meaning should not be taken yet. However, the intended meaning here is: “Tesaṃyevā” means of those states associated with the Path. “Padhānaṃ” means the effort associated with the Path. That effort is of great benefit for the attainment of the truth, which is called the realization of the Fruit, because without the Path, there can be no Fruit. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Caṅkī Sutta is finished.
292:
## 6. Esukārīsuttavaṇṇanā
This sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Esukārī Sutta. In that sutta, 'bilam olaggeyyuṃ' means they should cause a portion of meat to be hung up. By this, the custom of caravan leaders (sattha-dhamma) is shown. It is said that when a caravan leader is traveling through a great forest and an ox dies on the way, he takes the meat and hangs portions on the front of the wagons of all the traders, saying, 'Eat this and pay this much price.' There are those who eat the ox meat and those who do not; those who can pay the price and those who cannot. To recover the price for which the ox was bought, the caravan leader gives the portions to all the traders by force and takes the money. This is the custom of caravan leaders. Similarly, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'evameva kho' to show that Brahmins also prescribe four types of service (pāricariyā) according to their own nature, without obtaining the consent of the people.

'pāpiyo assa' means it would be very wicked. 'seyyo assa' means it would be beneficial. Alternatively, 'pāpiyo' means it would be a wicked and lowly self-existence (attabhāva); 'seyyo' means it would be a noble and excellent self-existence. 'seyyaṃso' means it is better. 'uccākulīnatā' means it is better by way of high birth. 'pāpiyaṃso' means it is worse. High birth is appropriate only in two classes: the Khattiya class and the Brahmin class. Having a splendid appearance (uḷāravaṇṇatā) increases in three classes, for a Vessa can also have a splendid appearance. Having great wealth (uḷārabhogatā) increases in all four classes; even a poor person or the lowest outcaste (Caṇḍāla) can indeed have great wealth.

Regarding the word 'bhikkhācariyaṃ', even a Brahmin with a hundred crores of wealth should wander for alms. Ancient Brahmins, even with eighty crores of wealth, would wander for alms once in a while. Why? So that when they have to wander for alms in times of poverty, they will not be criticized, saying, 'Only now have they started to wander for alms.' 'atimaññamāno' refers to a Brahmin who, having discarded the lineage of alms-gathering, makes a living through farming, trade, etc.; such a Brahmin is called one who despises (his tradition). 'gopo vā' means just as a cowherd who steals the goods he is supposed to protect is one who does what should not be done. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sections. 'asitabyābhaṅgaṃ' refers to a sickle for cutting grass and a carrying pole. 'anussarato' means because of recollecting the ancient family lineage of one's parents where one was born. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

## The Commentary on the Esukārī Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
293:
## 7. Dhanañjānisutta-vaṇṇanā

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Dhanañjāni Sutta. In that sutta, regarding the word 'Dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ', 'giri' means mountain. This is the name of the district located in the southern direction of the mountain that surrounds the city of Rājagaha. 'Taṇḍulapālidvārāya' refers to one of the gates named 'Taṇḍulapāli' among the thirty-two large gates and sixty-four small gates in the city of Rājagaha. 'Rājānaṃ nissāya' (depending on the king) means that when sent by the king with the instruction, "Go and collect the portion of the crops without harming the people," that person goes and seizes all the crops. Even when the people plead, "Venerable sir, do not destroy us," he says, "The grain in the royal palace is low; I have been ordered by the king to collect it in this way whenever I come; do not cry," and thus he robs and destroys the brahmins and householders by using the king as a pretext. He brings most of the seized grain to his own house and sends only a small amount to the royal palace. When the king asks, "Why did you oppress the brahmins and householders?" he replies, "Indeed, Great King, the crops in the fields were poor this time; therefore, even though I collected them without oppression, not much was obtained," and thus he robs and destroys the king by using the brahmins and householders as a pretext.

'Payo pīyataṃ' means "Please drink the fresh milk first." 'Tāva bhattassa' means that while sitting for a while after drinking the milk, the time for the meal will arrive. This indicates that they will bring the morning meal for us right here. In the words beginning with 'Mātāpitaro', one should support elderly parents by seeking out soft rugs and blankets, fine clothes, delicious food, and fragrant scents and flowers. One should support one's wife and children by performing various duties such as the naming ceremonies for the children. It should be understood that if this is not done, blame and criticism will arise.

'Adhammacārī' (unrighteous) refers here to 'adhamma' as the failure to observe the five precepts or the ten precepts. 'Upakaḍḍheyyuṃ' means they would be dragged to various hells to undergo punishments such as the fivefold binding.

448-453. 'Dhammacārī' refers to one who performs duties through righteous arts such as Sivavijjā. 'Paṭikkamanti' means they decline and perish. 'Abhikkamanti' means they progress and prosper. 'Seyyo' means superior or more excellent. 'Hīne' means low or inferior. 'Kālaṅkato ca Sāriputtā' means...
294:
The Blessed One spoke these words to the Elder Sāriputta with the intention, "Go to that Brahma realm and preach the Dhamma to him." The Elder also went at that very moment and preached the Dhamma to the Great Brahma. From that time onwards, even when speaking a verse of four lines, he did not speak anything that was apart from the Four Noble Truths.

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Dhanañjāni Sutta is finished.
## 8. Vāseṭṭhasutta-vaṇṇanā

The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Vāseṭṭha Sutta. In that sutta, "Icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍe" means in the forest grove not far from the village of Icchānaṅgala. The five brahmins beginning with Caṅkī were the chaplains (purohita) of King Pasenadi of Kosala. "Aññe ca abhiññātā" refers to many other well-known brahmins. It is said that those brahmins assemble in two places every six months. When they wish to purify their lineage (jāti), they assemble in the city of Ukkaṭṭhā in the presence of the brahmin Pokkharasāti for the purpose of purifying their lineage. When they wish to purify the mantras (Vedas), they assemble at Icchānaṅgala. At this time, they have assembled for the purpose of purifying the mantras. "Ayamantarā kathā" means that while they were walking about engaged in conversation suitable for their companionship, this other conversation arose in the midst of that talk. "Sīlavā" means one who possesses virtue. "Vattasampanno" means one who is accomplished in conduct.

"Anuññātapatiññātā" refers to those who have been authorized by their teachers saying, "You have learned," and who have also acknowledged it themselves saying, "Yes, teacher, we have learned." "Asmā" means "we are." "Ahaṃ Pokkharasātissa, Tārukkhassāyaṃ māṇavo" is intended to show, "I am the senior pupil and chief disciple of Pokkharasāti; this youth is the chief disciple of Tārukkha."

"Tevijjānaṃ" means of the brahmins who have mastered the three Vedas. "Yadakkhātaṃ" refers to even a single word that is explained according to its meaning and its phrasing. "Tatra kevalinosmase" means that because of knowing all of that, they have reached the end (perfection) in that matter. Now, wishing to make clear that state of perfection, he says the words beginning with "Padakasmā." Therein, "Jappe ācariyasadisā" means "In recitation, we are just like the teacher."
295:
"Kammunā" means by the ten courses of wholesome action. This is because this young man Vāseṭṭha previously said, "O friend, when one is virtuous," referring to the seven types of bodily and verbal actions. He said, "endowed with duties," referring to the three types of mental actions. One endowed with those mental actions is one endowed with conduct. "Cakkhumā" (The One with Vision) is an address to the Blessed One because of His possession of the five types of eyes.

"Khayātītaṃ" means transcending deficiency, which means complete. "Pecca" means having approached. "Namassanti" means they pay homage.

"Cakkhuṃ loke samuppannaṃ" (An eye arisen in the world) means having destroyed the darkness of ignorance in the world, He has appeared as an eye, enabling the people of the world to see their welfare in the present life and so forth.

Thus, being praised and requested by the young man Vāseṭṭha, the Blessed One, wishing to favor both individuals, said, "I will explain to you (the distinction of births)," and so on. There, "byakkhissaṃ" means I will explain. "Anupubbaṃ" (in order) means let the view of the Brahmins stand for a moment; I will explain in order starting from grass, trees, insects, and caterpillars. "Jātivibhaṅgaṃ" means the detailed classification of births. "Aññamaññā hi jātiyo" means the births of various beings are distinct from one another and are of various kinds.

"Tiṇarukkhe" (grass and trees): He began this teaching with the intention, "I will first teach the non-clung-to births (the world of insentient plants) and later the clung-to births (the world of sentient beings); in this way, the distinction of births will become clear." However, Elder Mahāsīva asked, "Venerable Sir, is it not proper to say that the non-clung-to (plants) are different due to the difference in seeds, while the clung-to (beings) are different due to the difference in kamma?" The answer was, "Yes, it is not proper. For kamma casts (beings) into a womb (yoni). These beings, produced by that womb, become of various appearances." In this context of "tiṇarukkhe," plants that have no heartwood inside but have heartwood outside, even at the minimum such as palms and coconuts, are just grass (tiṇa). All plants that have heartwood inside but no heartwood outside are called trees (rukkha). And those plants do not know, "We are grass, we are trees," or "I am grass, I am a tree." Even though they do not know, their form (liṅga) is a form produced by birth, resembling the original grass and so forth. Why? Because births are distinct from one another. The birth of grass is one thing, the birth of a tree is another. Even among grasses, the birth of a palm is one thing, the birth of a coconut is another. This should be understood in detail. By this statement, by the power of birth... (sentence incomplete).
296:
Those (palms, coconuts, etc.) are different by birth; that birth can be known as distinct from other births even without one's own claim or the instruction of others. If one were a Brahmin by birth alone, that person should also be known as distinct from the warrior caste, merchant caste, or menial caste without one's own claim or the instruction of others; however, they cannot be so distinguished. Therefore, one is not a Brahmin by birth. Later, however, He will make this meaning clear by uttering the verse beginning with "Yathā etāsu jātīsu."

Having thus shown birth in the non-clung-to (insentient grass and trees), wishing to show it in the clung-to (sentient beings), He said the words beginning with "Tato kīṭe." "Yāva kunthakipillike" means including up to small insects and ants. Here, those beings that go by leaping and flying are called "pataṅgā" (grasshoppers). "Aññamaññā hi jātiyo" means among those beings too, births are of various kinds by the power of colors such as blue, red, and so forth.

"Khuddake" refers to small animals such as black squirrels and so forth. "Mahallake" refers to large animals such as rabbits, cats, and so forth.

"Pādūdare" refers to snakes which have their bellies as feet; it means for those snakes, the belly itself constitutes the feet. "Dīghapiṭṭhike" means because snakes have only a back from head to tail, they are called "dīghapiṭṭhika" (long-backed beings).

"Udake" refers to beings born in water.

"Pakkhī" refers to birds. Because they go by means of wings, they are called "pattayāna" (wing-vehicles); because they go through the sky, they are called "vihaṅgama" (sky-goers).

Having thus shown the distinction of births of beings that frequent the land, water, and sky, now, wishing to reveal the purpose for which He showed that, He spoke the verse "Yathā etāsu." The meaning of that verse has been stated in brief. To show the matter to be stated here in detail Himself, He said the words beginning with "Na kesehi." There, the connection is as follows: The statement "There is no multiple characteristic born of birth among humans" should be understood as "there is none" in this way. What is that? "Na kesehi" (not by the hair) and so forth. There is no rule such as "The hair of Brahmins is like this, the hair of Khattiyas is like this," as there is in the case of elephants, horses, deer, and so forth. Everything should be connected in this manner.

"Liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ neva, yathā aññāsu jātīsu" (The characteristic born of birth is not present, as it is in other species) should be understood as the conclusion (nigamana) of the meaning already stated. There, the connection is: Thus, because...
297: Among humans, there are no distinct physical characteristics arising from birth, such as hair and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood: 'Among humans, distinguished as Brahmins and so on, there are no physical characteristics arising from birth, unlike in other species (animals).' Now, although there is no such distinction by birth, to show how the distinction of 'Brahmin' or 'Khattiya' arises, He spoke the verse beginning with 'Paccattaṃ'. In that verse, 'vokāraṃ' means distinction. The summary of the meaning here is: Just as animals have distinctions in the form of hair and so forth established by their species, there is no such distinction in the bodies of Brahmins and others. Even so, the distinction of 'Brahmin' or 'Khattiya' exists; that distinction is spoken of among humans only by name, and is expressed only by conventional usage. With these words, the Blessed One refuted the view of the young man Bhāradvāja. Now, if one were a Brahmin by birth, then even one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct would be a Brahmin. However, because the ancient Brahmins and other wise people in the world do not desire such a person to be a Brahmin, He spoke the eight verses beginning with 'Yo hi koci manussesu' to support the view of the young man Vāseṭṭha. In those verses, 'gorakkhaṃ' means guarding the fields or farming (kasikamma). 'Go' is a name for the earth, which is why He spoke thus. 'Puthusippena' means various crafts such as weaving and so forth. 'Vohāraṃ' means trade. 'Parapessena' means performing services for others. 'Issatthaṃ' means living by weapons, specifically holding the bow and spear. 'Porohiccena' means the work of a chaplain (purohita). Thus, by both the Brahmin tradition and worldly convention, He established that one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct is not a Brahmin. In this way, one is not a Brahmin by birth, but rather a Brahmin by qualities. Therefore, whoever is endowed with qualities, regardless of the family they are born into, is called a Brahmin; this is the proper reasoning here. Having established this meaning, and now wishing to manifest it through speech, He spoke the verse beginning with 'Na cāhaṃ brာhmaṇaṃ'. The meaning of that Pali is: I do not call a person a Brahmin just because they are born into any of the four classes, and specifically born from the womb of a mother praised by Brahmins, born of that lineage, born of that womb. Brahmins describe a Brahmin's pure path of arising as 'well-born from both sides of parentage,' meaning one with a pure conception...
298: Because of the perfection of the mother and also the perfection of the father, one is called 'yoni-ja' (born of a womb) or 'matti-sambhava' (born of a mother). I do not call one a Brahmin merely by such birth or being born from a mother's womb. Why? Because if that person has attachments (kiñcana) such as lust and so forth, they are merely called 'Bhovādī' (one who says 'bho, bho'), being distinguished from others who also have attachments only by that form of address. If one has attachments, one has obstacles. However, whoever is 'akiñcana' (without attachments) due to the absence of attachments like lust, regardless of where they are born, and is 'anādāna' (without grasping) due to the relinquishing of all grasping—that person who is akiñcana and anādāna, I call a Brahmin. Why? Because they have barred (bāhita) evil. To explain the remaining meaning, there are twenty-seven verses beginning with 'Sabba-saṃyojanaṃ chetvā'. In those verses, 'sabba-saṃyojanaṃ' refers to all ten fetters. 'Na paritassati' means they do not tremble or crave through craving (taṇhā). 'Saṅgātigaṃ' refers to one who has transcended attachments such as lust. 'Visaṃyuttaṃ' refers to one who is detached from the four types of birth or from all defilements. 'Naddhi' means a grudge (upanāha). 'Varatta' means craving (taṇhā). 'Sandāna' means a bond or shackle, which is a designation for the obsession with views (diṭṭhi-pariyuṭṭhāna). In 'sahanukkama', 'anukkama' refers to the knot used to enter a shackle, which is a name for the latent tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya). In 'ukkhittapaligha', 'paligha' refers to ignorance (avijjā). 'Buddha' refers to one who knows the Four Noble Truths. 'Titikkhati' means they endure. 'Khantibala' means the strength of patient endurance. That endurance is not called 'balānīka' (an army of strength) if it arises only once; it is called 'balānīka' only if it arises repeatedly. Because of such repeated occurrence, it is called 'balānīka'. 'Vatavanta' means one who possesses the dhutanga practices. 'Sīlavanta' means one who is endowed with qualities. 'Anussada' means one who is free from 'protuberances' (ussada) such as lust. There is also a variant reading 'anussuta', which means 'anavassuta' (one whose defilements do not leak). 'Danta' means one who has tamed the defilements. 'Na limpati' means not adhering. 'Kāmesu' means in the strands of sensual pleasure (kilesa-kāma and vatthu-kāma). In the phrase 'knows the end of suffering,' it refers to the fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of suffering in this very life. 'Pajānāti' means knowing through penetration. 'Pannabhāra' means one who has laid down the burden of the aggregates (khandha), defilements (kilesa), volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguna). The meaning of the word 'visaṃyutta' is as previously stated. 'Gambhīrapညည' means one who has wisdom that functions regarding deep objects. 'Medhāvi' means one who is endowed with natural wisdom.
299:
"Anāgārehi cubhayaṃ" means not mixing with both householders and the homeless (monks). It means being unmixed with both these groups. "Anokasārī" refers to a person who does not cling to the "oka," which is the dwelling place of the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Appiccha" refers to a person with few desires.

"Tasesu" refers to beings with craving. "Thāvaresu" refers to beings without craving.

"Attadaṇḍesu" refers to those who have taken up weapons. "Nibbutaṃ" refers to a person who is cooled through the cessation of defilements. "Sādānesu" refers to beings with grasping.

"Ohita" refers to that which has been laid down.

"Akakkasaṃ" refers to faultless speech. Even a tree with defects is called "sakakkasa" (rough/knotted). "Viññāpani" refers to speech that makes the meaning known. "Saccaṃ" refers to speech that is unfailing. "Udīraye" means speaks. "Yāya nābhisajje" means that by which one does not cause attachment or offense to others; it means speaking such non-harsh words.

"Dīghaṃ" refers to goods strung together with a cord. "Rassaṃ" refers to goods not strung together but scattered. "Aṇuṃ" refers to small goods. "Thūlaṃ" refers to large goods. "Subhāsubhaṃ" refers to good and bad goods. Strung goods may be of low value or high value. The same applies to short goods, etc. Although the entire range of goods is not covered by these specific terms, they are all encompassed by the term "subhāsubhaṃ."

"Nirāsaya" refers to a person without craving.

"Ālayā" refers to the attachments of craving. "Aññāya" means having known. "Amatogadhaṃ" refers to entering into the interior of Nibbāna (the Deathless). "Anuppattaṃ" means having reached.

"Ubho saṅgaṃ" refers to both these types of attachment. Merit causes attachment to the celestial realms, and demerit causes attachment to the lower realms. Therefore, the commentator says "both attachments." "Upaccagā" means having transcended.

"Anāvilaṃ" refers to a person free from the defilements that cause turbidity. "Nandībhavaparikkhīṇaṃ" refers to a person whose craving and existence are exhausted.

In the verse beginning with "Yo imaṃ," ignorance (avijjā) is called "palipatha" (the difficult path) because it causes deviation. It is called "dugga" (the dangerous track) because of its great difficulty. It is called "saṃsāra" because of the nature of wandering. It is called "moha" (delusion) because of the nature of being deluded. "Tiṇṇo" refers to one who has crossed the four floods. "Pāraṅgato" refers to one who has reached Nibbāna. "Jhāyī" refers to one who meditates by way of object-scrutiny (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and trait-scrutiny (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). "Anejo" refers to one who is without craving.
300:
"Anupādāya nibbuto" means one who is extinguished through the cessation of all defilements without taking up any grasping. "Kāme" refers to the two kinds of sensual pleasures. "Anāgāro" means being homeless. "Paribbaje" means wandering forth from the household life. "Kāmabhavaparikkhīṇaṃ" means one whose sensual desire and existence are exhausted.

"Mānusakaṃ yogaṃ" refers to the human bond, which is the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Dibbaṃ yogaṃ" refers to the divine bond, which is the five cords of celestial sensual pleasure. "Sabbayogavisaṃyuttaṃ" means one who is detached from all bonds of defilements.

"Ratiṃ" refers to delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Aratiṃ" refers to weariness in wholesome meditation. "Vīraṃ" refers to one who is energetic.

"Sugataṃ" refers to one who has gone to a good place, or one who has gone by a good practice.

"Gatiṃ" refers to rebirth. "Pure" refers to the past. "Pacchā" refers to the future. "Majjhe" refers to the present. "Kiñcanaṃ" refers to the defilement that causes anxiety.

"Mahesiṃ" refers to the Great Seer, so called because of seeking great virtues. "Vijitāvinaṃ" refers to one who has achieved victory.

In this way, the Blessed One showed that only an Arahant is a Brahmin by virtue. To show that the view of those who cling to the idea of being a Brahmin by birth is a wrong view held in ignorance, He spoke the two verses beginning with "Samaññā hesā." The meaning of those verses is: Whatever name and clan such as Brahmin, Khattiya, Bhāradvāja, or Vāseṭṭha is conceived, made, and fashioned—this is a mere designation in the world, a mere convention. Why? Because it comes from a collection; it comes by way of designation. This name and clan are conceived and given by relatives and kinsmen only at the time of birth in various places. If they did not designate it so, no one, upon seeing someone, would know "This is a Brahmin" or "This is a Bhāradvāja." This conceived name and clan is a long-held underlying tendency of view for the ignorant. For those beings who do not know that "This is just a name and clan, conceived for the sake of convention," it remains as a long-held underlying tendency of view in their hearts. Because of that underlying tendency, not knowing the truth, they do not speak the truth; they say "One is a Brahmin by birth" while remaining ignorant. This is the meaning.
301: In this way, showing that 'Those who adhere to the view "One is a Brahmin by birth" do not know this mere conventional designation; that view of theirs is indeed a bad view,' and now refuting the doctrine of birth in its literal sense while establishing the doctrine of kamma, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with 'Na jaccā' (Not by birth). Therein, to expand upon the meaning of the half-verse 'Kammunā' (By action), the passage beginning with 'Kassako kammunā' (A farmer by action) was spoken. In that context, 'Kammunā' refers to the volitional action (cetanā-kamma) that accomplishes present-day tasks such as farming. 'Paṭiccasamuppādadassā' refers to the wise who are accustomed to seeing dependent origination, understanding that 'because of this cause, this comes to be.' 'Kammavipākakovidā' refers to the wise who are skilled in the results of kamma, [knowing that] birth into a family worthy of respect or a family worthy of contempt occurs by the power of kamma, and other states of inferiority or superiority occur when inferior or superior kamma ripens. In the verse 'Kammunā vattati,' the terms 'loko' (world), 'pajā' (beings/generation), and 'satto' (being) have the same meaning; the difference is merely in the words. Here, by the first foot, the rejection of the view that 'There is a Great Brahmā, the Supreme, the Creator' should be understood. Indeed, the world of beings proceeds in various destinations (gati) only because of kamma; who then would be its creator? By the second foot, the Buddha shows that 'Even though one is produced by kamma in this way, one continues to exist during the course of life (pavattikāla) through kamma distinguished as past and present, experiencing pleasure and pain, and reaching various states such as inferiority and superiority.' By the third foot, he concludes that very meaning: 'Thus, in every way, beings have kamma as their bond; they continue to exist being bound by kamma alone, and not by any other cause.' By the fourth foot, he clarifies that meaning with a simile. Indeed, just as the linchpin is the bond for a moving chariot, and it cannot move without being connected to that linchpin, so too for the world of beings, kamma is the bond in both its arising and its persistence; without being connected to that kamma, it cannot arise or persist. Now, since the world is thus bound by kamma, wishing to show the state of excellence through excellent kamma, he spoke the two verses beginning with 'Tapena' (By austerity). Therein, 'Tapena' means by the austerity of the dhutaṅga practices. 'Brahmacariyena' means by refraining from sexual intercourse. 'Saṃyamena' means by virtue (sīla). 'Damena' means by the restraint of the sense faculties. By this excellent, pure, and sublime kamma, one becomes a Brahmin. Why? Because this Brahminhood is supreme, or it means this kamma is the supreme quality of a Brahmin. There is also a variant reading 'Brahmānaṃ'. The word-definition (vacanattha) here is: 'Brahmānaṃ' because it brings about (āneti) the sublime (brahma); it means it brings about the state of a Brahmin.
302:
In the second verse, 'santo' means one whose defilements are stilled. 'Brahmā Sakko' means he is called both Brahmā and Sakka. Such a person of this nature is not merely a brahmin; rather, to the wise who understand the distinction of a true brahmin, he is both Brahmā and Sakka. "O Vāseṭṭha, know it thus," is the meaning. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Vāseṭṭha Sutta is concluded.
## 9. Explanation of the Subha Sutta

The discourse beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Subha Sutta. Therein, 'Todeyyaputto' means the son of the Brahmin Todeyya, who lived in the village of Tudi. 'Ārādhako hoti' means one who accomplishes or fulfills. 'Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ' means the causal principle. 'Kusalaṃ' means the blameless state.

'Micchāpaṭipatti' (wrong practice) is the unwholesome practice that does not lead out from the round of suffering. 'Sammāpaṭipatti' (right practice) is the wholesome practice that leads out from the round of suffering.

In the terms beginning with 'mahaṭṭhaṃ', it is called 'mahaṭṭha' because it involves great benefit through many attendants or many buildings and implements. It is called 'mahākicca' (great task) because great matters such as naming ceremonies and other auspicious rites exist in this household life. It is called 'mahādhikaraṇa' (great affair) because great undertakings known as 'adhikāra'—such as "this must be done today, this must be done tomorrow"—exist in this household life. It is called 'mahāsamārambha' (great enterprise) because there is great exertion, described as the strain caused by the intense effort involved in the work of many people. 'Gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānaṃ' refers to the very work of those living the household life. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

In this household life, in the case of farming, the state of having many requirements should be understood by way of seeking implements such as the plowshare and so on. In commerce, however, the state of having few requirements should be understood by way of taking and exchanging goods that are already prepared. 'Vipajjamānaṃ' (failing) means that the work of farming may yield little fruit due to drought, excessive rain, etc., and the work of commerce may yield little fruit due to a lack of skill in gems, gold, etc.; it may even reach the point of losing the capital. Conversely, if it succeeds, it yields great fruit, as in the case of Cūḷantevāsika.

'Evameva kho' (even so) means that just as the work of farming yields little fruit when it fails, so too does the work of those living the household life yield little fruit. One who has not performed merit, when he dies...
303:
He is born in hell. It is said that a general named Mahādatta was a devotee of Brahmins (brāhmaṇabhatta). At the time of his death, hell appeared before him. When asked by the Brahmins, "What do you see?", he replied, "I see a house where blood flows." The Brahmins said, "O General, this is indeed the Brahma world." He asked, "O teachers, where is the Brahma world?" They replied, "It is above." He said, "To me, it appears below." Even though it appeared below, they insisted that the Brahma world is only above. When the general died, he was born in hell. Saying, "This man has found fault in our sacrifice," they took a thousand coins and gave them to have him removed from the house.

Conversely, when there is fulfillment, human action also has great fruit. One who performs good deeds is born in heaven after death. This matter is illustrated by the entire Guttila-vimāna story. Just as trade is of little fruit when it fails, so too is the state of a monk who does not fulfill the virtues (sīla) and exerts effort in wrong livelihood (anesanā). Such a monk attains neither the happiness of meditative absorption (jhāna) and so forth, nor heaven, the path, or the fruit. However, the state of a fulfilled monk has great fruit. A monk who fulfills the virtues and develops insight (vipassanā) can even reach the fruit of Arahantship.

He asks with the words, "Brāhmaṇā, bho Gotama," and so forth. Here, Subha the youth asks, "What shall I ask?" The Brahmins say, "There is no monk capable of fulfilling these five qualities; only a householder can fulfill them." But the ascetic Gotama repeatedly says, "O youth, whether it be a householder or a monk [I praise right practice]." Thinking, "He does not let go of the monk, and though it seems he is only asking me questions, I cannot remember them," he asks about the five qualities based on generosity (cāga). "Sace te agaru" means: if it is not a burden for you, O youth, to speak here as the Brahmins have designated, and if there is no discomfort, then speak. What is referred to by the words "Na kho me, bho"? It is difficult to speak in the presence of those who pretend to be wise. Such people find fault in every word and every letter. Truly wise people, however, praise what is well-spoken when they hear it. In the case of poorly spoken words, they straighten out whatever is contradictory in the Pāḷi, the words, the meaning, or the phrasing. There is no truly wise person equal to the Blessed One. Therefore, he says, "O Master Gotama, it is not a burden to me when your honor or someone like your honor is seated here." Truth (sacca) means truthfulness in speech. Austerity (tapa) means austere practice. Celibacy (brahmacariya) means abstinence from sexual intercourse. Study (ajjhayana) means the learning of mantras (Vedas). Generosity (cāga) means the relinquishing of material things.

"Pāpito bhavissati" means he will be led to a state of ignorance. "Etadavoca" means that when the Blessed One subdued him with the simile of the row of blind men, being unable to counter that statement, just as a weak dog rouses the prey and then to its master...
304:
...just as a weak, thin dog rouses the prey and then returns to its master's presence and retreats, even so the youth Subha, wishing to refer to his teacher Pokkharasāti, spoke the words beginning with "Brāhmaṇော". In that context, "Pokkharasāti" is the name of that Brahmin, and he is also called "Pokkharasāyī". It is said that his body was like a white lotus (puṇḍarīka). It was as beautiful as a silver archway erected in a city of the gods. His head was like dark blue sapphire. His beard appeared like a dark cloud across the moon. His eyes were like blue lotuses. His nose was well-rounded and pure like a silver tube. His palms, soles, and face were as beautiful as if treated with lac-dye. The appearance of this Brahmin was exceedingly beautiful. He was so majestic that he was fit to be crowned king in a place without one. Because he was like a lotus, people knew him as "Pokkharasāti". Some, however, knew him as "Pokkharasāyī" because he was not born from a mother's womb but in a lotus pond, sleeping upon a lotus. "Opamañña" means he was of the Upamañña clan. "Subhagavanika" means he was the lord of the Subhaga grove in the city of Ukkaṭṭhā. "Hassakaṃyeva" means it is merely ridiculous. "Nāmakaṃyeva" means it is merely lowly. That speech is empty because it lacks essence. Because it lacks essence, it is merely vain. Now, the Blessed One, in order to subdue the youth along with his teacher Pokkharasāti, spoke the words beginning with, "O youth, how is it?"

In that context, "Which of their words is more excellent?" means which speech is more praiseworthy. "Sammucā" means by way of worldly convention. "Mantā" means by way of reflection and deliberation. "Paṭisaṅkhāyā" means by way of understanding. "Atthasaṃhita" means connected with a reason or purpose. If speech spoken without abandoning worldly convention, but with reflection, understanding, and connection to a reason, is excellent, then: "Āvuta" means obstructed; "Nivuta" means hindered; "Ophuṭa" means overwhelmed; "Pariyonaddha" means enveloped.

Words such as "Gadhita" have the meanings already stated. "O Master Gotama, if that is the case" means if this reason exists. "Svāssa" means that due to the absence of smoke, ash, and so forth, that fire would be flaming, colorful, and radiant. "O youth, I too have such a simile" means I have a similar illustration. This is the meaning: just as a fire burning in dependence on fuel such as grass and wood is with defect because of the presence of smoke, ash, and embers...
305:
Just as it is so, the joy (pīti) that arises dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇā) is faulty because of the existence of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and so forth. However, just as a fire is pure when the fuel of grass and wood is abandoned and there is no smoke and such, similarly, the joy associated with the two supramundane jhanas (lokuttara-jhāna) is pure because of the absence of birth and so forth. This is the meaning.

Now, regarding the five qualities (dhamma) that the Brahmins have prescribed with generosity as the foremost, since those five qualities do not remain fixed as only five, they become six along with the nature of compassion (anukampā). Therefore, to show the fault of holding them as only five, the Buddha said, "Ye te māṇavā," and so forth. In that context, "anukampājātikaṃ" means the nature of compassion.

Regarding the question, "Where do you see this mostly?", why did the Blessed One ask this? Because this youth Subha had said, "A monk is not able to fulfill these five qualities; only a householder can fulfill them." Therefore, the Buddha asked this to make him speak with his own mouth that, "Only a monk can fulfill these qualities; a householder is not able to fulfill them."

In the passages beginning with "Na satataṃ samitaṃ saccavādī," a person who is a householder, even when there is no other interest at stake, still commits the usual false speech (musāvāda). Monks, however, do not speak two different words (falsehood) even if their heads are cut off with a sword. A householder is unable to guard the training rules (sikkhāpada) even for the duration of the three months of the rains retreat; a monk, however, is always possessed of virtue and is one who relies on ascetic practices. A householder is unable to undertake the Uposatha observance even for eight days a month; monks, however, are those who practice the holy life (brahmacariya) for as long as they live. A householder merely writes down the Ratana Sutta or Maṅgala Sutta in a book and keeps it; monks, however, always recite and study them. A householder is unable to give even the lottery-food (salākabhatta) without breaking the commitment; monks, however, give food and snacks even to crows, dogs, and so forth when there is no other recipient, and they also place offerings into the bowls of young monks and novices who carry their requisites. This is how the meaning should be understood. "Cittassāhamete" means, "I declare these five qualities to be the retinue of the mind of loving-kindness (mettā-citta)."

"Jātavaḍḍho" means one who was born and raised in that place. If a person was only born there but raised elsewhere, the roads and paths around the village would not be entirely clear and familiar to him; therefore, it says "jātavaḍḍho" (born and raised). Even for one born and raised there, if he has been away for a long time, the paths would not be entirely clear to him; therefore, it says "tāvadeva avasaṭaṃ," which means one who has just come out at that moment. "Dandhāyitattaṃ" means...
306:
"Dandhāyitattaṃ" means the state of taking a long time due to doubt, such as, "Is this the path or is this not the path?" "Vitthāyitattaṃ" means the state of the body becoming stiff or sluggish, just as the body of someone who is suddenly asked about a subtle matter becomes stiff. By the word "nateva," the Buddha shows the unhindered nature of his omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). For that person (the traveler), there might be an obstruction of knowledge due to the influence of Māra's deceptions and so forth; because of that, he might hesitate or become sluggish. But the omniscience of the Buddha is unhindered; it is shown that no one can create an obstacle to that omniscience.

In the passage, "Young man, just as a powerful conch-blower...," "balavā" means one endowed with physical strength. "Saṅkhadhamo" means a conch-blower. "Appakasirena" means easily, without trouble or pain. A weak conch-blower, even when blowing the conch, is unable to make it known to the four directions with the sound; his conch sound does not pervade everywhere. But the sound of a powerful one is pervasive; therefore, He said "balavā." In the passage "mettāya cetovimuttiyā," when "mettā" (loving-kindness) is mentioned, both access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā) are applicable. However, when "cetovimuttiyā" (liberation of mind) is mentioned, only absorption (appanā) is applicable. "Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ" refers to limited action, which means sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) karma. "Appamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ" refers to immeasurable action, which means fine-material or immaterial sphere (rūpāvacara/arūpāvacara) karma. Among these, only the karma of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) is intended here. Because it is performed by surpassing the limits of sense-sphere karma and expanding it through pervasion of directions, whether specifically or non-specifically, it is called "appamāṇakata" (immeasurable). "Na taṃ tatrāvasissati na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhati" means that sense-sphere karma does not remain or persist in that fine-material or immaterial sphere karma. What is meant? Sense-sphere karma is unable to get stuck or remain in the midst of that rūpa/arūpa-sphere karma, nor can it pervade or overwhelm the rūpa/arūpa-sphere karma to take its own place and persist. Rather, the rūpa/arūpa-sphere karma itself pervades and overwhelms the sense-sphere karma, just as a great flood pervades and overwhelms a small amount of water, and it takes its own place and persists. By blocking the result of that sense-sphere karma, it leads one to the company of the Brahmas. In all other parts, the meaning is clear.

## The Explanation of the Subha Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
307:
## 10. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Saṅgārava Sutta. In that sutta, "Cañcalikappa" means in the village of that name. "Abhippasannā" means having faith through the power of unwavering devotion. That Brahmin woman named Dhanañjānī was a noble disciple who was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and the wife of a Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. In former times, that Brahmin used to invite Brahmins from time to time and pay them honor and respect. However, after bringing this Brahmin woman to his home, he was unable to corrupt the mind of that beautiful woman of noble birth, and thus he could no longer perform the acts of honor for the Brahmins. Then, wherever the Brahmins saw him, they oppressed him, saying, "Now you no longer hold the views of the Brahmins; you do not even perform honor to the Brahmins for even a single day."

That Brahmin returned home, told the Brahmin woman about the matter, and said, "Lady, if you could guard your speech for just one day, I would like to offer alms to the Brahmins for a day." She replied, "Give your offerings wherever you please; how does this matter concern me?" That Brahmin invited the Brahmins, had milk-rice cooked with little water, cleaned the house, prepared seats, and had the Brahmins sit down.

The Brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, wearing a noble cloth and holding a ladle, while serving, stepped on the edge of her garment and slipped. Without even being mindful that she was serving the Brahmins, by the force of habit, she immediately recollected the Blessed One and uttered an exclamation of praise (udāna). When the Brahmins heard that exclamation, they became angry, saying, "This person belongs to both sides, both the Buddha's and the Brahmins'; she is a friend of the recluse Gotama. We will not accept his offerings." They threw away the food and departed. The Brahmin said, "Did I not tell you from the very beginning to guard your speech for just this one day? Now you have wasted this much milk, rice, and so on." Being extremely angry, he said, "This outcaste woman (vassalī) always speaks the praises of that shaven-headed recluse. Hey, you outcaste woman! Now I will go and challenge the doctrine of your teacher." Then the Brahmin woman said, "Go, Brahmin; when you go, you will know." She continued, "Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas... who could challenge the doctrine of that Blessed One." That Brahmin approached the Blessed One and—
308:
"Having cut what does one sleep soundly?
Having cut what does one not sorrow?
Of the killing of what single thing do you approve, Gotama?"
Thus he asked the question.

The Blessed One replied:
"O Brahmin, having cut anger, one sleeps soundly;
Having cut anger, one does not sorrow.
The noble ones praise the killing of anger,
Which has a poisoned root and a honeyed tip;
Having cut that anger, one does not sorrow."
Thus He answered the question.

That Bhāradvāja Brahmin ordained and attained Arahantship. His younger brother, named Akkosaka Bhāradvāja, heard that "My brother has ordained," approached the Blessed One, and reviled Him. Being disciplined by the Blessed One, he ordained and attained Arahantship. Another younger brother, named Sundarika Bhāradvāja, also approached the Blessed One, asked a question, and upon hearing the answer, ordained and attained Arahantship. Another younger brother, named Piṅgala Bhāradvāja, also asked a question, and at the conclusion of the explanation, ordained and attained Arahantship. The youth Saṅgārava was the youngest among them and was sitting with the Brahmins at a certain place for a meal on that day.

"Avabhūtā vā" means they are unprosperous and inauspicious. "Parabhūtā vā" means they have reached destruction. "Vijjāmānānaṃ" means while they are clearly present. "Sīlapaññāṇaṃ" means not knowing virtue and wisdom.

"Diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā" means having known specifically in this very life, having reached the end of defilements, and having attained Nibbāna, which is the further shore of all things known as perfections (pāramī), they claim the beginning of the holy life (brahmacariya). This is the meaning. "Ādibrahmacariyaṃ" means they claim to be the originators and progenitors of the holy life. "Takkī" means a logician. "Vီmamsī" means an inquirer, one who speaks thus after exercising the movement of wisdom. "Tesāhamasmi" means I am one among those Fully Enlightened Buddhas.

"Aṭṭhitavataṃ" means an unwavering practice of austerity (tapa); it is connected with the word 'predominant' (padhāna) and also with the word 'virtuous man' (sappurisa). The meaning is: The Venerable Gotama had an unwavering practice of effort; he had the practice of effort of the virtuous. There is...
309:
"When asked whether gods exist" — the youth Saṅgārava said this with the perception that "The Fully Enlightened One is declaring this meaning without knowing." "In such a case" means when there is a state of not knowing on your part. "It is a vain lie" means your words are useless and unproductive. In this way, the youth is said to be insulting the Blessed One with the charge of lying. "By a wise man" means by a wise human being. "But you, because of your ignorance, do not even know what I have answered," He shows. "Highly acclaimed" means clearly acclaimed in the world with a loud voice as "Adhideva." "Adhideva" means even children are called gods (deva) and goddesses (devī), but the actual gods are called "Adhideva," meaning they are superior to the humans who have received the names deva and devī in the world; they are the gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva). The remaining words are clear in all respects.
